_meta.id_rule: AW-NNN frozen at first ship, same discipline as R/X/W/T IDs

confidence_tiers.A: station-documented: every named node is a historically attested stop; coords good to ~1-3 km
confidence_tiers.B: corridor-documented: anchor nodes attested, path between reconstructed along known terrain line
confidence_tiers.C: scholarly reconstruction: sparse attested nodes (oases, ruins); intervening path is a best-fit line, honest density is LOW by design

_meta.shaping_note: t:'shaping' nodes are unnamed vertices added only to keep the drawn line on the historical terrain alignment (valley, coast, dune corridor) - they are geometry, not claims of settlement, and get no marker on the map
_meta.water_rule: no land segment may cross open water; attested crossings are their own segments with kind ferry/river, drawn dashed

decisions_locked.D1: water legs allowed as declared ferry/river segments, drawn dashed; never undeclared ocean shortcuts
decisions_locked.D2: pure historical layer - NO 2060 diegetic status; routes render identically across R/X/W zones
decisions_locked.D3: confidence rendered visually (solid A / long-dash B / dotted C) + stated in popup; reversible in viewer patch
decisions_locked.D4: full attested rosters for tier-A showpieces (69 Nakasendo, 53 Tokaido, 88 Shikoku)

_meta.ship_protocol: canonical filename ways_layer.json, CUMULATIVE full file each ship, real version in _meta.version

group_registry.south-asia-roads: South Asia — the great trunk roads

_meta.group_id_rule: frozen slug per network, never renamed; display group label may be reworded freely
_meta.segment_confidence: optional per-segment confidence A|B|C overrides route-level tier for that segment
_meta.verify_flag: optional node boolean 'v': true = coordinate pending verification (photo-manifest pattern)
_meta.antimeridian_rule: Split any segment at ±180. Guard FAILS on a lon jump >180 between consecutive nodes. ADOPTED at v3-B2 on the cartographer's request (optimization #5) when the layer's max |lon| was 141 and nothing came within 39 degrees of the line. IT FIRED FOR THE FIRST TIME AT v49-B48, forty-six batches later, on AW-250 the Manila Galleon — caught the unsplit draft on the first attempt. The rule was written before there was any data that could test it, sat dormant through 250 routes, and worked immediately when it was finally needed. Max |lon| is now exactly 180.00: the line is reached and split at, not jumped over.
_meta.join_node_convention: multi-segment routes repeat the junction node as last-of-prev and first-of-next — deliberate, renderer dedupes
_meta.sensitivity_rule: node-level "s": true and route-level "sensitive": true mark culturally sensitive locations. Renderer SHOULD offer hide / generalize-to-~10km / show rather than a binary — coordinate generalization is standard archaeological practice: it keeps the route's shape and loses the pinpoint. DISTINCT FROM "v" (coordinate pending verification) and from tier C (honestly sparse evidence). A flag that means two things means nothing.
_meta.tidal_rule: 'tidal' = a way that exists only between tides: seabed for six hours, sea for six. NEITHER land nor water, which is why it needed its own kind rather than a note. Exempt from the water rule (the guard samples against a coastline; a tideway is seabed and would fail for being what it is). RENDERER: these are the only segments in the layer that are lethal on a schedule — the Broomway has killed 100+ people. Suggest a distinct stroke rather than folding them into the ferry dash.
_meta.tier_density_rule: CORRECTED after a density audit. Tier A means EVERY NODE ATTESTED — it does NOT mean a fixed spacing. Density is a consequence of the road's own punctuation, not a criterion of the tier: post roads carry stations every ~8 km because horses need changing; pilgrim roads carry stages every ~25 km because walkers need sleeping; Roman viae carry mansiones every ~20 km. The original spec's '5-15 km' band was calibrated on the Nakasendo's 69 post stations and then wrongly applied to pilgrimages. A tier-A route is one where the roster is complete against its source, whatever spacing that produces.
_meta.census_rule: Roster loss is checked by census_ways.py against an EXTERNAL baseline (census_ways_baseline.json), per WORKBOOK_WRITER_PROTOCOL_v2 §3(c). The census deliberately does NOT live in this file: an in-file census is self-certifying — a stale base carries a stale census that agrees with its own stale routes, and the gate passes. Tested: six routes vanished, guard CLEAN. The baseline must sit outside the artifact it judges.
_meta.founding_date_rule: A CITY'S FOUNDING DATE IS NOT A STATEMENT ABOUT ITS SITE. Adopted at B67 after the same error was found SIX times: Portland ME ('harbours are where roads end'), Madison ('an 1836 plan'), Saskatoon ('an 1883 temperance colony'), Roseville and Davis ('railroad towns'), Bangalore ('a 1537 foundation'). Every one of those is true about a colonial charter and none of them is evidence about the ground. Teejop has effigy mounds; Wanuskewin has six thousand years; the Begur inscription names Bengaluru in 890 AD. Before recording a city as honestly off the map, probe the SITE — the indigenous name, the mounds, the inscription — not the incorporation.
_meta.writer_identity_gap: OPEN, RECORDED AT v69-B68. On 2026-07-17 a batch (B68-the-two-crossroads, AW-341/342) was merged into this layer that the ways-researcher instance has no record of authoring. Laurie reports no second ways instance running. The work is guard-clean, census-clean, correctly based on v68-B67, well-formed, and good — nothing was lost and nothing is wrong with it. THE POINT IS THAT NOBODY CAN TELL. This file records a VERSION and no WRITER: _meta.version cannot say who, batches_shipped cannot say whose, and census_ways.py reports CLEAN because it detects LOSS, not AUTHORSHIP — and --accept, which any writer runs as the documented workflow, moves the baseline regardless. The pipeline can prove the layer is CORRECT and cannot prove the layer is MINE. Per WORKBOOK_WRITER_PROTOCOL_v2: a name that does not encode a writer is a latent collision, and this is what one looks like when it does not lose anything. RESOLUTION NOT ATTEMPTED — the cause is undetermined and the honest record is that it is undetermined.
_meta.missed_junction_rule: ADOPTED AT B70 AFTER FINDING 28 OF THEM. Every check in this pipeline until now asked 'is a CLAIM false?' — the strict junction guard, the water rule, the tier hops, the census. Not one asked 'is there a junction I MISSED?' The answer was 28: the same town entered twice in different batches with coordinates a few hundred metres apart, so the routes passed through each other without touching. Arzúa on two Caminos, 81 m. Kyiv on the Varangian Way and the Via Regia, 283 m. Astorga, where the Vía de la Plata JOINS the Camino Francés, 246 m and unclaimed. The interlock was reported as 235 shared coordinates for fifty batches; it was 311. **A pipeline that only tests its own assertions cannot find the things it never asserted.** RUN THE NEAR-MISS SWEEP AT SHIP TIME: any two NAMED nodes on different routes under ~600 m are a candidate; same first word is near-certain. Judgement still required — Fornham All Saints and Fornham St Martin are two villages, St. Cloud and East St. Cloud are two banks, Brunnen and Treib are opposite shores, and none of those should be merged.
_meta.bidirectionality_rule: RULED v80-B80 (Kula Ring, AW-093). Two-way and seasonal traffic is recorded in the ROUTE NOTE, never as a schema attribute and never as mirrored routes. Direction is a property of the CARGO; this schema describes the PATH. A `direction` field would have to mean 'goods flow both ways' on the Kula and 'traffic ran one way' on a drove road or a slave road, and _meta.sensitivity_rule already established that a flag meaning two things means nothing. Mirrored routes would double the geometry, destroy the single-ring fact, and seed a permanent phantom in every near-miss sweep. Precedents now consistent: AW-093 Kula (soulava one way, mwali the other), AW-206 Pituri and Ochre (pituri south, ochre north, one set of tracks), AW-370 Cañada Real Conquense (north in June, south in November). REVERSIBLE: if the viewer ever needs to animate flow, add it in the renderer, not the layer.
_meta.shared_site_rule: RULED v80-B80. A site appearing in both the ways layer and the sacred layer is NOT duplicated, NOT cross-referenced by name, and carries NO new field. Names are not a join key — the two Mohawk Trails settled that, and the sacred layer has its own frozen IDs which this layer has never seen. One coordinate rendered twice is a CARTOGRAPHER problem and has been handed over as one (show-shared-nodes). CONFIRMED SHARED, both on AW-051 Old North Trail: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump (-113.65, 49.70) and Chief Mountain (-113.61, 48.93). Neither is flagged sensitive: both are mapped, signposted and publicly located, and the sensitivity flag protects places that pinpointing endangers, not places that matter. NOTE FOR THE SACRED LINE — the inherited ruling named THREE sites, but DEVILS TOWER IS NOT IN THIS LAYER AT ALL and never has been. Either the ruling was mis-scoped when written, or the ways layer is missing a road that reaches it. Undetermined, and recorded as undetermined.
_meta.note_only_edit_rule: FOUND v80-B80. merge_ways.py replaces a route WHOLESALE by frozen ID. A batch that patches only a note must therefore still carry the route's full segments, or the geometry is deleted — and the gates would mostly miss it. guard_ways.py catches a route with NO segments key (bad kind None), but census_ways.py compares ROUTE IDS and only WARNS on node loss above a 5% threshold: dropping every node from AW-051 and AW-093 is 0.58% of the layer and would have reported CLEAN. A PARTIAL segment loss inside a surviving route is invisible to both. Correct method, used for the three rulings in this batch: build the patch batch programmatically by deep-copying the live route and overwriting only the changed fields. Never retype a route to edit its prose.
_meta.densify_warrant_rule: FOUND v80-B80 on AW-062, the King's Road. Shaping nodes exist to satisfy the hop gate, and for nothing else. AW-062's note said no alignment between the anchors was drawn while the route carried four shaping nodes doing exactly that — on hops of 31 km and 35 km, a third of the densify threshold, so the gate had never asked for them. A shaping node placed where the gate did not demand one is an ASSERTION WEARING THE COSTUME OF GEOMETRY, and no check can see it: pre_check and guard_ways test hop LENGTH, never hop WARRANT. Before adding a shaping node, confirm the gate demanded it. Sibling of _meta.missed_junction_rule — a pipeline that only tests its own assertions cannot find what it never asserted.
_meta.enumeration_rule: FOUND v81-B81, and it supersedes probing as the FIRST method for every region and every theme. probe.py is CONFIRMATORY: it measures the distance from a place I already thought of to the nearest node. Its precision is excellent and its RECALL IS BOUNDED BY MY OWN RECALL — it can never surface a road nobody in this conversation happened to name. The correct first move is ENUMERATIVE: go to the domain's authoritative roster (UNESCO inscriptions, a national federation's register, an excavated corpus, a legal charter) and DIFF it against the layer. Probe second, to verify. MEASURED COST OF GETTING THIS BACKWARDS: probe-driven work on Iberia identified three pilgrimage routes; enumerating the Spanish roster surfaced fifteen to twenty. Recall was roughly 15-20% and there was no way to know it, because precision was 100% and precision is what FEELS like rigour. AND THE FAILURE IS INVISIBLE IN THE NUMBERS — see _meta.false_negative_rule.
_meta.false_negative_rule: FOUND v81-B81. A SMALL PROBE DISTANCE IS NOT COVERAGE. Probe distance measures coverage of GROUND; it says nothing about coverage of ROADS. Worked examples, all from the Spanish pilgrimage diff at v80-B80: Zaragoza/El Pilar probed 0.1 km — off the Ebro, a river. Guadalupe in Extremadura 0.4 km — off a cañada real. Valencia 0.3 km and Orihuela 0.5 km — off the Via Augusta, a Roman road. Málaga 0.0 km — off a coastal trade route. Santo Toribio de Liébana 30.8 km and looked nearly covered — the nearest node was the Camino del Norte passing overhead on its way somewhere else. Every one of those is a pilgrimage destination with NO PILGRIMAGE ROAD TO IT. ALWAYS ask which route the nearest node belongs to and whether that route has anything to do with the thing being looked for. A destination is not a road.
_meta.polyline_length_rule: FOUND v81-B81. THE LAYER'S GEOMETRY IS NOT A DISTANCE MEASUREMENT AND MUST NOT BE USED AS ONE. Each segment is a chain of great-circle hops between named nodes; a walked road winds between those nodes and climbs. Measured against sourced walking distances at B81: Camino Lebaniego polyline 43.6 km vs 72.7 km walked (60%); Camino de San Salvador 92.7 vs ~120 (77%); Fisterra 68.0 vs ~90 (76%). SO A POLYLINE LENGTH RUNS ROUGHLY 60-80% OF THE TRUE ROAD, and worst in mountains — the Lebaniego is the low figure because it climbs 1,050 m into Cabañes between two nodes 8 km apart. Densifying to close the gap would be FORBIDDEN under _meta.densify_warrant_rule: shaping nodes satisfy the hop gate, they do not measure roads. If a length is wanted, source it and put it in the note, which is where every length in this layer already lives. NEVER compute one from the geometry and never let a reader think the geometry is a survey.
_meta.shared_tail_rule: CONVENTION as of v85-B85, now used by five routes. Where a route merges into another and the two run as one road to a common destination, DRAW ONLY AS FAR AS THE MERGE. Camino Primitivo stops at Melide, Camino de Invierno at Silleda, the Mozárabe's Málaga arm at Baena, Camino del Sureste at Albacete, and the Ruta Teresiana's arms rejoin at Garcihernández rather than running doubled into Alba. Drawing the shared tail twice would MANUFACTURE A JUNCTION OUT OF AN IDENTITY, double the geometry, and seed permanent phantoms in the near-miss sweep — the same three objections that killed mirrored routes under _meta.bidirectionality_rule.
_meta.maritime_camino_gap: FOUND v87-B87. The Spanish federation records THIRTY maritime routes to Santiago alongside the land ones, from routes claimed for the first centuries to a Camino de la Antártida. This layer drew its first at B87 and has twenty-nine to go. The hole was structural, not incidental: AW-368 Camino Inglés is the LANDWARD TAIL of a sea road — pilgrims sailed to Ferrol or A Coruña from England, Ireland and Scandinavia — and its sea leg is still not drawn, so the route currently begins nowhere. Same for the Portugués coastal traffic and the Breton and Flemish crossings. A pilgrimage network that draws only the walking is drawing half a network.
_meta.wallace_roster_rule: DOMAIN SOURCE, opened v88-B88. Paul A. W. Wallace, 'Indian Paths of Pennsylvania' (PHMC, 1965) enumerates 131 NUMBERED paths plus 13 unnumbered cross-references and 9 named portages. Diffed against v85-B85 the layer held 11 of 152 — SEVEN PERCENT. This is the roster of record for Pennsylvania and every batch here should cite its Wallace number. THREE OF HIS FINDINGS ARE NOW LAYER RULES IN ALL BUT NAME. (1) Names are reversible: a path was named from either terminus, so the Kittanning Path from Chinklacamoose is the Chinklacamoose Path from Kittanning, and there are as many Venango and Wyoming paths as there were travellers heading there — frozen IDs matter more in this domain than anywhere in the layer. (2) A path is a BAND, not a line: graphed decade by decade it blurs, and in the Presque Isle portage area it is a mile or more wide. (3) DRY, LEVEL, DIRECT — paths took river terraces above flood level and well-drained valley ridges, not mountain spines; Wallace calls the Appalachian Trail a white man's imitation that gets this wrong. SCOPE WARNING: Wallace covers Pennsylvania only and says his book makes no pretense to be definitive. 152 is a FLOOR. New York needs Beauchamp and the NYS Museum trail maps; New England, New Jersey, Maryland and the Ohio country need their own rosters.
_meta.seasonal_road_rule: FOUND v89-B89. ROADS ARE NOT OPEN OR CLOSED, THEY ARE OPEN IN CERTAIN MONTHS, and a layer that draws them as permanent lines flattens that out. The set is now large enough to be an argument: AW-380 Camino de Invierno exists because O Cebreiro at 1,300 m kills people from November to March; AW-385 Camino Baztanés exists because Roncesvalles does the same; AW-403 Wyalusing Path is disqualified for half the year because John Ettwein counted THIRTY-SIX crossings of Muncy Creek, nothing in August and impassable in March; AW-370 Cañada Real Conquense runs north in June and south in November; AW-365's Baetis sailing season was February to April on the high water behind the harvest. Season belongs in the NOTE, never the schema — same ruling and same reasons as _meta.bidirectionality_rule.
_meta.old_town_rule: FOUND v90-B90, from Wallace. An 'Old Town' in this domain is a ROAD SIGN, NOT A SETTLEMENT. Chartier's Old Town, Kickenapaulin's Old Town, Kiskiminetas Old Town, Fish Basket Old Town — travellers navigated by places that were no longer inhabited, because the clearing, the water and the NAME survived the people who left. Wallace also records shelters every ten or twelve miles on the more important trails, marked on maps and surveys as Cock Eye's Cabin, Toby's Cabins, the Warriors Spring, Old King Nutimus. A LAYER THAT DREW ONLY LIVING PLACES WOULD LOSE THE NETWORK. Corollary for node typing: 'station' is the right type for these, not 'town', and abandonment is not a reason to omit a node — see also AW-062 Dunwich, drowned, still a terminus. MOST COMPLETE CASE, v115-B115: AW-478 runs between TWO places both called Sewickley Old Town, one on the Youghiogheny and one on the Allegheny, both named for the The-we-gi-la division of the Shawnee, and Wallace notes each 'is better known from the records as Sewickley Old Town, SINCE THE INDIAN OCCUPANTS LEFT EARLY IN THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY'. Not one abandoned node but an ENTIRE ROUTE consisting of them — a road whose both ends are memorials, reconstructed from records written after everyone had gone.
_meta.portage_rule: FOUND v91-B91. A PORTAGE IS WHERE A WATER SYSTEM STOPS BEING A ROAD, and it is the highest-value node type in the layer per kilometre drawn. Wallace names nine in Pennsylvania alone; five are now drawn and each joins two entire drainages: Presque Isle links Lake Erie to the Mississippi, Chautauqua does the same job a hundred km away, the Allegheny Big Portage joins the Gulf of Mexico to Chesapeake Bay, Great Bend joins the Chesapeake to Delaware Bay. TWENTY KILOMETRES OF WALKING IS THE ENTIRE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN TWO OCEANS. Corollary the layer should apply everywhere: wherever two river routes are drawn and their headwaters approach, LOOK FOR THE CARRY — it will be short, it will be named, and it will usually be the reason a fort or a treaty line is where it is. See also AW-371's Cachão da Valeira, a portage that stopped being one when it was blasted open. TWO NEW KINDS ADDED v120-B120. (1) AW-492, the Conestoga Portage, is not a road with a carry — it is A CANOE ROUTE with a carry, and Wallace calls it flatly THE MAIN CANOE ROUTE BETWEEN THE SUSQUEHANNA AND DELAWARE RIVERS. Eight roads leave Philadelphia in this layer and all of them walk; the busiest link between the two great rivers was people in boats, and only a portage entry found it. (2) AW-493, the Conococheague Portage, does NOT cross a watershed at all: the Conodoguinet reaches the Susquehanna and the Conococheague reaches the Potomac, and BOTH RIVERS END IN THE SAME BAY. It is a short cut between two long arms of one estuary — THE ONLY PORTAGE IN THE LAYER THAT SHORTENS A JOURNEY RATHER THAN ENABLING ONE. So the class is wider than 'where a water system stops being a road': some carries save time rather than making passage possible.
_meta.drowned_node_rule: CONFIRMED v92-B92, now twice. A NODE THAT IS UNDER WATER STAYS ON THE MAP, at the coordinate of the drowned place and not of the shore above it. AW-062 terminates at Dunwich, where St Felix's stood before the sea took the city; AW-420 begins at Jenuchshadego, Cornplanter's Town, flooded by the Kinzua Dam in 1965 after 174 years on the only Pennsylvania land the Seneca never ceded. DROWNING A NODE DOES NOT UNMAKE THE REASON A PATH BENT TOWARD IT. The two cases differ in a way worth keeping: one road was ended by a coast and the other by a decision. Related: _meta.old_town_rule — abandonment is not a reason to omit a node either.
_meta.hazard_coverage_gap: FOUND v93-B93 on AW-423. FOREST FIRE HAD NEVER ONCE BEEN RECORDED IN THIS LAYER, on any continent, in 420 routes. Flood, snow, ice, windfall, rapids, raiders, pirates, altitude and drought are all in here; fire was not. Martin Mack walked the Wapwallopen Path through burning woods on 19 April 1745 and treated it as an anecdote, which is the point — the eastern woods burned regularly and a path through burning country was a survivable difficulty, not a catastrophe. AUDIT QUESTION FOR EVERY DOMAIN: which hazards does this layer's evidence base systematically fail to mention? Journals record what SURPRISED the writer, so a hazard that was routine gets under-recorded precisely because it was routine.
_meta.gate_caught_me_note: v93-B93: pre_check.py refused batch93 because a sed edit had inserted unescaped quotes into a note, breaking the JSON. Because the shell used && the merge never ran and the layer was untouched. RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS THE FIRST TIME THE GATE STOPPED THE WRITER RATHER THAN THE DATA. Chain gate-then-merge with && every single time; never run merge_ways.py in a separate command from the pre_check that authorises it.
_meta.two_terminus_selection_rule: METHOD, adopted v94-B94. When a domain's body text is not in hand, PREFER THE PATHS WHOSE NAME CONTAINS BOTH TERMINI. Wallace states that where he had to coin a name he avoided the fanciful and used the two ends — Raystown-Chinklacamoose, Frankstown-Burnt Cabins, Standing Stone-Fort Littleton, Loyalhanna-Goschgoschink, and the five Kuskusky- paths. For those the endpoints are GIVEN by the source and only the intervening line is unknown, which is precisely the situation tier C anchors-only exists for. Drawing them is recording the source; drawing a single-name path without the text would be guessing at both ends. This is a constraint on WHICH routes get drawn next, deliberately chosen over drawing whatever happens to be interesting.
_meta.name_as_point_and_region: FOUND v94-B94, from Wallace, and it qualifies every node string in this domain. An Indian place name here is often BOTH A POINT AND A REGION: Lechawekink is the Forks where the Lehigh meets the Delaware AND a wide territory taking in Nazareth, Bethlehem and Allentown. Villages also PERAMBULATED — moved under pressure or when the soil was exhausted, rebuilt a few miles off, and carried the old name along, so there are several Goschgoschinks and several Kickenapaulin's Towns at different dates. A LAYER THAT FORCES EVERY NODE TO BE A POINT DISCARDS HALF OF WHAT THE NAME MEANT. Nothing to fix in the schema; the correction goes in the note, and a coordinate in this domain should be read as 'the place called X at the time in question', not as a survey mark.
_meta.source_extraction_method: SOLVED v95-B95, and it unblocks the whole Pennsylvania grind. Wallace's full text is on Internet Archive at /stream/indianpathsofpen00wall_djvu.txt, BUT THAT URL IS AN HTML VIEWER AND IS TRUNCATED SERVER-SIDE at about page 23 — path 3 of 131. Raising web_fetch's text_content_token_limit from 30,000 to 110,000 changed NOTHING; it was never the binding constraint. THE FIX IS THE PDF: fetch indianpathsofpen00wall.pdf with pdf text extraction on. No navigation chrome means roughly 2.5x more book per token, and it reached path 10 on the first try. GENERAL LESSON FOR ANY SOURCE: when an archive text looks truncated, check whether you are fetching a VIEWER or a FILE, and prefer the PDF with extraction over the HTML transcript. REMAINING LIMITATION: every fetch restarts at page 1, so the book cannot be paged into. The only clean solution is to get the 784 KB djvu.txt onto disk in /mnt/user-data/uploads, where the container can grep it per path — bash has no network route to archive.org, so that upload is the one step this researcher cannot perform alone.
_meta.gate_ordering_rule: FOUND v95-B95, a sequencing error by this researcher. In B95 the shell ran merge, then guard, then census --accept as separate statements — and the GUARD FAILED (false junction on AW-433) while census --accept still moved the baseline forward. The baseline was therefore advanced over a layer with a known violation. It was repaired within the minute, but the ordering was wrong. CORRECT ORDER, CHAINED WITH && THROUGHOUT: pre_check → merge → guard → nearmiss → ONLY THEN census --accept. The census is the last gate, not a bookkeeping step to run alongside the others, because accepting a baseline is what makes a state canonical. See also _meta.gate_caught_me_note. REPEATED v102-B102 IN A NEW FORM: the guard failed because a NEW group_id was registered in the _meta step that ran AFTER it. Registering a group is not bookkeeping, it is part of making the batch valid. CORRECT ORDER IS NOW: pre_check → merge → REGISTER ANY NEW group_id → guard → nearmiss → census --accept, chained with && throughout. Twice in three batches this researcher has put a _meta write on the wrong side of the guard.
_meta.source_pull_list: OPEN v95-B95. See SOURCES_TO_PULL.md. Laurie is downloading source texts that web_fetch cannot usefully deliver, because every fetch restarts at page 1 and cannot page into a document. A file on disk in /mnt/user-data/uploads can be grepped per path at trivial cost; bash has no network route to archive.org, so the download is the one step the researcher cannot do. PRIORITY 1 is Wallace's djvu.txt (784 KB), which unblocks ~100 undrawn Pennsylvania paths AND allows the 25 tier-C anchors-only routes already shipped to be upgraded in place. PRIORITY 2 is New York, and the important finding there is that THERE IS NO WALLACE FOR NEW YORK — no single numbered roster. It must be assembled from Beauchamp 1905 (Perch Lake, which carries 'Indian trails' in its subject headings and is easy to miss behind a mounds title), Beauchamp 1900 (Aboriginal Occupation, with two map plates in pockets), and Parker 1922 (corroborative; NYSAA says it is almost identical to Beauchamp). NEW YORK THEREFORE NEEDS A ROSTER BUILT BEFORE ANYTHING IS DRAWN — the Spanish pilgrimage job, not the Pennsylvania job.
_meta.rival_destination_rule: FOUND v97-B97 on AW-440, the Camino de Uclés. NOT EVERY ROAD IN A PILGRIMAGE NETWORK IS TRYING TO REACH THE SAME PLACE. Uclés is the seat of the ORDER of Santiago and the second great Jacobean shrine in Spain, and its road runs 144 km EAST from Madrid, away from Compostela — with red arrows carrying the Cross of Santiago instead of yellow arrows and the scallop, its own credential, and its own certificate, the Uclessiana. A different arrow, a different passport, a different certificate, and the same saint. THE LAYER MUST NOT ASSUME A NETWORK CONVERGES just because most of its members do; convergence is a finding, not a definition, and a route that runs the other way is evidence about the network rather than an exception to it. Compare AW-375 Fisterra-Muxía, which runs away from Santiago to older ground, and AW-394 the Traslatio, which runs the wrong way down time. Three of the thirty-odd Iberian pilgrim roads decline the destination.
_meta.borrowed_legal_status_rule: FOUND v98-B98, and it recurs across three continents. A DEVOTIONAL ROUTE USUALLY SURVIVES BY BORROWING SOMETHING ELSE'S LEGAL STATUS. The Caravaca arms run on waymarked GR long-distance footpaths (GR-252, GR-253), which in Spain are maintained legal objects with numbers. AW-376, the Romería del Rocío, runs on the Cordel de Triana and the Cañada Real de los Isleños because a vía pecuaria is public in perpetuity — a million-person pilgrimage kept alive by grazing law. GENERALISATION FOR THE LAYER: nothing in this domain is built for pilgrims. Pilgrims use what is there — Roman military roads (Via Nova, Calzada de los Blendios), frontier supply corridors (Lorca), wool roads (Ruta de la Lana), drove roads, and modern footpath law. When asking why a devotional route runs where it does, ask FIRST what the corridor was for before it was holy.
_meta.wallace_text_on_disk: SOLVED v99-B99. Wallace's complete text is now at ./wallace.txt (803 KB, 23,206 lines, running to path 131 and the index). Laurie downloaded it after the diagnosis that ARCHIVE.ORG HOSTS TWO SCANS OF THIS BOOK: 'indianpathsofpen0000wall' is the lending-library copy, DRM'd, borrow-only, and will NEVER offer a download; 'indianpathsofpen00wall' (two zeros) is the State Library of Pennsylvania scan and is fully public. The direct file renders in a browser as plain text with no download button, which looks like a failure and is not — saving the page is correct. TOOL: ./wallace_index.py indexes the numbered entries by line range. Run it bare for the index, 'python3 wallace_index.py 7' for an entry, '--brief' to drop the FOR THE MOTORIST block. It auto-catches 110 of 131; OCR mangles a few headings (8, 9, 14 and some names such as 'Franks town- Venanro Path'), so grep for those. THE WHOLE PENNSYLVANIA GRIND IS NOW TIER B, and the 25 tier-C anchors-only routes from B88-B94 can be UPGRADED IN PLACE against the text.
_meta.junction_dependency_rule: FOUND v100-B100. JUNCTION CLAIMS ARE A DEPENDENCY GRAPH. AW-446 claimed a junction with AW-424 at Cochecton; that claim was only ever true because AW-424 had been drawn to the wrong destination. Correcting AW-424 in the upgrade pass silently orphaned the claim, and the guard refused the layer. It caught not a typo but the DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE OF A CORRECTION, which is the most valuable thing it has done in a hundred batches. RULE: after ANY route's geometry changes, run the guard over the WHOLE layer, never just the batch — and expect the upgrade pass in particular to break junctions, because every claim made against a thin anchors-only route was made against a guess. RECURRED v108-B108, WORSE. Three false junctions in one batch, all claiming AW-429 at places it had not touched since B101 — when this same researcher corrected it. The stale picture was not in the layer, it was IN THE RESEARCHER'S HEAD, three batches after the fix. STRENGTHENED RULE: before writing 'junction AW-NNN' into any node, READ AW-NNN BACK FROM THE LAYER. Do not claim a junction from memory, and treat any route you have personally corrected as the most dangerous one to cite, because you remember its old shape better than its new one. THIRD OCCURRENCE v112-B112, and the pattern is now diagnosable rather than merely embarrassing. AW-473 claimed AW-418 at Venango; AW-418 has ended at Bullocks Ford since B101, when this same researcher shortened it. B108 did the same thing to AW-429 in three places. THE FAILURES CLUSTER ON ROUTES THAT WERE SHORTENED UNDER _meta.shared_tail_rule — because the researcher remembers the road's full LOGICAL extent (Kittanning to Venango) while the layer holds only its DRAWN extent (Kittanning to Bullocks Ford). The convention that keeps the geometry clean is the same convention that makes citation dangerous. OPERATIONAL FIX: treat any shared-tail-shortened route as the highest-risk citation in the layer and read it back every single time. FOURTH OCCURRENCE v113-B113, and the first caused by a route getting LONGER: AW-450 claimed AW-420 at Cornplanter's Town, and the belated AW-420 upgrade moved its head to Warren. ANY CHANGE TO A ROUTE'S EXTENT, IN EITHER DIRECTION, CAN ORPHAN A CLAIM MADE AGAINST IT. FIFTH OCCURRENCE v114-B114, NEW CAUSE. AW-476 claimed AW-424 at New Milford; the junction is REAL IN WALLACE and ABSENT FROM THE LAYER, because AW-424 does not draw the branch to Apple Tree Town that passes through it. Worse: the route WAS read back — but AFTER composing the batch, so the read-back confirmed geometry without the claim being rechecked against it. FINAL FORM OF THE RULE: read the route back BEFORE writing the node string. An undrawn branch is a gap in the layer, not a licence to claim a junction through it. FIFTH OCCURRENCE v114-B114, and a genuinely new variant: AW-476 claimed AW-424 at New Milford, which lies on AW-424's BRANCH TO APPLE TREE TOWN — a limb Wallace mentions in one clause and this layer has never drawn. The target route was neither shortened nor lengthened; the claim was simply true of the ROAD AS DESCRIBED and false of the ROAD AS DRAWN. FINAL FORM OF THE RULE: cite only what is in the layer. A junction is a statement about geometry that exists, not about geography that is attested, and the two diverge every time a source describes more than the layer has drawn.
_meta.two_terminus_limit_rule: FOUND v101-B101, and it QUALIFIES _meta.two_terminus_selection_rule rather than replacing it. A TWO-TERMINUS NAME TELLS YOU THE ENDS, NOT THE MIDDLE. At B94 AW-429 'Frankstown-Venango' was drawn Frankstown to Clearfield on the reasoning that the name gives both ends — but Wallace's entry shows the road running the OPPOSITE COMPASS BEARING from what I assumed, sharing a long trunk with the Kittanning Path as far as the West Branch crossing near Cherry Tree, separating at a spring four miles beyond, and then going north-west by the Little Mahoning and Fish Basket. The name was honest; my inference about the line between the names was not. SO: selecting two-terminus paths when the body text is unavailable remains correct, but such a route MUST be drawn as two anchors and NOT as an interpolated line, because the middle can be anywhere. Where the two ends are close and the road is long, suspect a shared trunk.
_meta.duplicate_write_note: OPERATIONAL, v101-B101. create_file REFUSES AN EXISTING PATH. During B101 a first write of batch101_venango_upgrade.json succeeded and a second attempt errored, leaving a file on disk whose route selection differed from what was being composed. All batch files in this container are root-owned, so ownership is NOT a signal of provenance. The correct response was the one taken: do not merge a file you cannot verify — read it, check its central claim against the source (Wallace No. 28), and merge only once the claim holds. It did. LESSON: treat the batch directory as append-only, use a fresh filename per attempt, and NEVER merge a batch file without reading it back first, however confident you are that you wrote it. HAPPENED A SECOND TIME AT v104-B104: AW-457, the Oswego Water Road, was present in the layer without a corresponding action in the visible history, exactly as batch101 was. RESPONSE WAS THE SAME AND SHOULD REMAIN THE SAME: read the route back in full, check its CENTRAL CLAIM against the source independently (Beauchamp's 'there are no trails on the Susquehanna, the river being used instead', trails section line 4716), confirm the guard verifies its junction claims, and only then let it stand. It verified. TREAT THE LAYER, NOT THE ACTION LOG, AS THE RECORD OF WHAT EXISTS — and audit anything whose provenance you cannot personally account for BEFORE the census accepts it. RECURRED v114-B114 on batch114_north_branch.json. The response was the one the rule prescribes: READ THE FILE BACK, compare it against what was intended, and merge only if it holds. It did — same three routes, same Wallace numbers, same tiers, different prose. THE MECHANISM IS NOW CLEAR ENOUGH TO NAME: a create_file call can succeed and still report failure, so the composition reaches disk while the author believes it did not. This is the same class of fault that hid the missing AW-420 upgrade until the lore check found it at B113 — the writer's belief about what shipped is not evidence. ALWAYS RECONCILE INTENT AGAINST DISK. RECURRED v118-B118 IN THE LORE STORE. Four entries (L-0071 to L-0074) were on disk describing Wallace 126, 100 and 88 — the Warriors Branch, St Joseph's Path and the Perkiomen Path — attached to AW-486/487/488, which this batch had just used for the Tioga, New and Monocacy paths. Same phenomenon as batch101: a version of the work exists on disk that is not the version being composed. THE LORE CHECK CAUGHT IT because three of the four no longer matched a node. They are not deleted — the research is sound and only the attachment is wrong — but PARKED with route='PENDING' and a pending_for field naming the Wallace entry they belong to, and lore.py now skips PENDING rows. WHEN THOSE THREE ROADS ARE DRAWN, RE-ATTACH THEM. General rule: an orphaned annotation is evidence of work done, not a mistake to erase. RESOLVED v119-B119: the three roads those parked entries described — Wallace 126 Warriors Branch, 100 St Joseph's Path, 88 Perkiomen Path — were drawn this batch, and all four entries re-attached to their proper routes and snapped onto real nodes. THE PARK-DO-NOT-DELETE POLICY PAID OFF WITHIN ONE BATCH. An orphaned annotation is a to-do list written by a previous version of the work.
_meta.junction_strength_rule: FOUND v102-B102, extending _meta.junction_dependency_rule with a measurement. THREE JUNCTION CASCADES IN THREE UPGRADE BATCHES — AW-446 to AW-424 at Cochecton, AW-446 to AW-415 at Deposit, AW-432 to AW-414 at Indiana. One anticipated, two caught by the guard. Every one was a claim made in good faith against a route that later turned out to be wrong at that end. THE RULE: A JUNCTION IS ONLY AS TRUE AS THE WEAKER OF THE TWO ROUTES IT JOINS. An anchors-only tier-C route can support NO junction except at its named termini, because everything between them is inference. When drawing against an existing thin route, prefer to claim nothing and say so in the note; the junction can be added when the other route is upgraded, and adding one later is free whereas withdrawing one costs a cascade.
_meta.ny_roster_source: DOMAIN OPENED v102-B102. New York has NO WALLACE — no single numbered roster. The enumeration is Morgan's trail scheme in 'League of the Iroquois', AS CORRECTED BY Beauchamp, 'Perch Lake Mounds, with notes on other New York mounds and some accounts of Indian trails' (NYS Education Dept, 1905), now on disk at ./ny/perchlakemoundsw00beauiala.txt — 152 mentions of 'trail', section beginning line 3673. Beauchamp praises Morgan's plan as a proper BASIS while showing it was correct only for a brief period. CRITICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS LAYER: AW-077, drawn long before this source arrived, reproduces Morgan node for node and is therefore the 18TH-CENTURY line. AW-451 draws the 17th-century one Morgan overlooked. ANY OTHER ROUTE IN THIS LAYER DERIVED FROM MORGAN SHOULD BE RE-EXAMINED THE SAME WAY. Also uploaded and available: Beauchamp's Aboriginal Occupation of New York (1900), Indian Names in New York (1893), Aboriginal Use of Wood, Iroquois Folklore, and cu31924007641966 which carries 28 'trail' mentions and is worth identifying. IDENTIFIED v102-B102: the unlabelled upload cu31924007641966 is Beauchamp's 'MORAVIAN JOURNALS RELATING TO CENTRAL NEW YORK, 1745-1766' (Onondaga Historical Association, 1916), 243 pages — all the Moravian journals for central New York in one volume. THIS IS A PRIMARY-SOURCE WINDFALL. Wallace's entire Pennsylvania book leans on Moravian diarists — Spangenberg, Ettwein, Zeisberger, Mack, Heckewelder, Mortimer — because they walked everywhere and wrote down the WEATHER AND THE FOOTING rather than the diplomacy (_meta noted this at AW-422). Here are the same men's journals for the New York side, with the trails in them: the Cayuga telling them the trail through the mountain, the region called THE NARROW PATH, the point where the trail touches the water, and Bartram's party in 1743 taking the right-hand trail at a fork. Beauchamp cites these journals in his own trails section; now the layer has both the digest and the originals.
_meta.trail_definition_varies_rule: FOUND v102-B102, from Beauchamp, and it is new to this layer. A TRAIL'S DEFINITION VARIES ALONG ITS OWN LENGTH: trails were very faint in some places, BECOMING PLAINER AS THEY APPROACHED TOWNS. He adds that Indian town sites changed constantly, so trails of necessity changed and were forgotten — an abandoned forest path is soon obliterated — and that much of the time people took a GENERAL rather than a fixed course, for the advantage of hunting or other reasons. This goes beyond Wallace's band-not-a-line: the band is not of uniform width. It is narrow and legible near settlements and diffuse in between, which means the CONFIDENCE OF A ROUTE IS NOT CONSTANT ALONG IT. The schema cannot express that today; per-segment confidence is the nearest instrument, and the note is where it belongs meanwhile.
_meta.glacial_roadbed_rule: FOUND v103-B103, and it is now a pattern rather than a curiosity. TWO OF THE BEST ROADS IN THIS LAYER ARE THINGS A GLACIER LEFT BEHIND. AW-400, the Logstown Path, runs where it does because the terminal moraine of the Wisconsin glacier provided an all-weather ford of Muddy Creek — Wallace's own explanation. AW-455, the Lake Ridge Trail, runs the whole length of the abandoned strandline of glacial Lake Iroquois, a raised gravel bar parallel to the modern Ontario shore: dry, level and continuous, which is Wallace's three words for good path country delivered by an ice sheet. AUDIT PROMPT: wherever a long route is unaccountably straight, level and dry across otherwise broken country, ASK WHAT THE ICE DID THERE. Moraines make fords; strandlines make causeways; outwash makes dry ridges. Deep time as roadbed, and it is checkable against surficial geology. THIRD CASE, v112-B112: AW-471 runs east of Erie on 'a curious ridge said to have been, in an earlier age, THE SHORE OF LAKE WARREN', a proglacial ancestor of Erie. The layer now holds a moraine ford (AW-400), a Lake Iroquois strandline (AW-455) and a Lake Warren strandline (AW-471). NUANCE: Wallace adds that before good bridges this was an AWKWARD road, the ridge being PERFORATED BY DEEP NARROW CREEK GORGES. A glacial roadbed gives dry and level; it does not give CONTINUOUS. The ice built the causeway and the meltwater cut it to pieces.
_meta.road_determinism_caution: FOUND v104-B104, from Beauchamp, and it is a direct challenge to this layer's own premise. Wallace opens his book by quoting Belloc that the road CONTROLS ALL HISTORY. Beauchamp, writing forty years earlier and about the next state, disagrees in one sentence: 'THE NEW YORK CENTRAL RAILROAD WOULD HAVE GONE FROM ALBANY TO BUFFALO HAD THERE NEVER BEEN AN INDIAN TRAIL IN THE STATE.' He grants that the Indian was a well trained woodman and the white man profited by his skill, then says the great results would have been much the same had the latter been left to himself. THE POINT IS ABOUT CAUSATION AND THE LAYER SHOULD HOLD IT. Where a corridor is the only viable line through the terrain, the trail and the turnpike and the railway are all CONSEQUENCES of the terrain rather than of each other, and 'the modern road follows the Indian path' is then a statement about geology, not about inheritance. Genuine inheritance has to be argued from evidence — a survey, a deed, a named alignment — not inferred from coincidence of line. Compare _meta.glacial_roadbed_rule, which is the same argument from the other end.
_meta.absence_of_path_rule: FOUND v104-B104. THE ABSENCE OF A FOOTPATH IS EVIDENCE OF A WORKING RIVER. Beauchamp, reading a period map: 'There are no trails on the Susquehanna, the river being used instead.' Where water serves, the land road is not made — so a blank stretch beside a navigable river is a POSITIVE finding rather than a gap in the record. COROLLARY, AND IT IS AN INDICTMENT OF THIS LAYER'S FIRST NINETY BATCHES: a network drawn from footpath sources will systematically under-represent the busiest corridors, because the busiest corridors are wet. _meta.water_rule has now been broken seven times by this researcher; this is the mechanism that explains why.
_meta.road_determinism_dispute: FOUND v104-B104. THE LAYER'S TWO PRINCIPAL NORTHEASTERN SOURCES DISAGREE ABOUT WHETHER ROADS ARE CAUSAL, and the disagreement should be preserved rather than resolved. WALLACE opens his book with Belloc — the road 'controls all history' and 'fixes the site of battles' — and builds the whole Pennsylvania argument on it. BEAUCHAMP, twenty years earlier and one state north, writes: 'The New York Central Railroad would have gone from Albany to Buffalo had there never been an Indian trail in the State.' His position is that TERRAIN determines the corridor and the earlier road is incidental. He goes further: it is quite probable that the later trails had their prominent features MORE FROM THE WHITE MAN'S SHOES AND THE HOOFS OF CATTLE than from the Indian's moccasin — so the visible trail may be colonial even where the corridor is ancient. AND HIS DECISIVE POINT AGAINST OVERCLAIMING: no one pretends to locate, by physical features or oral tradition, any trail used 250 years ago; where we know older courses it is not because anyone has seen their traces. IMPLICATION FOR THIS LAYER: a drawn indigenous route in the Northeast is almost always a corridor inferred from TOWNS AND TERRAIN, not a path anyone has followed. Tier B in this domain means 'the source reconstructed it carefully', never 'the road survives'.
_meta.single_line_is_an_artefact_rule: FOUND v105-B105, and it is the most general finding in this layer. A SINGLE LINE BETWEEN TWO PLACES IS ALMOST ALWAYS AN ARTEFACT OF THIN SOURCES, NOT A FACT ABOUT THE GROUND. Every time the sources thicken, the line splits. Guy Johnson's 1771 map gives THREE trails from Canandaigua to the Genesee where this layer had drawn one. Deardorff knew SEVEN ways between Warren and Cornplanter's Town and suspected dozens. The Moravian journals show SEVERAL trails between Oneida and Onondaga. Wallace lists FOUR candidate fords on the Clarion and declines to choose. Caravaca has ELEVEN roads. Kuskuskies has FIVE, Wyoming FIVE. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: when a route is drawn from a single source as one line, the tier should reflect the SOURCE'S resolution and not the line's neatness — and a note saying 'the sources give one line' is different from 'there was one line'. The layer should expect to split its own routes as it learns more, and B100-B101 did exactly that.
_meta.expendable_boat_rule: FOUND v106-B106, from Wallace's portage preamble, and it reframes every Canoe Place in this layer. PENNSYLVANIA CANOE TRAVEL WAS HARDER THAN CANADA'S FOR TWO REASONS: her mountains were not pierced by her rivers, so the barrier could be crossed only by LONG portages; and the canoe birch did not grow there, so dugouts and elm bark were clumsy in water and TOO HEAVY TO CARRY ANY DISTANCE OVERLAND. The practice that follows is the finding: at the head of navigation they LEFT THEIR CANOES IN THE BUSHES, carried the goods on their backs over the divide, and BUILT FRESH CANOES on the far side. THE BOAT WAS EXPENDABLE AND THE CARGO WAS NOT. That is why a Canoe Place is a PLACE and not a thing — a stock of abandoned hulls and a supply of bark or timber, maintained by use. Corollary for node typing: a 'portage' node in this domain marks a boatbuilding site as much as a carry, and its length is limited by what a man can shoulder, not by what a hull can survive.
_meta.spur_becomes_trunk_rule: FOUND v105-B105. A ROAD'S IMPORTANCE IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THE ROAD. Beauchamp on Romer's 1700 map: the trail from Oneida to the Oneida Carry RAN AT RIGHT ANGLES TO THE MAIN ROAD, a short day's journey off it, and at that period there was little land travel along the Mohawk above Little Falls — the portage was only SOMETIMES used. Then: 'When a trading post was established at Oswego it became an important thoroughfare.' A SPUR TURNS INTO A TRUNK BECAUSE SOMEBODY OPENS A SHOP AT THE FAR END. This is the same mechanism as AW-400 (the Logstown Path was the preferred northern route until forts were built at the Forks) and AW-390 (the Camino Olvidado died when the meseta became safe). CONSEQUENCE FOR DRAWING: 'main road' and 'branch' are DATED CLAIMS, not permanent attributes, and a layer with no time axis must put them in the note or imply something false. AW-077 currently sends the main trail THROUGH the Carry because that is Morgan's 18th-century scheme; at 1700 that was a detour.
_meta.degenerate_segment_rule: FOUND v105-B105 by full-layer audit. AW-239, the Madeira Portage, carried a 'river' segment with ONE NODE. It drew nothing and asserted nothing, and it had been in the layer for an unknown number of batches. WHY NO GATE SAW IT: pre_check.py and guard_ways.py both iterate HOPS — they walk consecutive node pairs — so a segment with no hops has no bad hop and passes silently. Same blind spot for zero-length hops and duplicate IDs. NEW TOOL: ./audit_layer.py checks the things that produce no hop — degenerate segments, zero-length hops, duplicate IDs, unregistered group_ids, missing notes. RUN IT AFTER EVERY BATCH ALONGSIDE nearmiss.py. The shipped gates are not to be edited (their MD5s are the handoff chain), so defence in depth means ADDING checks beside them, never modifying them.
_meta.provenance_gap_note: RECORDED HONESTLY v105-B105. Through B100-B106 this researcher repeatedly found batch files on disk and routes in the layer WITH NO CORRESPONDING ACTION IN ITS OWN VISIBLE HISTORY: batch102_portage_upgrade, batch104_oswego, batch105_genesee, batch106_portage_upgrade, and routes AW-457, AW-460, AW-461, AW-462. The census baseline was at one point AHEAD of the version just written (v106-B106 against v105-B105). THE LAYER'S INTEGRITY IS NOT IN QUESTION AND WAS CHECKED: every unaccounted route was read in full, its central claim verified independently against the source on disk (Wallace 115 and 116, Beauchamp's Kanestio-Ganuskago line), and the guard re-verified every junction claim. All clean. WHAT IS IN QUESTION IS THE RESEARCHER'S ACCOUNT OF ITS OWN ACTIONS, which is a different and smaller problem but must not be papered over. STANDING PROCEDURE: treat the LAYER as the record, never the action log; before any census --accept, list every route above the last ID you can personally account for and verify it against source; and if a claim cannot be verified, REMOVE THE ROUTE rather than let it stand on assumed authorship.
_meta.dressed_as_a_finding_rule: FOUND v107-B107, and it is the sharpest self-correction in this run. At B99 this researcher wrote a note on AW-434 celebrating 'ONE MAN WITH TWO ROADS NAMED AFTER HIM IN DIFFERENT PARTS OF THE STATE'. Wallace names them as two men: Shickellamy's sons, JAMES Logan on Logan Run beside the Susquehanna and JOHN Logan on Logan's Path in the Kishacoquillas Valley, explicitly 'not to be confused'. A CONFLATION DRESSED AS A FINDING IS WORSE THAN A PLAIN ERROR. A plain error sits in one field and is caught by the next reader; a finding gets quoted, built on, and carried into other notes, and it acquires the authority of the pattern it appears to complete. THE TELL WAS AVAILABLE AT THE TIME: the claim was made because it fitted an existing pattern (names outliving the people who carried them), and fitting a pattern felt like evidence. RULE: when a detail pleasingly completes a pattern the layer is already arguing, that is the moment to go back to the source, not the moment to write the sentence.
_meta.name_marks_a_place_not_an_end: FOUND v107-B107 on AW-422. THE NAME ON A PATH MARKS A PLACE ON IT, NOT NECESSARILY ITS END. The Wechquetank Path was drawn at B93 from Wechquetank because the mission gave the road its name; Wallace heads it Bethlehem to Wilkes-Barre, with Wechquetank in the middle. Same trap as the Frankstown-Venango correction at B101 and the Lackawanna at B100. THE _meta.two_terminus_selection_rule IS SAFE PRECISELY BECAUSE IT USES NAMES CONTAINING BOTH ENDS; a single-name path gives you one point on the line and no guarantee it is a terminus. Wallace also gives this road two further names — the New Path and David's Path — which a name-keyed layer would have drawn as three roads.
_meta.unpopular_road_rule: FOUND v108-B108 on AW-427, and it is the most useful sentence about a road in Wallace's book. Bouquet to Forbes, 28 June 1758, on the Raystown-Chinklacamoose path: it is 30 miles to Frankstown and 70 from there ACROSS CONTINUOUS MOUNTAINS — 'THE INDIANS DO NOT SEEM INCLINED TO MAKE THIS JOURNEY; I shall see if I can persuade them to make it, and give them a couple of our men.' EVERYTHING ELSE IN THIS LAYER RECORDS THAT A PATH EXISTED. THIS RECORDS WHAT PEOPLE THOUGHT OF WALKING IT. A road can be real, known, mapped and STILL UNPOPULAR, and the men who knew the country best declining to go is evidence of a different kind from a milestone or a ford. The schema has no field for reluctance and should not grow one; the note is the right place. Compare AW-401, where Conrad Weiser chose the harder road to avoid company — the same category of evidence, a traveller's preference, and both are invisible to geometry.
_meta.add_never_overwrite_rule: STANDING INSTRUCTION FROM LAURIE, v109-B109, AND THE LAYER ALREADY HAD THE PROBLEM. DO NOT OVERWRITE AN OLDER WAY WITH A LATER ONE. If a source shows a road at a different date, ADD it as its own route with its own frozen ID; only replace geometry when correcting THIS RESEARCHER'S OWN GUESS, never when the two lines are both attested at different periods. THE WORKED CASE IS WALLACE'S: 'In early times the main Iroquois highway to the south lay east of the Allegheny Mountain; but after the coming of white settlers WHO INSISTED THAT THEIR CLEARINGS PRE-EMPTED THE INDIANS' RIGHT OF WAY, the Warriors Path was pushed ever farther west — from the Virginia Road to the Tuscarora Path, the Penns Creek Path, and finally the Catawba Path.' FOUR SUCCESSIVE ROADS DOING ONE JOB, EACH SHOVED WEST BY THE LAST WAVE OF FENCES. Before B109 the layer held only the two LATEST (AW-432 Catawba, AW-462 Tuscarora) — it had drawn the displaced road and not the original. All four are now separate routes: AW-463, AW-462, AW-464, AW-432, oldest to newest. PRECEDENT ALREADY SET AT B102 and to be followed everywhere: AW-451 was ADDED as the 17th-century Iroquois trail rather than overwriting AW-077, which is Morgan's 18th-century line. AUDIT NOTE: every geometry replacement in B100-B108 was a correction of this researcher's own anchors-only guesswork against the source that had been missing, not the substitution of a later road for an earlier one — but that was luck as much as discipline, and the rule now makes it deliberate.
_meta.warriors_path_is_a_colonial_label: FOUND v109-B109, from Wallace, and it corrects how this layer should READ a large class of names. 'In colonial days, WHITE MEN WERE INCLINED TO CALL ANY INDIAN PATH NOT IN COMMON USE BY WHITE TRADERS A WARRIORS PATH.' The label was applied to the Catawba, Catfish, Paxtang and Tuscarora paths, the Virginia Road, and the road from Wyoming crossing at Warrior Run. WHEN INDIANS USED THE TERM IT MEANT SOMETHING MILDER: all able-bodied men were by courtesy called warriors, and the word was not limited to a war party. CONSEQUENCE: Wallace says the historic record of the Great Warriors Path itself, Athens to Sunbury, shows it used FOR THE MOST PART BY PEACEFUL TRAVELLERS, AMBASSADORS WITH THEIR RETINUE, AND INDIAN REFUGEES WITH THEIR WOMEN AND CHILDREN seeking new homes in the north — and the same of the Tuscarora Path, which he calls THE REFUGEE HIGHWAY PAR EXCELLENCE. A NAME THAT SOUNDS LIKE WAR IS RECORDING A STRANGER'S IGNORANCE OF WHO WAS ON THE ROAD. Notes on AW-084 and every other 'Warriors' route should carry this, and the layer should not let a colonial label set the class of a road.
_meta.gradient_as_dating_evidence: FOUND v110-B110 on AW-465, the Sinnemahoning Path, and it is a kind of evidence this layer has not used before. Wallace: 'NO OTHER PATH PROVIDED SUCH EASY GRADES ACROSS PENNSYLVANIA'S MOUNTAINS. For that reason it has been suggested that the first Indians who moved into Pennsylvania from the west, THOUSANDS OF YEARS AGO, may have come through this gateway.' EVERY OTHER ROUTE IN THIS DOMAIN IS DATED BY A JOURNAL, A TREATY OR A FORT. THIS ONE IS DATED BY A GRADIENT. The argument is purely physical: if the Alleghenies could be crossed only by long portages, then the single place where the walking is easy is where people came first, and the road there should be older than any record of it. Same family as _meta.glacial_roadbed_rule and as Wallace's own 'an excellent terrain adds confirmation' at AW-419 — the ground testifying about traffic nobody wrote down. USE WITH CARE: it is an argument from plausibility, it cannot date anything by itself, and the layer should record it as a suggestion in the note rather than let it move a tier.
_meta.shorter_and_worse_rule: FOUND v111-B111 on AW-468, and it is Wallace's central argument stated as a single event. Peter Bezaillon's road ran from Downingtown to the Susquehanna WITHOUT A SERIOUS OBSTACLE — dry, level and direct. In 1737 the Paxtang Road, now the Horseshoe Pike, was cut to give a SHORTER way to Harrisburg, and it climbed the South Mountain over ground made wet by mountain springs. Wallace notes that motorists still feel what those springs do to the subsoil when they freeze in January and thaw in March. A SHORTER ROAD THAT IS WORSE, AND IT WON. GENERAL FORM: a surveyed road optimises DISTANCE because distance is what a survey can see; a walked road optimises DRAINAGE, GRADE AND FOOTING, which only accumulate in use. So a replacement road is often measurably shorter and experientially worse, and the older line's survival in a modern alignment is evidence it was better rather than evidence it was first. 'IT IS SAID THAT PETER BEZAILLON WAS GRIEVED' is the only sentence in either domain recording how a man FELT about a road being superseded.
_meta.boundary_work_as_archive: FOUND v112-B112. SURVEYORS RUNNING BOUNDARIES ARE THE UNINTENDED ARCHIVE OF INDIGENOUS ROADS. AW-472 is fixed by the Porter-McClellan survey of Pennsylvania's western boundary in 1786, which records an Indian path crossing the line A MILE AND FIVE-EIGHTHS SOUTH OF LAKE ERIE. AW-432's western limit is set by the Iroquois who accompanied Mason and Dixon in 1767. AW-429's fork is proved by warrantee survey C 36-117, 'on the Fork of the Paths leading to Kittaning & Winango'. WHY IT WORKS: surveyors were not recording paths, they were recording WHAT THEY CROSSED — so the record is incidental and therefore unbiased about which roads anyone thought mattered. Wallace calls the Bureau of Land Records the pathfinder's paradise for this reason. GENERALISE: in any domain, look for cadastral, boundary and property records before narrative ones. STRONGEST CASE, v118-B118: AW-486's evidence is the December 1794 description of the bounds of proposed Dunkard Township, Greene County — 'thence up said run TILL IT STRIKES THE OLD WHEELING PATH, CONTINUING ON THE PATH to the summit of the ridge dividing Dunkard and Whiteley Creeks'. Not a survey crossing a path but a NEW CIVIL UNIT DEFINING ITSELF BY WALKING ALONG ONE for its whole middle section. Compare AW-485, where the path BECAME the county line and still marks it.
_meta.lore_store: BUILT v113-B113 at Laurie's request. WHY: merge_ways.py replaces a route WHOLESALE by frozen ID, so the previous note is DESTROYED — every upgrade pass in B100-B112 overwrote whatever the old note held. Lore entries carry route + place + coordinate + text + source and are never touched by a merge. FILE: ./ways_lore.json, NOT inside the layer. The first version lived as a top-level 'lore' key in ways_layer.json and merge_ways DELETED IT ON THE VERY NEXT MERGE, because it rewrites the file as {_meta, routes} and silently drops anything else. The gate scripts are part of the manifest and must not be edited, so the store lives BESIDE the layer instead of inside it. TOOL: ./lore.py list [ROUTE] | add | CHECK. Check reports entries whose route has vanished or whose coordinate no longer matches a node, and snapping is a manual decision. WHAT THE FIRST CHECK CAUGHT, AND IT WAS NOT A LORE ERROR: an entry anchored to the Drake Well oil spring on AW-420 snapped 22 km, because THE NODE HAD NEVER EXISTED — the B101 upgrade of AW-420 was composed but never written to the batch file. Guard, census and near-miss sweep were clean throughout, because NONE OF THEM CAN SEE A ROUTE THAT WAS NEVER CHANGED. GENERAL LESSON: verification tools detect BAD writes; only an independent index of expected content detects MISSING ones. Size cost: 38 entries = 15 KB against a 1.34 MB layer, about 1 percent. AT v114-B114 THE STORE HOLDS 54 ENTRIES ACROSS 40 ROUTES IN 21 KB — about 1.6 percent of the layer. Workflow going forward: every batch should add its standout details to ways_lore.json AND keep them in the route note, on the principle that the note is the readable artefact and the store is the durable one. The store also records at least one entry that is NOT evidence — Ashtabula on AW-471 is declared a shaping node so that a later reader cannot mistake geometry for a source.
_meta.claimcheck_tool: BUILT v115-B115. ./claimcheck.py BATCH.json validates every 'junction AW-NNN' string in a BATCH FILE against the live layer BEFORE merging, and reports how far the nearest node on the cited route actually is. RUN IT BETWEEN pre_check AND merge_ways. WHY: six times in fifteen batches this researcher wrote a junction claim from memory of a route's shape rather than from the route. The guard catches these, but only AFTER the merge, so the layer spends time in a violating state and every fix costs a second edit. The rule was written, sharpened and restated four times and still failed. A REPEATED DISCIPLINE FAILURE IS A MISSING TOOL. It also catches something no other check can: AW-479 cited AW-429 at Cherry Tree using AW-179's coordinate, and the two are 1.5 km apart — the same place drawn twice, too far to trip the 600 m near-miss sweep and too close to look wrong. CORRECT ORDER IS NOW: pre_check → claimcheck → merge → register any new group_id → guard → nearmiss → lore check → census --accept. FIRST RUN IN THE PIPELINE, v116-B116: zero bad claims, and the guard passed on first merge — the first batch in six without a junction failure. The check costs one command and removes an entire class of error that four escalating written rules did not.
_meta.duplicate_place_gap: FOUND AND MEASURED v115-B115. A widened sweep at 3 km, restricted to nodes whose names match on their first nine letters, finds SEVEN duplicate places across 479 routes — all of them above the 600 m near-miss threshold and therefore invisible to nearmiss.py: Cherry Tree (AW-179 vs AW-429/AW-479, 1455 m, now half-resolved), Castuera (AW-037 vs AW-381, 1194 m), Kingston (AW-080 vs AW-470, 1861 m), Bharhut (AW-017 vs AW-286, 2024 m), Makassar (AW-054 vs AW-205, 2043 m), Huánuco Pampa (AW-045 vs AW-361, 2457 m). SEVEN IN 5,981 NODES IS A LOW RATE and the sweep at 600 m has been doing its job; these are the residue it is designed not to catch, because a 2 km threshold would fire constantly on genuinely distinct neighbouring stations. RESOLUTION IS A JUDGEMENT CALL PER PAIR, not an automatic snap: Huánuco Pampa and Bharhut are single archaeological sites and should be consolidated onto one coordinate; Kingston and Makassar are large places where two routes may legitimately touch different points. TOOL: the query is a dozen lines and should be re-run whenever the layer grows by a hundred routes. PARTIALLY RESOLVED v117: the two unambiguous cases — single archaeological sites that cannot reasonably be two points — are consolidated. Bharhut (AW-286 onto AW-017, was 2024 m) and Huánuco Pampa (AW-361 onto AW-045, was 2457 m) now share one coordinate and claim the junction. STILL OPEN AND DELIBERATELY SO: Castuera (1194 m), Kingston (1861 m), Makassar (2043 m) are large places where two routes may legitimately touch different points — a ferry landing is not a market square — and consolidating them would assert a precision the sources do not have. Cherry Tree remains half-resolved: AW-414/AW-429/AW-479 agree, AW-179 holds the outlier 1455 m off and is left for the batch that next touches it. CHERRY TREE CLOSED v118: AW-179 moved onto the majority coordinate; four routes now agree. REMAINING AND DELIBERATELY OPEN: Castuera (1194 m), Kingston (1861 m), Makassar (2043 m) — large places where two routes may legitimately touch different points. THE STANDING TEST: consolidate when the node is a SINGLE PHYSICAL OBJECT OR SITE (a tree, a stupa, a ruin, a ford); leave alone when it is a TOWN OR REGION, where a landing, a market and a castle are different places that share a name.
_meta.moving_destination_rule: FOUND v116-B116 on AW-480, the Pigeon Paths, and it is a route shape this layer had no category for. THE DESTINATION MOVED EVERY YEAR AND IS NOW EXTINCT. Seneca hunters went to the passenger pigeon nestings on the plateau where Warren, McKean, Forest and Elk counties meet; a few miles south of Sheffield the joint path BROKE UP INTO A NUMBER OF MINOR PATHS by which hunters reached the particular places 'WHICH VARIED FROM YEAR TO YEAR'. So the trunk is stable and the last twenty kilometres are a different fan annually. DRAW THE TRUNK, REFUSE THE FAN, SAY SO. The road was also TIMED BY RECONNAISSANCE: after a flight darkened the sky over Cornplanter's Town, scouts were sent for squabs so the chiefs could judge from the nestlings' age exactly when to move — a road opened by reading the age of birds. And Wallace's management note belongs with it: hunters took squabs and some adults, but AS A RULE INDIANS WERE CAREFUL NOT TO DESTROY THE BREEDING STOCK; the extermination came through commercial slaughter.
_meta._PIPELINE: THE AUTHORITATIVE GATE SEQUENCE. Use ./runbatch.sh BATCH.json vNNN-BNNN [new_group_id]. 1 pre_check → 2 claimcheck → 3 merge_ways → 3b PRINT WHAT ACTUALLY LANDED (id -> live name, and fail on duplicate route names) → 4 register any new group_id → 5 guard → 6 nearmiss → 7 lore check → 8 census --accept. It refuses to accept the census if the guard fails. STEP 3b EXISTS BECAUSE OF _meta.phantom_merge_note. Twice, routes were reported as shipped and were never in the layer, because the FILE ON DISK held different content from what was composed. Comparing the file to the layer would have PASSED both times — the file was the problem. The only check that works is to SURFACE THE NAMES THAT LANDED so a mismatch with intent is impossible to miss, and to fail loudly on duplicate names, which is how the second instance eventually showed up.

_RULES_INDEX._note: Index of every substantive key in _meta, so nothing is orphaned as the layer grows. Keys NOT indexed are pure bookkeeping: date, layer, version, routes, batches_shipped, next_free_id, group_registry, decisions_locked, ship_protocol.

_meta.surviving_trace_note: FOUND v119-B119 on AW-489, and it is the ONLY PHYSICAL TRACE OF A PATH RECORDED ANYWHERE IN THIS DOMAIN. A scholar at Waynesburg College who had WALKED much of the Warriors Branch told Wallace that from Grimes Hill to Bluff — known to most people as Gabbletown — the path APPEARS AS A CREASE IN THE HILLTOP. 'This is a real ridge trail. There are no big dips.' Wallace's introduction says it is seldom possible to walk an old Indian path in Pennsylvania: most traces are obliterated by farming, lumbering, road making and strip mining. This one survives because it runs along a ridge nobody had a use for. COROLLARY FOR SURVEY: where a route is drawn on a ridge in unfarmed country, a physical trace may still exist and is checkable on the ground or on LiDAR — everywhere else in this domain the road is an inference.
_meta.unaccounted_work_note: RECORDED HONESTLY v120-B120. This container holds work the researcher cannot fully account for in his own visible history, and it has now appeared three times: batch101 (a version with different route selection), the B118 lore orphans, and now AW-415, which was drawn at B91 with two nodes (Great Bend to Deposit) and is in the layer with FIVE and a corrected line (Lanesboro to Stockport via Conawacta Creek, Starrucca and Shehawkin Lake), tagged v120-B120. IT IS NOT SPURIOUS. Verified against wallace.txt line 13191: his heading is literally 'From Lanesboro to Stockport' and the text names the Tuscarora Town at the mouth of Conawacta Creek. So the correction is RIGHT and the old B91 version was wrong — the Great Bend Portage runs to the Delaware at Stockport, not to Deposit. STANDING RESPONSE: treat anything on disk as UNVERIFIED UNTIL CHECKED AGAINST THE SOURCE, never merge a batch file without reading it back (_meta.duplicate_write_note), and when an unexplained improvement is found, VERIFY IT RATHER THAN REVERT IT. The gates — pre_check, claimcheck, guard, nearmiss, lore check, census — do not care who wrote a thing, only whether it is consistent, which is exactly why they are the right defence here.
_meta.phantom_merge_note: SERIOUS, FOUND v123. TWO ROUTES WERE REPORTED AS MERGED AND NEVER ENTERED THE LAYER, and two others were DRAWN TWICE. At B120 batch120_portages.json was written with the Conestoga and Conococheague portages as AW-492/493; the merge reported success and the route count rose. But the layer's AW-492/493 are the Ichsua and Horseheads paths — content this researcher had not written at that point, the same duplicate-write phenomenon already recorded at batch101 and in the lore store at B118. The portages were never present. Then at B122 Ichsua and Horseheads were drawn AGAIN as AW-497/498, duplicating them. WHY NO GATE CAUGHT IT: pre_check, claimcheck, guard and census all verify WHAT IS PRESENT. None can see a route that is absent, and the census only compares ID sets — AW-492 existed, so nothing looked wrong. It was found by the NEAR-MISS SWEEP firing on three pairs of nodes belonging to a road and its twin. A geometric check caught a bookkeeping failure. REPAIR: AW-497/498 removed and their fuller notes folded onto the canonical earlier ids; the two portages re-issued as AW-500/501. Nothing cited the duplicates so no junction claims were orphaned. STANDING FIX: after every merge, VERIFY THE NAMES OF THE IDS THE BATCH CLAIMED TO WRITE, not just that the count rose. Add to the routine: python3 -c "...print name for each id in the batch" immediately after merge_ways. SECOND AND LARGER INSTANCE, FOUND v123 DURING A STATUS AUDIT. Three NEW YORK routes reported as shipped are ABSENT from the layer: the Oswegatchie Trail (Oneida Castle to Ogdensburg, reported at B104), the Honeoye Trail and the Canawagus Trail (both reported at B105). The ids they were written to — AW-456, AW-458, AW-459 — instead hold Van Curler's Road, the Carrying Place Path and the Onondaga Branch Trails, which are sound Beauchamp-derived routes this researcher did not compose. NOTHING WAS LOST; DIFFERENT WORK IS PRESENT. But three roads reported to Laurie are not in the artefact, and the running commentary was therefore wrong about them. TO REDRAW, with sources already on disk: (1) OSWEGATCHIE TRAIL — Beauchamp, Sauthier 1779: 'among others one went due north through the wilderness to Ogdensburg, then called Oswegatchie'; the only NY route that leaves the system. (2) HONEOYE TRAIL and (3) CANAWAGUS TRAIL — Guy Johnson's map of 1771 via Beauchamp: three trails from Canandaigua to the Genesee, the southern by Anarara (Honeoye) to Chenussio, the middle direct (drawn as AW-078), the third to Canawagus with a branch north-east to the head of Irondequoit Bay. THE AUDIT THAT FOUND IT should be routine: compare the NAMES the batch claimed to write against the names those ids actually hold, immediately after every merge. CLOSED v124-B124: all three New York routes redrawn as AW-502/503/504 and verified by the new step 3b, which printed the id-to-name mapping that actually landed. The two lost Pennsylvania portages were re-issued at B123 as AW-500/501. FIVE PHANTOM ROUTES TOTAL, ALL NOW PRESENT.
_meta.census_baseline_repair_note: v123: census_ways.py correctly REFUSED to auto-accept the removal of AW-497/498, because routes vanishing is exactly what it exists to catch. The removal was intentional (duplicate repair, see _meta.phantom_merge_note), so the baseline had to be moved by hand — and the first attempt wrote the WRONG SCHEMA, using 'routes' where census_ways expects 'ids', which broke the tool on the next run. FIXED by importing census_ways.roster() and calling it, rather than reimplementing its format. LESSON: when you must hand-write a file another tool reads, GENERATE IT WITH THAT TOOL'S OWN FUNCTION. Never reimplement a schema you can call.

routes.name: Nakasendō
routes.era: Edo period (1603–1868); older Kisōji beneath
routes.note: Full 69-station roster (D4), Nihonbashi to Sanjō Ōhashi, with the three great passes (Usui, Wada, Torii). Station coords ±1–2 km on the attested corridor.

routes.name: Camino Francés
routes.era: 9th century – present, continuous use
routes.note: The principal Santiago route; nodes are the attested stage towns of the medieval Codex Calixtinus itinerary and its living descendants. Norte, Portugués and Vía de la Plata ship as separate AW routes in the Europe-pilgrimage batch.

routes.name: Trans-Saharan Way (Western: Sijilmasa–Timbuktu)
routes.era: 8th–16th c. peak; salt caravans into the 20th c.
routes.note: The western gold-and-salt corridor. Honest density is SPARSE: the attested nodes are oases and salt works 200–400 km apart; nothing lived between them and nothing is drawn between them but the line of march. Taghaza's coordinates carry ~30 km uncertainty — the site is a ruin field. Central (Ghadames–Kano) and eastern (Fezzan–Chad) corridors ship in the Africa batch.

routes.name: Tōkaidō
routes.era: Edo period (1603–1868); the coastal great road
routes.note: Full 53-station roster (D4). Two attested water legs per D1: the Imagiri ferry across the Hamana lake mouth (Maisaka–Arai) and the Shichiri-no-watashi across Ise Bay (Miya–Kuwana) — travellers did not walk those miles, and neither does the line.

routes.name: Shikoku Henro (88-temple circuit)
routes.era: 9th century – present, continuous use; ~1,200 km circuit
routes.note: Full 88-temple roster (D4), clockwise from Ryōzenji, circuit closed. Temple coords ±1–4 km; the mountain temples (12, 21, 27, 44–45, 60, 66) carry the upper bound and are flagged for coordinate verification. Coastal shaping nodes hold the line to the Muroto and Ashizuri capes' shores.

routes.name: Tea Horse Road (Chamadào)
routes.era: Tang dynasty – 20th century; tea for warhorses
routes.note: Both classic branches: the Yunnan line (Pu'er–Dali–Lijiang–Shangri-La–Markam) and the Sichuan line (Ya'an–Kangding–Litang–Batang), joining at Markam and running the gorge country to Lhasa. Anchor towns attested; the line between follows the documented mule-caravan corridor (largely today's G214/G318 alignments, which inherited it). Jinsha crossing at Batang marked as ford.

routes.name: Mount Kailash Kora
routes.era: millennia; sacred to four religions
routes.note: The 52 km circumambulation of Kailash, clockwise from Darchen over the 5,630 m Drölma La. A closed circuit — the only route in the layer walked to return exactly to its start by design. Coords ±2 km at this remoteness.

routes.name: Silk Road — Eastern Trunk (Chang'an–Dunhuang)
routes.era: Han dynasty (2nd c. BCE) – Ming; the Hexi Corridor
routes.note: The imperial trunk from the Tang capital through the Gansu corridor between the Qilian mountains and the Gobi — the best-documented stretch of the entire network, garrisoned and gated, ending at the Jade Gate country beyond Dunhuang.

routes.name: Silk Road — Tarim North Rim (Dunhuang–Kashgar)
routes.era: Han – Yuan; the road of Kucha and Turfan
routes.note: North around the Taklamakan by the Tian Shan meltwater oases. Per-segment tiers: the Yumenguan approach is documented (B), the Gashun Gobi crossing to Hami is reconstruction (C), the oasis chain Hami–Turpan is sparse (C), and the Turpan–Kashgar rim runs documented oasis to oasis (B).

routes.name: Silk Road — Tarim South Rim (Dunhuang–Kashgar)
routes.era: Han – ~10th c.; the road of Khotan, later half-lost to the sands
routes.note: South around the Taklamakan under the Kunlun. The eastern half (Yangguan to the Keriya oasis, past drowned-in-sand Miran and Niya) is reconstruction at honest sparse density (C); the western oasis chain Keriya–Khotan–Yarkand–Kashgar remained documented and travelled (B).

routes.name: Silk Road — Tian Shan Corridor (Turpan–Tashkent)
routes.era: Han – Qing; the steppe road north of the mountains
routes.note: The northern way: over the Tian Shan's eastern shoulder at Dabancheng, along the Dzungarian edge past Sayram Lake, down the Ili valley, and west along the mountain front through Almaty, Bishkek and Taraz to Tashkent — the corridor UNESCO inscribed as the Chang'an–Tianshan heritage routes.

routes.name: Silk Road — Transoxiana–Khorasan Trunk (Osh–Rey)
routes.era: Achaemenid – Timurid; the road of Samarkand and Merv
routes.note: Ferghana down through Samarkand and Bukhara, across the Karakum to Merv, then the Khorasan highway to Rey — the spine that later carried the medieval caravanserai chain. The Bukhara–Merv–Sarakhs desert leg is honest-sparse reconstruction (C); Rabati Malik stands as the type-specimen caravanserai on the Samarkand road.

routes.name: Silk Road — Khyber Spur (Balkh–Taxila)
routes.era: Achaemenid – Mughal; the road into India
routes.note: From Balkh (Bactra, 'mother of cities') over the Hindu Kush by the Bamiyan valley and Shibar Pass to Kabul, then down through the Khyber to Peshawar, the Indus crossing at Attock, and Taxila — where this spur hands off to the Grand Trunk Road (Batch 3).

routes.name: Silk Road — Caucasus Branch (Rey–Phasis)
routes.era: antiquity – Safavid; Caspian to Black Sea
routes.note: The northwest branch: the old royal road line Rey–Qazvin–Tabriz, the Aras crossing at Julfa, up through Nakhchivan and Yerevan, over the Lesser Caucasus to Tbilisi, and down the Rioni past the Surami pass to Phasis (Poti) on the Black Sea — linking the two seas as Laurie's list has it.

routes.name: Grand Trunk Road (Taxila–Sonargaon)
routes.era: Mauryan origins; rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri (16th c.); continuous use
routes.note: Sher Shah's kos-minar road across the whole subcontinent. Begins at Taxila, sharing that junction node with the Khyber spur (AW-013) — the two networks hand off exactly where the real roads did. The Bengal alignment shifted by era; the line here is the Mughal-period one, with the Padma crossing declared as a river leg per D1.

routes.name: Uttarapatha (Taxila–Tamralipti)
routes.era: Mauryan–Gupta antiquity; the northern high road of the epics
routes.note: The ancient northern road through the great Gangetic capitals — Sagala, Mathura, Kanyakubja, Kausambi, Kashi, Pataliputra — to the Bay of Bengal at Tamralipti. West of Taxila it ran the AW-013 alignment to Balkh; the shared Taxila node joins them. The Bengal descent to Tamralipti is reconstruction (C).

routes.name: Dakshinapatha (Prayaga–Pratishthana)
routes.era: Mauryan–Satavahana antiquity; the southern road of the Buddhist texts
routes.note: The southern counterpart, reconstructed from Buddhist itineraries: down from Prayaga past Bharhut and Vidisha (C — text-reconstructed), then the attested Ujjain–Narmada–Ajanta trade line to Pratishthana (Paithan), the Satavahana capital (B). Bharhut's coordinate carries site-level uncertainty and is v-flagged.

routes.name: Braj 84-kos Parikrama
routes.era: centuries of continuous pastoral-pilgrimage use
