routes.note: Type specimen for the diffuse 'Indo-Gangetic pastoral tracks' list item: the attested circumambulation of the Braj cow-country around Mathura — Vrindavan, Nandgaon, Barsana, Govardhan — a closed circuit walked for centuries. The wider unmapped pastoral web is flagged as honestly unmappable; see ship note. DEFERRAL CLEARED: AW-075 (Narmada) and AW-076 (Panchkroshi) join this as type specimens; the diffuse pastoral web remains undrawn because it has no line.

routes.name: Incense Route (Qana–Gaza)
routes.era: ~7th c. BCE – 2nd c. CE; frankincense and myrrh
routes.note: The 2,000 km frankincense road from the Hadhramaut ports up the western Arabian interior to Petra and Gaza. Arabian legs are honest-sparse reconstruction (C) — oasis kingdoms 150–350 km apart; Timna's coordinate is v-flagged. The Negev descent (Petra–Avdat–Haluza–Gaza) is the UNESCO-inscribed section and runs documented (B).

routes.name: King's Highway (Aqaba–Damascus)
routes.era: Bronze Age – present; the plateau road of Edom, Moab and Ammon
routes.note: The biblical Derech HaMelech along the Transjordan plateau rim — Petra, Kerak, Madaba, Rabbath Ammon, Jerash — still a living road, as Laurie's list notes.

routes.name: Via Maris (Pelusium–Damascus)
routes.era: Bronze Age – Roman; the Way of the Sea
routes.note: The coastal great road linking Egypt to the northern empires: across north Sinai, up the Philistine and Sharon coasts, inland through the Megiddo pass, past Hazor and over the Golan shoulder to Damascus.

routes.name: Ottoman Hajj Road (Istanbul–Mecca)
routes.era: Ottoman period (16th–19th c.); the Darb al-Hajj al-Shami
routes.note: The Sultan's pilgrimage road: the Bosphorus crossing declared as a ferry (D1), the Anatolian menzil chain through the Cilician Gates to Damascus, then the fort-guarded Syrian Darb down the Hejaz — the line the Hejaz Railway later followed. Joins the King's Highway world at Damascus and the Incense Route's oases at Tabuk, Hegra and Medina: three networks, shared nodes, as it was.

routes.name: Camino del Norte
routes.era: 9th century – present; the coastal way
routes.note: The Cantabrian-coast route, the oldest documented Santiago way, hugging the shore from Irún to Ribadeo before turning inland through Mondoñedo and Sobrado to join the Francés world at Arzúa.

routes.name: Camino Portugués
routes.era: 12th century – present
routes.note: Lisbon to Santiago by the central way — Santarém, Tomar, Coimbra, Porto, the Minho crossing at Valença–Tui — the major Portuguese limb of the network, as Laurie's list has it.

routes.name: Vía de la Plata
routes.era: Roman road; pilgrimage use from the Middle Ages
routes.note: The Silver Way — the Roman Iter ab Emerita Asturicam become pilgrim road, Seville north through Mérida, Cáceres, Salamanca and Zamora to hand its pilgrims to the Francés at the shared Astorga node. Covers Laurie's list items 40 and 49 in one line, which is what they historically were. DENSITY CORRECTION: rebuilt on the Antonine Itinerary's Iter ab Emerita Asturicam plus the surviving stage towns. 14 named nodes to 25; spacing 46 km to ~21. The Roman mansiones whose sites are argued carry v-flags. The name is a red herring, incidentally: there was never any silver on it. Pláta is most likely Arabic balaṭa, a paved way — the Romans built it, al-Andalus named it for what it was made of, and Castilian heard a precious metal.

nodes.n: El Cubo de la Tierra del Vino

routes.name: Via Francigena
routes.era: Sigeric's itinerary, 990 AD; the road far older
routes.note: REBUILT ON THE SOURCE. In 990 Archbishop Sigeric of Canterbury went to Rome for his pallium, and somebody in his party wrote down every stop of the way home — eighty submansiones, numbered LXXX to I, surviving in a single manuscript. That list is the Via Francigena: not a road anyone designed but a road one man walked, once, whose secretary kept count. The nodes here ARE Sigeric's, numbered as he numbered them, so the route reads backwards from the Channel because that is the direction he was going. HONESTY: roughly a quarter of the eighty identifications are argued in the scholarship — Sigeric's clerk wrote Old English ears onto Latin and Lombard place-names and some of the results match nothing on any map — and every contested one carries a v-flag. Junctions AW-100 the Pilgrims' Way at Canterbury and AW-057 the ViaJacobi at Lausanne.

nodes.n: X Sce Petir in Pail (Ponte a Rigo)
XXIX Sce Stephane (Santo Stefano di Magra)
XXXIX Sce Andrea (Corte Sant'Andrea, the Po)
XL Sce Cristine (Santa Cristina e Bissone)

routes.name: St Olav's Way (Gudbrandsdalsleden)
routes.era: 11th century – present; to Nidaros
routes.note: The principal path of the network, Oslo up the Gudbrandsdal valley and over the Dovrefjell to St Olav's shrine at Nidaros Cathedral, Trondheim — in use since the saint-king's death in 1030. DENSITY CORRECTION: 11 named nodes to 18; spacing 45 km to ~27. The road's hinge is the Dovrefjell, and Norway's founding oath is named for it: enhet og troskap til Dovre faller — unity and loyalty until the Dovre mountains fall — sworn at Eidsvoll in 1814 when the constitution was written. The pass this pilgrim road crosses is the metaphor a nation used for permanence.

routes.name: St Kevin's Way
routes.era: 6th c. onward; the road to Kevin's Glendalough
routes.note: D4 upgrade in place — frozen ID, 3 nodes to 12. The pilgrim road from Hollywood over the Wicklow Gap to Glendalough, ~30 km, following the King's River up and the Glendasan down: the way Kevin himself is said to have walked to his hermitage, and the way pilgrims followed after him. Tier B — the corridor is the attested one (the valleys admit no other line) but the modern waymarking fixes a path that was never fixed. The Valleymount branch joins near Ballinagee and is not drawn.

routes.name: Pilgrim's Road to Clonmacnoise
routes.era: early medieval; along the Eiscir Riada
routes.note: The esker-ridge causeway across the midland bogs to the monastic city of Clonmacnoise — the dry road nature laid down in glacial gravel and the monks made a highway. Second type specimen for the 'Monk's Road' item.

routes.name: Amber Road (Gdańsk–Aquileia)
routes.era: Bronze Age – Roman; the road of Northern Gold
routes.note: Baltic amber south through Calisia (Kalisz — Poland's oldest attested town, named by Ptolemy on exactly this road), the Moravian Gate, Roman Carnuntum on the Danube, and the Pannonian towns to Aquileia at the head of the Adriatic.

routes.name: Via Egnatia (Dyrrachium–Byzantium)
routes.era: 2nd c. BCE Roman; vital Ottoman artery into the 19th c.
routes.note: The Adriatic-to-Bosphorus road: over the Albanian mountains past Lake Ohrid, through Heraclea and Pella to Thessaloniki, then coastal Thrace by Amphipolis and Philippi to Byzantium — the land bridge between the two halves of the Roman world, kept alive by the Ottomans as Laurie's list notes.

routes.name: Via Appia (Rome–Brundisium)
routes.era: 312 BCE onward; regina viarum
routes.note: The Queen of Roads on its itinerary-documented mansiones: the dead-straight Pontine run through Tres Tabernae and Forum Appii, Capua, Beneventum, then the southern line by Venusia and Silvium to Tarentum and the sea at Brundisium. DENSITY CORRECTION: rebuilt on the Antonine Itinerary's station list. 18 named nodes to 26; spacing 31 km to ~24. And one node is not a road at all: Forum Appii is a BARGE LANDING. The Appia crosses the Pontine Marshes, and travellers who could afford it skipped nineteen miles of it by night-boat, towed by a mule along a canal beside the road. Horace took it in 37 BC and wrote it up — the mosquitoes, the frogs, the drunk boatman who moored the barge and went to sleep, the passengers who did not notice until dawn. The oldest complaint about public transport in Europe is about this node.

routes.name: Alte Salzstraße (Lüneburg–Lübeck)
routes.era: Middle Ages; the white-gold road of the Hanse
routes.note: Lüneburg's salt to Lübeck's herring fleets: the Elbe crossing at Artlenburg, the ox-cart line through Mölln, sixty miles that funded two Hanseatic cities. DENSITY CORRECTION: 4 named nodes to 9; spacing 24 km to ~12. Short and consequential: Lüneburg had the salt, Lübeck had the Baltic, and between them lay one hundred kilometres and the entire Hanseatic herring trade. Salt from here cured the herring that fed Europe through Lent, and the warehouses at both ends — Lübeck's Salzspeicher still standing on the Trave — are the visible remains of a road.

routes.name: The Ridgeway
routes.era: ~5,000 years of use; Britain's oldest road
routes.note: The chalk high road along the Wessex downs and Chilterns scarp: Avebury's Overton Hill past Barbury, Wayland's Smithy and the Uffington White Horse to the Thames ford at Goring, then the Chiltern crest to Ivinghoe Beacon. STRUCTURAL CORRECTION (B18): this is the MIDDLE THIRD of one road. The Ridgeway, the Wessex Ridgeway, the Icknield Way (AW-098) and the Peddars Way together form the Greater Ridgeway, ~580 km of chalk from the Channel to the Wash. AW-098 shares this route's Ivinghoe Beacon terminus.

routes.name: Tin Route (Ictis–Massalia)
routes.era: Bronze Age – classical antiquity
routes.note: Reconstructed from Diodorus and Pytheas: Cornish tin gathered at the tidal island of Ictis (St Michael's Mount), shipped across to Gaul (declared sea leg, D1), then the classical 'thirty days' overland by the Loire–Rhône axis to Massalia. The Gaulish line is scholarly best-fit — tier C throughout.

routes.name: Highland Drove Road (Skye–Falkirk Tryst)
routes.era: 16th–19th c.; cattle to the trysts
routes.note: The great cattle road south: beasts swum across the Kylerhea narrows from Skye (declared water leg — the drovers' cattle genuinely swam it), Glen Shiel, the Corrieyairack, and down by Dalwhinnie and Crieff to the Falkirk Tryst, where 150,000 head changed hands in a season.

routes.name: Cañada Real Soriana Occidental
routes.era: Mesta charter 1273; seasonal use for 750 years
routes.note: Type specimen of Spain's nine royal cañadas — 90 varas wide by law since Alfonso X — running the merino flocks from the Soria highlands down through Guadalajara and Toledo to winter pasture in La Serena.

routes.name: Tratturo Magno (L'Aquila–Foggia)
routes.era: pre-Roman; codified by the Aragonese Dogana (1447)
routes.note: The greatest of the Abruzzo–Puglia tratturi, legally surveyed at 111 metres wide: the sheep road from the Gran Sasso down the Adriatic flank to the Tavoliere winter plains at Foggia. Tier A because the width and line are literally in the land registry.

routes.name: Trans-Saharan Way (Central: Ghadames Road, Tripoli–Kano)
routes.era: classical Garamantian roots; peak 9th–19th c.
routes.note: The central corridor: Tripoli through the Jebel Nafusa to Ghadames 'the pearl of the desert', down the Tassili edge to Ghat, through the Aïr past Iferouane to Agadez, and south to Kano's gates. Honest density is oasis-sparse; the line between is the line of march, nothing more.

routes.name: Trans-Saharan Way (Eastern: Fezzan–Bornu Road, Tripoli–Kukawa)
routes.era: Garamantian antiquity – 19th c.; the Bornu road
routes.note: The eastern corridor down the Fezzan: Tripoli to Murzuk, through the Tummo gap past Madama, along the Kawar oasis chain (Séguédine, Dirkou, Bilma of the salt pans) to Lake Chad and Kukawa, capital of Bornu. The Kawar line is the best-watered crossing of the entire Sahara — which is why empires fought over it for a thousand years.

routes.name: Hajj Road of Mansa Musa (Niani–Mecca)
routes.era: the 1324 pilgrimage; corridor in use for centuries either side
routes.note: The Sahelian hajj corridor as walked in legend in 1324: from Niani (whose very location scholars still argue — flagged) down the Niger to Timbuktu and Gao (deliberately sharing AW-003's river stretch; both roads used it), east past debated Takedda to Agadez, up the Kawar and Fezzan, along the northern oasis line through Awjila and Siwa to Cairo — then the documented Egyptian darb al-hajj (B) through Sinai and down the Red Sea coast to Medina and Mecca. Several outbound variants are attested; this is the defensible consensus corridor, not a claim of the emperor's exact footprints.

routes.name: Nile Corridor (Meroe–Cairo)
routes.era: Kushite antiquity – present; the river road
routes.note: The land paths paralleling the river that stitched East Africa to the Mediterranean: from Meroe of the pyramids through Napata and Kerma — the deep-history line by the river towns — past the cataract portages to Aswan, then the thickly attested Egyptian valley road to Memphis and Cairo. The Nubian reach is tier C (alignments shifted between the river line and desert cuts like the Korosko road, noted as variant); Egypt is B. Where the river carried the freight, the path carried the feet beside it.

routes.name: Gold Road (Wangara Road, Timbuktu–Begho)
routes.era: ~11th–17th c.; the Akan gold feeder
routes.note: The southern feeder that made the Saharan trade worth making: Wangara (Dyula) merchants carried gold up from the Akan forest edge at Begho through Bondoukou and Kong to the Niger entrepôts at Djenné and Timbuktu — where it crossed to AW-003's salt caravans. Begho is a ruin field; its coordinate and Kong's early alignment carry site-level uncertainty. **CHECKED IN B58 AND IT IS STILL LOAD-BEARING.** This road — drawn fifty batches ago as a gold road — IS the corridor that carries labour into the Ivorian cocoa belt today: Bobo-Dioulasso sits on it at 0 km, Bondoukou at 1 km, Djenné at 1 km, Kong at 31 km. Workers come down it from Burkina Faso and Mali to the forest, which is 300–1,000 km, and the road is six hundred years old. Nobody chose it; the geography did, and the railway of 1904 and the highway after it were laid along the same line for the same reason the Dyula walked it. AW-307 draws the forest leg and carries the honest numbers.

routes.name: Swahili Caravan Road (Bagamoyo–Ujiji)
routes.era: older roots; peak documented use 18th–19th c.
routes.note: The central of the Swahili coast–interior roads: from Bagamoyo ('lay down your heart') opposite Zanzibar, through Morogoro and Mpwapwa, across the Ugogo plateau to Tabora — the great crossroads — then west past the Uvinza salt springs to Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika. Type specimen for the coast–interior network; the Kilwa and Mombasa feeders are siblings, not yet drawn. DEFERRAL CLEARED: the Kilwa and Mombasa feeders ship as AW-072 and AW-073. **CORRECTED IN B59: this is a slave road and the note did not say so.** The Zanzibar caravans carried ivory AND people, and the efficiency is the horror: **the enslaved carried the ivory**, so one caravan moved two commodities and both were sold at the coast. Perhaps 1.5 million people came down this line in the 19th century. Livingstone watched the Nyangwe massacre at the far end in 1871, and his account is a large part of why Zanzibar's market closed in 1873. Flagged `sensitive`.

routes.name: Qhapaq Ñan — Highland Trunk (Quito–Uspallata)
routes.era: Inca imperial road (15th–16th c.) over older Wari and regional alignments
routes.note: The Camino Real de la Sierra: the spine of the 30,000 km system, Quito to the Uspallata valley through Ingapirca, Cajamarca, Huánuco Pampa, Cusco, the Titicaca shore, Tiwanaku and the Altiplano, Potosí country, the Quebrada de Humahuaca, and the Argentine valles. Cities and major tambos are attested; the drawn line follows the documented corridor between them. Stone-paved original sections remain the working footpaths of the sierra to this day.

routes.name: Qhapaq Ñan — Coastal Road (Tumbes–Arica)
routes.era: Inca imperial road over Chimú and coastal predecessors
routes.note: The Camino de los Llanos, the desert twin of the highland trunk: Tumbes down the whole Peruvian coast through Chan Chan, Pachacamac and the Nazca valleys to Arica. Ends there honestly — the continuation across the Atacama despoblado to Copiapó existed but at a sparseness this drawn line does not pretend to know; it can ship later as a C extension. DEFERRAL CLEARED: the Atacama despoblado continuation ships as AW-071 at tier C.

routes.name: Camino Real de Tierra Adentro (Mexico City–Santa Fe)
routes.era: 1598–1882; the Royal Road of the Interior, 2,560 km
routes.note: The silver road: Mexico City through the mining towns — Querétaro, Zacatecas, Durango, Parral, Chihuahua — across the desert jornadas to El Paso del Norte, up the Rio Grande past the Jornada del Muerto to Santa Fe. UNESCO-inscribed; town alignment is tier A. The waterless jornada stretches are rendered as anonymous shaping vertices — the parajes there were campsites, not settlements, and the line does not promote them. DENSITY CORRECTION: this route was tier A throughout while its NAMED nodes averaged 109 km apart — tier-A in name and tier-C in fact. The fix is not to invent parajes but to say what is true: the Bajío and Zacatecas half is A, densely towned and UNESCO-surveyed; north of Durango the jornadas are genuinely empty and the road is C. The gap in the nodes was the desert, not the research.

routes.name: Natchez Trace
routes.era: millennia of Choctaw–Chickasaw–Natchez use; boatmen's return road c. 1785–1830
routes.note: The old walking road from the Mississippi at Natchez to the Cumberland at Nashville, worn hip-deep into the loess in places. Tier A — the alignment is surveyed metre-by-metre under the National Parkway. George Colbert's ferry over the Tennessee is drawn as the two-kilometre water leg it was; the water rule does not care how short the water is. DENSITY CORRECTION: rebuilt on the NPS stand roster — the inns, mounds and fords the Parkway surveys metre by metre. 13 named nodes to 30; spacing 57 km to ~24. The stands are the road's real punctuation: a boatman walking home from Natchez slept at one every night, and they are why the Trace has a rhythm rather than a length. **CORRECTED IN B59.** This note described boatmen walking home and said nothing about the other traffic. The Trace was also the last leg of the COFFLE ROAD (AW-311): about a million people were walked from the Upper South to the cotton frontier between 1790 and 1860, chained in pairs, and the ones bound for Natchez came down this surface. **Kaintucks north and coffles south, at the same time, on the same road.** Forks of the Road at Natchez was the second-largest slave market in the South, two kilometres from this route's terminus.

routes.name: Great North Road (Chaco)
routes.era: Ancestral Puebloan, ~9th–12th c.
routes.note: Nine metres wide, engineered dead-straight for fifty kilometres due north from Chaco Canyon to Kutz Canyon — a road that connects almost no settlements and may never have been 'for' travel at all; archaeologists read it as a cosmological axis as much as a route. The surveyed road itself is tier A; the debated continuation to Salmon and Aztec ruins ships as a C segment, because the argument belongs on the map.

routes.name: Peabiru Path (São Vicente–Asunción)
routes.era: pre-Columbian Guaraní–Inca contact path; Cabeza de Vaca walked it 1541–42
routes.note: The transcontinental path of Guaraní tradition from the Atlantic at São Vicente over the Serra do Mar and across the Paraná plateau to Asunción — the stretch Cabeza de Vaca's crossing documents. Drawn to Asunción and stopped there honestly: the traditional continuation to the Andes and Potosí is attested as idea more than alignment. The Paraná is crossed by declared ferry at the Guairá reach. DEFERRAL CLEARED: the Andes reach ships as AW-074 at tier C, ending at Samaipata.

routes.name: Old North Trail (Calgary–Fort Collins)
routes.era: in use for millennia along the Rocky Mountain front; Blackfoot lifeline
routes.note: The travois road along the spine of the Rockies. LAURIE'S RULING: drawn to the full traditional extent, with per-segment tiers doing the honest work. The Blackfoot core (Calgary to Helena, tier B) is documented, and the mountain front dictates its line — Head-Smashed-In and Chief Mountain sit on it. The southern reach (Helena to Fort Collins, tier C) rests on tradition, not survey: the trail is said to have run from the far north to Mexico, and this is the Montana-to-Colorado-front stretch of that saying. Lethbridge is deliberately omitted — it lies ~60 km out on the plains, off the front, and reads as a modern-road artifact rather than a travois line. SHARED-SITE RULING (v80-B80, see _meta.shared_site_rule): Head-Smashed-In and Chief Mountain also belong to the sacred layer. They are NOT duplicated, NOT cross-referenced by name, and carry NO new field. Names are not a join key here any more than anywhere else — the two Mohawk Trails settled that. A site in two layers is one coordinate rendered twice, which is a CARTOGRAPHER problem, not a schema problem, and it has been handed over as one. Neither node is flagged sensitive: both are mapped, signposted, publicly located landmarks, and the sensitivity flag exists to protect places that pinpointing endangers, not to mark places that matter.

routes.name: Varangian Way of the East (Neva–Constantinople)
routes.era: ~8th–11th c.; the road from the Varangians to the Greeks
routes.note: The route that made Rus: up the Neva and Volkhov to Novgorod, up the Lovat to the volok country where boats were dragged overland past Usvyaty and Vitebsk to the Dnieper at Gnyozdovo, down the great river through Kyiv to the rapids — portaged again, under arms — then the coastwise Black Sea run that Constantine VII documented station by station in De Administrando Imperio. Eleven segments, four kinds: this route is why the D1 ruling exists. Water legs render dashed; the two portages are honest land.

routes.name: Mekong River Trade Road (Jinghong–delta)
routes.era: centuries of continuous use; the river as road
routes.note: The river and its landing towns from Yunnan to the South China Sea: Jinghong down through the Golden Triangle to Luang Prabang, Vientiane and the Lao reaches, broken — as it always was — at the Khone Falls, where everything walked. The falls portage is the route's defining fact: the one place the river road became a land road, and the reason the Mekong never carried through-traffic the way the Yangzi did. Below, the Cambodian reaches to Phnom Penh and the delta mouth.

routes.name: Maritime Spice Route (Ternate–Basra)
routes.era: antiquity – age of sail; the monsoon road
routes.note: The one route in this layer that is primarily water, shipped under the D1 ruling: the sailing corridor from the clove islands through the Java Sea and the Malacca Strait, across the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea on the monsoon, to Hormuz, Siraf and up the Shatt al-Arab to Basra. The two open-ocean monsoon crossings (Lamuri–Galle, Calicut–Muscat) are exactly that — open water sailed on the season, not coastline hugged — and the line says so by running straight. A river spur reaches Palembang, Srivijaya's seat 80 km up the Musi, the toll-gate of the whole eastern trade.

routes.name: Great North Road (Lusaka–Morogoro)
routes.era: ancient migration and trade corridor; motorable road 20th c.
routes.note: The corridor the modern Zambia–Tanzania road inherited: up the Muchinga escarpment through Mpika and the Tunduma gap to Mbeya and Iringa, meeting the Swahili caravan road (AW-044) at Morogoro — the two networks share that junction node deliberately. Tier C: the alignment is a composite of migration and trade traditions under a modern road, drawn as corridor, not survey.

routes.name: Camino de Madrid
routes.era: Roman road over the Fuenfría; pilgrim use from the medieval period; waymarked as a named camino in the 1990s
routes.note: Madrid to Sahúgún, where it hands off to the Camino Francés (AW-002) at a shared node. Honest tiering: the ROAD is old — the Fuenfría carries a preserved Roman calzada, and the Segovia–Valladolid–Tierra de Campos corridor is genuinely medieval — but the NAME is new. Madrid was a minor town until 1561, so this was never a great pilgrim artery; it is a real old road that modern waymarking rebranded. The line follows the attested stage towns.

nodes.n: Santa María la Real de Nieva

routes.name: ViaJacobi
routes.era: medieval Jakobsweg; the Alte Etzelstrasse was a trade road by the 10th c.; waymarked as SwitzerlandMobility route 4
routes.note: Rorschach on the Bodensee to Genève, ~450 km along the foot of the Alps — the Swiss limb of the Jakobsweg. Tier B by the sources' own admission: the medieval routes were never clearly defined, weather rerouted pilgrims mid-journey, and the modern line detours where the original became a road. Specific stretches ARE attested: the Alte Etzelstrasse (10th-c. trade road), the Tüfelsbrugg of Etzel (1117), and the Brünigweg, whose pilgrim status a surviving pilgrimage pfännig attests. TWO declared water legs per D1 — Brunnen–Treib on the Vierwaldstättersee and Merlingen–Spiez on the Thunersee — both still rowed today. Hands off to the Via Francigena (AW-026) at Lausanne, where the road to Rome parts from the road to Santiago. The northern variant via Luzern and the Konstanz, Wattwil and Fribourg branches are attested alternates, not drawn.

routes.name: Clare Priory Way
routes.era: medieval; Clare Priory founded 1248 — the first Augustinian house in England
routes.note: The best-attested of the limbs: the Cathedral names this explicitly as a route used by medieval pilgrims travelling from Clare Priory to the Abbey, ~31 km. The corridor is certain; the exact village sequence is reconstructed from the line of the land, so the intermediate settlements carry verification flags. HONEST GAP: the drawn line measures ~21 km against the attested 31 km, so the true road wandered considerably more than this reconstruction shows. The anchors are right; the meander is missing.

routes.name: Lark Valley Way (Ely–Bury)
routes.era: commemorates the monks who came from Ely to the Abbey c.1020
routes.note: ~48 km up the River Lark from the Isle of Ely to the shrine, through Mildenhall at the halfway mark. Honours the monks sent from Ely and St Benet's to take charge of Edmund's body when Canute raised the stone shrine. The river is the route's logic — the Lark runs from Bury down to the Great Ouse at Ely, and the road ran beside it.

routes.name: First Benedictines' Way (St Benet's–Bury)
routes.era: commemorates the twenty monks from St Benet's Abbey, c.1020
routes.note: The longest limb, ~129 km from the Broads to the shrine — in the footsteps of the first Benedictines, the twenty monks who came from St Benet's to take charge of Edmund. Passes Venta Icenorum at Caistor St Edmund, the Roman town the Iceni's country became, and the attested overnight stages at Dunston and Diss.

routes.name: Icknield Way to Bury (Thetford–Bury)
routes.era: the Icknield Way is prehistoric; the pilgrim use medieval
routes.note: ~30 km from Thetford Priory to the shrine, past the medieval stone Barnham Cross on the Norfolk–Suffolk boundary and along the Icknield Way through the King's Forest to West Stow. Taken not for the modern waymarking but for the road under it: the Icknield Way is prehistoric, and is very likely the oldest thing in this batch by several thousand years. Thetford's Priory of the Canons of the Holy Sepulchre aided pilgrims bound for Jerusalem — this limb begins where longer roads began.

routes.name: The King's Road (Dunwich–Hoxne–Bury)
routes.era: 10th c., under King Athelstan's patronage; alignment lost
routes.note: RULED v80-B80: tier C, ANCHORS ONLY, alignment inexplicably lost. Also called the King's Highway and St John's Road: a pilgrim path attested by NAME in the 10th century under Athelstan's patronage, running from St Felix's at Dunwich to the Abbey at Bury by way of Hoxne. Three things are honest to say and the note says all three. First, the road is real in the record but its alignment is, in the source's own word, inexplicably lost — the only modern reconstruction is one walker's re-imagining, so nothing between the anchors is drawn. Second, Hoxne is the TRADITIONAL martyrdom site, not an established one; Edmund's relics were translated from a site nobody can locate. Third, Dunwich is gone — the sea took the city, and the terminus here is where St Felix's stood, not where anything stands. This is the Old North Trail ruling applied: draw the tradition, and say plainly what it rests on. THE CORRECTION THAT CAME WITH THE RULING: this route previously carried FOUR shaping nodes between the three anchors while its own note said nothing between the anchors was drawn. The note was right and the geometry was lying. The anchor hops are 31 km and 35 km — a third of the 110 km densify threshold — so the shaping nodes were never structurally required; they were decoration that drew a line no one can attest, on the one route in the layer whose entire finding is that the line is lost. They are gone. Lesson for the next writer, and it is not a small one: DENSIFY IS A GATE-SATISFYING TOOL, NOT A DRAWING TOOL — a shaping node added where the gate did not demand one is an assertion wearing the costume of geometry, and the guard cannot see it because the guard tests hop length, not warrant.

routes.name: Red River Trails — West Plains Trail
routes.era: an Indigenous path before the carts; oxcart use 1820s–1870s
routes.note: The oldest of the three, and originally an Indigenous path. Down the west bank of the Red to Pembina, then west and south onto the higher ground — the gravel beach ridges of glacial Lake Agassiz, which is why it was also called the Ridge Trail — to avoid the Red's swamp bottoms. Rejoins the river at Georgetown and Fort Abercrombie, south to Lake Traverse, through the Traverse Gap, and down the whole Minnesota River valley by Traverse des Sioux to Mendota and St. Paul. BRAIDING CAVEAT applies (see group note): no oxcart trail was ever one line.

routes.name: Red River Trails — East Plains Trail
routes.era: in common use from the 1840s; Kittson's cart trains moved to it in 1854
routes.note: Also called the Middle Trail, and shorter than the West Plains it branched from. Shares the West Plains line from Pembina to Breckenridge, then strikes east out of the Red River Valley across the upper Pomme de Terre and Chippewa valleys to St. Cloud and Sauk Rapids on the Mississippi, and down its east bank to St. Paul. Norman Kittson moved the company's cart trains here in 1854 when Sibley retired — a business decision that redrew the map.

routes.name: Red River Trails — Woods Trail (Crow Wing Trail)
routes.era: cut in autumn 1844; established by 1846; in use through the 1860s
routes.note: The last trail cut, and cut for one reason: safety. In summer 1844 Métis carters attacked Dakota hunters, and that year's traders could not go home the usual way. They struck northwest up the Mississippi to Crow Wing, west up that river to Otter Tail Lake, and northwest to the Red. Inferior terrain, superior safety — it ran within Ojibwe country the whole way, and many Métis carters had Ojibwe kin. Follows the Lake Agassiz beach ridge, fords the Red Lake River at the Old Crossing near Huot, and crosses the Mississippi at Old Crow Wing. A road drawn by a killing.

routes.name: Maumee–Wabash Portage (Lake Erie–Ohio River)
routes.era: pre-contact Miami corridor; French, British and American contest 1680s–1830s
routes.note: One of the great continental portages: Lake Erie up the Maumee, the carry at Kekionga, down the Little River to the Wabash, and the whole Wabash to the Ohio and the Mississippi beyond. This is the water road between the St. Lawrence and the Gulf, and the reason Kekionga was the most fought-over ground of the early republic — Harmar, St. Clair and Fallen Timbers were all about who held the carry. River segments follow the river; the portage is honest land.

routes.name: Trappers Trail (Fort Laramie–Bent's Fort)
routes.era: 1830s–1850s; the Cherokee Trail later overlaid much of it
routes.note: The Front Range corridor, ~640 km along the base of the Rockies from Fort Laramie on the North Platte to Bent's Fort on the Arkansas, threading the whole South Platte fur-post cluster. Four posts — St. Vrain, Jackson, Vasquez, Lupton — stood within about 25 km of each other, all built and abandoned inside a decade: a boom and bust you can walk in an afternoon. The 1849 Cherokee Trail overlaid much of the same line, which is where the modern naming confusion enters.

routes.name: Grand Canal (Beijing–Hangzhou)
routes.era: Sui unification 605–609; Yuan realignment to Beijing 1280s; Shandong summit works 1411; northern reaches failed after the Yellow River shifted in 1855
routes.note: REBUILD. The candidate roster gave 45 km of Wuxi–Suzhou with a fabricated Taihu crossing; this is the whole thing — ~1,780 km, the longest artificial waterway of the pre-modern world, and the artery that fed a capital 1,700 km from its rice. Note what it does NOT do: it never crosses Taihu. It was engineered to stay clear of open water, because a squall on a lake kills a loaded grain barge. The one water it cannot avoid is the Yangtze, and there boats left the canal at Guazhou and crossed to Zhenjiang under their own power. Per-segment tiers: the Jiangnan reach is A — still navigable, precisely mapped, continuously used for 1,400 years — while the northern reaches are B, documented but silted and abandoned after 1855 when the Yellow River jumped its bed and took the Shandong summit's water with it. The Nanwang summit is typed as a PASS, because that is what it is: a watershed crossing, engineered in 1411 by Bai Ying, who solved the problem of pushing boats over a divide. LENGTH CAVEAT: the drawn line measures ~1,395 km against the canal's real ~1,780 km. The difference is meander this node density does not capture, not a claim about the route.

routes.name: Via Augusta (Pyrenees–Gades)
routes.era: Republican roots on an older Heraklean Way; rebuilt and named under Augustus, 8–2 BCE
routes.note: REBUILD, and now the longest Roman road in the layer at ~1,500 km — the Pyrenees to the Atlantic at Gades, laid over an older Iberian track the Greeks called the Heraklean Way. The candidate roster gave three Alicante points that backtracked 150 km and placed Torrevieja's salt lakes on it; the road ran INLAND through Ilici and Orcelis, and Torrevieja's salt is an 18th-century industry. Tier B: every city is certain and the milestones are abundant, but the line between them is reconstructed. The Carthago Nova leg is drawn as main-line per common usage, though some itineraries carry it as a branch — flagged. SELF-CAUGHT: the first draft of this rebuild put Orcelis before Ilici and backtracked ~20 km north — the same reversal defect the original candidate data was rejected for. Caught pre-merge.

routes.name: Kumeyaay Trade Road (coast–mountain–desert)
routes.era: millennia of use; the shell-bead road east
routes.note: The Kumeyaay road across three worlds in ninety miles: Pacific shore, oak-and-pine mountains, and the desert sink to the Colorado. Shell beads went east and obsidian, agave and pottery came back — a trade that worked precisely because the ecologies were unlike. SOURCES: published archaeology and public place names ONLY. Tier C is honest — the corridor is documented at landscape scale, the exact village-to-village line is not, and the specific ceremonial locations that would make it precise are not published, so they are not drawn. The route carries a sensitivity flag; Cuyamaca carries a node-level one.

routes.name: Qhapaq Ñan — Atacama Despoblado (Arica–Copiapó)
routes.era: Inca imperial road; the southern despoblado crossing
routes.note: DEFERRAL CLEARED. AW-046 stopped at Arica because the Atacama continuation was too sparse to draw honestly at tier B. It is drawn here at tier C, where sparseness is the correct answer rather than a failure: the despoblado de Atacama is the driest desert on Earth, and the nodes are ports and oases 150–250 km apart because nothing lived between them. Quillagua on the Loa is the exception — a genuine oasis in the absolute desert, and one of the driest inhabited places ever recorded. This deferral was about EVIDENCE, not sensitivity.

routes.name: Kilwa Caravan Road (Kilwa–Lake Nyasa)
routes.era: Kilwa's gold-trade heyday 12th–16th c.; caravan road documented into the 19th
routes.note: DEFERRAL CLEARED — the southern sibling AW-044's note promised. From Kilwa Kisiwani, the island city that controlled the Sofala gold trade and whose Great Mosque still stands, inland by Liwale and Songea to Lake Nyasa. The island is reached by a declared ferry per D1 — Kilwa's whole power rested on being just offshore, close enough to trade and far enough to be defended.

routes.name: Mombasa Caravan Road (Mombasa–Lake Victoria)
routes.era: older roots; documented caravan use 18th–19th c.
routes.note: DEFERRAL CLEARED — the northern sibling. From Mombasa's harbour inland by the Taita Hills and Taveta to the foot of Kilimanjaro, then west by Arusha and the Rift lakes to Lake Victoria at Mwanza. The mountain is the road's logic: Kilimanjaro's meltwater makes a green line across dry country, and the caravans followed the water.

routes.name: Peabiru — Andes Reach (Asunción–Samaipata)
routes.era: pre-Columbian Guaraní–Inca contact; the reach Cabeza de Vaca's crossing gestures at
routes.note: DEFERRAL CLEARED, and the terminus is the point. AW-050's note called the Andes continuation 'attested as idea more than alignment', and that remains true — this is tier C and deliberately sparse across the waterless Chaco Boreal. But it ends somewhere exact: Samaipata, the Inca frontier fort built to WATCH FOR GUARANÍ RAIDS. The Peabiru is the road the Inca were watching for. Its western end is the wall raised against it, which is the most eloquent possible proof the path was real. The traditional continuation to Potosí is drawn beyond, more faintly attested still.

routes.name: Narmada Parikrama
routes.era: millennia; continuously walked
routes.note: DEFERRAL CLEARED — type specimen for what the 'Goshala paths' entry could not be. The only river on Earth circumambulated along its entire length: from the source at Amarkantak down one bank to the sea, across, and back up the other — roughly 2,600 km, traditionally walked over three years, three months and thirteen days. Pilgrims must never cross the river, only walk beside it, which is why it is a circuit and not a road. A closed loop that takes years to close. The diffuse pastoral web the candidate roster gestured at has no line to draw; THIS is what an attested Indian circuit looks like.

routes.name: Panchkroshi Yatra (Kashi)
routes.era: ancient; continuously walked; five stages
routes.note: DEFERRAL CLEARED — second type specimen. The ~88 km circuit tracing the sacred boundary of Kashi, walked in five stages with a night at each of the five halts. It defines the city by walking around it: everything inside the line is Kashi, and the line exists only because feet keep drawing it. Coordinates are approximate to the stage-halt villages rather than surveyed — the circuit is certain, the polyline is a reconstruction of a road that has moved with the city's edge.

routes.name: Mohawk Trail (Albany–Onondaga)
routes.era: pre-contact Haudenosaunee route; the only water-level gap through the Appalachians
routes.note: The most consequential corridor in eastern North America: the Mohawk valley is the ONLY water-level gap through the Appalachian barrier, and whoever held it held the continent's interior. Three carries define it — Cohoes Falls, where the Mohawk drops off the plateau; Little Falls, where it drops again; and the Oneida Carry at Fort Stanwix, the divide between Atlantic drainage and the Great Lakes. Extended west past Laurie's roster to Onondaga, where it meets AW-078 and AW-079 at the Haudenosaunee council fire.

routes.name: Seneca Trail (Geneseo–Onondaga)
routes.era: pre-contact; the east–west trail of the Five Nations
routes.note: The western limb of the Great Iroquois Trail, running the north ends of the Finger Lakes from Seneca country to Onondaga. It threads the confederacy itself — each lake a nation, each nation a fire. Coordinates from Laurie's roster, which are sound; the distance column was decorative and discarded.

routes.name: Onondaga–Susquehanna Trail
routes.era: pre-contact; the road from the council fire to the Susquehanna
routes.note: South from Onondaga down the Tioughnioga to the Susquehanna at Binghamton, then downriver west and south to Tioga Point at Athens — the gateway where the Chemung meets the Susquehanna and the road to the Ohio country opened. Third limb of the Onondaga junction. PRIMARY-SOURCE CONFIRMATION FOUND v162-B162, and explicitly checked against this session's own test for whether a diary entry documents a real route or a one-off trek before being used. Zeisberger and Frey's 1753 diary (Beauchamp's Moravian Journals) describes travelling this exact corridor by water: up the Susquehanna to the fork at Zeninge (Otsiningo, this route's own Binghamton node — identified by name in Gen. J. S. Clark's editorial notes on the same diary), then up the Tiohujodha branch (the Tioughnioga, this route's own name for the same river) past a fourth fork (Schio) to a fifth (Onogariske), then overland the final 50 miles. This passes the route's own bar for inclusion: named by multiple travelers (the diarists explicitly compare their trip to 'Bro. Joseph' [Spangenberg]'s 1745 journey, and rejoin his exact trail near Lake Ganneratareske), a guide who evidently knew the water systems and forks by name, and the diarists' own explicit distinction between 'we could see no traces of a trail' (true wilderness, briefly, right after leaving the canoe) and 'the trail that comes up from Owego, and is quite clearly defined here' once they rejoined the known road. Not drawn as new geometry — this whole diary resolves to corridors already on the layer (this route, plus AW-401/AW-550 for the final overland leg), which is itself the finding worth recording: three separate documented attempts to reach Onondaga from the Tioga area (Owego overland, this water route, and the 1750 Cammerhoff road via Cayuta Lake/AW-556) were real known options, chosen between rather than invented fresh each time.

routes.name: Minisink Trail
routes.era: pre-contact Lenape/Munsee route; the Old Mine Road follows part of it
routes.note: The Lenape road from the Minisink country on the Delaware over the Shawangunk ridge to the Esopus landing on the Hudson at Kingston — the line that carried the interior to tidewater before any European drew it.

routes.name: Catskill Path (Kingston–Unadilla)
routes.era: pre-contact Esopus/Munsee route across the Catskill divide
routes.note: West from the Hudson up the Esopus, over the Catskill divide, and down the Delaware headwaters to the Susquehanna at Unadilla. Tier C — the corridor is real but the alignment is reconstructed. FLAGGED: Laurie's roster gives 'Slide Mountain — mountain pass', which is a data artifact. Slide is the highest Catskill peak at 1,274 m and no trade path crosses a summit; the real divide crossing is the low saddle near Pine Hill, and the line is drawn there instead.

routes.name: Mahican–Wappinger River Trail
routes.era: pre-contact Wappinger and Mahican route along the Hudson's east bank
routes.note: The east-bank road up the Hudson from Wappinger country into Mahican country, ending at Schodack — the Mahican council seat, whose name means 'fire place'. Tier C: the corridor is certain (the river dictates it) but the line is reconstructed from the creek mouths and council sites rather than surveyed. INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED v168-B168: C.G. Hine's 1906 Post Road account, walked and written without reference to Beauchamp, gives Schodack the identical gloss — a Dutch rendering of the Indian Esquatak, 'the fireplace of the nation,' the Mohican council seat. Two unrelated sources naming the same site the same way is about as good as corroboration gets for a place name.

routes.name: Lake Champlain Water Road
routes.era: millennia of canoe use; the Mohawk–Abenaki corridor between the Hudson and the St. Lawrence
routes.note: The water road between two worlds: south to the Hudson and the Atlantic, north down the Richelieu to the St. Lawrence and Canada. Every army that ever tried to split the American colonies came this way, because the lake IS the road. Drawn as river-kind per D1 — the segment vocabulary's inland-water kind — and dashed accordingly. Nobody walked this; they paddled it.

routes.name: Great Warriors Path (Athawominee)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Haudenosaunee–Cherokee war and trade road
routes.note: Athawominee, the Great Warriors Path: the Iroquois country to the Cherokee country down the whole Great Valley of the Appalachians, ~1,300 km. It carried war parties north and south for centuries before it carried a single settler, and then it carried all of them — the Great Wagon Road inherited its line, and so did much of modern I-81. Long Island of the Holston is where treaties were signed on it. FLAGGED: New Echota is anachronistic as a southern terminus — the Cherokee capital there dates only to 1825, while the path is centuries older; Chota, the Overhill capital now drowned under Tellico Lake, is the period-appropriate node and both are drawn.

routes.name: Occaneechi Path (Great Trading Path)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Virginia–Catawba trade road; Occaneechi monopoly broken 1676
routes.note: The Great Trading Path southwest from the Virginia fall line to the Catawba and Cherokee country. Its centre of gravity was an island: the Occaneechi held a fortified town in the Roanoke where the path crossed, and taxed every pelt that went by — a monopoly built on a ford. Bacon's Rebellion destroyed them in 1676 and the tollgate with them, after which the path ran free and the trade moved to Charles Town's men. FLAGGED: Augusta as a southern terminus is late (founded 1736); the path's older southern reach ran to the Catawba towns and on by other names.

routes.name: Old Sauk Trail (Detroit–Chicago)
routes.era: pre-contact Sauk and Potawatomi route; became US-12
routes.note: The great east–west trail across the southern Michigan and Indiana country, Detroit to Chicago, skirting the southern tip of Lake Michigan — the one land route between the eastern and western Great Lakes basins that avoids going round the top. Saline sits on salt springs, which is why it is on the road at all. The trail became a stage road, then US-12; the line under the asphalt is the older thing.

routes.name: Athiamiowee (the Path of the Armed Ones)
routes.era: pre-contact Miami route; contested through the 1790s
routes.note: Athiamiowee — in Miami, the path of the armed ones — running south from Kekionga to the Ohio down the Great Miami. It shares its northern node with AW-066's Maumee–Wabash portage, because Kekionga was the hinge of the whole interior: from that one town, water ran to the Gulf by the Wabash, to the Gulf by the Miami, and to the Atlantic by the Maumee. Carries a second divide crossing at Loramie, the carry between the Maumee and the Great Miami — the same portage the Miami and Erie Canal would later buy with dynamite.

routes.name: Chilkoot Trail (the grease trail)
routes.era: Tlingit trade road for centuries; opened to outsiders 1880; 30,000 stampeders 1897–98
routes.note: A gold-rush trail only for eighteen months, and a Tlingit trade road for centuries before that. The Chilkoot Tlingit held the pass as a monopoly and packed eulachon oil — 'grease' — inland to the interior Athabaskans, carrying furs back; they guarded it so jealously that outsiders were barred until 1880, and even then the Tlingit worked as packers on their own road. Then the Klondike, and 30,000 people over the Golden Stairs in a single winter, each hauling a tonne of goods up in relays because the Mounties would not let a man into Canada with less. The full NPS stage roster. FLAGGED: the Sheep Camp coordinate is suspect — the official trail distance to the summit (3.5 mi / 5.6 km) is SHORTER than the drawn chord (7.9 km), which is impossible; the distances match the survey, so the coordinate is what needs verifying.

routes.name: Mojave Road (Colorado–Afton)
routes.era: pre-contact Mojave (Pipa Aha Macav) trade road; army wagon road 1860s
routes.note: The Mojave were runners: they crossed the desert on foot to the Pacific and back, trading Colorado River produce for coastal shell, and thought nothing of a journey that killed most people who tried it. The road's design is a single idea — it is a CHAIN OF SPRINGS, each about a day apart, and every named node here is water. Piute, Rock, Marl, Soda. Miss one and you die; that is the whole engineering. Pairs with AW-070 Kumeyaay as the layer's second shell-bead road. EXTENSION AVAILABLE: the trade road continued west from Afton over the Cajon Pass to the Gabrielino and Chumash coast; that half needs its own reconstruction and is not drawn.

routes.name: Hohokam Shell & Turquoise Route
routes.era: Hohokam, ~300 BCE–1450 CE; the O'odham corridor after
routes.note: Glycymeris shell from the Gulf of California went north and turquoise came south, and the proof is in the ground: Snaketown alone yielded shell bracelets by the thousands, cut and carved 500 km from the sea that made them. Tier C — the corridor is inferred from where the shell ENDS UP rather than surveyed, which is the honest situation for a trade that left artefacts instead of a roadbed. FLAGGED, anachronistic names on ancient places: San Xavier is a 1692 mission built at Wa:k, a Sobaipuri O'odham village far older than the church; Nogales is a modern border town on an old southern link. The places are right; the names are late. Quitobaquito is drawn on the roster's jog west — a detour that costs 20 km and buys the only reliable water in the driest country on the route, which is a trade any walker would make.

routes.name: Naches Pass Trail
routes.era: Yakama route across the Cascades; wagon road 1853
routes.note: The Yakama road over the Cascade crest, carrying dried salmon and horses west to the Puget Sound peoples and shell and dentalium back — a trade between a wet world and a dry one, forty miles apart and utterly unalike. The 1853 Longmire wagon train forced the first wheels over it and had to lower them down the eastern scarp on ropes. FLAGGED: Fort Steilacoom is an 1849 army post at the western end of a route centuries older; the terminus is the Sound, not the fort. The Toppenish–Walla Walla leg is drawn through Wallula Gap, where the Columbia cuts the basalt and every road in the interior had to pass.

routes.name: Ala Kahakai (the ala loa)
routes.era: the ancient ala loa, the long trail that ringed the island
routes.note: The shoreline stretch of the ala loa — the 'long trail' that once ringed Hawai'i island entirely, carrying chiefs, tax collectors and everyone else along the coast where the fishing was. Its southern terminus is the point: Pu'uhonua o Hōnaunau is a place of refuge, and if you broke a kapu the law was that you could be killed on sight UNLESS you reached it first. The trail ends at a sanctuary you had to outrun the executioner to reach. FLAGGED: Hulihe'e Palace (1838) and the Cook Monument (1874) are late names on ancient ground; the places are older than the labels.

routes.name: The Kula Ring
routes.era: pre-contact; documented by Malinowski 1915–18; still practised
routes.note: The only route in this layer that carries nothing anyone needs. Soulava (shell necklaces) travel one way around the ring and mwali (armshells) travel the other, forever, and no man keeps either — you receive a valuable, hold it a while, and pass it on, and your name travels with it. The exchange creates the partnership; the partnership is the point; the goods are the excuse. Ordinary trade rides along beside it. RULED v80-B80 — BIDIRECTIONALITY STAYS IN THE NOTE (see _meta.bidirectionality_rule). A CLOSED RING drawn once. The two rejected alternatives, and why: a `direction` attribute would have to mean 'the goods flow both ways' here and 'the traffic ran one way' on a drove road or a slave road, and _meta.sensitivity_rule already settled that a flag meaning two things means nothing; two mirrored routes would double the geometry, destroy the one fact the ring is FOR (it is one ring, whichever way you sail it), and plant a phantom in every future near-miss sweep — every node zero metres from its own twin, forever. The deciding argument is that direction is a property of the CARGO and this schema describes the PATH. AW-206, the Pituri and Ochre Road, already made this call in prose and shipped: pituri south, red ochre north, one set of tracks. The ruling ratifies the precedent rather than inventing a rule.

routes.name: The Sawei Tribute Route (Satawal–Yap)
routes.era: pre-contact; the outer-island tribute network to Yap
routes.note: Drawn in the direction the canoes actually sailed — inward, from Satawal 900 km east to Yap — because the sawei was a tribute network and tribute flows one way. The outer islanders carried mats, rope and shell to Yap and received in return the right to Yap's land and food when a typhoon took theirs, which on low atolls is not tribute so much as insurance. It worked because of the navigators: Satawal and Lamotrek held the deep-sea wayfinding knowledge that made 900 km of open Pacific a road rather than a barrier. Sea segments per D1, drawn straight — which is correct here, not lazy: open-ocean sailing IS the great circle.

routes.name: Nōti Raureka (Browning Pass)
routes.era: opened c.1700 by Raureka's crossing; knowledge later made tapu
routes.note: REBUILD. Laurie's roster gave the modern Greenstone Track's DOC huts; this is the ara tawhito underneath the whole idea. Pounamu is found only on Te Tai Poutini, the West Coast, and Kā Tiritiri o te Moana stood between it and everyone else. Around 1700 a Kāti Wairaki woman named Raureka walked from Lake Kaniere up the Arahura, over this 1,411 m pass, and down to South Canterbury ALONE, carrying a pounamu toki. She showed Ngāi Tūhaitara what her stone could do, and — more consequentially — she told them the way. Ngāi Tahu crossed, fought Kāti Wairaki for three or four generations, and took the pounamu trade. Her generosity destroyed her people. The pass later became TAPU after a party died there in snow: a road closed by law rather than by disuse, and by 1865 only one living kaumātua had walked it.

routes.name: Nōti Taramakau (Harper Pass)
routes.era: pre-contact; seasonal use; the principal pounamu crossing
routes.note: REBUILD. The most important crossing of the Southern Alps for Māori seeking pounamu, and the reason is arithmetic: at 962 m it is among the LOWEST passes in the range, which on a mountain wall is the whole argument. Known by its rivers rather than a name — Taramakau on the west, Hurunui on the east — and used seasonally, when the snow allowed. The first European over it in 1857 was guided by four Māori, which is the usual shape of these discoveries.

routes.name: wukalina Walk
routes.era: Country walked for tens of thousands of years; THIS walk established 2018
routes.note: MODERN — 2018, and the note says so, per Laurie's ruling that it earns its place for what it represents. palawa-owned and palawa-guided, the only walk of its kind, and the fifteen-year project of Elder Clyde Mansell: land is the blueprint of our culture. It exists because a famous extinction was false — the textbooks say the last Tasmanian Aboriginal died with Trukanini in 1876, but 47 people survived detention on Wybalenna, and it is their descendants who guide this. In palawa kani, wukalina means woman's breast: the Country understood as nurturer. It is also where the mob watched for British ships and lit signal fires to warn the islands to hide the women and children. krakani lumi, the standing camp, sits on removable footings — taken away, within a season there would be no trace. FLAGGED: Ansons Bay is dropped from Laurie's roster; the walk ends at larapuna.

routes.name: Icknield Way
routes.era: prehistoric; in use before the Romans, before the Saxons, before the road
routes.note: STRUCTURAL: the Icknield Way and AW-034 the Ridgeway are the SAME ROAD. Together with the Wessex Ridgeway and the Peddars Way they form the Greater Ridgeway, ~580 km of chalk from the Channel to the Wash — AW-034 is its middle third. They are shipped as separate AWs because they are separately named and separately attested, and they share the junction node at Ivinghoe Beacon where one name ends and the other begins. Same treatment as Uttarapatha and the GT Road. The road follows the chalk because chalk drains: in a wooded, boggy island the high dry line was the only line. Junctions with AW-059 at Icklingham. AW-061 (Thetford–Bury) is a pilgrim SPUR off this road, not a rival to it. The Peddars Way continues northwest from Knettishall to the Wash and is available on request.

routes.name: The Harrow Way
routes.era: prehistoric; the Hoary Way
routes.note: The Hoary Way — hoary meaning grey, meaning old. FLAGGED: it is often called the oldest road in Britain, and that claim is repeated more confidently than it is evidenced; the layer draws the corridor and declines the superlative. Tier C accordingly: the western reach in particular is reconstructed from place-names and alignment rather than survey. Runs the chalk from the Devon coast east past Stonehenge — which it predates — to Farnham, where it hands off to AW-100 and the two roads become one line to the Channel. What later pilgrims walked to Canterbury was already immeasurably old when they walked it.

routes.name: Pilgrims' Way (Winchester–Canterbury)
routes.era: the North Downs trackway dates to ~600–450 BC; pilgrim use from 1172
routes.note: The road is two thousand years older than the pilgrimage. The North Downs trackway is archaeologically dated to roughly 600–450 BC; Becket was murdered in 1170 and canonised in 1172, and the pilgrims who then walked to his shrine were inheriting a route that had been walked since the Iron Age. The saint did not make the road — the road was there, and the shrine was placed at the end of it. Joins AW-099 at Farnham and hands off to AW-026 the Via Francigena at Canterbury, where the road to Rome begins: a walker could step from the Iron Age chalk onto the road to St Peter's without breaking stride.

routes.name: Lindisfarne Pilgrims' Way
routes.era: since Aidan's founding in 635; the poles are the modern marking of an ancient crossing
routes.note: FIRST TIDAL ROUTE IN THE LAYER. Holy Island is an island twice a day and a peninsula twice a day, and the pilgrim way crosses the sands on foot — not the modern causeway — following a line of poles with refuge boxes on stilts for those who misjudge. Cuthbert's island, Aidan's island, the Lindisfarne Gospels' island, and the place the Vikings hit first in 793. The theology is in the geography: a monastery you can only reach when the sea permits, and cannot leave when it does not. The tidal segment is neither land nor water and is typed accordingly.

routes.name: The Broomway
routes.era: attested since at least the 1400s; the only road to Foulness before 1922
routes.note: The deadliest path in Britain, and it was a commuter route. For six centuries it was the ONLY way to Foulness — islanders walked it to market, coffins were carried along it, and it has drowned something over a hundred people, the ones recorded. It runs across Maplin Sands roughly 400 m OFFSHORE of the island, marked historically by brooms: bundles of twigs stuck in the seabed, replaced as they rotted. The sands flood faster than a person walks, fog arrives without warning, and the compass is the only thing that saves you. Tier C — the landing heads are approximate and flagged; the line itself was never fixed because the sands move. A road that exists for six hours and drowns for six.

routes.name: Watling Street (Dubris–Viroconium)
routes.era: an older British trackway metalled by Rome from 43 AD; the name is Saxon
routes.note: The road Rome found rather than invented — a British trackway already running from the Kent beaches to the Midlands, which the legions straightened and metalled after 43 AD. The name is Saxon: they called it after a tribe who had settled at Verulamium, so the road carries the name of people who arrived centuries after it was built and used it anyway. Three junctions on one road: it BEGINS at Canterbury with AW-100 and AW-026 (the Iron Age chalk and the road to Rome), CROSSES the Icknield Way at Dunstable, and CROSSES the Fosse Way at High Cross — Venonis, a place that is nothing but an intersection and was important for exactly that reason.

routes.name: Ermine Street (Londinium–Eboracum)
routes.era: 1st c. AD; the road to the north
routes.note: London to York, the spine of Roman Britain's north road. It has a hole in it: the Humber. There was no bridge and Rome never built one — traffic went by FERRY from Winteringham to Petuaria, which is drawn here as a declared crossing per D1. An imperial trunk road that stops at a river and gets in a boat is a useful corrective to the idea that Rome engineered its way past everything. Junctions with AW-105 at Lindum and AW-106 at Eboracum, where the road north continues under another name.

routes.name: Fosse Way (Isca–Lindum)
routes.era: c. 47 AD; first as a frontier, then as a road
routes.note: The straightest long road in Britain and possibly anywhere: over ~370 km from Exeter to Lincoln it never deviates more than about 10 km from a straight line. It is straight because it was not originally a road at all — it was the FRONTIER, the limit of the conquest around 47 AD, a line drawn across an island to say this far. Then the conquest went further and the border became a highway. Junctions: AW-099 the Harrow Way at Ilchester (a Roman town on a prehistoric track), AW-103 at High Cross, AW-104 at Lindum.

routes.name: Dere Street (Eboracum–Inveresk)
routes.era: c. 71 AD; the invasion road into Caledonia
routes.note: The road built to conquer Scotland, which never quite worked. It runs from York north through the fort chain to Corbridge, THROUGH Hadrian's Wall at the Portgate — a hole deliberately left in the empire's own barrier so the road could keep going — and on to the Forth. The wall-gate node type earns its second use here after the Silk Road's Jade Gate: two empires, two walls, and both of them cut a door in the wall for a road, because a barrier you cannot trade through is a barrier you cannot afford. Junction with AW-104 at Eboracum.

routes.name: Sarn Helen (Segontium–Moridunum)
routes.era: late 1st c. AD; the gold road of Wales
routes.note: The road exists for one reason and it is at Dolaucothi: the only Roman gold mine in Britain, worked with aqueducts and hushing on an industrial scale, and this road is how the gold left. Tradition names the whole thing for Elen Luyddog — Elen of the Hosts — who in the Mabinogion's Dream of Macsen Wledig asks her husband the emperor to build roads across her country so her armies can move, and he does. A road named after a woman in a dream, running to a gold mine that was entirely real. Tier C: several stretches are inferred between the forts rather than surveyed, and the north–south alignment through mid-Wales is debated.

routes.name: Tro Breizh
routes.era: attested from the 12th c.; suppressed by the Revolution; revived 1994
routes.note: A CLOSED LOOP of ~600 km around Brittany, touching the graves of all seven founding saints — Samson, Malo, Brieuc, Patern, Corentin, Paul Aurelian, Tugdual — whose seven cathedral cities are the seven nodes. The medieval belief is the reason it earns its place in this layer above almost any other pilgrimage: if you did not walk the Tro Breizh in life, you walked it AFTER DEATH, advancing the length of your own coffin every seven years. A circuit with no exemption and no end. Same closed-ring geometry as Shikoku, Kailash and the Kula.

routes.name: North Wales Pilgrim's Way (to Ynys Enlli)
routes.era: medieval; Enlli a pilgrim island since the 6th c.
routes.note: ~210 km from Holywell to the tip of the Llŷn and across to Ynys Enlli, Bardsey — the island of twenty thousand saints. THREE pilgrimages to Enlli counted as ONE to Rome, which tells you what the crossing was worth and what it cost: Bardsey Sound is a tide race that has drowned pilgrims in every century, and the boat is drawn as a declared ferry per D1 because no one ever walked it. Begins at St Winefride's Well, which has never stopped flowing and has been a place of pilgrimage for thirteen centuries without a break. Junctions with AW-107 Sarn Helen at Caernarfon — the pilgrim road to the saints' island crosses the Roman road to the gold mine. HONEST GAP: the drawn line measures ~144 km against the attested ~210 km. The route wanders considerably more through the Hiraethog moors and the Llŷn than this node density shows. The anchors are right; the meander is missing. Same caveat as AW-058.

routes.name: Tóchar Phádraig
routes.era: a pre-Christian chariot road to the mountain; a pilgrim road since the 5th c.
routes.note: Older than Patrick and older than Christianity: a chariot road running to Cruach Phádraig when the mountain was already sacred, later rebranded as the saint's causeway to the peak where he is said to have fasted forty days. ~35 km from Ballintubber Abbey — which has held Mass continuously since 1216, through suppression, roofless, for over 800 years without a break. The Boheh Stone on the road bears Neolithic rock art AND the Rolling Sun: twice a year, on 18 April and 24 August, the setting sun appears from that exact stone to ROLL DOWN the shoulder of Croagh Patrick. The stone was placed to watch it. The road goes to a mountain that was a calendar before it was a shrine.

routes.name: Corlea Trackway
routes.era: the oaks were felled in the winter of 148/147 BC
routes.note: The most precisely dated ancient road on Earth, and the shortest route in this layer by an order of magnitude. Not 'around 150 BC' — dendrochronology gives the felling of the oaks to the WINTER OF 148/147 BC, a single season, twenty-two centuries ago. Two kilometres of oak planks on birch runners laid across a raised bog, built to carry weight the bog could never carry: it took hundreds of mature oaks and an organised community, and it SANK within about a decade. It may never have been meant to work. The scale is wrong for cattle or carts and right for ceremony — a road to somewhere that mattered, built once, magnificently, and abandoned to the peat that then preserved it perfectly for two thousand years. Tier A: excavated plank by plank.

routes.name: Via Regia (Frankfurt–Kyiv)
routes.era: royal road under the Königsbann from the 8th c.; the great east–west of Europe
routes.note: The King's Road — not a metaphor. It was under the Königsbann, the royal peace: the crown guaranteed the safety of anyone travelling it, and in return took the tolls. A road that is a legal instrument as much as a surface. It ran the whole breadth of the continent, and it CROSSES AW-113 the Via Imperii at Leipzig, which is why Leipzig exists at all — the city is the intersection, and its fair grew from the crossroads and made it rich. Drawn Frankfurt to Kyiv; the fuller Council of Europe route reaches Santiago westward and is not drawn.

routes.name: Via Imperii (Stettin–Verona)
routes.era: medieval Reichsstraße; the great north–south of the Empire
routes.note: The Empire's road: the Baltic to the Alps and on to Rome, the line an emperor rode to be crowned. Crosses AW-112 the Via Regia at Leipzig, and the two together are the reason a marsh village on the Pleisse became one of Europe's great fair cities — Leipzig is a CROSSROADS that grew a town, not a town that acquired roads. Drawn to Verona and stopped there deliberately: beyond it the road to Rome runs by the Via Romea Germanica and merges with the network AW-026 the Via Francigena already draws, so it is not duplicated. The two roads to Rome cross the Alps by different doors — the Francigena at the Great St Bernard, this one at the Brenner.

routes.name: Westfälischer Hellweg (Duisburg–Paderborn)
routes.era: prehistoric line; Charlemagne's Saxon-war road from 772; salt road after
routes.note: Charlemagne's road into Saxony, and the reason the Ruhr's cities sit in a line: Duisburg, Essen, Bochum, Dortmund, Unna, Soest, Paderborn are beads on a string, and the string came first. The name is the point — Hellweg, from hell meaning bright or cleared: a road kept open to a lance's width on either side, cleared by royal order so an army could not be ambushed in the forest. It ran the loess strip between the marshes and the hills, the only dry line across Westphalia, and it carried salt for a thousand years after the wars ended.

routes.name: Via Claudia Augusta (Altinum–Augusta Vindelicum)
routes.era: completed 47 AD by Claudius, on his father Drusus's line of 15 BC
routes.note: The first Roman road over the Alps to the Danube country, and one of the few whose completion date is on a stone: Claudius finished it in 47 AD along the line his father Drusus forced in 15 BC. It crosses at the Reschen — a lower, gentler door than the Brenner, which is why the legions used it first and why the Empire's centre of gravity in the north is Augsburg rather than anywhere else. Junctions with AW-113 the Via Imperii at Augsburg: a Roman road and a medieval imperial road ending at the same town fourteen centuries apart, because the geography did not change.

routes.name: Hærvejen / Ochsenweg (Viborg–Hamburg)
routes.era: prehistoric ridge line; army road and ox road through the 19th c.
routes.note: Two names, two truths. Hærvejen is the ARMY ROAD; Ochsenweg is the OX ROAD — and the oxen won: up to 50,000 head a year were walked south from Jutland to the German markets, the largest livestock movement in northern Europe. It runs the watershed ridge of the peninsula because that is the ONLY line: Jutland is fjords to the east, bog and heath to the west, and the spine between them is the one dry road — the same logic as the Esker Riada and the Lake Agassiz beach ridges. Passes Jelling, where Harald Bluetooth's stone calls itself Denmark's birth certificate, and Hedeby, the Viking town that was the hinge between the North Sea and the Baltic. Completes the drover network beside the Highland Drove Road and the Spanish and Italian cañadas.

routes.name: Slighe Mhór (the Great Way)
routes.era: attested in the annals from the birth of Conn Cétchathach; the esker is 10,000 years older
routes.note: The greatest of the five, and the only road in this layer that is also a BORDER: the Slighe Mhór divided Ireland into Leth Cuinn, Conn's Half to the north, and Leth Moga, Mug's Half to the south. A line you walk that is also a line you do not cross. It runs the Esker Riada — a gravel ridge dumped by a retreating ice sheet ten thousand years before anyone walked it, and the only dry line across a country of impassable bog. Ireland's central road was laid by a glacier; people merely found it. Junctions with AW-029 at Clonmacnoise, the monastery that sits where the road meets the Shannon, which is why it was built there and why it was sacked so often.

routes.name: Slighe Midluachra (the north road)
routes.era: the road of the Táin; attested in the annals and the epic alike
routes.note: The road north to Ulster, and the road the Táin Bó Cúailnge is fought along — Medb's army goes up it and Cú Chulainn holds it alone at the fords. It threads the Moyry Pass, the Gap of the North, a defile between bog and mountain that is the ONLY way an army can enter Ulster from the south: two thousand years later the English fortified the same gap for the same reason. Ends at Dunseverick on the Antrim coast. Emain Macha, the Ulster royal seat, sits on it.

nodes.n: Moyry Pass (the Gap of the North)

routes.name: Slighe Cualann (the southeast road)
routes.era: pre-Christian; the road that made Dublin
routes.note: The road southeast to Cuala, the Wicklow country — and the reason Dublin is where it is. It crossed the Liffey at Áth Cliath, the ford of hurdles: a causeway of woven branches laid over the tidal river. The city's Irish name is still Baile Átha Cliath, the town of the hurdle ford, so the capital of Ireland is named after a road crossing on this route. The Vikings came later and built beside the ford because the ford was already the reason to be there. A road that named a city.

nodes.n: Áth Cliath (the ford of hurdles, Dublin)

routes.name: Slighe Dála (the southwest road)
routes.era: pre-Christian; the road to Munster through Osraige
routes.note: The road southwest out of the Tara country through Osraige — Ossory, the buffer kingdom that spent a thousand years being fought over precisely because this road ran through it. Crosses the Curragh, the great plain of Kildare, which has been open grazing and horse country continuously for at least two millennia and is one of the oldest unbroken land-uses in Europe. Runs on to the Shannon at Limerick and the Munster kingdoms beyond.

routes.name: Slighe Asail (the west road)
routes.era: pre-Christian; the least attested of the five
routes.note: The faintest of the five, and honestly drawn as such. The annals put it running west from Tara past Loch Uair — Lough Owel in Westmeath — and there the firm evidence stops. The continuation to Cruachain, the Connacht royal seat, is inference from narrative logic rather than record: a road from one royal capital toward another is the obvious guess, but a guess it remains, and the note says so rather than letting the line imply otherwise. Tier C for the whole road and doubly so beyond the lake.

routes.name: Zlatá stezka — Prachatice branch
routes.era: attested from 1010; the oldest of the three branches; salt until 1706
routes.note: The oldest branch of the Golden Path, and it is golden because Bohemia has no salt. Passau had it, Bohemia had none, and the Šumava stood between — so for seven centuries pack-horse trains carried salt northeast over the forest and brought grain, malt and beer back. At its height thousands of Saumpferde a year moved on this line, and the tolls made Prachatice rich enough that its houses are still painted with the fact. Nothing wheeled ever used it: the forest was too dense and the grades too steep, so it stayed a PACK road for its entire working life and the sunken hollow-ways are still legible in the trees. OLD-GROWTH: passes within a few km of Boubínský prales, a reserve since 1858 and among the oldest protected forests anywhere.

routes.name: Zlatá stezka — Vimperk branch
routes.era: opened 14th c.; the Winterberger Steig
routes.note: The middle branch, opened when the Prachatice line could no longer carry the traffic — a road built because another road was full. Runs Passau by Freyung and Philippsreut to the Strážný pass and down to Vimperk. THE OLD-GROWTH BRANCH: Boubín stands between this line and the Prachatice one, and the reserve declared around it in 1858 exists because a forester named Josef John argued that a piece of the forest should be left to be itself. The salt roads went either side of it and it survived in the gap.

routes.name: Zlatá stezka — Kašperské Hory branch
routes.era: opened 14th c.; the Bergreichensteiner Steig
routes.note: The northern and highest branch, over the Bučina saddle at ~1,150 m — the roughest crossing of the three and the last to open. It climbs the Kvilda plateau, which is bog on top of a mountain: the salt trains crossed a raised peat moor at the roof of the forest, and the corduroy of logs they laid to do it is still under the moss. Kašperské Hory was a gold town before it was a salt town, which is the other reason the whole network is called golden.

routes.name: Osudareva Doroga (the Sovereign's Road)
routes.era: built and used ONCE, August 1702
routes.note: The strangest road in this layer. In August 1702 Peter the Great had a road cut ~260 km through virgin Karelian taiga and bog from the White Sea to Lake Onega, and then DRAGGED TWO FRIGATES ALONG IT. Some five thousand peasants built it in weeks; the ships went overland on rollers; from Onega they took the Svir to Ladoga and in October Peter stormed Nöteborg, which had held for ninety years, because a fleet arrived from a direction that had no water. The road was used once and abandoned to the forest the same season. Tier C and deliberately sparse: the two ends are certain, the corridor is traceable in the taiga in places, and the named waypoints between are contested — a road built in weeks, used for one campaign, and left. The forest took most of it back within a generation and is still holding it.

routes.name: Wildnis Road — Ragnit to Kaunas (WB corridor)
routes.era: raiding corridor 1384–1402, documented in the Littauischen Wegeberichte
routes.note: Drawn from the Littauischen Wegeberichte — a hundred route reports the Teutonic Order compiled between 1384 and 1402 to raid into Lithuania through die Wildnis, the Great Wilderness, which contemporaries called the last primeval forest of ancient Europe. THE FOREST WAS MADE BY THE WAR THAT NEEDED TO CROSS IT: the Wildnis had Prussian settlements and hillforts until the raiding depopulated it, people left because raids made life untenable, and the trees closed over the empty ground — after which the Order needed guides to cross the wilderness its own violence had grown. The reports open by vouching for their leitsleute, local Prussian and Lithuanian scouts selling knowledge of their own country; one, Gedutte, is credited with several thousand square miles of it. Tier C, and honestly so: the place-names were written down in Old German, badly distorted from Lithuanian, and MANY CAN NO LONGER BE LOCATED AT ALL. Only the anchors are drawn. The forest ate its own place-names.

routes.name: Wildnis Road — Insterburg to Vilnius (WB corridor)
routes.era: raiding corridor 1384–1402; the deep road
routes.note: The long raid: out of Insterburg, across the Wildnis by the Rominta forest, and on to Merkinė and Vilnius — the route that let armoured cavalry bypass the frontier defences entirely and arrive at the Lithuanian interior with no warning. The Wegeberichte log **alka** — pagan sacred groves — among the waypoints, sacred places demoted to navigation markers by the men who came to destroy them. The reports also note where to water horses and where to loot for fodder, because a Reise had to eat the country it burned. The Rominta forest on this line survived as a royal hunting reserve into the 20th century for the same reason Błowieża did: kings wanted it kept. Tier C — anchors only; the wilderness between is honest emptiness, exactly as the sources leave it.

routes.name: Rathad nam Mèirleach (the Thieves' Road)
routes.era: the cattle-raiding centuries, c.1500–1750
routes.note: The Drove Road's shadow, and it belongs in the same group: AW-036 took cattle to market and this one took them without asking. The caterans of Lochaber raided the fat lowlands of Moray and drove the beasts home the back way through the forest and the passes, where no one could follow fast and the trees hid a herd. It runs through the last Caledonian pinewoods — Rothiemurchus and Abernethy, remnants of the forest that once covered the Highlands, and among the only native pine old-growth left in Britain. FLAGGED: the name attaches to several routes and the alignment is variously reported; this is the Lochaber–Moray corridor at tier C, with the intermediate nodes flagged. Drawn as a corridor, not a survey.

routes.name: Rennsteig
routes.era: first documented 1330 as Rynnestig; the ridge is older
