routes.note: ~170 km along the crest of the Thüringer Wald, and like the Fosse Way and the Slighe Mhór it is a road that is also a LINE: it rides the watershed between the Elbe and the Weser — rain falling a metre apart on it ends up in different seas — and for centuries it was the political border too, between Thuringia and Franconia and then between a scatter of statelets, so the forest beside it is studded with boundary stones cut by rivals who agreed only about where the ridge was. The name most likely comes from Rain, a boundary, not from rennen, to run. Walkers still carry a stone from the Werra at Hörschel the whole way and throw it in the Saale at Blankenstein. OLD-GROWTH: the Vessertal reserve on the line holds unlogged beech and spruce stands.

routes.name: Hämeen Härkätie (the Ox Road of Häme)
routes.era: medieval; Finland's oldest known road
routes.note: Finland's oldest known road, ~160 km from the sea to the lakes — Turku Castle on the coast to Häme Castle in the interior, the two poles of medieval Finland, with nothing but forest between them. The name is the cargo: oxen walked it. It matters because Finland is a country with almost no roads and enormous water — travel here was by lake and river and frozen surface, and a LAND road across the forest was the exception that had to be argued for. Long stretches are still gravel through the trees.

routes.name: Kongevegen over Filefjell (Oslo–Bergen)
routes.era: the medieval main line between Norway's two cities; rebuilt as a king's road 1793–1843
routes.note: The road between Norway's two cities, and the whole problem of Norway is in it: the country runs north–south and the mountains run east–west, so a road from Oslo to Bergen must climb the Filefjell and then RUN OUT at Lærdal, where the Sognefjord begins and the land stops. From there it was a boat. The fjord leg is drawn as declared water per D1 and it is not a shortcut — it is the road. Passes Borgund, whose stave church has stood beside the route since about 1180 and is among the best-preserved wooden buildings in Europe, kept by the same cold that made the road hard.

routes.name: Eriksgatan (the Eriksgata)
routes.era: codified in the provincial laws c.1296 and the land law c.1350; ridden into the 16th c.
routes.note: A CLOSED RING that is a constitutional procedure. A newly elected king of Sweden was not yet king: he had to RIDE THE CIRCUIT, sunwise, presenting himself to each province's ting, and at each one he swore to uphold that province's law and the province swore him its allegiance — and gave him HOSTAGES to guarantee his safe passage to the next. A coronation performed as a journey, in which the crown is not placed on a head but walked into by consent, province by province, and can be refused. Crosses the Tiveden, the forest wall between Götaland and Svealand — a wilderness so notorious that crossing it was the hard part of being crowned. Tier C: the law names the provinces and the assembly places, but the road between them is reconstructed from the ting-sites, not surveyed. Eighth closed ring in the layer.

routes.name: Via Augusta — Coastal Branch (Carthago Nova–Gades)
routes.era: Phoenician coastal line from the 8th c. BC; Roman road under Augustus
routes.note: THE GARUM ROAD. AW-069's main line turns INLAND at Cartagena through Basti and Acci to reach Córdoba; this branch hugs the sea instead, and the two rejoin at Gádes — one road going round a mountain range both ways. It exists because of fermented fish. Rome's most valuable condiment was made here: Malaca, Sexi and Baelo Claudia were factory towns whose salting vats are still in the ground, and the sauce went out along this line to the whole empire. The towns are older than the road and older than Rome — Malaca is a Phoenician foundation, and its name may come from the Punic for SALT, because the fish were being salted here seven centuries before a Roman surveyor arrived. Shares both termini with AW-069, exactly.

routes.name: Via Maritima Cambriae (Isca–Moridunum)
routes.era: late 1st c. AD; the south Wales frontier road
routes.note: The coastal road west out of Isca Augusta — the legionary fortress at Caerleon, one of only THREE permanent legionary bases in all Britain, alongside York and Chester, and the only one whose amphitheatre still stands open to the sky. The road runs the narrow habitable strip between the mountains and the Severn, past the fort under Cardiff Castle, to Moridunum — 'sea fort' in Brythonic — where it JUNCTIONS AW-107 Sarn Helen. That matters: Sarn Helen carried Dolaucothi's gold north through the mountains, and this road is how it reached the sea. A gold road needs a port.

routes.name: Antonine Wall Military Way
routes.era: built c.142 AD; abandoned c.162 AD
routes.note: THE NORTHERNMOST ROAD THE ROMAN EMPIRE EVER BUILT, and it is made of turf. Antoninus Pius pushed 160 km beyond Hadrian's Wall, threw a rampart across Scotland's narrow waist from the Clyde to the Forth with sixteen forts and this road running behind it — and then, about twenty years later, walked away and went back to the stone wall. That contrast is the whole point: Hadrian built in stone because he meant it to last; Antoninus built in TURF, and it did not. The high-water mark of the empire is a bet that did not pay. Tier A — excavated fort by fort and UNESCO-inscribed. Its western end at Old Kilpatrick is ~15 km from Glasgow; its eastern end is on the Forth, and AW-036's Falkirk tryst is on its line — cattle drovers later gathered where the legions had stopped.

routes.name: The Vistula (Kraków–Gdańsk)
routes.era: the grain artery; peak 16th–17th c.
routes.note: Not a road — the artery of Poland, and for two centuries the reason western Europe could eat. Grain from the szlachta estates was floated down to Gdańsk by flisacy on rafts, and Gdańsk shipped it to Amsterdam; Kazimierz Dolny's granaries and Gdańsk's wealth are the same fact seen twice. It JUNCTIONS AW-112 the Via Regia at Kraków and AW-030 the Amber Road at BOTH Toruń and Gdańsk — the river crosses the two great land roads of Poland and shares their nodes. And it carries the Błowieża connection: in 1409 Jagiełło hunted the primeval forest through the winter, salted the meat, and floated it down to Grunwald — a forest with no roads through it provisioned an army by water, which is why the forest is still there.

routes.name: Nemacolin's Path (Cumberland–the Forks of the Ohio)
routes.era: pre-contact Lenape/Shawnee trail; blazed for wagons 1750; Braddock's Road 1755
routes.note: A road with a man's name on it because he was PAID to show it. Nemacolin, a Lenape, was hired by Thomas Cresap in 1750 to mark out the old path from Wills Creek to the Monongahela — an Indigenous trail already there, made legible to wagons. Five years later Braddock widened it to drag artillery at the Forks of the Ohio and was destroyed a few miles short of it; Washington, who had already lost Fort Necessity on the same line the year before, buried him IN the road and marched the survivors over the grave so it could not be found. The National Road later followed it and US-40 follows that. A footpath, a wagon track, a military road, a turnpike, a federal highway — one line, five names, and the first name is a man who knew where it went. CROSS-CONFIRMED v149-B149 against Wallace No. 71 ('Nemacolin's Path, The Braddock Road'), a much more detailed entry describing the same road, termini, and history (Nemacolin hired 1750-52 by Cresap/Gist for the Ohio Company, Braddock's 1755 approach, Washington's earlier Fort Necessity defeat) at far finer resolution than this route's existing anchors. NOT a correction — the existing geometry is not contradicted, only coarser than Wallace's. One waypoint added (Half King's Rock, where Wallace's text says the path genuinely forks: north via Jumonville Glen to Christopher Gist's plantation and onward to either the Forks of the Ohio or Redstone, versus west via Hopwood directly to Uniontown/Brownsville). Wallace also records that at dawn on May 28, 1754, Washington interviewed the Half King (Tanacharison) here before attacking the French party hidden at Jumonville Glen — the opening action of what became the French and Indian War, staged at a fork of this very road.

nodes.n: Half King's Rock (Braddock's route forks here: north via Jumonville to Gist's Plantation and Pittsburgh, or west via Hopwood to Uniontown/Brownsville)

routes.name: Raystown Path (Harris's Ferry–Fort Pitt)
routes.era: pre-contact trader's path; the Forbes Road, 1758
routes.note: The other road to the Forks, and the one that worked. Forbes cut his road along the old Raystown Path in 1758 — slower than Braddock, fort by fort, Loudoun to Bedford to Ligonier — and the French burned Duquesne and left before he arrived: a road so obviously arriving that the war ended without a battle. It JUNCTIONS AW-084 the Great Warriors Path at Harris's Ferry AND Carlisle, which is the point — the Warriors Path ran north–south down the Great Valley and this one crosses it westward, and everything that happened in the Ohio country came through that intersection. CROSS-CONFIRMED v151-B151 against Wallace No. 96, a 500-line entry describing the same road at far greater resolution — same termini (Paxtang/Harrisburg to Fort Pitt), same major waypoints (Carlisle, Shippensburg, Burnt Cabins, Fort Littleton, Bedford/Raystown), and the same acknowledgement that the path's course changed constantly and had multiple contemporary variants (a fork at Shippensburg reuniting near Burnt Cabins; disputed final approaches to the Juniata and up the Allegheny Mountain). Not a correction — existing geometry is not contradicted, only coarser than Wallace's own hedge-filled detail. Wallace himself calls a coherent single picture of this path 'difficult to present.'

nodes.n: Fort Pitt (the Forks of the Ohio)

routes.name: Great Minquas Path
routes.era: pre-contact; the beaver road, contested 1630s–1670s
routes.note: The beaver road. The Susquehannock — whom the Dutch called Minquas — carried pelts east from the Susquehanna to the Delaware, and whoever held the path's eastern end got the trade: the Dutch built for it, the Swedes built for it, they fought each other over it, and the English took it from both. Philadelphia sits where it does partly because this is where the path met the river. Tier C — the two ends are certain and the corridor is documented in the trade records, but the line between is reconstructed. The Susquehannock were destroyed by 1675 and the road they made outlived them by centuries under other names.

routes.name: Toronto Carrying-Place Trail
routes.era: pre-contact; the short road to the upper lakes
routes.note: THE PORTAGE THAT NAMED A CITY, and it named it from a hundred kilometres away. Tkaronto is Mohawk for 'where there are trees standing in the water' — the fish weirs at the Narrows between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching, at the FAR end of this trail. The name slid down the route: first the Narrows, then the trail to the Narrows, then the trail's Lake Ontario mouth, then the fort there, then the town, then the city. Toronto is named after a fishery it cannot see. The route itself is the short cut to the upper Great Lakes — up the Humber, carry to the Holland, down to Simcoe, out by the Severn to Georgian Bay — skipping the whole long way round by Niagara and Erie and Huron. Which is why the French built at both ends of it and why the British bought it in 1787.

routes.name: Niagara Portage (the Carrying Place)
routes.era: pre-contact Seneca carry; French from 1720; the Devil's Hole massacre 1763
routes.note: The one obstacle that closed a continent. Everything moving between the lower and upper Great Lakes — every pelt, every gun, every barrel — came out of the water at Lewiston, went up a 100 m escarpment on human backs, and went in again above the falls. Eleven kilometres of climb decided who held the interior of North America, and the Seneca held it first and portaged for hire. In 1763, during Pontiac's War, they ambushed a British supply train at Devil's Hole on the carry and killed some eighty men in an afternoon, which is what the carry was worth. Tier A: surveyed, excavated, and still legible on the escarpment.

routes.name: Iroquois Trail — the Western Door (Geneseo–Buffalo)
routes.era: pre-contact; the western limb of the Great Iroquois Trail
routes.note: The last limb, and it completes the road: with AW-077 and AW-078 the Great Iroquois Trail now runs unbroken from Albany to Lake Erie, which is what the Haudenosaunee called their own confederacy — the Longhouse, with the Mohawk keeping the Eastern Door and the Seneca the Western. This is the Western Door. It junctions AW-078 at Geneseo and ends where the trail meets the lake at Buffalo Creek, beside AW-141's carry.

routes.name: Fox–Wisconsin Waterway (Green Bay–Prairie du Chien)
routes.era: pre-contact Ho-Chunk and Meskwaki route; Marquette and Jolliet, 1673
routes.note: MADISON'S HONEST ANSWER: not this route, but the great route of that country — and it passes ~50 km north of the city, which was founded in 1836 as a planned capital and sits on no ancient road at all. What this IS: the door between two oceans. A ~2 km carry at Portage separates water that reaches the Atlantic by the Great Lakes and the St Lawrence from water that reaches the Gulf by the Wisconsin and the Mississippi. Marquette and Jolliet crossed it in June 1673 and opened the interior of the continent to France; everything French in the Mississippi valley came through a portage a person can walk in twenty minutes. The Ho-Chunk and Meskwaki had used it for centuries and knew exactly what it was worth, which is why they fought so hard over who could cross. **CORRECTED IN B67.** This note said Madison 'sits on no ancient road at all' because it is an 1836 plan. That is a fact about a townsite deed, not about the ground: Teejop, the isthmus, carries one of the densest concentrations of effigy mounds anywhere, built 700–1200 AD, and the university is standing on some. AW-337 draws it.

routes.name: Kennebec–Chaudière (the Height of Land)
routes.era: Abenaki canoe road; Arnold's march, 1775
routes.note: PORTLAND'S HONEST ANSWER: Maine's great route is a river, and it starts at Augusta, not Portland — Portland is a harbour, and harbours are where roads END. This is the Abenaki road from the Atlantic watershed to the St Lawrence: up the Kennebec, over the Height of Land at the Chain of Ponds, down the Chaudière to Quebec. Arnold took 1,100 men up it in the autumn of 1775 with the wrong boats — green pine bateaux that leaked, built by a contractor in a fortnight — and arrived at Quebec with about 600, having eaten the dogs. The Abenaki had been crossing it for centuries in birchbark, which weighs a fifth as much and does not rot in a season. Tier C: the carries are known and the intervening line is the river. **CORRECTED IN B66.** This note said Portland was honestly off the map because 'Maine's great route is a river, and harbours are where roads END.' The river part is right; the harbour part is a walker's assumption. AW-334 draws the Wabanaki coast, which is a CONTINUOUS ROAD by canoe inside the islands — and on that road a harbour is a node, not a terminus. Portland is on the map now, and it was my measurement that was off, not the town.

routes.name: Rian Bó Phádraig (the Track of Patrick's Cow)
routes.era: an ancient road; the Patrick legend medieval
routes.note: CORK'S HONEST ANSWER: Cork is old — monastery in the 600s, Viking town by 915 — but it is not on a great road, because Cork's connections went BY SEA, which is what a Viking port is for. AW-120 the Slighe Dála stops at Limerick, 86 km off. The nearest ancient road is this one: a linear earthwork running from Cashel over the Knockmealdowns to Ardmore, ~90 km, parts of it still a visible bank in the fields. The name is the story — the track is said to have been worn by Patrick's cow searching for her stolen calf, bellowing all the way, which is a folk etymology laid over a road that was already there and already unexplained. Tier C: the earthwork survives in stretches; the full line is reconstructed between them.

routes.name: Sibirsky Trakt (Moscow–Kyakhta)
routes.era: decreed 1689, built 1730s–1830s; superseded by the Trans-Siberian from 1903
routes.note: The longest road on Earth: ~9,000 km from Moscow to the Chinese border at Kyakhta, and for two centuries the only land link between Europe and China. It was the TEA ROAD — caravans took sixteen months to bring Chinese tea to Moscow, and the tea was said to taste better for it because the dry cold cured it, so 'caravan tea' fetched a premium over the sea-shipped kind for arriving slowly. It was also the road to exile: Dostoevsky walked part of it in irons, and so did a hundred thousand others — the Trakt carried tea one way and prisoners the other, on the same surface, past each other. Named nodes are the post towns; shaping nodes carry the line between them, because at this scale my density is coarser than the road's was — it had stations every 25–40 km.

routes.name: From the Varangians to the Arabs (the Volga Road)
routes.era: ~8th–11th c.; older than the road to the Greeks and richer
routes.note: AW-052'S SIBLING, and for two centuries the more profitable one. The Rus went two ways from the north: down the Dnieper to the Greeks, and down the VOLGA to the Arabs — and this is the road that explains why Swedish fields are full of Arab silver. Hundreds of thousands of Abbasid dirhams have come out of Scandinavian soil; Gotland alone has hundreds of hoards. The silver came UP this river, in exchange for furs, wax, honey and slaves sold at Bulgar, where Ibn Fadlan met the Rus in 922 and wrote down the ship-burial nobody else recorded. Shares Staraya Ladoga and Novgorod with AW-052 — the two roads are one road until the water forks. Carries a real portage: Vyshny Volochyok, the 'high portage', where boats crossed from Baltic drainage to Caspian. Itil, the Khazar capital at the delta, was so completely destroyed that its site is still argued over.

routes.name: Darb al-Arba'in (the Forty Days Road)
routes.era: pharaonic roots; the great slave road 16th–19th c.; camel drives still run it
routes.note: Forty days by camel from Darfur to the Nile, ~1,700 km, and the name is a measurement of endurance. It carried gold, ivory and ostrich feathers north — and it carried PEOPLE: for three centuries this was one of the great slave roads of Africa, and hundreds of thousands were walked up it, of whom a large fraction did not arrive. The route is marked by bones. Between the wells at Bir Natrun, Selima and Kharga there is nothing at all, which is why tier C is not a limitation here but a description: the sparse nodes ARE the road, because water is the only thing that exists on it. Junctions AW-042 the Nile Corridor at Asyut. Camel drives still walk it to Egypt today. **FLAGGED `sensitive` IN B59** — an inconsistency: the note always said this was a slave road; the flag was missing.

routes.name: The Gold Road of Zimbabwe (Great Zimbabwe–Sofala)
routes.era: ~11th–15th c.; the road that made Kilwa rich
routes.note: THE ANSWER TO A QUESTION AW-072 ALREADY ASKED. Kilwa's note says the island city controlled the Sofala gold trade — this is where the gold came FROM. Great Zimbabwe's builders mined the plateau and moved gold down the Save valley to Sofala, the southernmost Swahili port; from there it went up the coast to Kilwa and out into the Indian Ocean world. The traffic ran both ways: Chinese celadon, Persian glass and a Kilwa coin have come out of the ground AT Great Zimbabwe, 400 km inland, which is how we know a stone city on a African plateau was wired into a trade system reaching to Guangzhou. Tier C — the two ends are certain and the corridor is inferred from the finds, which is the honest situation for a road that left artefacts rather than a surface.

routes.name: Yeongnam-daero (Hanyang–Dongnae)
routes.era: Joseon dynasty; one of the Nine Great Roads
routes.note: The great southeastern road of Joseon, ~380 km from the capital to the sea at Dongnae, and the country's main artery in both directions of history. Scholars walked UP it to sit the civil service examination in Hanyang, and by preference over Mungyeong Saejae, because the pass's name puns on 'hearing good news' and a candidate wanted every omen he could get. In 1592 Konishi Yukinaga landed at Busan and marched DOWN the same road in reverse, taking Seoul in twenty days — the road that carried scholars to their futures carried an invasion to the capital at the speed the road allowed. Mungyeong Saejae's three gates were built afterward, which is the usual order of these things.

routes.name: The Amole Road (Danakil–Mekele)
routes.era: centuries; still walked
routes.note: The road that carried MONEY, literally. Salt cut from the Danakil flats was shaped into bars called amole, and amole WAS currency in Ethiopia — a standard bar bought a standard thing, into the twentieth century. The Afar cut it with poles from a salt pan in one of the hottest places measured on Earth, and camel caravans walked it up 2,000 m to the highland markets at Mekele, two days and a world away. So the caravans were not carrying goods to be sold for money; they were carrying the money. Still walked today, and still cut with poles.

routes.name: Kumano Kodō — Nakahechi
routes.era: imperial pilgrimages from the 10th c.; UNESCO 2004
routes.note: The Camino's only equal on paper: Kumano Kodō and the Camino de Santiago are the ONLY TWO pilgrimage routes inscribed on the World Heritage list, and they are formally twinned — walk both and you are a Dual Pilgrim. They walk toward opposite things: Santiago goes to an apostle's bones, Kumano goes to three shrines that are a waterfall, a rock and a river, worshipped before anyone thought to name a god in them. Retired emperors made this pilgrimage over a hundred times between them, and by the medieval period so many commoners were on it that the phrase was ari no Kumano-mōde — THE KUMANO PILGRIMAGE OF THE ANTS, a column of people visible from the ridges. The oji shrines are the road's punctuation, ninety-nine of them. The Hongū–Shingū leg is drawn as RIVER because pilgrims took the boat down the Kumano-gawa; it is not a shortcut, it is the rite.

routes.name: The Shu Roads (Chang'an–Chengdu)
routes.era: Warring States plank roads; the Stone Cattle Road legend c.316 BC
routes.note: 蜀道之难，难于上青天 — 'the road to Shu is harder than the road to heaven', wrote Li Bai, who came from there. These are the zhàndào, the PLANK ROADS: holes chiselled into vertical cliff, beams driven into the holes, planks laid across the beams, and a gallery of timber hanging over a gorge for kilometres at a time. TWO STORIES LIVE ON THIS ROAD. The first is the Stone Cattle Road: Qin told Shu it had cattle that shat gold and would gift them; Shu cut a road through the mountains to receive them; Qin's army marched down the road Shu had built and destroyed Shu in 316 BC — a road built by the victim, for the invader, out of greed. The second is Han Xin's, 206 BC: he BURNED the plank roads behind him to prove he was never coming back, then made a great show of repairing them while his army crossed at Chencang — 明修栈道，暗度陈仓, and it is still one of the Thirty-Six Stratagems. Junctions AW-008 the Silk Road's eastern trunk at Chang'an: the road to Rome and the road to Shu started from the same gate.

nodes.n: Jianmen Pass (one man may hold it)

routes.name: Angkor Royal Road (Angkor–Phimai)
routes.era: Jayavarman VII, r. 1181–1218
routes.note: A king who built a WELFARE STATE along his roads. Jayavarman VII's Preah Khan stele records 121 dharmasala — 'houses with fire' — set along the royal roads about a day's walk apart, and 102 hospitals, each with a stated staff and a stated ration, endowed by the crown. This road to Phimai carries seventeen of them, and it is a raised laterite causeway with arched bridges, one of which — Spean Praptos at Kompong Kdei, fourteen arches — still carries traffic eight hundred years on. Whether it was charity or infrastructure or propaganda is a question the stele does not answer and the road does not care about; the fire-houses are there either way. Tier C — the two ends and the Dangrek crossing are certain, the dharmasala locations are partly surveyed and partly not, and the line between is corridor rather than survey.

nodes.n: Prasat Ta Muen Thom (the Dangrek gate)

routes.name: The Norse Sea Road of Ireland (Dublin–Limerick)
routes.era: Hiberno-Norse, 9th–12th c.
routes.note: CORK'S ANSWER, and it required allowing water. Every one of Ireland's coastal cities is a Viking foundation — Dublin, Wexford, Waterford, Cork, Limerick — because the Irish built monasteries and cattle-kingdoms and had no use for a town on a tidal river, and the Norse had no use for anything else. This sea road is the ring they made: longphorts a day's sail apart around the south coast, trading each other's slaves and silver. And it CLOSES A LOOP the layer already had: AW-119 the Slighe Cualann reaches Áth Cliath and AW-120 the Slighe Dála reaches Limerick, both from Tara — so the five land roads run out from the hill, and this one runs round the outside and joins their ends. Ireland's Gaelic roads and its Norse road are the same circuit, drawn by people who wanted opposite things.

routes.name: Cuyahoga–Tuscarawas Portage (Lake Erie–the Ohio)
routes.era: pre-contact; an international border 1785–1805
routes.note: CLEVELAND'S ANSWER, and the strangest fact in the portage group: THIS FOOTPATH WAS AN INTERNATIONAL BORDER. The Portage Path — thirteen kilometres of carry between the Cuyahoga, which reaches the Atlantic by Lake Erie, and the Tuscarawas, which reaches the Gulf by the Ohio — was written into the Treaty of Fort McIntosh in 1785 and the Treaty of Greenville in 1795 as the boundary of the United States. West of the trail was Indian country; east of it was not. A trail worn by feet became a line on a map became a sovereignty. Cleveland sits at its northern mouth for exactly that reason, and Akron's name is Greek for 'summit' — the top of the carry.

routes.name: The Wampum Road (Canarsee–Fort Orange)
routes.era: pre-contact shell trade; the Dutch circuit 1620s–1660s
routes.note: BROOKLYN'S ANSWER, and it explains a node the layer already had. Wampum was made from quahog and whelk shells, and the best beds were on Long Island Sound — so Brooklyn's Canarsee sat on the raw material of the northeast's CURRENCY. The Dutch worked out the circuit fast: buy wampum on Long Island, carry it up the Hudson, trade it at Fort Orange for beaver, ship the beaver to Amsterdam. Which means AW-077's Fort Orange — the Mohawk Trail's eastern door — is where the shells met the furs, and this road is the other half of that transaction. Money grew on a beach in Brooklyn and was spent 250 km up a river. Tier C: the trade is thoroughly documented, the physical line is the river and is not. Junctions AW-080 at Rondout and AW-077 at Fort Orange.

routes.name: The Jurassic Way (Stamford–Banbury)
routes.era: prehistoric; the limestone ridge road
routes.note: BANBURY'S ANSWER. Britain's prehistoric roads are all the same idea in different rock: the Ridgeway rides chalk, and this one rides the JURASSIC LIMESTONE belt that runs diagonally across England from the Humber to Dorset — a band of well-drained high ground through a country that was otherwise clay, forest and bog. Walk the geology and you stay dry. Ends at Banbury, which is a crossroads on it and has been a market since before the nursery rhyme sent a fine lady there on a white horse. Tier C — the corridor is the outcrop, which is certain; the line along it is reconstructed.

routes.name: The Thames (Cricklade–London)
routes.era: prehistoric navigation; the Oxford crossing from the Saxon period
routes.note: OXFORD'S ANSWER, and it required allowing water. Oxford is a FORD — Oxenaford, where the oxen crossed — and a ford is a place a road meets a river, so the honest route through Oxford is the river itself. The Thames was southern England's main line long before any road was metalled: everything heavy moved on it, and the towns on it are all crossings or wharves. It JUNCTIONS AW-034 the Ridgeway at Goring, which is the good one — the Ridgeway comes off the chalk to cross the Thames at the Goring Gap, so at that node the oldest road in Britain meets the oldest highway in Britain, and neither of them is a road.

routes.name: Via Devana (Camulodunum–Duroliponte–Durovigutum)
routes.era: 1st c. AD
routes.note: CAMBRIDGE'S ANSWER. The Roman road from Colchester northwest through Duroliponte — the fort and bridge at Cambridge, the crossing of the Cam that the town is named for — to Godmanchester, where it JUNCTIONS AW-104 Ermine Street. FLAGGED: 'Via Devana' is not a Roman name at all. It was invented in the 18th century by a Cambridge don, Charles Mason, who assumed the road ran on to Deva (Chester) and named it accordingly; the Romans called it nothing we know. A road named by an academic guess, and the guess stuck. Tier C for the alignment, which is patchy between the certain crossings.

routes.name: The Siskiyou Trail (Sacramento–the Columbia)
routes.era: pre-contact Indigenous route; HBC brigade trail from 1826
routes.note: ROSEVILLE AND DAVIS'S HONEST ANSWER: both are railroad towns, 1864 and 1868, and sit on no ancient road — but the great route of their country runs past Sacramento about 25 km from each. The Siskiyou Trail is the Indigenous road up the Sacramento Valley and over the Siskiyous to the Columbia, used by the Wintu, Shasta, Takelma and others long before the Hudson's Bay Company's Southern Party walked it as a fur brigade trail from 1826, before it was a gold road, a stage road, a highway and finally Interstate 5. The whole west-coast corridor of the United States is an Indigenous footpath with six centuries of pavement on it. Tier C: the corridor is certain, the line is the valley. **CORRECTED IN B67.** This note said Roseville and Davis 'sit on no ancient road' because they are railroad towns. The valley floor was Nisenan and Patwin and among the most densely populated non-agricultural landscapes on Earth. AW-339 draws the trans-Sierra road they used, which the railway was later laid along.

routes.name: The Trans-Borneo Way (Kapuas–Müller–Mahakam)
routes.era: pre-colonial Dayak route; the forest-product trade
routes.note: KALIMANTAN'S ANSWER, and it is the Fox–Wisconsin of the tropics: a carry over the Müller Range joins the Kapuas, Indonesia's longest river, flowing west to the Java Sea, with the Mahakam flowing east to the Makassar Strait — so a single portage crosses the third-largest island on Earth. What moved on it was FOREST: gaharu (agarwood) worth more by weight than silver, damar resin, rattan, edible birds' nests, and the casque of the helmeted hornbill — 'golden jade', which Ming China valued ABOVE elephant ivory and carved into belt ornaments. The Dayak upriver cut it; the Malay and Bugis downriver shipped it; Beijing wore it. Tier C — the rivers are certain and the Müller crossing is attested, but the corridor's fine line is not surveyed.

routes.name: Kōshū Kaidō
routes.era: Edo period; the third of the Gokaidō
routes.note: The Gokaidō's escape route, and it was designed as one. The shogunate built it as the road the Tokugawa would flee ALONG if Edo fell — west through the mountains to Kōfu, a Tokugawa stronghold, and on to the Nakasendō; the 44 stations are close together and the terrain is defensible for exactly that reason. It has fewer daimyo processions and more freight than the Tōkaidō, because it was never meant to impress anyone. Full station roster. JUNCTIONS AW-001 the Nakasendō at Shimosuwa — the road out of Edo meets the road to Kyoto, which was the point: two ways to leave.

routes.name: Ōshū Kaidō
routes.era: Edo period; the fourth of the Gokaidō
routes.note: The road to the north, and it STOPS at Shirakawa — which is the fact. Shirakawa-no-seki was the ancient barrier gate, the line beyond which lay Michinoku, 'the road's end', the deep north that classical Japan regarded as the edge of the civilised world. Poets had been writing about crossing it for eight hundred years before Bashō walked out through it in 1689 and made the Oku no Hosomichi out of what he found. An imperial highway that ends where the poetry says the country does. Drawn from Utsunomiya, where it branches off AW-165's trunk — the two roads share the first seventeen stations out of Edo and are not duplicated here.

routes.name: Nikkō Kaidō
routes.era: Edo period; the fifth of the Gokaidō
routes.note: A road built to visit one dead man. Ieyasu is enshrined at Nikkō as Tōshō-daigongen, and this road exists so his descendants could process there in state — twenty-one stations, and at the end the most extravagantly decorated building in Japan, put up by a dynasty that governed by sumptuary law and forbade everyone else such things. The final approach is lined with over ten thousand cryptomeria planted by a single retainer, Matsudaira Masatsuna, who could not afford a lantern and gave trees instead; they are still standing, and it is the longest avenue of trees on Earth. AW-164 the Ōshū Kaidō branches off this trunk at Utsunomiya.

routes.name: Shio no Michi (the Salt Road)
routes.era: medieval; the Chikuni Kaidō
routes.note: A ROAD THAT BECAME AN IDIOM. Salt from the Japan Sea at Itoigawa to landlocked Shinano, ~120 km over the mountains, by ox and by back. In about 1567 the Hōjō and Imagawa cut off Takeda Shingen's salt to starve him out — and Uesugi Kenshin, who had been at war with Shingen for a decade and would be again, sent his own salt down this road to his enemy, reportedly saying that he fought with swords and not with salt. 敵に塩を送る — teki ni shio wo okuru, 'to send salt to one's enemy' — is still current Japanese for aiding a rival in his hour of need. Whether Kenshin did it is argued; that the language kept the road is not.

routes.name: Saba Kaidō (the Mackerel Road)
routes.era: Nara period onward; the Wakasa Kaidō
routes.note: A ROAD WHOSE LENGTH IS A RECIPE. Kyoto is landlocked and the nearest sea is Wakasa Bay, eighteen ri away. Mackerel landed at Obama were salted, loaded, and RUN to Kyoto through the night — and the walk takes almost exactly as long as the cure: the fish that leaves Obama raw-salted arrives in Kyoto perfectly done. The road's length and the recipe's time are the same number. That is why Kyoto has saba-zushi and why the porters ran instead of walked. The old saying on it is 京は遠ても十八里 — 'Kyoto is far, but only eighteen ri' — which is a boast, a complaint, and a schedule at once.

routes.name: Kōyasan Chōishi Michi
routes.era: Kūkai's road from 816; the stone pillars set 1265–1285
routes.note: The most precisely marked road in this layer: 180 stone pillars — chōishi — one every chō, 109 metres, all the way up. They were set between 1265 and 1285, and MOST OF THE ORIGINAL STONES ARE STILL IN PLACE, so the road is still counting down to Kōya exactly as it did seven hundred years ago. It begins at Jison-in because Kūkai's mother lived there: women were barred from Kōyasan until 1872, so she waited at the bottom and he is said to have walked down nine times a month to see her. A road with its own milestones, starting at the place his mother was not allowed past. UNESCO, with Kumano.

routes.name: Kumano Kodō — Kohechi
routes.era: medieval; the direct road between the two sacred mountains
routes.note: THE ROAD BETWEEN TWO RELIGIONS. The Kohechi runs ~70 km from Kōyasan to Kumano Hongū over three passes above 1,000 m — the hardest of the Kumano routes, and it exists to join Shingon Buddhism's mountain to Kumano's older, stranger syncretism, where the gods were a waterfall and a rock before anyone gave them Buddhist names. Walking it is an argument that the two are the same thing. Barely one pilgrim in fifty takes it, because it is vertical. COMPLETES A CHAIN: AW-168 climbs to Kōya, this crosses to Hongū, and AW-152 goes on to Nachi — three routes, two junctions, one road from the foot of one holy mountain to the falls at the end of the other.

routes.name: Kumano Kodō — Ōhechi
routes.era: medieval; the coastal way
routes.note: The long way round, and it was chosen ON PURPOSE. The Nakahechi crosses the peninsula's neck in a week; the Ōhechi goes all the way round the coast and takes twice as long, and Edo-period pilgrims took it anyway because the point was never arrival. It hugs the rock past Kushimoto at the peninsula's tip — the southernmost point of Honshū — where the sea has stood the Hashigui-iwa in a line pointing offshore like a broken bridge. Junctions AW-152 at BOTH ends: Tanabe and Nachi, the same two nodes the Nakahechi uses, so the two roads are a loop with the whole peninsula inside it.

routes.name: Kumano Kodō — Iseji
routes.era: Edo period revival; the road between the two
routes.note: THE ROAD BETWEEN JAPAN'S TWO HOLIEST PLACES. Ise Jingū is the shrine of Amaterasu, the imperial ancestor, rebuilt from new timber every twenty years for thirteen centuries; Kumano is older, wilder, and worships a waterfall. This road joins them — ~170 km down the ria coast over pass after pass, and the Edo pilgrim's logic was simply to do BOTH while out. Its stone paving is the best preserved in the Kumano network, because the rain here is among the heaviest in Japan and unpaved track would have washed away; the stones are a response to weather, and they outlasted the reason. Junctions AW-152 at Shingū.

routes.name: Ōmine Okugakemichi
routes.era: Shugendō, attributed to En no Gyōja, 7th c.
routes.note: The hardest road in the layer, and it is not a road so much as a RIDGE you are meant to suffer along. ~170 km down the spine of the Kii peninsula from Yoshino to Kumano, over peaks the whole way, walked by yamabushi — mountain ascetics of Shugendō, which is Buddhism and Shinto and mountain-worship fused into one practice whose method is hardship. En no Gyōja is said to have opened it in the 7th century. Sanjōgatake on this line is STILL CLOSED TO WOMEN, one of the last such places in Japan, and the argument about it is live. The gyōja crossed here to be remade; the road's purpose is not to take you somewhere but to take something out of you. Junctions AW-152 and AW-169 at Hongū.

routes.name: Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage (33 temples)
routes.era: traditionally founded 718; revived by retired Emperor Kazan c.988
routes.note: JAPAN'S OLDEST PILGRIMAGE CIRCUIT — older than Shikoku by three centuries, and the model Shikoku copied. Thirty-three because that is how many forms Kannon takes to save beings, per the Lotus Sutra: the number is a doctrine, and the route is the number walked. ~1,000 km wandering Kansai in an order that makes no geographic sense whatever, because the sequence is the point and efficiency is not. TEMPLE 1 IS SEIGANTŌ-JI AT NACHI — the same ground as Kumano Nachi Taisha, so the Saigoku BEGINS where AW-152 ends: a pilgrim arriving at the falls has finished one pilgrimage and is standing at the first stop of another. Temple 30, Hōgon-ji, is on Chikubushima in Lake Biwa and reached by declared ferry per D1.

routes.name: Dewa Sanzan (the Three Mountains)
routes.era: attributed to Prince Hachiko, 6th c.; yamabushi ever since
routes.note: A PILGRIMAGE OF DEATH AND REBIRTH, walked in that order. Haguro is the present, Gassan is the past — the mountain of death — and Yudono is the future: you climb through your own dying and come down reborn. Haguro's approach is 2,446 stone steps under cedars four hundred years old, past a five-storey wooden pagoda a thousand years old that was built without nails. And YUDONO IS THE SECRET: pilgrims are forbidden to describe what is there — 'speak not of what you see, hear not of what is spoken.' Bashō came in 1689, the greatest travel writer in the language, and wrote that he could not write about it. He kept the rule. Whatever is at Yudono is the only thing in this layer that no one will say.

routes.name: Nagasaki Kaidō (the Sugar Road)
routes.era: Edo period; Japan Heritage 'Sugar Road', 2020
routes.note: SUGAR CAME UP IT AND EUROPEANS WENT DOWN IT. For two centuries Nagasaki was the ONLY hole in a closed country — Dejima, an artificial island where the Dutch were penned — and everything foreign entered Japan through it and travelled this road. Sugar was the cargo, and you can still eat the evidence: the towns along the way have distinctive sweets — Saga's maruboro, Ogi's yōkan — because sugar was available HERE when it was not available anywhere else, and the confectionery survived the trade route by three hundred years. The traffic ran the other way too: the Dutch owed the shogun a periodic journey to Edo, so Kaempfer, Thunberg and Siebold all walked this road, and most of what Europe knew about Japan before 1854 was seen from it.

routes.name: The Minisink Trail (Delaware–Navesink)
routes.era: pre-contact Lenape route; the shell road
routes.note: THE OTHER WAMPUM ROAD. AW-157 carries Long Island's shells up the Hudson; this one carries the Jersey shore's shells inland — the Lenape walked ~160 km diagonally across New Jersey from the Navesink beaches to the Minisink country on the Delaware, and the trail is named for both ends: Minisink and Navesink, the people of the stony country and the people of the point. Two peoples named for their landscape, joined by a road named for both. Junctions AW-080 at Minisink Island, where the Jersey shell road meets the Lenape road north to the Hudson. Tier C — the corridor is documented in colonial deeds and place-names; the line is reconstructed.

routes.name: The Burlington Path (Delaware–Raritan)
routes.era: Lenape path; the Lower Road from the 1680s; the King's Highway after
routes.note: New Jersey is an ISTHMUS and this is where you cross it. The Delaware reaches Philadelphia; the Raritan reaches New York Bay; between them is sixty kilometres of land, and everything moving between the two greatest cities of colonial America had to walk that gap. The Lenape knew it first, the Quakers made it the Lower Road in the 1680s, it became the King's Highway, and then US-206 — and the reason New Jersey is the most crossed and least noticed state in America is written into this line. Boats at both ends; feet in the middle. The whole state is a portage.

routes.name: The Great Shamokin Path (Shamokin–Kittanning)
routes.era: pre-contact; the east–west trunk of Pennsylvania
routes.note: Pennsylvania's east–west trunk, ~300 km from the Susquehanna forks to the Allegheny — the road that made Shamokin the capital of Indian Pennsylvania and Kittanning the door to the Ohio country. It junctions AW-084 the Great Warriors Path at BOTH Shamokin and Great Island, which is the whole geography of the colony in one fact: the Warriors Path runs north–south down the valley, this one runs east–west across the ridges, and where they cross is where every treaty was argued and every war began. Shamokin under Shikellamy was a multi-nation town — Iroquois, Delaware, Shawnee, Tutelo — governed as an Iroquois protectorate over the Susquehanna, which is what a crossroads produces when it is left alone long enough.

routes.name: The Kittanning Path (Standing Stone–Kittanning)
routes.era: pre-contact Delaware and Shawnee route over the Allegheny Front
routes.note: The short way over the wall. The Allegheny Front is a 500-metre escarpment running the length of Pennsylvania, and there are very few places to climb it — Kittanning Gap is one, which is why this path exists and why the Pennsylvania Railroad later put Horseshoe Curve within sight of it. Cherry Tree at its western end is the CANOE PLACE: the head of navigation on the West Branch, and later the corner of the Fort Stanwix treaty line of 1768, so a tree became a boundary of the British Empire. In 1756 Armstrong marched up this path and burned Kittanning — Captain Jacobs's town — in the first American offensive of the war. The path was there first and outlasted the town. CHERRY TREE CONSOLIDATED v118: this node sat 1455 m from the coordinate AW-414, AW-429 and AW-479 already shared — above the 600 m near-miss threshold and therefore invisible to the sweep, but plainly one place. IT IS A SINGLE NAMED TREE used as a corner of the 1768 Fort Stanwix purchase line; it cannot be two points. Three routes against one, so the majority coordinate wins. Recorded because consolidating a shared node is a decision, not a tidy-up: it silently moves geometry on a route the batch was not otherwise touching.

nodes.n: Cherry Tree (the Canoe Place) — junction AW-414, AW-429, AW-479

routes.name: The Tulpehocken Path (Shamokin–Philadelphia)
routes.era: pre-contact; Conrad Weiser's road, 1730s–50s
routes.note: ONE MAN'S ROAD. Conrad Weiser lived at Womelsdorf on this path, and walked it for twenty years: Philadelphia to Shamokin, Shamokin to Onondaga, back again — a German farmer raised among the Mohawk who became the interpreter between the Iroquois Confederacy and the Pennsylvania government, and who was trusted by both because he could be trusted by both. Pennsylvania's Indian policy for a generation was one man walking. When he died in 1760 an Iroquois speaker said that they had lost their interpreter and that the road was now dark — which was about a man and about this line at once. Junctions AW-084 at Shamokin and AW-139 the Great Minquas Path at Philadelphia. CROSS-CONFIRMED AND UPGRADED v153-B153 against Wallace No. 113 — a much more detailed entry naming the same road (Shamokin to Weiser's/Womelsdorf, Iroquois embassies from Onondaga to Philadelphia) but tracing dozens of waypoints this route's coarser anchors skipped: Boile Run round Mahanoy Mountain, a Mahanoy Creek ford, Mouse Creek valley to Urban, Hooflander Mountain, Fisher Ridge, a Mahantango Creek crossing at Klingerstown (now added as a node, replacing an unnamed shaping point that stood roughly there without gate warrant), a gap in Mahantango Mountain, Pine Creek valley through Sacramento and Valley View to Hegins, Broad Mountain, Joliett, Lorberry Creek to Swatara Creek, and a gap in Second Mountain crossed by an 18-inch cliffside shelf near Pine Grove (added as a waypoint) before Bethel, Rehrersburg and Host to Womelsdorf. WALLACE ALSO RECORDS AN ALTERNATE, SHORTER BUT WORSE ROUTE: Lewis Evans' 1749 map calls it 'Scarce passable for 3 Steep Mountains,' the same shorter-and-worse pattern already documented at AW-468 (shorter_and_worse_rule). AND HE FLAGS THE PHILADELPHIA CONTINUATION AS A DIFFERENT NAME IN EARLY DAYS: before the Weiser's-to-Reading road existed, travelers continued on what was called the Allegheny Path (AW-396) rather than the Tulpehocken Path proper — this route's own Reading-Pottstown-Norristown-Philadelphia continuation is therefore better understood as that later, distinct naming, not re-labeled here since the geometry itself is not contradicted.

nodes.n: Pine Grove (Second Mountain gap, an 18-inch cliffside shelf)

routes.name: The Forbidden Path (Tioga–the Genesee)
routes.era: pre-contact; closed to outsiders by Iroquois law; forced 1779
routes.note:
A ROAD THAT WAS ILLEGAL TO WALK. The Haudenosaunee forbade outsiders this path — hence the name colonists gave it — because it ran straight into the Seneca heartland, and a nation that controls the only road to its own towns controls who arrives. It worked for a century and a half. In 1779 Sullivan's expedition forced it under orders from Washington to destroy the Seneca and Cayuga towns so completely that the country would be uninhabitable, and burned some forty settlements, their orchards and their standing corn. Washington's name in Iroquois has been Hanadagayas — Town Destroyer — ever since. Junctions AW-079 at Tioga Point and AW-078 at Geneseo: the Forbidden Path is the missing edge that closes the Haudenosaunee network, and it is the one they did not want drawn.

RESTORED v144-B144: this route was mistakenly overwritten at v142-B142 by a researcher who read Wallace No. 24 (also titled 'Forbidden Path,' also starting at Athens) and assumed it was correcting this route's geometry against a newly-available primary source. It was not — this route predates wallace.txt being on disk, belongs to a different group ('Haudenosaunee trails,' not the Wallace-sourced 'pa-indian-paths'), and was never cited to Wallace at all; its reasoning is independent (the symbolic closing of the Haudenosaunee network, Sullivan's 1779 campaign) rather than a specific route tracing. Wallace's own path 24 is now drawn separately as AW-515. add_never_overwrite_rule applies: two differently-sourced roads sharing a folk name are not the same claim, and only one of them should ever have been touched.

routes.name: The Great Carrying Place (Albany–Ticonderoga)
routes.era: pre-contact carry; the Great Warpath, 1690–1783
routes.note: THE MOST STRATEGIC TWENTY KILOMETRES IN NORTH AMERICA. At Fort Edward the Hudson turns west and stops being useful; from that bend a carry of ~20 km reaches Lake George, and Lake George reaches Champlain, and Champlain reaches the Richelieu and the St Lawrence. So a canoe can go from New York harbour to Montreal with one walk in the middle — which means whoever holds this carry can cut the American colonies in half, and everybody knew it. The corridor was called the Great Warpath and it was fought over for a century: William Henry, Ticonderoga, Saratoga. Burgoyne came down it in 1777 to split the rebellion and it ended his army. On the carry that year a woman named Jane McCrea was killed by Burgoyne's own Indian allies; the story travelled faster than he did, and the militia that turned out in fury destroyed him at Saratoga — a murder on a portage decided a war and, arguably, a country. Junctions AW-077 and AW-157 at Fort Orange, AW-083 at Ticonderoga.

routes.name: The Adirondack Canoe Route (Old Forge–Plattsburgh)
routes.era: pre-contact Mohawk and Abenaki canoe route
routes.note: The Adirondacks are ROAD-POOR ON PURPOSE, and that is this batch's honest finding. The Mohawk called them Couchsachraga — the dismal wilderness — and nobody lived there: Haudenosaunee and Abenaki both claimed it as hunting ground and neither could hold it, so a mountain range the size of Vermont sat empty between two peoples who used it and would not settle it. Same shape as Błowieża: a wilderness preserved by being contested. What crossed it was water. This is the canoe road — Fulton Chain to Raquette to Long Lake, then the INDIAN CARRY at Stony Creek Ponds, ~2 km of portage that is the whole point of the route, joining the Raquette watershed to the Saranac, and out to Champlain. Tier C: the carries are attested and named, the rest is lakes.

routes.name: The Sacandaga Path (Mohawk–Raquette)
routes.era: pre-contact Mohawk hunting road into Couchsachraga
routes.note: The Mohawk door into the dismal wilderness. Sacandaga is said to mean 'land of the waving grass' — the drowned vlei country at the river's mouth, now under a reservoir — and the path ran up it from the Mohawk valley into the high country to hunt and not to stay. It junctions AW-077 the Mohawk Trail at Amsterdam and AW-183 at Raquette Lake, which is what makes it useful: it is the LAND door to a water road, and the two together take you from Albany's river to Champlain without ever needing the Great Carrying Place. Tier C — a hunting path, documented as a corridor and not as a line, through country the Iroquois deliberately kept empty.

routes.name: Darb al-Hajj al-Maghribi (Fez–Cairo)
routes.era: from the 9th c.; the Maghreb's road to Mecca
routes.note: THE ROAD THAT MADE THE MAGHREB ONE PLACE. Nearly 4,000 km along the whole North African littoral, and it is the reason a scholar in Fez and a scholar in Cairo read the same books: every year the caravan left the west and every year it came back, and what it carried besides pilgrims was ideas, manuscripts, lawyers, gossip and disease. Ibn Battuta stepped onto it at Tangier in 1325, aged twenty-one, meaning to reach Mecca; he did not see Morocco again for twenty-four years and by then he had been to China. He set out on a pilgrimage and arrived at a life. The Sirtica — the desert coast round the Gulf of Sirte — is the hard part and always was: no water, no towns, and the caravan crossed it in one push. Junctions AW-039/AW-040 at Tripoli and AW-041/AW-042 at Cairo.

routes.name: The Almoravid Road (Marrakesh–Sijilmasa)
routes.era: Almoravid, 11th c.; the road that founded a capital
routes.note: MARRAKESH EXISTS BECAUSE OF THIS ROAD. The Almoravids came out of the Sahara, took Sijilmasa and its gold in 1054, and then founded a new city in 1070 at the far end of the Atlas crossing — Marrakesh is a road's northern terminus that grew into a capital, sited where the mountain pass meets the plain because that is where the gold arrived. The crossing itself is the Tichka, and the road runs down the Dadès and the Ziz oases on the far side, each one a green line in red rock. Junctions AW-003 at Sijilmasa: this is the last hundred kilometres of a road that starts at Timbuktu.

routes.name: Mauretania Tingitana Road (Baelo–Volubilis)
routes.era: 1st–3rd c. AD; abandoned beyond the Loukkos c.285
routes.note: A ROMAN PROVINCE THAT COULD ONLY BE REACHED FROM ANOTHER CONTINENT. Rome never took the Rif, so Mauretania Tingitana had NO LAND ROAD east to the rest of Roman Africa — and the empire simply administered it as part of the Diocese of SPAIN, governed across the water and supplied by boat from Baelo Claudia. It is drawn here the way it was reached: a declared ferry across the Strait, junctioning AW-133 the Via Augusta's coastal branch at Baelo, and then a road that runs south and stops. Tocolosida is the last fort. Around 285 Rome pulled back to the Loukkos and abandoned Volubilis, which then kept going without them for four hundred years, Latin-speaking and Christian and quietly on its own, until Idris arrived in 788 and founded a dynasty out of it.

routes.name: Roman Africa Coastal Road (Rusaddir–Leptis Magna)
routes.era: 1st–5th c. AD; the granary road
routes.note: THE ROAD THAT FED ROME. Africa Proconsularis supplied something like two-thirds of the city's grain, and it came down to these ports and across to Ostia — which means the Roman mob was fed by Tunisia and everyone knew it, and it is why Genseric's Vandals taking Carthage in 439 was not a provincial loss but a stranglehold. Thysdrus's amphitheatre, the third largest in the empire, stands in a town nobody has heard of because olive oil paid for it. AW-187 shows why this road STARTS at Rusaddir rather than Tangier: the Rif was never taken, so Roman North Africa was two pieces, and this is the eastern one. Junctions AW-039/AW-040/AW-185 at Tripoli.

routes.name: The Ghana Road (Sijilmasa–Koumbi Saleh)
routes.era: 8th–12th c.; superseded when Ghana fell and Mali rose
routes.note: THE SAME DESERT, AN OLDER ENDING. AW-003 runs Sijilmasa to Timbuktu; this ran Sijilmasa to KOUMBI SALEH, and it is the earlier road — the original gold road, when the empire at the far end was Ghana and not yet Mali. Al-Bakri wrote it up in 1068 from Cordoba without leaving Spain, describing a king who held court with gold-collared dogs and a capital of two towns, one Muslim and one not, six miles apart. Aoudaghost was the Sanhaja town Ghana took and the Almoravids took back. Then Ghana fell, Mali rose, and the road's southern end MOVED east to Walata and Timbuktu — the caravans kept crossing the same sand and simply arrived somewhere else. Shares Sijilmasa AND Taghaza with AW-003: two roads, one desert, three hundred years apart. Tier C — Koumbi Saleh's identification with Ghana's capital is probable, not proven, and Aoudaghost's is argued.

routes.name: The Straight Road (Zhidao, Xianyang–Jiuyuan)
routes.era: built 212–210 BC by Meng Tian
routes.note: 直道 — THE STRAIGHT ROAD, and it is straight for the same reason the Fosse Way is: it was not built to go somewhere, it was built to ARRIVE. Qin Shi Huang wanted armies at the Xiongnu frontier in days rather than weeks, so Meng Tian drove ~700 km of highway up to 60 m wide across the Ordos in about two and a half years with a labour force in the hundreds of thousands. It rides the Ziwu Ling ridge the whole way — high, dry, and unambushable — which is the same logic as the Ridgeway's chalk and the Esker Riada's gravel, executed by an empire with a quota. THEN IT CARRIED ITS BUILDER HOME DEAD. Qin Shi Huang died on tour in 210 BC; Li Si concealed the death and brought the body down this road in a closed carriage, with a cart of rotting abalone travelling alongside so nobody would notice the smell. The first emperor's road delivered the first emperor's corpse, in secret, under fish. Junctions AW-008 at Xianyang.

routes.name: The Tang–Tibet Road (Tangbo Gudao, Chang'an–Lhasa)
routes.era: opened by Princess Wencheng's journey, 641 AD; over a hundred embassies each way
routes.note: A ROAD NAMED FOR A WOMAN'S HOMESICKNESS. In 641 the Tang sent Princess Wencheng ~3,000 km to marry Songtsen Gampo; the journey took roughly three years. At the pass west of Xining she is said to have looked back, found she could no longer see anything of China, and thrown down her bronze mirror — which broke in two and became two hills. The pass has been called RIYUE SHAN, the Sun and Moon Mountain, ever since, and it is on this map because a homesick teenager dropped a mirror there thirteen centuries ago. What followed was the road itself: over a hundred embassies each way, Buddhism, tea, and eventually the treaty pillar that still stands at the Jokhang with the peace terms cut in both languages. Junctions AW-008 at Chang'an and AW-006 the Tea Horse Road at Lhasa.

nodes.n: Riyue Shan (the Sun and Moon Mountain)

routes.name: The Five-Foot Way (Wuchi Dao, Chengdu–Bhamo)
routes.era: Qin, 3rd c. BC; the southwestern silk road
routes.note: 五尺道 — THE FIVE-FOOT WAY, named for its WIDTH: five Chinese feet, about 1.2 m, because that is all the gorges would allow. An imperial road you could not pass a cart on. And the story on it is the best in Chinese geography: in 128 BC Zhang Qian, marooned in Bactria on the far side of the world, walked through a market and SAW SICHUAN CLOTH AND QIONG BAMBOO on a stall. He asked where they came from. India, he was told; merchants bring them. So he worked out, four thousand kilometres from home, that there was a road from his own country to India that his own government did not know about — one that bypassed the Xiongnu entirely. He reported it; Emperor Wu sent expedition after expedition to find the southern end; the tribes along it would not let a single one through, and the Han never opened it. China discovered its own back door by finding its own goods in a foreign market, and then could not walk through it. Junctions AW-153 at Chengdu and AW-006 at Dali.

routes.name: The Lychee Road (Lizhi Dao, Fuling–Chang'an)
routes.era: Tang, mid-8th c.; built for one woman's fruit
routes.note: 荔枝道 — A ROAD BUILT SO ONE WOMAN COULD EAT FRESH FRUIT. Yang Guifei loved lychees; lychees spoil in about three days; the nearest lychees to Chang'an grew a thousand kilometres away in Sichuan. So the Tang ran a post relay: riders galloping day and night, changing horses at every station, carrying fruit north on a schedule set by rot. Horses were ridden to death. Men were ridden to death. Du Mu wrote the line that outlived the dynasty: 一騎紅塵妃子笑，無人知是荔枝來 — 'a single horseman in the red dust, and the consort smiles; nobody knows it is the lychees arriving.' Within a few years An Lushan rebelled, the court fled Chang'an, the army mutinied on the road and demanded Yang Guifei's death, and the emperor gave her up. The lychee road is remembered as the emblem of what she cost — which is a convenient story about a woman, and worth saying so. Tier C: the corridor is attested and argued, and several variant alignments are proposed. Junctions AW-008 at Chang'an.

routes.name: The Qinghai Road (Qinghai Dao, Xining–Dunhuang)
routes.era: Tuyuhun road, 4th–7th c.; the main line after Tibet took the Hexi in the 760s
routes.note: THE DETOUR THAT BECAME THE ROAD. For centuries this was the Silk Road's poor relation — a southern bypass round the Hexi Corridor through Tuyuhun country and the Qaidam, longer and colder and higher than the proper road. Then in the 760s Tibet took the Hexi Corridor and the proper road CLOSED, and for the better part of a century everything that still moved between China and the west moved through here instead. Tuyuhun made a kingdom out of being the alternative. The Dulan tombs on this line have given up Sogdian and Byzantine silks, which is what a detour looks like in the ground. Tier C — the Qaidam alignments are multiple and seasonal and the sources disagree. Junctions AW-191 at Xining and AW-008/AW-009/AW-010 at Dunhuang.

routes.name: The Fall Line Road (Philadelphia–Petersburg)
routes.era: pre-contact; the King's Highway after 1650; US-1 now
routes.note: WASHINGTON'S ANSWER, and it is a geological one. The Fall Line is where the piedmont's hard rock meets the coastal plain's sediment: every river crossing it breaks into rapids, and rapids are the head of navigation. So a boat coming up from the sea STOPS at the same latitude on every river along the eastern seaboard — and a city grew at every stop. Philadelphia, Wilmington, Baltimore, Georgetown, Fredericksburg, Richmond, Petersburg are not a coincidence and not a plan; they are an outcrop. This path connected the heads of navigation before anyone built a city on any of them, and the cities came later and sat on the path. Junctions AW-139 at Philadelphia and AW-085 the Occaneechi Path at Petersburg.

routes.name: The Potomac Path (Georgetown–Cumberland)
routes.era: pre-contact; Washington's road west, 1753; the C&O Canal after
routes.note: THE ROAD WASHINGTON COULD NOT STOP THINKING ABOUT. He walked it in 1753 as a twenty-one-year-old carrying an ultimatum to the French, and he spent the rest of his life trying to turn it into a canal — the Potomac reaching the Ohio was his fixed idea, the Patowmack Company his project, and the whole geography of the federal capital's site is downstream of the conviction that the Potomac was a highway to the interior. It was not: the C&O Canal ground west for twenty-two years and reached Cumberland in 1850, eight years AFTER the B&O railroad got there, obsolete on arrival and stopping exactly where this footpath had always stopped. Junctions AW-195 at Georgetown and AW-137 Nemacolin's Path at Cumberland — so from the federal city you can now walk the layer to the Forks of the Ohio.

routes.name: The Schoharie Path (the Mohawk–the Esopus)
routes.era: pre-contact Mohawk route; the Palatine road, 1712
routes.note: MIDDLEBURGH'S ANSWER, and it carries a man from one route in this layer to another. The Schoharie is the Mohawk's largest tributary and it flows NORTH out of the Catskills, so this path is the mountains' back door to the Mohawk valley. In 1712 a few hundred Palatine Germans — shipped to New York by Queen Anne to make naval stores, a scheme that failed — walked here in WINTER without permission and settled the Schoharie flats; the patent holders evicted them, and many walked on to Pennsylvania. One of the boys was Conrad Weiser, who lived with the Mohawk here, learned the language, went south with the rest, and became the interpreter on AW-180 the Tulpehocken Path. Two routes in this layer are joined by a childhood. Junctions AW-077 at Schoharie Crossing and AW-081 at Phoenicia.

routes.name: The Susquehanna Turnpike (Catskill–Unadilla)
routes.era: chartered 1800, built 1801–04, over an older Catskill–Susquehanna corridor
routes.note: RENSSELAERVILLE'S ANSWER, and it is honestly a LATE one: this is a turnpike of 1800, not an ancient way, though it follows the older Catskill–Susquehanna corridor over the Helderberg edge. FLAGGED for that reason — same class as the Camino de Madrid's 1990s waymarking, drawn because the road under it is real. What it did was decant New England: for thirty years this was the road settlers took west out of the Hudson to the Susquehanna and beyond, paying tolls the whole way, and the turnpike company went broke when the Erie Canal opened in 1825 and everyone went north instead. Rensselaerville is on it because the road climbs the escarpment there. Junctions AW-081 the Catskill Path at Unadilla.

routes.name: Akeman Street (Verulamium–Corinium)
routes.era: 1st c. AD
routes.note: BICESTER'S ANSWER — the town sits beside Alchester, the Roman town this road was built to reach. Akeman Street runs diagonally across the grain of southern England from Watling Street to the Fosse Way, and it is the connective tissue of Roman Britain: three of the four great roads meet it. It crosses the RIDGEWAY at Tring, which is the good junction — a Roman surveyor's line cutting a prehistoric chalk track at right angles, the newest road in Britain crossing the oldest, and the crossing point is why Tring is there. The name is Saxon again, as Watling Street's is: the people who inherited these roads named them, and the names stuck harder than the empire did. Junctions AW-103 at Verulamium, AW-034 at Tring, AW-105 at Corinium.

routes.name: The Lake Erie Shore Path (Buffalo–Detroit)
routes.era: pre-contact; the south shore road, broken by the Black Swamp until the 1890s
routes.note: CLEVELAND'S AND BUFFALO'S SECOND ROAD, and the string that ties the whole south shore together — it junctions FOUR existing routes: AW-141/AW-142 at Buffalo, AW-156 at Cleveland, AW-066 at Maumee Bay, AW-086 at Detroit. But the interesting thing about it is the hole. West of Sandusky lay the GREAT BLACK SWAMP: four thousand square kilometres of drowned forest, elm and ash standing in a metre of water over clay that would not drain, mosquito-ridden and effectively impassable, left behind when glacial Lake Maumee emptied. The path did not cross it — nothing crossed it — and travellers went round or took a boat, which is why northwest Ohio was the LAST part of the old northwest settled, decades after land further west. It was finally ditched and tiled out of existence between the 1850s and the 1890s and is now some of the flattest farmland on the continent. A swamp that shaped a century of settlement, and there is nothing left of it to see.

routes.name: Kuninkaantie (the King's Road, Turku–Vyborg)
routes.era: medieval; the postal road of the Swedish realm from the 14th c.
routes.note: HELSINKI'S ANSWER — and Helsinki is younger than the road it sits on. Gustav Vasa founded the town in 1550 to compete with Tallinn; the King's Road had been running past the spot for two centuries by then, because the coast dictated the line and the town came later. This is the postal road of the Swedish realm: Bergen to Stockholm, across the Åland by boat, Turku to Vyborg and on to the Neva. It carried the mail, the bishops, the tax collectors and the king, and the medieval churches along it are the milestones — grey stone, one per parish, all facing the road. Junctions AW-130 the Ox Road of Häme at Turku, where Finland's two oldest roads meet at a castle.

routes.name: The Neman Road (the Baltic–the Dnieper)
routes.era: ~9th–13th c.; the western Varangian variant
routes.note: MINSK'S ANSWER, and Minsk is a WATERSHED. The Neman runs to the Baltic; the Svisloch runs through Minsk to the Berezina, the Dnieper and the Black Sea — and the two systems very nearly touch in the country south and west of the city. So this is the third Varangian road: not the Dnieper (AW-052) and not the Volga (AW-147), but the Neman line, the western way from the Baltic to the Black Sea. The name may be from mena, exchange — a trading place where two seas almost meet, though the etymology is argued like everything else here. In 1797 the Russians finally cut the Berezina Canal through the same watershed to do by engineering what portage had done by muscle. Tier C: the Neman route is far less documented than the Dnieper one and the carry's exact line is not fixed. Junctions AW-126 at Ragnit and Kaunas, AW-127 at Vilnius, AW-052 at Rogachev.

routes.name: The Palghat Gap Road (Muziris–Kaveripattinam)
routes.era: Sangam era; the Roman pepper trade, 1st–3rd c. AD
routes.note: THE ONLY DOOR IN A 1,600 KM WALL. The Western Ghats run the length of peninsular India and the Palghat Gap is the one significant break in them — forty kilometres wide, and the sole reason Kerala and the Tamil country are connected by land at all. Everything went through it. Rome's pepper came out this way: the Muziris Papyrus records ONE cargo worth about seven million sesterces, enough to buy 2,400 hectares of Egyptian farmland, and Pliny complained that India drained Rome of fifty million a year and that this was what 'our luxuries and our women cost us.' The proof is in the ground — Roman coin hoards cluster at the Gap's EASTERN end, around Coimbatore and Karur, exactly where you would set them down after carrying them through. The Gap also lets the monsoon through, so Coimbatore gets rain the rest of Tamil Nadu does not: a hole in a mountain range that moves money and weather. Kodumanal on this line is the road made visible: an excavated Sangam-era workshop town where beryl, carnelian and sapphire were cut, with Tamil-Brahmi graffiti on the potsherds — a bead factory in the middle of the Gap, working stones from three directions for customers on two coasts.

routes.name: The Coromandel Road (Kanchipuram–Nagapattinam)
routes.era: Pallava and Chola; the road to the ports for Southeast Asia
routes.note: CHENNAI'S ANSWER — and Chennai is late (1639) while Mylapore beneath it is not: Ptolemy knew the port, and Kanchipuram inland was the Pallava capital and one of India's seven sacred cities. This road links the capital to its ports, and the ports faced EAST. From Nagapattinam in 1025 Rajendra Chola launched a fleet across the Bay of Bengal and raided Srivijaya — an Indian navy attacking Sumatra, which is not the direction anyone expects Indian history to run. Mamallapuram's shore temples were carved by the same people for the same reason: the sea was the front door. Junctions AW-203 at Kaveripattinam.

routes.name: The Macassan Trepang Route (Makassar–Marege')
routes.era: annual voyages from at least c.1720; banned 1906–07
routes.note: THE ROAD THAT BROUGHT AUSTRALIA A WORD BEFORE IT BROUGHT THE PEOPLE. Every year the northwest monsoon carried Makassan praus from Sulawesi to the Arnhem Land coast — Marege', they called it — and every year the southeast trades carried them home. They came for trepang, boiled and dried it on Yolŋu beaches, and sold it into China: so a Chinese appetite for sea cucumber wired northern Australia into Asian trade for two centuries. It was NOT invasion and not settlement; it was a seasonal partnership. Yolŋu men crewed the praus back to Sulawesi and some stayed. Yolŋu languages carry Makassarese loanwords still — rupiah for money, djambatan for jetty, and BALANDA for a white person, from Makassarese for 'Hollander'. Aboriginal Australians had a word for Europeans, learned from Indonesians, BEFORE they met any. Tamarind trees still grow on those beaches from Macassan seeds. South Australia taxed and then banned the trade in 1906–07 and a two-century relationship stopped by legislation.

routes.name: The Pituri and Ochre Road (the Mulligan–Bookartoo)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Birdsville Track later followed it
routes.note: TWO GOODS, ONE ROAD, OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS — the Kula Ring's logic in the driest inhabited country on Earth. PITURI (Duboisia hopwoodii, a nicotine shrub chewed with ash) grew only in the Mulligan River country of southwest Queensland, and travelled south and outward a thousand kilometres and more. RED OCHRE came the other way: Bookartoo, in the Flinders near Parachilna, produced ochre so valued that expeditions of seventy or eighty men walked up from the Diamantina to fetch it and carried thirty-kilogram loads home — hundreds of kilometres, annually, and men died doing it. The two traffics crossed on the same tracks. Tier C by the same standard as AW-090 the Hohokam shell road: the corridor is inferred from WHERE THE GOODS END UP rather than surveyed, which is the honest situation for a trade that left artefacts instead of a roadbed. The Birdsville Track was later laid along it, which is the usual order of these things.

routes.name: The Persian Royal Road (Sardis–Susa)
routes.era: Darius I, c.500 BC; Herodotus described it c.440 BC
routes.note: THE ROAD THE POST OFFICE STOLE ITS MOTTO FROM. Herodotus counted it: 111 stations, ninety days on foot, about 2,700 km — and then described the angareion, the royal courier relay that did the same distance in SEVEN, fresh horse and fresh rider waiting at every stage. 'Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds.' That sentence is about THIS ROAD. An architect cut a loose translation of it into the New York post office in 1912 and it has been the unofficial motto of the United States Postal Service ever since — a Greek historian's line about Persian horsemen, carved on an American building, describing a road built by Darius. Alexander marched down it in the other direction and the stations were still working.

routes.name: Sacbe 1 (Cobá–Yaxuná)
routes.note: A HUNDRED KILOMETRES OF PAVED HIGHWAY BUILT FOR PEOPLE ON FOOT. The Maya had no wheels in use and no draft animals — and they built this: sacbe, 'white road', eight metres wide, raised up to two and a half metres on a limestone causeway, surfaced in white plaster, running DEAD STRAIGHT for about a hundred kilometres from Cobá to Yaxuná with almost no deviation across country that offered no reason to be straight. The white surface is the tell: plastered limestone catches moonlight, so the road could be walked at night. Nobody needed a highway this wide to walk on. It was almost certainly POLITICAL — Cobá throwing a line across the peninsula toward Chichén Itzá's country and daring it to be crossed. Drawn with shaping nodes because the straightness IS the artefact: there is nothing between the ends but road.

routes.name: Darb Zubaydah (Kufa–Mecca)
routes.era: Abbasid; built out by Zubayda bint Ja'far, d. 831
routes.note: BAGHDAD'S ANSWER, AND IT IS NAMED FOR THE WOMAN WHO PAID FOR THE WATER. The Abbasid hajj road ran ~1,400 km from Kufa to Mecca across country that would kill you, and Zubayda bint Ja'far — Harun al-Rashid's wife and cousin — spent her own fortune making it survivable: wells, cisterns, birkas, milestones, and rest houses, station after station. Told what it would cost, she is said to have answered that she would pay if every stroke of the pick cost a dinar. At Mecca she built the Ayn Zubayda, an aqueduct from the Hunayn valley that watered the city for more than a thousand years. The greatest pilgrim road in Islam carries a woman's name because she is the reason anyone survived it — which is a rarer kind of monument than the ones men build to themselves. Junctions AW-041 at Medina and Mecca.

routes.name: The Yam Road (Khanbaliq–Karakorum)
routes.era: örtöö relay from c.1234; Marco Polo described it c.1290
routes.note: THE FASTEST INFORMATION ON EARTH UNTIL THE TELEGRAPH. The yam was a relay: stations every 25–45 km, horses standing ready, and a rider carrying a paiza — a tablet of authority — could commandeer a fresh mount and go on. At its height something like 1,400 stations, and a courier could cover 350 km in a day by never resting the same horse twice. Marco Polo wrote it up in detail because there was nothing like it in Europe and would not be for six hundred years. This is the road between the two capitals: the old one at Karakorum and the new one Kublai built at Khanbaliq. At Karakorum in 1254 William of Rubruck found a silver tree in the khan's courtyard, made by GUILLAUME BOUCHER, a goldsmith from Paris taken prisoner in Hungary — four pipes pouring wine, mare's milk, mead and rice ale, with a silver angel on top blowing a trumpet. A Frenchman's drinking fountain in Mongolia, at the end of a road that carried news faster than anything until wire. Junctions AW-068 the Grand Canal at Beijing.

routes.name: The Kra Isthmus Portage (Takua Pa–Chaiya)
routes.era: from at least the 2nd c. AD; the shortcut round the Strait
routes.note: THE SHORTCUT AW-054 DOES NOT TAKE. The Malay peninsula narrows to about 44 km at the Kra, and crossing it on foot saves roughly 1,500 km of sailing round Singapore — and, more to the point, saves you the Strait of Malacca and everyone waiting in it. So for centuries goods came ashore at Takua Pa on the Andaman side, walked, and went back to sea at Chaiya on the Gulf: an isthmus used as a valve. Takua Pa has given up Tamil inscriptions and Indian beads; Chaiya was a Srivijayan seat. Ptolemy knew the crossing. Thai kings have been proposing a canal here since 1677 and it has still not been dug, which makes this the most persistently contemplated 44 km on Earth. Tier C — the two ports are certain and the overland line between them is inferred.

routes.name: The Casiquiare (the Orinoco–the Amazon)
routes.era: used by the Ye'kuana and others for millennia; Humboldt proved it 1800
routes.note: THE ONLY PLACE ON EARTH WHERE TWO GREAT RIVER SYSTEMS ARE NATURALLY JOINED. The Orinoco simply SPLITS: about a third of its upper flow leaves and runs south down the Casiquiare into the Rio Negro and thence to the Amazon. So a canoe can go from the Caribbean to the Atlantic — four thousand kilometres, two basins — WITHOUT PORTAGING ONCE, which is why this route has no portage node in a layer full of them. European geographers refused to believe it for two centuries because rivers are not supposed to do that; Humboldt paddled it in 1800 and settled the argument. The people who live there had known it forever and had been saying so, and being disbelieved, the entire time. Tier C — the waterway is certain, the nodes are the settlements on it.

routes.name: The Old Connecticut Path (Shawmut–Hartford)
routes.era: pre-contact Nipmuc trail; Hooker's company walked it in 1636
routes.note: THE ROAD THAT FOUNDED HARTFORD, AND THEN EMPTIED THE TOWNS ON IT. In 1636 Thomas Hooker's congregation of about a hundred walked this Nipmuc trail from Newtowne to the Connecticut with a hundred and sixty cattle, two weeks on foot, and founded Hartford at the end of it — a colony established by a congregation that simply left. But the darker fact is who was already on the path: Hassanamesit at Grafton was one of Eliot's PRAYING TOWNS, Christian Nipmuc settlements strung along this trail. In King Philip's War the praying Indians — converts, neutral, on the colony's own side — were rounded up and interned on Deer Island through the winter of 1675–76, and something like half of them died of exposure and starvation. **The road they lived beside was the road they were marched down.**

routes.name: The Bay Path (Newtowne–Agawam)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Bay to the Connecticut, from 1636
routes.note: Boston Bay to the Connecticut River, and it exists because of one man's arithmetic. William Pynchon worked out that the head of navigation on the Connecticut was where the fur would come to meet the sea, founded Agawam there in 1636, and this path is the line between his warehouse and his market. Quaboag and Quinsigamond on it were Nipmuc towns before they were English ones. The path later became the Post Road's UPPER branch — the inland route — while AW-216 took the shore, which is why New England has had two ways from Boston to New York since before it had roads.

routes.name: The Mohawk Trail — Massachusetts (Pocumtuck Path)
routes.era: pre-contact Pocumtuck route; the Mohawk raiding road
