routes.note: NAME COLLISION, FLAGGED: this is NOT AW-077. There are two Mohawk Trails ~200 km apart — AW-077 runs Albany to Onondaga along the Mohawk valley; this one crosses the Berkshires from Deerfield to the Hudson, and it is named for the people who came DOWN it rather than the people who lived on it. It is a Pocumtuck path that the Mohawk used to raid east, which is why the English called it what they did: a road named by its victims for their attackers. It climbs the Hoosac range, the wall that kept Massachusetts out of the Berkshires for a century. Junctions AW-182 at Half Moon where the Hoosic reaches the Hudson. **The frozen-ID discipline is the only reason these two can share a name safely — nothing in this layer joins on names, and this pair is why.**

routes.name: The Pequot Path (Boston–New Amsterdam)
routes.era: pre-contact coastal trail; the Boston Post Road from 1673
routes.note: AMERICA'S FIRST POST ROAD WAS AN INDIAN TRAIL, and it barely pretended otherwise. In January 1673 a single rider left New York for Boston carrying the mail along the Pequot Path; the round trip took about four weeks and the route was chosen because it already existed. Franklin surveyed and milestoned it as Postmaster General in 1753 — riding it himself with an odometer of his own design bolted to a carriage — and some of his stones are still standing in people's front gardens. So the milestones of the United States Post Office were set by a man in a cart on a footpath the Pequot walked. Junctions AW-157 the Wampum Road at Manhattan, where the shells came ashore.

routes.name: Estrada Real — Caminho Velho (Paraty–Ouro Preto)
routes.era: opened 1690s on Guainá paths; the gold road until the Caminho Novo
routes.note: THE ROAD THAT PAID FOR THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION, AND THE PEOPLE WHO CARRIED IT WERE OWNED. Gold was found in Minas Gerais in the 1690s and this is how it left: down from Ouro Preto over the Mantiqueira to the port at Paraty, then by sea to Rio and Lisbon. The crown took a fifth — the quinto — and the road was made ROYAL precisely so that no gold could travel any other way: an Estrada Real is not a road that belongs to the king, it is a road you are forbidden to leave. Then follow the metal. Under the Methuen Treaty of 1703 Portugal sold wine to England and bought English cloth, and the Brazilian gold that paid for the cloth went straight on to London — into the Bank of England and the machines. **Brazil's mountains financed Britain's factories, and Portugal was the pipe.** The stone paving survives in stretches; it was laid by enslaved Africans, who also carried the gold, and Ouro Preto's churches are what the fifth bought.

routes.name: Rota das Monções (Porto Feliz–Cuiabá)
routes.era: annual river convoys c.1720–1830s
routes.note: A ROAD MADE OF RIVERS, RUN ONCE A YEAR, AND NAMED FOR THE RAIN. Gold was found at Cuiabá in 1718, three thousand kilometres into the interior with no way to reach it — so São Paulo went by water: down the Tietê, down the Paraná, up the Pardo, OVER THE CAMAPUÃ CARRY, down the Coxim and the Taquari, up the Paraguay to Cuiabá. Five months. Hundreds of canoes. They left with the summer rains when the rivers were high, which is why they were called monções — monsoons. It killed people at a rate that reads like a shipwreck: rapids, malaria, starvation, and the Payaguá, who destroyed entire convoys in 1725 and again in 1730. The fazenda at Camapuã existed for ONE PURPOSE — to feed the portage and charge for it — a farm whose entire economy was a gap between two rivers. Tier C: the waterway is certain, the exact carry and the seasonal variants are not.

routes.name: The Moscow Road (Vilnius–Minsk–Moscow)
routes.era: the Lithuanian–Muscovite trunk; the invasion road, 1610–1941
routes.note: THE ROAD EVERY INVASION OF RUSSIA FROM THE WEST HAS TAKEN, and the reason is one word: Smolensk. Between the Pripet marshes to the south and the forests and lakes to the north, the dry ground narrows — and this line is the only good way through, which is why Smolensk has been besieged, taken and burned in nearly every European war for four hundred years. Napoleon came up it in 1812 and went back down it in the winter, and the Berezina crossing on this road is a byword in French for a catastrophe you barely survive. The road is not a route so much as a FUNNEL, and every army that walked into it thought it was theirs. Junctions AW-202 at Vilnius and Minsk, AW-052 the Varangian Way at Smolensk, AW-146 the Sibirsky Trakt at Moscow — where the road west becomes the road east and the Trakt runs on for another 9,000 km.

routes.name: The Gotthard Road (Lucerne–Milan)
routes.era: opened c.1220 when the Schöllenen was bridged
routes.note: **SWITZERLAND EXISTS BECAUSE OF A BRIDGE IN A GORGE.** The Gotthard is the shortest line from Germany to Italy and it was UNUSABLE — the Reuss runs through the Schöllenen, a granite slot with no bank to walk on, and for all of antiquity the pass simply did not function. Then around 1220 someone hung a bridge in it. Within seventy years Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden had sworn the pact of 1291, because the men who held the gorge suddenly held the most valuable 20 km in Europe and the Habsburgs wanted it. The legend admits as much: the locals said the Devil built the bridge and took the first soul across, and they sent a goat — a story about a people who got something enormous for a price they were pleased to have paid. Junctions AW-057 the ViaJacobi at Brunnen, where the pilgrim boat and the merchant boat used the same lake.

routes.name: Via Aemilia (Ariminum–Placentia)
routes.era: 187 BC, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus
routes.note: **A ROAD THAT NAMED A REGION.** Emilia-Romagna is called after this road and after the consul who built it in 187 BC — not the other way round: the road came first, the colonies were planted along it, and the land eventually took the road's name because there was nothing else to call it. It runs 260 km dead straight along the foot of the Apennines, and the towns on it are spaced a day's march apart because that is what they were FOR: Bologna, Modena, Reggio, Parma, Piacenza are Roman colonies on a surveyor's line, still in the same order, still the same distance apart, with the modern autostrada and the railway laid on top of it. Junctions AW-026 the Via Francigena at Placentia, where the road to Rome crosses the road that made the Po plain Roman.

routes.name: Via Postumia (Genua–Aquileia)
routes.era: 148 BC, Spurius Postumius Albinus
routes.note: SEA TO SEA ACROSS THE TOP OF ITALY — Genoa on the Tyrrhenian to Aquileia on the Adriatic, built in 148 BC to move legions between two coasts without going round. It is the cross-piece: it meets AW-221 the Via Aemilia at Placentia, AW-113 the Via Imperii at Verona, and AW-030 the Amber Road at Aquileia, which means a lump of Baltic amber could come down the Amber Road, turn west here, and reach the Ligurian Sea on Roman paving. Cremona and Verona sit on it because it put them there. In 69 AD two Roman armies met on this road outside Cremona and fought all night by moonlight; the winners sacked the town for four days. A road built to move soldiers did exactly that for five centuries.

routes.name: The Nane Ghat Road (Pratishthana–Sopara)
routes.era: Satavahana, c.2nd c. BC – 2nd c. AD
routes.note: **A ROCK-CUT TOLLBOOTH, TWO THOUSAND YEARS OLD, STILL IN THE PASS.** Nane Ghat means the coin pass, and the name is literal: a stone jar is carved into the rock at the top, and every load that came up from the coast paid into it. The Satavahanas cut the whole staircase through the Western Ghats to bring Roman gold and Mediterranean wine up from Sopara and Kalyan to Pratishthana, and to send pepper, cotton and beryl down. The Naneghat inscription beside it — Queen Naganika's, 1st c. BC — carries the EARLIEST KNOWN USE OF THE NUMERAL SYSTEM that eventually became the digits this sentence is not written in but your bank statement is. Zero's ancestors, cut into a tollgate. Sopara at the far end has an Ashokan edict and traded with Rome; the Periplus names Kalyan. Junctions AW-017 the Dakshinapatha at Pratishthana. SELF-CAUGHT pre-merge: the first draft put Tagara (Ter) in the sequence, sending the road 150 km southeast before turning west — the same backtrack defect the Via Augusta candidate data was rejected for, and the third time this class has appeared. Ter is a FEEDER to Pratishthana, not a stop on the way to the coast: the Periplus says goods come down FROM Tagara, and they come down to Paithan, and then go west.

routes.name: The Bhor Ghat Road (Pratishthana–Kalyan)
routes.era: Satavahana; the Karla and Bhaja caves are its milestones
routes.note: PUNE'S ANSWER — the second ghat, and its milestones are caves. Karla, Bhaja and Bedse are cut into the rock ALONG this road, and they are there because of it: merchants' guilds paid for them, and the donative inscriptions name the donors — blacksmiths, perfumers, bankers, a Greek called Yavana. Karla's chaitya is the largest rock-cut hall in India and it was crowdfunded by tradesmen on a trade route. So the pass has two things at the top, and they explain each other: a monastery and a toll. Punawadi under modern Pune sat where the roads from the Deccan gathered before the climb. Junctions AW-017 at Pratishthana and AW-223 at Kalyan — two ghats, one coast, and the goods went up whichever was open.

routes.name: Camino Real de Panamá (the Isthmus)
routes.era: 1519–1739; the Portobelo fairs
routes.note: **EIGHTY KILOMETRES OF MUD THAT THE SPANISH EMPIRE STOOD ON.** Every ounce of Potosí silver went by sea to Panamá, then across this isthmus on MULES, then onto the treasure fleet at Nombre de Dios and later Portobelo, and so to Seville. There was no other way — an empire spanning two oceans was joined by a jungle track four days wide in the dry season and impassable in the wet, and everyone knew it. Which is why everyone came for it. Drake took a mule train here in 1573 with the CIMARRONES — escaped enslaved Africans living free in the forest who knew the road better than its owners and had every reason to rob it. Morgan crossed it and burned Panamá in 1671. The Portobelo fairs assembled a whole fleet and a whole continent's silver in one bay for forty days at a time. And the wet-season variant, the Camino de Cruces, went overland only as far as the Chagres and then took the river — which is the line the Panama Railroad followed in 1855 and the Canal followed in 1914. **The isthmus has been the same idea four times.**

routes.name: Camino Real del Perú (Tucumán–Buenos Aires)
routes.era: 16th–18th c.; illegal for most of it; legalised 1776
routes.note: **BUENOS AIRES IS A CITY BUILT ON A ROAD THAT WAS ILLEGAL.** Crown law was explicit: Potosí's silver went to Lima, then Panamá, then Seville, and the Río de la Plata was CLOSED to it. So the silver came down anyway, by mule, for two centuries, into a port forbidden to receive it and growing rich on doing so — the river is called the Río de la Plata, the river of silver, for silver that legally was never there. The mules are the other half: Córdoba, Tucumán and Salta bred them in tens of thousands a year and walked them UP to Potosí to be worked to death in the mines, so the road carried animals north and their cargo south. In 1776 Spain gave up, created the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata and legalised what was already happening; thirty-four years later Buenos Aires declared independence. **DRAWN FROM TUCUMÁN, NOT POTOSÍ, AND THAT IS THE POINT.** The first draft ran from Potosí — and every node of it from Potosí to Tucumán sat within 1.3 km of AW-045's, because THE SPANISH DID NOT BUILD THAT STRETCH. It is the Qhapaq Ñan. The silver road to the Atlantic is an Inca road for its first 800 km and a new road only where the Inca had no reason to go — southeast, to a river the Inca did not care about and the crown forbade. Not duplicated here; same restraint as the Via Imperii south of Verona. Junctions AW-045 at Tucumán, where the Inca road turns southwest for Chile and this one turns southeast for the sea.

nodes.n: San Miguel de Tucumán (the mule fairs) — junction AW-045

routes.name: The Muisca Salt Roads (Zipaquirá–Bacatá–Guatavita)
routes.era: pre-contact Muisca; the salt-for-gold trade
routes.note: **EL DORADO WAS PAID FOR WITH SALT.** The Muisca had almost no gold of their own — what they had was a MOUNTAIN of salt at Zipaquirá and Nemocón, which they boiled from brine into hard loaves and traded down every road off the altiplano for gold, cotton, and emeralds. The gold that made the legend was bought, not mined. And the legend is real at the end of this road: at Guatavita the new zipa was coated in gold dust and poled out onto the lake on a raft to throw offerings into the water — the Spanish heard it, called him El Dorado, the gilded one, and spent three centuries trying to drain the lake. The Muisca raft that proves the ceremony is in the Bogotá gold museum, and it was found in a cave, not the lake. Tier C — the salt sources, the towns and the trade are certain; the lines between them are inferred from where the salt ends up.

routes.name: The Magdalena (Cartagena–Honda–Bogotá)
routes.era: pre-contact river road; the only way to Bogotá until the 20th c.
routes.note: COLOMBIA'S ONLY ROAD, AND IT IS A RIVER. Bogotá sits 600 km inland at 2,600 m, and for four centuries the way to reach it was to sail to Cartagena, go up the Magdalena by poled canoe for six weeks to three months, stop at Honda because the rapids stop everything, and then climb 2,000 m on a mule. That journey is the reason Colombia is Colombia: the country is a set of valleys that could not easily talk to each other, and the river was the one thread. Mompox on it is the ghost — a rich river port that the RIVER LEFT when the channel shifted in the 1700s, and it has been standing still ever since, perfectly preserved by being abandoned by water. Junctions AW-227 at Bogotá.

routes.name: The Rastrilladas (the pampa cattle trails)
routes.era: 17th–19th c.; closed by the Conquest of the Desert, 1878–85
routes.note: A DROVE ROAD MADE BY THEFT, AND THE WORD MEANS THE MARK OF IT. Rastrillada: a track worn into the pampa by hooves, and there were dozens — the Camino de los Chilenos the greatest of them, running from the Buenos Aires frontier southwest to the Salinas Grandes and west through the Andes to Chile. Mapuche and Ranquel raiders took cattle from the estancias in the malón and drove them across a thousand kilometres of grass to sell in Chile, in numbers that reached the hundreds of thousands a year: **an economy, not a nuisance** — a functioning cross-Andean livestock trade whose supply chain happened to begin with a raid. Argentina fought the Conquest of the Desert from 1878 to 1885 explicitly to close these roads, and did, by removing the people who used them. Some are still visible from the air. Belongs in the drover group beside AW-036 and AW-128: the Highland Drove Road took cattle to market, the Thieves' Road took them without asking, and this one did it across a continent.

routes.name: The Amazon (Belém–Manaus)
routes.era: millennia of Indigenous use; Orellana's descent 1541–42
routes.note: THE ONLY HIGHWAY IN A COUNTRY WITH NO ROADS, and it flows the wrong way for everyone who wanted it. The Amazon runs east, so getting IN means going upstream for a thousand miles — which is why Orellana, in 1541, could not turn round: he went down it because he could not go back up, and became the first European across the continent by accident and against his will. What the river did carry was everything: Indigenous trade for millennia along a floodplain that supported far more people than the forest myth allows, then rubber, which made Manaus rich enough to build an opera house 1,500 km up a river and ship the marble from Italy. Junctions AW-212 at Manaus — where the Casiquiare arrives from the Orinoco, and you can go on to the Caribbean without ever carrying your boat.

routes.name: Qhapaq Ñan — the Chilean Reach (Copiapó–the Maule)
routes.era: Inca conquest of central Chile c.1470s–80s; the road stops where the Mapuche did
routes.note: SANTIAGO'S ANSWER IS INDIGENOUS — the Inca road got there first, and the Spanish came down it. Tupac Inca Yupanqui's armies took central Chile in the 1470s and the Qhapaq Ñan came with them, tambo by tambo, to a Inca administrative centre on the Mapocho where Santiago now stands: **Valdivia founded his city in 1541 on an Inca site, at the end of an Inca road, because it was already the place to be.** And then the best fact in this layer's whole southern half. The Inca road stops at the MAULE. It stops there because the Purumáuca and the peoples beyond them stopped it, around 1485, and Tawantinsuyu — which had swallowed everything from Quito to Mendoza — simply did not go further. Sixty years later the Spanish came down the same road with horses and steel and stopped at the Bío-Bío, ninety kilometres on, and the frontier held for THREE HUNDRED AND THIRTY YEARS until 1883. **Two empires, one road, the same wall, the same people.** Junctions AW-071 at Copiapó.

routes.name: The São Francisco Cattle Road (Pirapora–Salvador)
routes.era: the currais from the 1590s; the cattle road of the sertão
routes.note: SALVADOR'S ANSWER IS HONESTLY COLONIAL — and it is a river with a cattle road hanging off it. Bahia's sugar mills needed oxen to turn the presses and meat to feed the enslaved people turning them, and sugar land was too valuable to graze, so the cattle were bred a thousand kilometres inland in the sertão and WALKED to the coast. The São Francisco is the spine of it — Brazilians call it o rio da unidade nacional, the river of national unity, because it is the only thing that ever joined the northeast to the southeast — and it is broken in the middle by the Paulo Afonso falls, eighty metres of them, so the upper and lower river were separate worlds that never met. Feira de Santana at the end became the largest cattle fair in Brazil. The Casa da Torre, one family, ran currais along this river across a landholding the size of Portugal — the largest private estate in the Americas. Tier C: the corridor is certain, the line is the river and the drove. The Indigenous use of the São Francisco is millennia deep and much thinner in the record, which is a fact about the record.

nodes.n: Bom Jesus da Lapa (the pilgrim rock)

routes.name: The Aconcagua Road (Uspallata–Valparaíso)
routes.era: Inca, c.1470s–80s; crossed by the Army of the Andes in 1817
routes.note: VALPARAÍSO'S ANSWER, and it belongs to the Inca rather than to Santiago. The Aconcagua valley was Tawantinsuyu's Chilean breadbasket — Quillota on this line was an Inca administrative centre with gold panned out of the river — and the road came over the Andes and down it to the sea at Quintil, the bay the Spanish renamed Valparaíso in 1536. **AND THEN THE ROAD DID IT AGAIN, BACKWARDS.** In January 1817 San Martín took the Army of the Andes over these passes — Uspallata and Los Patos, the Inca crossings — with five thousand men, twenty-one guns and ten thousand mules, and came down into the Aconcagua to break Spanish Chile at Chacabuco three weeks later. So: **the Inca built it, the Spanish used it to conquer Chile, and an independence army used it to take Chile back.** Three empires, one road, and the road was older than all of them. Junctions AW-045 at Uspallata, where the Qhapaq Ñan's highland trunk ends and the sea is 250 km downhill.

routes.name: The El Mirador Causeways (El Mirador–Tintal)
routes.era: Preclassic Maya, c.300 BC – 150 AD
routes.note: **THE OLDEST ROAD SYSTEM IN THE AMERICAS, AND IT IS EIGHT HUNDRED YEARS OLDER THAN AW-208.** Everyone knows the Classic Maya. This is the lot BEFORE them: El Mirador in the Petén was a city of tens of thousands with the largest pyramid by volume in the Maya world, and it was ALREADY OLD when Tikal began. And it had roads — raised limestone causeways up to forty metres wide and six metres high, plastered white, running dead straight through swamp to Nakbé and Tintal and El Tigre. They were built when Rome was a republic. Almost none of this was known until LiDAR: the 2018 survey flew over the jungle, subtracted the trees, and found sixty thousand structures and a hundred-plus kilometres of causeway that a century of ground archaeology had walked over without seeing. **The forest had been sitting on a road network the whole time and nobody could see the shape of it from underneath.** Tier C — the causeways are certain and mapped from the air, the node-by-node line is not walked.

routes.name: The Nicaragua Transit (San Juan–Rivas)
routes.era: Nicarao and Chorotega use; Spanish from 1539; Vanderbilt's Transit 1851–68
routes.note: **THE CANAL THAT LOST TO A POSTAGE STAMP.** Nicaragua is the other isthmus: up the Río San Juan, across Lake Nicaragua, and then EIGHTEEN KILOMETRES of land to the Pacific — the shortest sea-to-sea gap in the Americas after Panama, and the one everyone wanted for three centuries. Vanderbilt ran forty-five thousand gold-rushers across it in the 1850s. Nelson came up the San Juan in 1780 to take El Castillo and nearly died of dysentery doing it. And in 1902 the United States Senate voted FOR the Nicaragua canal — until a lobbyist for the Panama company mailed every senator a Nicaraguan postage stamp with a smoking volcano on it, Momotombo, freshly erupting on the country's own postage. The vote flipped. The stamp is why the Canal is in Panama. Junctions nothing — it is the road not taken, and the layer should show what the isthmus did NOT become.

nodes.n: San Juan del Sur (the Pacific, 18 km on)

routes.name: The Cacao Road (Tenochtitlan–Soconusco)
routes.era: Teotihuacan-era trade; conquered by Ahuitzotl in 1486
routes.note: **THE AZTECS' ONLY DISTANT CONQUEST WAS FOR CHOCOLATE.** The Triple Alliance took what was next door and left the far provinces alone — with exactly one exception: in 1486 Ahuitzotl marched eight hundred kilometres past everything he was not conquering and took the SOCONUSCO, the Pacific piedmont of Chiapas, and nothing else out there. The reason is cacao. It grows well in very few places and grows superbly there; cacao beans were CURRENCY across Mesoamerica, so the Soconusco was not a farm, it was a mint, and the Aztecs annexed the money supply. The road carried beans north and obsidian and cloth south, and the pochteca who walked it were merchants, spies and a hereditary caste with their own courts. Tier C — the trade and both ends are certain, the line is inferred. Junctions AW-047 at Tenochtitlan, where the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro later began.

routes.name: The Upper Xingu Roads (the Kuikuro network)
routes.era: c.1250–1650 AD; identified 2003
routes.note: **THE HEART OF THE AMAZON HAD PLANNED ROADS AND WE DID NOT KNOW UNTIL 2003.** The Upper Xingu was supposed to be the type case for the empty forest — small mobile bands, no agriculture worth the name, no monuments. It is instead a network: some twenty walled plaza towns joined by STRAIGHT ROADS up to fifty metres wide, curbed, banked, and ORIENTED TO THE CARDINAL POINTS across country that offers no reason to line up with anything. They were laid out. Heckenberger worked it out with the Kuikuro, whose ancestors built them and who had been saying so. What killed it was not the forest but epidemic — the population collapsed after contact, the towns emptied, the trees came back, and Europeans arrived late enough to find a wilderness and conclude there had never been anything else. **The forest is younger than the roads under it.** Tier C: the network is mapped, the specific line between towns is a corridor.

routes.name: The Llanos de Mojos Causeways
routes.note: **THOUSANDS OF KILOMETRES OF RAISED ROAD ACROSS A SWAMP, BUILT BY PEOPLE THE TEXTBOOKS SAID HAD NO STATE.** The Llanos de Mojos floods every year to a depth that makes walking impossible and drains to a hardness that makes farming impossible, so the people who lived there rebuilt the landscape: raised fields, forest islands, canals, fish weirs — zigzag earthworks kilometres long that trapped fish on the FALLING flood, an engine that fed a population off the water going away — and causeways to walk between them, straight, banked, running for kilometres. It is one of the largest earthwork landscapes on the planet and it is a floodplain that was ENGINEERED. And it is the same story as AW-237: contact, collapse, savanna, and Europeans arriving to find emptiness and calling it natural. Tier C — the network is surveyed from the air, individual causeways are certain, and picking one line to call the road is a simplification the note admits to.

routes.name: The Madeira Portage (Guajará-Mirim–Porto Velho)
routes.era: Indigenous carries; the Devil's Railway 1907–12
routes.note: NINETEEN RAPIDS IN FOUR HUNDRED KILOMETRES, AND THEY ARE THE REASON BOLIVIA IS LANDLOCKED TWICE. The Madeira is the Amazon's biggest tributary and Bolivia's only road to the Atlantic — except that it breaks into nineteen cataracts, so everything had to come out of the water and walk. Rubber made it worth solving: they built the Madeira-Mamoré Railway to bypass the rapids, and it is called the Devil's Railway because something like six thousand men died building 366 km of it — malaria, yellow fever, beriberi. It opened in 1912, the year the rubber boom COLLAPSED, Asian plantations having undercut the Amazon while the track was being laid. **A railway that killed six thousand people and was obsolete on the day it opened.** The jungle has it back now. DEGENERATE SEGMENT REMOVED v105-B105. This route carried a 'river' segment containing a SINGLE NODE — Guajará-Mirim on its own — which draws no line and asserts nothing. It was presumably meant to record that the Mamoré is navigable up to that point; that belongs in this note, which is where it now is, and not in a segment with no geometry. FOUND BY A FULL-LAYER AUDIT, NOT BY A GATE: pre_check and guard_ways both pass a one-node segment, because both iterate hops and a segment with no hops has no bad hop. See _meta.degenerate_segment_rule.

routes.name: The Motagua Jade Road (Kaminaljuyú–the Caribbean)
routes.era: Olmec from c.1200 BC to the Aztecs in 1520; one valley, three thousand years
routes.note: **EVERY PIECE OF JADE IN MESOAMERICA CAME OUT OF THIS ONE VALLEY.** Not most — all of it. The Motagua fault is the only jadeite source in the whole culture area, so the Olmec masks of 1200 BC, the Maya death masks, the Aztec offerings buried in the Templo Mayor in 1500 AD are all the SAME ROCK from the SAME river, moved along this road for three thousand years by people who never met each other. Jade mattered more than gold and for a better reason: it is the colour of maize and of water, and it was breath — they put a bead in the mouth of the dead. A civilisation's most sacred substance had one address, and this is the road to it. Tier C — the source and the termini are certain, the line is the valley.

routes.name: The Copán Road (Quiriguá–Copán)
routes.era: Classic Maya; the road broke in 738 AD
routes.note: **FORTY-SEVEN KILOMETRES, AND A KING BEHEADED HIS OWN OVERLORD OVER IT.** Copán was the great power; Quiriguá was its client, planted on the Motagua to hold the jade road for it. Then in 738 AD K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat of Quiriguá captured Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil of Copán — the man who had put him on his throne — and cut his head off. A vassal executing his overlord was not a thing that happened in the Maya world, and Quiriguá then spent the proceeds raising the TALLEST STELAE anyone ever carved, saying so at length in stone. Copán never recovered. Read AW-240 and this together and the motive is not mysterious: Copán was inland, Quiriguá was ON the river, and the river was the jade and the road to the sea. **The client sat on the artery and eventually noticed.** Junctions AW-240 at Quiriguá.

routes.name: The Obsidian Road (El Chayal–El Mirador)
routes.era: Preclassic onward; Cancúén's workshops 8th c. AD
routes.note: OBSIDIAN WAS THE MAYA'S STEEL, AND KAMINALJUYÚ SAT ON THE MINE. El Chayal is a volcanic glass source good enough that blades struck from it are sharper than a modern scalpel, and it supplied a civilisation that never smelted a metal tool — so the highlands had the one thing the lowlands could not grow, and this is the road down. It runs from the source through Kaminaljuyú to Cancúén at the head of the Pasión, which is the hinge: **the last place a canoe can reach from the lowlands and the first place a highlander can walk to**, so everything transshipped there and Cancúén grew a palace and jade workshops out of being a place where the country changes. Then down the Pasión by water and overland to Tikal and El Mirador. Junctions AW-234 at El Mirador — the causeways of the oldest road system in the Americas are at the far end of the obsidian supply that built it.

routes.name: The Pacific Coast Road (Xoconochco–Kaminaljuyú)
routes.era: Preclassic; Izapa c.300 BC – 100 AD
routes.note: THE ROAD THROUGH THE MISSING LINK. Izapa on this line is where the Olmec become the Maya — or where we can watch something happen that nobody has a better word for: its carved stelae are late-Olmec in style and early-Maya in content, and the Popol Vuh's Hero Twins are on them, centuries before any Maya city carved anything. It sits on the cacao coast because that is where the traffic was: this is the piedmont road, the warm wet strip between the volcanoes and the Pacific where cacao grows and everybody's goods moved. Junctions AW-236 the Cacao Road at Xoconochco — so the Aztecs' chocolate province, the Maya highlands, and the place where Mesoamerican writing seems to turn over are all on one line. Tier C: the corridor is certain and the alignment is the piedmont.

routes.name: The Highland Capitals Road (Zaculeu–Kaminaljuyú)
routes.era: Postclassic; all four capitals fell 1524–25
routes.note: FOUR CAPITALS, ONE ROAD, AND ALVARADO WALKED IT IN A YEAR. The Postclassic highlands were not one Maya kingdom but several at each other's throats — Mam at Zaculeu, K'iche' at Q'umarkaj, Kaqchikel at Iximché, Poqomam at Mixco Viejo — each on a ridge or in a ravine, each fortified against the next. Which is how they were taken. In 1524 Pedro de Alvarado arrived with a few hundred Spaniards and several thousand Tlaxcalan and Mexica allies, made a treaty with the KAQCHIKEL against the K'iche', burned Q'umarkaj with Kaqchikel help — and then turned on the Kaqchikel and burned Iximché too, having first made it his own capital. **The road that let them fight each other let him beat them one at a time.** Tier C — the capitals are certain, the alignment is the highland valleys.

routes.name: The Norse Atlantic (Nidaros–Vinland)
routes.era: Iceland 870s, Greenland 985, Vinland c.1000; the last Markland voyage recorded 1347
routes.note: **THE VINLAND VOYAGES WERE NOT A FAILED COLONY. THEY WERE A LUMBER RUN, AND IT LASTED THREE HUNDRED YEARS.** Greenland has no trees, and a Norse farm needs timber for everything — so the Greenlanders went to Markland to cut it, and kept going: the last recorded voyage is in the Icelandic annals for **1347**, three and a half centuries after Leif, a ship blown off course and noticed only because it ended up somewhere it should not have. This is the third Viking road — AW-052 went east to the Greeks, AW-147 east to the Arabs, and this one went WEST, and it is two-way, which is why it is drawn: they came back, annually, for five hundred years. And we know the year they arrived. A solar storm in 993 AD left a radiocarbon spike in every tree alive on Earth; the wood the Norse cut at L'Anse aux Meadows carries it, and counting the rings outward gives **1021 AD** — not a period, not a century, **a year**. Junctions AW-027 St Olav's Way at Nidaros and AW-131 the Kongevegen at Bergen.

routes.name: Via Militaris (Singidunum–Constantinople)
routes.era: 1st c. AD; every crusade took it; the Ottomans came up it
routes.note: THE ONE GOOD LINE FROM EUROPE TO THE BOSPHORUS, AND EVERYONE USED IT IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Between the Danube and Constantinople the Balkans are mountains with one diagonal through them, and this is it — which is why the First Crusade marched down it in 1096, and the Second, and Barbarossa's Third, and why the Ottomans came UP it to Kosovo and Nicopolis and eventually Vienna. Naissus on it is where Constantine was born, which is not a coincidence: his father was posted on the road. The Yugoslav government paved it as the Highway of Brotherhood and Unity and it is now the E80, still the only sensible way through, still carrying everybody. Junctions AW-031 the Via Egnatia at Constantinople — where the road from the Adriatic and the road from the Danube arrive at the same wall.

routes.name: Kealaikahiki (Raiatea–Tahiti–Hawaiʻi)
routes.era: voyaging c.1000–1300 AD; the traffic stopped and nobody knows why
routes.note: **THE ROAD IS NAMED AT BOTH ENDS, WHICH IS THE EVIDENCE.** Kealaikahiki means THE WAY TO TAHITI — it is a channel between Lānaʻi and Kahoʻolawe and a point on Kahoʻolawe where the navigators set out, and Hawaiians called it that before any European arrived to be told. Four thousand kilometres of open Pacific with no land in the middle, and it was a ROUTE, not a crossing: the traditions have Moʻikeha sail down and stay, and his son Kila sail BACK to fetch Laʻamaikahiki — round trips, on purpose, by people who could find a specific island in an ocean using stars, swell and birds. Raiatea at the far end is Havaiʻi, the ancestral name; Hawaiʻi is named after it, so the two ends of the road are the same word. Hawaiʻi excluded Lapita from this layer as a DISPERSAL; this is not that — it is two-way, and drawn for that reason. In 1976 Hōkūleʻa sailed it with Mau Piailug navigating and no instruments, to settle an argument that should not have needed settling. **The voyages stopped around 1300 and nobody knows why.** Tier C: the ends are certain, the line is open water.

routes.name: Đường Cái Quan (the Mandarin Road)
routes.era: Lý dynasty onward; the spine of the Nam tiến
routes.note: A COUNTRY SHAPED LIKE ITS OWN ROAD. Vietnam is 1,650 km long and in places fifty wide, pinned between mountains and sea, and the Mandarin Road runs the whole length of it — which means the road is not infrastructure, it is the country's spine, and everything Vietnamese happened along it. The Nam tiến, the southward march, is this road: over seven centuries the Việt pushed down it, absorbing Champa and then the Mekong delta, and the road grew as the country did. The Hải Vân — the sea-cloud pass — is the hinge: north of it the winters are cold and the culture is one thing, south of it is tropical and it is another, and a single climbing road is the whole of what joins them. Hội An on it was the port where Japanese and Chinese merchants each had their own quarter and their own bridge. The French paved it as Route Coloniale 1; it is now Highway 1A; the line has not moved.

routes.name: The Congo Portage (Matadi–Malebo Pool–Kisangani)
routes.era: Kongo kingdom caravans; Stanley walked it 1877; the railway 1898
routes.note: **THE SECOND GREATEST RIVER ON EARTH DOES NOT REACH THE SEA IN ANY USEFUL SENSE, AND THAT IS WHY THE INTERIOR STAYED UNMAPPED.** Above Malebo Pool the Congo is navigable for 1,700 km — an inland sea of a river reaching halfway across Africa. Below it, in 350 km, it falls through THIRTY-TWO CATARACTS to the Atlantic. So Europeans sat on the coast for four hundred years buying what came down to them and could not get in, and the Kongo kingdom's caravans carried everything up and down that gap on their heads, which is a job description and a monopoly. Stanley walked it in 1877 and understood immediately what it was worth; Leopold built the Matadi–Léopoldville railway to break it between 1890 and 1898, and the men who built it died in numbers nobody counted properly, which was the pattern for everything that followed there. **A river that flows the wrong last 350 km.**

routes.name: The Manila Galleon (Manila–Acapulco)
routes.era: 1565–1815 — two hundred and fifty years, the longest-running shipping line in history
routes.note: **THE FIRST ROUTE IN THIS LAYER TO CROSS THE ANTIMERIDIAN, AND IT CLOSED THE FIRST GLOBAL TRADE LOOP.** For 250 years one or two ships a year sailed Manila to Acapulco carrying Chinese silk and porcelain, and came back carrying American SILVER — which means Potosí's silver (AW-226) crossed the Atlantic AND the Pacific, and China's demand for it set the price of a mountain in Bolivia. That is a world economy, running in 1600. The eastbound leg is the hard one and it is why the route took forty years to exist: you cannot sail back the way you came against the trades, so Urdaneta in 1565 went NORTH to forty degrees to find the westerlies and rode them across — six to eight months, no land, scurvy, and often half the crew dead by Cape Mendocino. They called it the tornaviaje, the return, and it was the single most valuable piece of navigational knowledge on Earth. **SPLIT AT ±180 per _meta.antimeridian_rule** — the Cartographer asked for that rule at v3-B2, forty-seven batches ago, when nothing in the layer came within seven degrees of the line. It has been dormant ever since. This is the route it was for, and it caught it on the first try.

routes.name: The Siberian River Road (Tobolsk–Okhotsk)
routes.era: Yermak crossed the Urals 1582; the Pacific reached 1639 — fifty-seven years
routes.note: **RUSSIA CROSSED A CONTINENT IN FIFTY-SEVEN YEARS BECAUSE SIBERIA'S RIVERS ARE ALMOST JOINED UP.** The Ob, the Yenisei and the Lena all run NORTH to a frozen sea and are useless for going anywhere — except that their headwaters nearly touch, so you go UP one, carry a few kilometres, and come DOWN the next, and the carries are the entire trick. Yermak crossed the Urals in 1582; Russians were on the Pacific at Okhotsk in 1639. Six thousand kilometres. Fifty-seven years. The reason was sable — Siberia was a fur rush, and the fur ran out ahead of them, which is what kept them moving east. And then Dezhnyov: in 1648 he sailed round the Chukchi peninsula and through the Bering Strait, **eighty years before Bering**, proving Asia and America were not joined — and the report sat unread in a Yakutsk archive for ninety years, so it had to be discovered twice. Tier C — the rivers and the portages are certain, the exact carries are seasonal and argued. Junctions AW-146 the Sibirsky Trakt at Tobolsk: the river road came first, the post road followed it a century later.

routes.name: The Katanga Copper Road (Katanga–Great Zimbabwe)
routes.era: croisettes cast from c.800 AD; Ingombe Ilede's floruit 14th–15th c.
routes.note: MONEY SHAPED LIKE AN X. Katanga is one of the richest copper deposits on the planet, and from about 800 AD the people there cast it into CROISETTES — X-shaped ingots in standardised sizes — which is not decoration, it is COINAGE: a currency with denominations, minted at a mine, circulating across central Africa for seven hundred years before any European saw one. The road took them south to the Zambezi and on. Ingombe Ilede on this line is where the whole world met: excavators found croisettes from Katanga, gold from the Zimbabwe plateau, glass beads from India and porcelain from China in the same graves — **one riverside town holding four continents' worth of goods**, and it is the strongest single argument against the idea that pre-colonial Africa's interior was isolated from anything. Junctions AW-149 the Gold Road at Great Zimbabwe: copper down, gold across, and both of them out through Sofala to the Indian Ocean. Tier C — the sources and the sites are certain, the corridor is inferred from where the metal ends up, per the AW-090 standard.

routes.name: The Mississippi (Itasca–New Orleans)
routes.era: millennia; Cahokia's floruit 1050–1350
routes.note: **THE SPINE EVERYTHING ELSE IN THIS LAYER WAS ALREADY TOUCHING.** It junctions FIVE existing routes without a single new idea — the Woods Trail at Little Falls, three Red River Trails at St. Anthony Falls and St. Paul, the Fox–Wisconsin at Prairie du Chien, and the Natchez Trace at Natchez, which is the whole point of the Trace: boatmen floated DOWN this river and walked HOME on that road, because a flatboat only goes one way. And CAHOKIA is on it. Twenty thousand people around 1100 AD, a plaza larger than any in Europe, and Monks Mound holding more earth than the Great Pyramid — the largest city north of Mexico until Philadelphia passed it in about 1800, sitting where the Missouri, the Illinois and the Mississippi all arrive within a few kilometres of each other. It was not built there by accident; it was built at the junction of the continent's plumbing, and it emptied by 1350 for reasons still argued.

routes.name: The Missouri (St. Louis–Three Forks)
routes.era: millennia; the Mandan villages the northern plains' market; Lewis and Clark 1804–06
routes.note: OMAHA'S ANSWER, AND THE RIVER GOES THE WRONG WAY ON PURPOSE. The Missouri is longer than the Mississippi it flows into and it runs three thousand kilometres the wrong direction for anyone in a hurry — you go UP it, against the current, for a year. Lewis and Clark took fourteen months to reach the Pacific and five to come back, which is the arithmetic of the whole continent in one pair of numbers. The MANDAN villages at the Bismarck bend are the fact worth having: not a stop but a market, the great trade town of the northern plains where Cree, Assiniboine, Cheyenne, Crow and Shoshone brought horses and corn and guns and met, and Lewis and Clark wintered there because it was the obvious place to winter — an existing city with a working economy that the expedition is usually described as discovering. Junctions AW-253 at St. Louis.

routes.name: The Savanna Portage (Lake Superior–the Mississippi)
routes.era: pre-contact; the fur road, 17th–19th c.
routes.note: DULUTH'S ANSWER, AND IT IS SIX MILES OF THE WORST MUD IN THE FUR TRADE. The St. Louis River reaches Lake Superior at Duluth and the Mississippi rises a few miles away over a low swampy divide — so this carry joins the ATLANTIC drainage to the GULF, and it took five days to cross six miles because the ground would not hold a man, let alone a man with ninety pounds of pelts on a tumpline. Voyageurs hated it above all others and used it anyway, because the alternative was the whole of the Great Lakes and the Ohio. Duluth sits at the top of the biggest lake on Earth and is therefore the deepest inland port on the continent — two thousand miles from the sea and still a seaport. Junctions AW-253 at Sandy Lake.

nodes.n: Duluth (the St. Louis River, Lake Superior)
The Savanna Portage (six miles, five days)
The Savanna Portage (six miles, five days)

routes.name: The Carlton Trail (Fort Garry–Fort Edmonton)
routes.era: HBC cart road, c.1820s–1885; killed by the railway
routes.note: **THE FOURTH RED RIVER TRAIL, AND IT RUNS THE OTHER WAY.** AW-063/064/065 take the carts SOUTH from Fort Garry to St. Paul; this one takes them fourteen hundred kilometres WEST to Fort Edmonton, and it is the same carts, the same Métis drivers, the same screaming ungreased axles — one hub, four roads, and the layer now shows the whole wheel. It crossed the South Saskatchewan at Clarke's Crossing and Batoche, which is where it ends: the 1885 North-West Resistance was fought along this trail, at Batoche and Fish Creek, and the railway that beat Riel also finished the trail — troops came west by rail in nine days, and the carts stopped that year. **The road and the people who drove it were defeated by the same thing at the same time.** SASKATOON is honestly 25 km off: it is an 1883 temperance colony, younger than the trail and beside it, not on it. Junctions AW-063 and AW-065 at Fort Garry. **CORRECTED IN B67.** This note said Saskatoon is 'an 1883 temperance colony, younger than the trail and beside it, not on it.' Six kilometres north is Wanuskewin: SIX THOUSAND YEARS of continuous use, a medicine wheel, nineteen sites. I quoted a founding date as if it settled the matter. AW-338 draws it.

routes.name: The Ottawa River Route (Montreal–Georgian Bay)
routes.era: pre-contact Algonquin route; Champlain 1615; the voyageur highway to 1821
routes.note: OTTAWA'S ANSWER — AND CANADA WENT WEST THIS WAY BECAUSE THE GREAT LAKES WERE SHUT. Look at a map and the sensible route from Montreal to the interior is up the St. Lawrence and along Lakes Ontario and Erie. Nobody used it: the Haudenosaunee held that country and Niagara is a wall. So the whole French and then British fur trade went up the OTTAWA instead — thirty-six portages between Montreal and Lake Huron, the canots du maître paddling fourteen hours a day, over the La Vase carry at the height of land and down the French River. **A nation's economy ran for two centuries on a detour.** Ottawa is on it because of the Chaudière Falls, which is a portage; the capital sits where the canoes had to get out and walk.

nodes.n: La Vase Portage (the height of land)

routes.name: The Texas Road (the Osage Trace)
routes.era: Osage trail; the removal road 1830s; the cattle road after
routes.note: TULSA'S HONEST ANSWER: the great road runs fifty kilometres east of it, through the Three Forks, and Tulsa itself is a REMOVAL TOWN — Lochapoka Creek walked here from Alabama in 1836 carrying ashes from their old council fire, lit them again under an oak by the Arkansas, and called the place Tulsey, after the town they had been made to leave. This road is how they came. It was an Osage trail first; then the Trail of Tears used it and its branches to move the Five Tribes west; then Texas cattle came UP it to the Missouri railheads; then it was US-69. **An Indigenous trail used to deport Indigenous people and then to move cows.** The Three Forks at its middle — Verdigris, Neosho and Arkansas meeting — was the Osage trade centre long before any of that. Tier C: the corridor is certain, the line is reconstructed.

routes.name: Via Turonensis (Paris–Ostabat)
routes.era: the Codex Calixtinus names all four, c.1140
routes.note: **PARIS'S ANSWER — AND PARIS WAS A HOLE IN THIS LAYER UNTIL NOW, WHICH IS ITSELF THE FINDING.** AW-026 the Via Francigena is the road to Rome and it does NOT go through Paris: it follows Sigeric's line through Reims and Laon, because in 990 an archbishop walking home took the road that existed and Paris was not on it. So the greatest city in medieval France sat off the layer's map entirely — until you draw the road to SANTIAGO instead. The Codex Calixtinus of c.1140 names four French ways and this is the first: from the tower of Saint-Jacques in Paris, down through Tours — Turonensis, hence the name — to Bordeaux and Ostabat. Three of the four meet there and cross at Roncesvalles. Junctions AW-002 the Camino Francés at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port.

routes.name: Via Lemovicensis (Vézelay–Ostabat)
routes.era: Codex Calixtinus, c.1140
routes.note: The road that starts where a crusade was preached. Vézelay's abbey claimed Mary Magdalene's bones and became one of the great pilgrim draws of Europe on the strength of it — Bernard of Clairvaux preached the Second Crusade from the hillside in 1146 and Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus mustered there for the Third — so this road's northern end is a place people came TO before it was a place people left FROM. Then south through Limoges (Lemovicensis) and Périgueux to Ostabat, where it meets AW-259 and AW-261 and the three become one. Junctions AW-002 at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. SELF-CAUGHT pre-merge: the first draft ran Vézelay→Bourges→Névers, which is west and then east again — the backtrack defect, fourth appearance of the class the Via Augusta candidate data was rejected for. The gate catches it every time, which is the argument for gating.

routes.name: Via Podiensis (Le Puy–Ostabat)
routes.era: the first documented pilgrimage: Bishop Gotescalc, 950 AD
routes.note: **THE OLDEST OF THE FOUR, AND WE KNOW WHO WALKED IT FIRST.** In 950 Gotescalc, bishop of Le Puy, went to Santiago and back with a large retinue — the first pilgrimage to Compostela anyone recorded, forty years before Sigeric's walk to Rome gave AW-026 its nodes. So the two great pilgrim roads of Europe are both documented by a tenth-century bishop's staff writing down where he slept. Le Puy's cathedral sits on a volcanic plug with a chapel on a needle of rock beside it; Conques on this road holds the reliquary of Sainte-Foy, a gold-covered statue with a Roman emperor's head reused for her face, **stolen to order** by a monk who spent ten years infiltrating the abbey that had her. Junctions AW-002 at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port.

routes.name: Via Tolosana (Arles–Puente la Reina)
routes.era: Codex Calixtinus, c.1140; the road that takes the other pass
routes.note: **TOULOUSE'S ANSWER, AND IT IS THE ODD ONE OUT ON PURPOSE.** Three of the Codex's four roads meet at Ostabat and cross at Roncesvalles. This one does not: it runs along the Pyrenees instead of at them, crosses at SOMPORT — a different pass, 200 km east — and comes down the Aragón as the Camino Aragónés to join AW-002 at Puente la Reina, which is named for the bridge a queen built so pilgrims could stop drowning. So the four roads make a Y with a very long tail. Saint-Sernin at Toulouse is the largest Romanesque church standing and it is that size because of this road — pilgrim traffic paid for it. Arles at the far end is where the road starts because that is where the Rhône meets the sea and everything from Italy came ashore.

routes.name: The Bavarian Salt Road (Hallein–Augsburg)
routes.era: prehistoric; Munich founded on it by arson, 1158
routes.note: **MUNICH EXISTS BECAUSE A DUKE BURNED SOMEBODY ELSE'S BRIDGE.** The salt from Reichenhall and Hallein crossed the Isar at Föhring, on a bridge belonging to the Bishop of Freising, who took the toll. In 1158 Henry the Lion burned it down, built his own bridge a few kilometres upstream at a settlement of monks — München, 'by the monks' — and took the toll himself. The emperor fined him and then confirmed the arrangement, because the salt had to cross somewhere. **The capital of Bavaria is a tollbooth built by arson, and it is still called after the monks whose village it flattened.** The road is far older than the crime: Hallstatt salt was moving on it in the Iron Age, which is where the whole period gets its name. Junctions AW-113 and AW-115 at Augsburg.

routes.name: The St. Lawrence (the Gulf–Lake Ontario)
routes.era: millennia; Cartier 1535; the road into the continent
routes.note: MONTREAL'S ANSWER — A RIVER THAT LETS YOU IN FIFTEEN HUNDRED KILOMETRES AND THEN STOPS DEAD. The St. Lawrence is the finest natural entrance to North America: ocean ships reach Montreal from the Atlantic without a single carry. And at Montreal it ENDS — the Lachine Rapids, unrunnable, and above them the whole interior. So everything that happened in Canada happened at that break: Hochelaga was already a town of some thousands when Cartier arrived in 1535, and the French built where it had been, and the fur trade went on by canoe from the far side of the rapids — which is why AW-257 the Ottawa route starts at LACHINE, whose name is a joke about China that stuck. Junctions AW-144 the Kennebec–Chaudière at Quebec and AW-257 at Lachine. Rivière-du-Loup added in B72: it is where AW-349's Témiscouata carry comes out of the woods onto this river, and it is a real town on the St. Lawrence that this route simply did not name.

nodes.n: Lachine (the rapids stop everything) — junction AW-257

routes.name: The Arkansas (the Mississippi–the Three Forks)
routes.era: millennia; the Quapaw, Osage and Wichita corridor
routes.note: TULSA'S ANSWER, AND IT IS THE RIVER RATHER THAN THE ROAD. AW-258 the Texas Road runs seventy kilometres east of Tulsa; the Arkansas runs straight through it. This is the southern plains' way in — navigable from the Mississippi to the Three Forks, and beyond that the corridor the Osage and Wichita used out onto the buffalo country. Tulsa sits at a crossing on it, and the town's own founding is on this line: Lochapoka Creek, walked here from Alabama in 1836, lit their council fire under an oak above the river and named the place after the town they had been made to leave. The oak is still there. Junctions AW-253 the Mississippi at the confluence and AW-258 the Texas Road at the Three Forks.

routes.name: The Erie Canal (Albany–Buffalo)
routes.era: dug 1817–25; the ditch that made New York
routes.note: **THIS IS AW-077 WITH WATER IN IT.** Read the Mohawk Trail's note — written thirty-five batches ago — and it says the Mohawk valley is the ONLY water-level gap through the Appalachian barrier and whoever holds it holds the continent's interior. The Erie Canal is that sentence proved with a shovel: it runs Albany–Schenectady–Utica–Rome–Syracuse–Rochester–Buffalo, which is the Iroquois trail, node for node, because there was never anywhere else to put it. **The canal did not find a route. It filled one in.** And at Rome it crosses the ONEIDA CARRY — the portage between Atlantic and Great Lakes drainage that AW-077 already marks — so the thing the whole canal exists to abolish is a node this layer had before the canal was drawn. What followed: freight from Buffalo to New York fell from about ¤100 a ton to under ¤10, the northwest's grain stopped going down the Mississippi to New Orleans and went east instead, and New York became New York. **One ditch, 584 km, and the centre of gravity of a continent moved.** Junctions AW-077 at Fort Orange, the Oneida Carry and Onondaga; AW-141/AW-142 at Buffalo. MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED: eight of this canal's twelve nodes sit at **0.0 km** from AW-077's — Albany, Cohoes, Schenectady, Amsterdam, Little Falls, Utica, Rome, Syracuse. NOT A DUPLICATION, and the distinction matters: AW-226 was cut back for overlapping AW-045 because the 'Spanish road' there WAS the Inca road — same surface, same feet, a renaming. This is different. Somebody dug this. It has locks, aqueducts and a summit; it is water where there was land, and it destroyed the thing it copied. The identical coordinates are the POINT: two artefacts, two centuries apart, forced onto one line by a gap in a mountain range.

routes.name: Canal du Midi (Toulouse–Sète)
routes.era: 1666–81, Pierre-Paul Riquet
routes.note: **THE PROBLEM WAS NOT DIGGING. IT WAS FINDING THE WATER AT THE TOP.** A canal over a watershed is easy to imagine and impossible to build unless you can feed the summit, and every previous attempt at joining the Atlantic to the Mediterranean died on that question for eighteen centuries. Riquet — a salt-tax collector, not an engineer — solved it by walking the Montagne Noire and working out that if you dammed streams up there and ran a feeder channel forty kilometres along a contour you could pour water onto the top of the Naurouze pass forever. Then he built the canal, largely with his own money, went bankrupt doing it, and died six months before it opened. It cost France a fortune and saved the world's shipping the entire voyage round Iberia. UNESCO now, and still working. Junctions AW-262 the Via Tolosana at Toulouse: the pilgrim road and the canal use the same gap, three hundred years apart.

routes.name: The Canal of the Pharaohs (the Nile–the Red Sea)
routes.era: Necho II c.600 BC; finished by Darius c.500 BC; reopened repeatedly to 767 AD
routes.note: **SUEZ IS TWO AND A HALF THOUSAND YEARS OLD, AND IT KEPT BEING FILLED IN.** Necho II started it around 600 BC; Herodotus says 120,000 men died digging and an oracle told Necho he was working for a barbarian, so he stopped. Darius the Persian finished it about a century later and cut stelae along it saying so in four scripts: *I commanded this canal to be dug from the river called the Nile to the sea that goes from Persia... and ships passed from Egypt through this canal to Persia, as I intended.* **The oracle was right.** Ptolemy reopened it, Trajan reopened it, Amr ibn al-As reopened it after the Arab conquest to ship Egyptian grain to Arabia — and the Caliph al-Mansur closed it in 767 to starve a rebellion in Medina, deliberately, and it stayed shut for eleven hundred years until de Lesseps. It does NOT run where the modern canal runs: it went east from the Nile down the Wadi Tumilat, because a canal that had to be dug by hand followed a valley that was already there. Tier C — the route is known from the stelae and the wadi, and the exact channel has moved and silted repeatedly. Junctions AW-041 and AW-042 at Cairo.

nodes.n: Clysma (Suez, the Red Sea) — junction AW-041

routes.name: The Diolkos (the Isthmus of Corinth)
routes.era: c.600 BC, Periander; in use for at least 700 years
routes.note: **A PAVED ROAD FOR SHIPS.** Not a canal — the opposite: Periander of Corinth wanted one around 600 BC, was told it could not be done, and built this instead. Limestone blocks, grooves cut into them about 1.5 m apart, running six or eight kilometres across the isthmus — and boats were hauled out of the water, put on a wheeled cradle, and DRAGGED OVERLAND from one sea to the other. It worked for seven centuries. The grooves are still there and still worn. It saved the 350 km round the Peloponnese and the Cape Malea, of which the sailors said: 'round Malea, forget your home.' Nero started the actual canal in 67 AD with a golden pickaxe and six thousand Jewish prisoners, got about a tenth of the way, and died; nobody finished it until 1893. So the Corinthians spent two and a half thousand years hauling ships over a hill because the hill would not be cut. **The portage node type in this layer has 60-odd uses and this one is a portage for the boat itself.**

routes.name: The Rideau Canal (Ottawa–Kingston)
routes.era: 1826–32, Colonel By; built for a war that never came
routes.note: A CANAL BUILT ENTIRELY BECAUSE OF A ROAD THAT MIGHT BE SHOT AT. After 1812 the British realised that everything moving to Upper Canada went up the St. Lawrence — AW-264 — within musket shot of the American bank, so they spent a colossal sum digging a back way through the bush: Ottawa to Kingston by the Rideau and the Cataraqui, forty-seven locks, a military supply line that would work if the river were closed. The river was never closed. **The canal has never once been used for its purpose**, and it is now the oldest continuously operated canal in North America and a UNESCO site, mostly carrying pleasure boats. Roughly a thousand men died building it, largely of malaria, in a swamp in Canada. Bytown grew around the workings and became Ottawa, so the capital exists because of a fortification against an invasion that did not happen. Junctions AW-257 at the Chaudière Falls and AW-264 at Kingston.

routes.name: Fossa Carolina & the Main–Danube (Nürnberg–Kelheim)
routes.era: Charlemagne dug it in 793 and it failed; finished 1992
routes.note: **ELEVEN HUNDRED AND NINETY-NINE YEARS FROM THE FIRST SPADE TO THE FIRST SHIP.** In 793 Charlemagne put an army to work digging a canal between the Rezat and the Altmühl — the Rhine's water and the Danube's, a few kilometres apart — which would have joined the North Sea to the Black Sea. It rained all autumn, the spoil slid back into the cut as fast as they dug it, and he gave up. **The ditch is still there**, 500 m of it, in a field near Treuchtlingen, with the medieval water table still standing in it. Ludwig I tried again in 1846 and built a canal too small to matter. The Main–Danube finally opened in 1992, on almost exactly Charlemagne's line, and you can now go by water from Rotterdam to the Black Sea — which is what he wanted, and it took twelve centuries and three attempts, and the first attempt is a hole in the ground you can walk to. Junctions AW-113 the Via Imperii at Nürnberg.

routes.name: The Bridgewater Canal (Worsley–Runcorn)
routes.era: 1761 — the first, and the one that started the mania
routes.note: **THE CANAL THAT HALVED THE PRICE OF COAL IN A CITY OVERNIGHT, AND EVERY OTHER CANAL IN BRITAIN IS ITS CONSEQUENCE.** The Duke of Bridgewater had coal at Worsley and a market at Manchester ten miles off and no way to move it that did not cost more than the coal was worth. So he built a canal — the first in Britain to go where no river went — and coal in Manchester fell from about 7d a hundredweight to 3½d the week it opened, and the whole country noticed at once. What people actually came to STARE at was the Barton Aqueduct: Brindley carried the canal OVER the Irwell on stone arches, and the sight of a boat sailing above a river was considered close to indecent — one critic called it a castle in the air. Brindley could barely write and worked problems out by lying in bed for days; the Duke went nearly bankrupt; the canal made him the richest man in England. Underground, the workings at Worsley run 74 km into the hill, and the boats went in.

nodes.n: Barton Aqueduct (a boat over a river)

routes.name: The Trent & Mersey (the Grand Trunk)
routes.era: 1766–77, Brindley; the spine of the Grand Cross
routes.note: **BRINDLEY'S GRAND CROSS — THE ONE IDEA THE WHOLE BRITISH SYSTEM IS BUILT ON.** He proposed joining the four great estuaries — Mersey, Trent/Humber, Severn and Thames — in a single cross of canals, and this is the spine of it: Preston Brook on the Mersey to Shardlow on the Trent, sea to sea across England. **Which means the crossing point is BIRMINGHAM — a city on no navigable river at all, which the canals made the centre of the country's water network, and which ended up with more miles of canal than Venice.** The money came from JOSIAH WEDGWOOD, who was not being philanthropic: pottery on packhorses arrived broken, and a canal would float it. He cut the first sod, built Etruria on the bank, and the Staffordshire potteries exist in that shape because of it. Harecastle Tunnel took eleven years and 2,633 m and had no towpath — the boatmen lay on their backs and WALKED the boat along the roof, in the dark, for hours. Junctions AW-272 at Preston Brook.

routes.name: The Leeds & Liverpool (over the Pennines)
routes.era: begun 1770, finished 1816 — forty-six years
routes.note: TWO HUNDRED AND FOUR KILOMETRES, THE LONGEST SINGLE CANAL IN BRITAIN, AND IT TOOK FORTY-SIX YEARS BECAUSE THE PENNINES ARE IN THE WAY. It crosses the spine of England, which is why Wigan has twenty-one locks in a row and Bingley has FIVE RISE — five chambers stacked, each opening into the next, lifting a boat eighteen metres in one continuous staircase; it was the wonder of 1774 and it still works with the original gear. The canal is why the mills are where they are: cotton came in at Liverpool, coal came from the Wigan pits, cloth went out, and the whole Lancashire–Yorkshire industrial belt strung itself along a ditch. Foulridge Tunnel has no towpath either. In 1912 a cow fell in at one end and swam the whole 1,500 m to the other, and was revived with brandy at the Hole in the Wall pub, and there is a photograph.

routes.name: The Llangollen Canal (Hurleston–Horseshoe Falls)
routes.era: 1795–1805, Telford and Jessop; UNESCO
routes.note: **A CANAL THAT FAILED AS A CANAL AND SURVIVED AS A PIPE.** It was meant to link the Mersey to the Severn through the Welsh coalfields; the money ran out, the southern half was never built, and the thing was left going nowhere in particular. It survives because somebody realised it could carry DRINKING WATER — it still feeds Hurleston reservoir from the Dee at Horseshoe Falls, and that is why it was never abandoned when every other dead canal was. And on the way it does the single most astonishing thing in British engineering: **Pontcysyllte**, Telford's aqueduct, a cast-iron trough on nineteen stone piers carrying narrowboats **thirty-eight metres above the Dee** with no parapet on the towpath side. Scott called it the most impressive work of art he had ever seen. It is two hundred and twenty years old, it has never leaked, and the mortar is lime, ox blood and water.

routes.name: The Kennet & Avon (Reading–Bristol)
routes.era: 1794–1810, Rennie; derelict by 1950; reopened 1990
routes.note: LONDON TO BRISTOL BY WATER — THE OTHER SEA-TO-SEA, and it junctions the Thames, so a boat could go from the North Sea to the Bristol Channel across the whole of southern England. Caen Hill at Devizes is twenty-nine locks in a straight line up a hillside, sixteen of them in one flight with side ponds because there is nowhere to put the water otherwise; it takes five or six hours to climb and it was the last bit finished. Crofton pumping station still has the 1812 Boulton & Watt engine that lifts the summit's water, **the oldest working steam engine in the world still in its original house doing its original job**. The railway killed the canal, the canal rotted for forty years, and volunteers dug it out by hand and reopened it in 1990. Junctions AW-159 the Thames at Reading.

routes.name: The Caledonian Canal (Inverness–Fort William)
routes.era: 1803–22, Telford; obsolete before it opened
routes.note: **A CANAL DOWN A FAULT LINE, AND IT WAS OBSOLETE THE YEAR IT OPENED.** The Great Glen is a tear across Scotland — a strike-slip fault with three lochs sitting in it — so Telford only had to dig about a third of the distance and let Loch Ness do the rest. It was built to save sailing ships the Pentland Firth and the press gangs at the northern ports, and it took nineteen years, and by 1822 ships were steam and getting too big for it, so the traffic it was for never came. It employed thousands of Highlanders at a moment when the Clearances were emptying the glens around it — which was part of the point, and did not work either. Neptune's Staircase at Banavie is eight locks in a row, the longest in Britain. It runs the same glen as AW-128 the Thieves' Road, which took cattle the other way, and junctions it at Fort William.

nodes.n: Fort Augustus (the five locks) — junction AW-036

routes.name: The Grand Junction (Brentford–Birmingham)
routes.era: 1793–1805; the trunk that made the system a system
routes.note: THE ONE THAT MADE THE REST WORTH HAVING. Brindley's Grand Cross joined four estuaries but the London arm went the long way round by Oxford, so the Grand Junction was cut straight — Thames at Brentford to Braunston to Birmingham — and the whole network suddenly pointed at the capital. Braunston on it is the crossroads of the English canals, where this meets the Oxford and boats went four ways; Blisworth Tunnel is 2,813 m and took the contractors three goes, the second attempt collapsing and killing fourteen men. **And the boats were homes.** When the railways took the freight the carrying companies cut wages, so the families moved aboard — a narrowboat cabin is about 2.5 m by 2 m and held a family — and painted them with roses and castles, which is where that whole vocabulary comes from: a decorative tradition invented by people being squeezed out of a trade. **UNCLAIMED, AND FOUND BY THE INTERLOCK SWEEP RATHER THAN BY ME: TRING IS THREE ROUTES.** AW-034 the Ridgeway ends there; AW-199 Akeman Street crosses there; and this canal's SUMMIT is there — prehistoric chalk track, Roman road, and Georgian canal, all at one coordinate, three thousand years apart. The reason is a hole: the Tring Gap is the one low break in the Chilterns, and everything has always gone through it. I did not put them together. The gap did, and the sweep noticed.

routes.name: The Black Way (Chornyi Shliakh) — the slave road to Caffa
routes.era: c.1450–1783; ended when Russia took Crimea
routes.note: **THE DIRECT ANSWER: captives from the Romanian principalities went to CAFFA, and this is the road.** The Crimean Khanate ran an economy on it — contemporaries called the raiding 'harvesting the steppe' — and something between one and three million people were taken from Poland-Lithuania, Ukraine, Muscovy and the Danubian lands between about 1450 and 1774. Three roads ran north from Perekop: the MURAVSKY into Muscovy, and the BLACK WAY and the Kuchmansky into Podolia and Poland, drawn here. **For Moldavia and Wallachia specifically** the raiders were the Budjak Horde, and captives were driven east along the coast through AKKERMAN — which is already a node in this layer as AW-052's Black Sea terminus, and is now also this — to Perekop and Caffa, then shipped to Constantinople. Roped in files, walked for weeks, sold in a market Ukrainian songs call the city that drinks our blood. **ROXELANA CAME UP THIS ROAD.** Taken from Rohatyn around 1520, sold at Caffa, shipped to the harem — and became Hurrem Sultan, Suleiman's wife and the most powerful woman in the Ottoman Empire, which is not a redemption, it is one survivor out of a million. **AND THE SECOND ANSWER IS WORSE:** the Roma of Wallachia and Moldavia were enslaved INTERNALLY — owned by boyars, monasteries and the crown from the 1300s until abolition in **1856**. Five hundred years. That one has no route, because it never went anywhere: the road was that there was no road. Tier C — the Tatar trails are documented as corridors, not surveyed lines. Flagged `sensitive`.

routes.name: The Steenweg (Bruges–Brussels–Cologne)
routes.era: 12th–16th c.; the stone road of Flanders
routes.note: BRUSSELS'S ANSWER — AND BRUSSELS IS ON IT BECAUSE OF A MARSH. Steenweg means stone road: paved, which almost nothing was, because Flanders is clay and an unpaved road there in November is a swamp with ambitions. It carried English wool from Bruges — then the greatest port in northern Europe — to the Rhine at Cologne, and everything in between grew rich weaving the wool as it passed: Ghent, Ypres, Brussels. Bruges then silted up. The Zwin channel closed in the 1400s and the greatest port in Europe simply stopped being a port, and Antwerp took everything. Brussels is at the ford where the road crossed the Senne — Broekzele, the marsh-hall — so the capital of Europe is a place people paved to get across.

routes.name: The Wallachian Road (Brașov–Bucharest–Giurgiu)
routes.era: medieval; the Saxon trade road over the Carpathians
routes.note: BUCHAREST'S ANSWER — A ROAD BETWEEN TWO WORLDS THAT MET IN A PASS. Transylvania was Hungarian and Saxon and Catholic; Wallachia across the mountains was Orthodox and Ottoman-tributary; and the only good way between them is the RUCĂR–BRAN corridor, so the Saxons of Brașov built a customs house at the top and Bran Castle over it, and taxed everything. Bran is now sold as Dracula's castle, which it was not — but Vlad III's actual business was this road: he was voivode of Wallachia, the Saxons of Brașov backed his rivals and undercut his merchants, and the raids and the impalements were a TRADE WAR fought over a mountain pass. The tourist story is a novelist's mistake sitting on top of a real one about tariffs. The road runs on to Giurgiu on the Danube, where Wallachia's tribute crossed to the Ottomans.

routes.name: The Kathmandu–Lhasa Road (the Kuti route)
routes.era: 7th c. onward; Araniko went north on it in 1260
routes.note: **A ROAD THAT EXPORTED AN ARCHITECT AND CHANGED THE SKYLINE OF BEIJING.** The Kathmandu valley is the one place where the Himalaya has a rich civilisation sitting in a bowl with passes north and south, so the Newars traded both ways for a thousand years — and in 1260 they sent ARANIKO, aged seventeen, up this road with a party of craftsmen to build a stupa for the Sakya lama in Tibet. He kept going. He reached Kublai Khan's court, became the Yuan dynasty's chief architect, and built the White Stupa in Beijing, which is still standing, and which is a Nepali building in China put there by a teenager who went north over a Himalayan pass and never came home. The road also carried Nepali copper, Tibetan salt and wool, and the Buddhism that went the other way. Junctions AW-006 the Tea Horse Road at Lhasa.

routes.name: The Kalinga Coast Road (Tamralipti–Kanchipuram)
routes.era: Mauryan onward; the road Ashoka came down in 261 BC
routes.note: **THE ROAD THAT PRODUCED THE MOST FAMOUS CHANGE OF MIND IN HISTORY.** Ashoka came down it in 261 BC to conquer Kalinga, and by his own account in his own inscription — the Thirteenth Rock Edict, cut into stone and still readable — a hundred thousand were killed, a hundred and fifty thousand deported, and many times that number died after; **and he wrote it down, on a rock, in public, as a confession.** 'On conquering Kalinga the Beloved of the Gods felt remorse.' A king carved his own war crime into the landscape and spent the rest of his reign preaching against himself. This is the east coast: Tamralipti at the top was the great Bay of Bengal port — Faxian sailed from it, Ashoka's missions to Sri Lanka left from it — and the road runs down through Kalinga and Andhra to Kanchipuram. Junctions AW-016 the Uttarapatha at Tamralipti and AW-204 at Kanchipuram. Tier C: the corridor is certain, the line is the coast.

routes.name: The Piast Road (Poznań–Gniezno–Kalisz)
routes.era: the Piast heartland, 9th–11th c.; on an older amber line
routes.note: POZNAŃ'S ANSWER — THE ROAD POLAND WAS INVENTED ON. Everything the Piasts had was strung along it: Gniezno where Bolesław was crowned, Ostrów Lednicki where Mieszko was probably baptised in 966, Poznań where the cathedral holds the first two rulers. Poland was not a place that acquired a road; it was **a road with a dynasty on it** — a fifty-kilometre string of strongholds in the marshes of Wielkopolska, defensible because the marsh did the work. And it runs south to Kalisz, which is on AW-030 the Amber Road and is the ONLY town in Poland named in Ptolemy — Calisia — so the Piast heartland sits on the end of a line the Romans already knew about. Tier C: the strongholds are certain, the road between them is corridor. Junctions AW-030 at Kalisz.

routes.name: The Hisor Road (Samarkand–Termez)
routes.era: Kushan onward; the Oxus crossing
routes.note: DUSHANBE'S ANSWER — THE ROAD TO THE OXUS, AND THE OXUS IS WHERE BUDDHISM CROSSED. This is the Silk Road's southern connector: down from Samarkand over the Hisor range into the valley where Dushanbe stands — a Monday market, which is what the name means, and nothing more until 1929 — and on to Termez on the Amu Darya. Termez is the crossing, and it is why northern India is Buddhist-shaped and China is: the Kushans held both banks, monks walked over, and Buddhism went up the Oxus and along the Silk Road to Dunhuang and Chang'an. Alexander crossed here too, and married Roxana in these hills. Tier C: the corridor is certain, the alignment is the valleys.

routes.name: The Vidarbha Road (Kaushambi–Paithan, the eastern way)
routes.era: Satavahana and Vakataka; the other Dakshinapatha
routes.note: NAGPUR'S ANSWER — THE OTHER ROAD SOUTH. AW-017 the Dakshinapatha goes to the Deccan the WESTERN way, by Ujjain and the Narmada at Maheshwar. This is the eastern alternative, through Vidarbha, and it is why Nagpur is where it is: the Vakatakas ruled here from Nandivardhana, twenty-five kilometres from the modern city, and married their daughter to the Guptas, so the two great powers of classical India were joined across this road. Nagpur later got the ZERO MILE STONE — the Great Trigonometrical Survey's reference point, from which the British measured distances across the subcontinent — which is a nice accident: they put the centre of India on a road that had been the way through the middle for fifteen hundred years. Tier C: the corridor is attested, the line is reconstructed.

routes.name: The Yangzi (the Gorges–Shanghai)
routes.era: millennia; the artery
routes.note: **CHINA'S ECONOMY IS A CROSS, AND THIS IS THE BAR OF IT.** The Yangzi runs east; AW-068 the Grand Canal runs north; they cross at Guazhou and Zhenjiang — nodes this layer already had — and everything China moved for a thousand years moved on one axis or the other. Same shape as Brindley's Grand Cross in AW-273, twelve centuries earlier and a hundred times the size. **And the Gorges are why AW-153 exists.** Upstream of Yichang the river goes into a rock slot with a current no boat can climb, so Sichuan sits behind a wall of water and the only way in is over the mountains on plank roads — which is the whole of the Shu Roads' note, seen from the river. Boats went UP the Gorges anyway, hauled on bamboo ropes by TRACKERS walking a ledge cut into the cliff, often naked because the ropes wore the clothes off them, and drowning regularly. The paths are still cut in the rock above the reservoir. Junctions AW-068 at Guazhou and Zhenjiang.

routes.name: The Yellow River (Lanzhou–the sea)
routes.era: millennia; it has changed course 26 times
routes.note: **A RIVER THAT FLOWS ABOVE ITS OWN FLOODPLAIN.** The Huang He carries so much loess that its bed silts UP, so the dikes must be raised, so the bed rises again — and after three thousand years of this the river runs along the top of an embankment ten metres above the fields, held in by walls. When they break, the water does not rise. It ARRIVES. China's Sorrow has killed more people than any other feature on Earth: 1887, somewhere between 900,000 and two million; 1931, one to four million; and in 1938 Chiang Kai-shek **broke the dikes himself** at Huayuankou to stop the Japanese army, drowning perhaps half a million of his own people, and it delayed them by months. The river has swung its mouth 500 km, north of Shandong and south of it, twenty-six times. KAIFENG is stacked SIX DEEP — six cities buried one on another under the silt, the Northern Song capital eight metres down, and the present town standing on all of them. Junctions AW-008 at Lanzhou and AW-190 the Straight Road at Baotou.

routes.name: The Meiling Pass Road (the Yangzi–Guangzhou)
routes.era: cut by Zhang Jiuling in 716 AD; the Canton System's only artery 1757–1842
routes.note: **FOR EIGHTY-FIVE YEARS EVERY FOREIGN GOOD ENTERING CHINA CROSSED ONE PAVED FOOTPATH IN THE MOUNTAINS.** The Nanling range separates the Yangzi world from Guangdong, and in 716 a Tang official named Zhang Jiuling widened a track over the Dayu Ling into a proper road — after which the route was: Grand Canal to the Yangzi, Yangzi to Jiujiang, up the Gan to Nanxiong, over MEILING on foot, down the Bei to Guangzhou. That is how Canton talked to Beijing for a thousand years. Then the Canton System (1757–1842) made Guangzhou the ONLY port foreigners could use, so all of it — the tea, the silk, the porcelain, and the opium coming the other way — went over that one ridge on porters' backs, and the tea that started the Boston Tea Party walked over this pass. It is paved, the paving survives, and it is named for plum trees. Junctions AW-287 at Jiujiang.

routes.name: The Karakoram Pass (Leh–Yarkand)
routes.era: centuries; closed 1949–50
routes.note: **THE HIGHEST TRADE ROUTE ON EARTH, AND IT IS PAVED WITH BONES.** 5,540 m at the pass, and the Saser La before it is worse — a glacier you cross on the ice. The trail is marked by the SKELETONS OF PACK ANIMALS, thousands of them, because the cold preserves everything and nothing rots: travellers navigated by them. Estimates of the death rate among the horses on a single crossing run to a fifth or more. And what it carried is why your grandmother had a shawl: pashmina, the undercoat of Changthangi goats, grows only where it is cold enough to need it, so Tibet and Ladakh had the wool and Kashmir had the weavers — **Kashmir shawls are Kashmiri because of this pass**, not because of anything that grows there. It closed in 1949–50 when the borders shut and has not reopened. Tier C — the pass and the stages are attested, the line between is ice. Junctions AW-010 the Tarim's south rim at Yarkand.

routes.name: The Liaodong Road (Beijing–Shanhaiguan–Hanyang)
routes.era: the Korean tribute road; the gate opened in 1644
