routes.note: **ONE MAN OPENED ONE GATE AND A DYNASTY ENDED.** Shanhaiguan is where the Great Wall runs into the sea — the First Pass Under Heaven, the hinge of the whole northern frontier, and the Ming held it against the Manchus for decades. In 1644 Li Zicheng's rebels took Beijing, the emperor hanged himself in his garden, and the Ming general Wu Sangui — holding Shanhaiguan, caught between a rebel in his capital and a Manchu army at his gate — chose the Manchus and **let them through**. They took Beijing in a fortnight and ruled China for 268 years. The wall worked until somebody decided it should not. The road is also KOREA'S: the Uiju-daero carried some five hundred tribute embassies to Beijing over five centuries, and Korean scholars walked it and wrote up everything they saw — the yeonhaengnok, hundreds of travel diaries, which are one of the best records of Qing China that exists. Junctions AW-068/AW-210 at Beijing and AW-150 at Hanyang.

routes.name: The Zayton Route (Quanzhou–Malacca)
routes.era: Song and Yuan; Quanzhou's floruit 11th–14th c.
routes.note: **THE GREATEST PORT IN THE WORLD, AND YOU ARE WEARING ITS NAME.** Marco Polo said Quanzhou took a hundred ships of pepper for every one that reached Alexandria; Ibn Battuta said its harbour was the largest he had seen anywhere, and he had seen most of them. Arabs called it ZAYTON, from the olive trees along its walls — and the glossy cloth that shipped from it took the port's name into Europe as SATIN. What is left is stranger than the trade: Quanzhou has the ruins of a MANICHAEAN temple, the only one standing on Earth; a mosque built in 1009; Hindu temple carvings reused in a Buddhist one; and a Muslim cemetery holding two companions of the Prophet, by tradition. A Chinese city with a Persian religion's last building in it. Then the Ming closed the sea in the 1370s and the harbour silted and Quanzhou stopped, so completely that Europe forgot which city Zayton had been. Junctions AW-289 at Guangzhou, AW-248 at Quy Nhơn, AW-054 at Malacca.

routes.name: The Amur (Nerchinsk–Nikolayevsk)
routes.era: Russian descent 1643–89; lost at Nerchinsk; retaken 1858
routes.note: **THE FIRST TREATY CHINA EVER SIGNED WITH A EUROPEAN POWER WAS WRITTEN IN LATIN, BECAUSE NEITHER SIDE COULD TALK TO THE OTHER.** Russia came down the Amur in the 1640s looking for grain — Siberia could not feed itself and this was the one warm valley — and ran straight into the Qing, who regarded it as the Manchu homeland's back door. Albazin was besieged twice. And in 1689 at Nerchinsk the two empires met and had **no common language at all**, so the negotiation was conducted through Jesuit priests in the Russian and Chinese suites translating everything into LATIN, and the treaty was signed in Latin, Russian and Manchu — no Chinese. Russia gave up the Amur entirely and got the caravan trade to Beijing instead. She took it back in 1858, when the Qing were losing the Second Opium War and could not argue. Harbin on the Sungari branch is younger than the argument: the Russians built it in 1898 for a railway. Junctions AW-146 the Sibirsky Trakt at Irkutsk is NOT claimed — they are 600 km apart and the connection is overland; the note says so rather than the map implying it.

routes.name: The Irrawaddy (Bhamo–the Bay of Bengal)
routes.era: millennia; Pagan 1044–1287
routes.note: **THIS COMPLETES ZHANG QIAN'S ROAD, 2,100 YEARS LATE.** AW-192 ends at Bhamo because that is where the Five-Foot Way runs out of mountain and finds a river — and this is the river. Put them together and you have the road Zhang Qian deduced from a bolt of Sichuan cloth in a Bactrian market in 128 BC: Chengdu to the Bay of Bengal, the southwestern silk road, the back door the Han spent decades failing to open. It works. It always worked. The tribes simply would not let the Chinese use it. PAGAN sits on it: ten thousand temples raised between 1044 and 1287 on a dry plain by kings who kept building them until the treasury broke, and about 2,200 still standing — then the Mongols came in 1287 and the building stopped in one year. The river is still Burma's only real road. Junctions AW-192 at Bhamo.

routes.name: The Yukon (Bennett–St. Michael)
routes.era: millennia of Athabaskan use; 1898
routes.note: **SEVEN THOUSAND HOMEMADE BOATS LEFT ONE LAKE IN A SINGLE WEEK.** This is what AW-088 was FOR: the whole point of hauling a tonne of goods over the Chilkoot was to reach Bennett, cut down the trees, build a boat, and wait for the ice. In the spring of 1898 about seven thousand of them were waiting, and when the lake broke on 29 May they all went at once — a flotilla of amateur carpentry, 800 km down a river most of them had never seen, to a goldfield already staked. The river was an Athabaskan road for thousands of years before that and is still the only way through most of interior Alaska. Junctions AW-088 the Chilkoot at Bennett: the trail and the river are one journey, and the layer now shows both halves.

routes.name: The Iditarod Trail (Seward–Nome)
routes.era: Athabaskan and Iñupiaq trails; a mail route from 1908; the serum run 1925
routes.note: **THE DOG THAT GOT THE STATUE RAN THE LAST LEG. THE DOG THAT DID THE WORK IS LESS FAMOUS.** In January 1925 diphtheria broke out at Nome; the only antitoxin was in Anchorage; the port was frozen, the planes would not start at −50°C, and the trail was the only thing left. Twenty mushers and about 150 dogs relayed the serum 1,085 km in five and a half days through a blizzard. TOGO, aged twelve, ran the longest and worst leg — some 420 km including the Norton Sound ice, which was breaking up, in the dark. BALTO ran the final 88 km into town, and got the statue in Central Park. Both facts are true and only one of them is remembered. The trail itself is older than either: Athabaskan and Iñupiaq routes strung together as a mail road in 1908, and it is now a race, which is the usual fate of a road that stops being needed.

routes.name: The Melos Obsidian Route (Melos–Franchthi)
routes.era: **c.11,000 BC** — the oldest sea route known anywhere
routes.note: **THE OLDEST ROUTE IN THIS LAYER BY SEVEN THOUSAND YEARS, AND IT IS A SEA CROSSING.** Franchthi Cave on the Argolid has obsidian in its Mesolithic layers — around 11,000 BC, possibly earlier — and every piece of it comes from MELOS, a hundred and thirty kilometres away across open water. Melos was never joined to the mainland; there is no sea level low enough. So people in the Greek Mesolithic — no farming, no pottery, no metal, no writing for another seven thousand years — were **building boats, crossing open sea out of sight of land, and coming back**, repeatedly, for a rock. And they were coming back: the obsidian is in the cave, so the traffic was two-way, which is the test this layer applies to Lapita and Rapa Nui and which this passes by thirteen thousand years. It is the earliest evidence of seafaring anywhere on Earth. **We have no idea what the boats were.** Tier C: the two ends are certain from the geochemistry, and there is nothing in between but water and inference.

routes.name: The Sweet Track & the Post Track (Somerset)
routes.era: **the Post Track 3838 BC; the Sweet Track 3807/3806 BC** — dated to the winter
routes.note: **WE KNOW THE WINTER IT WAS BUILT.** Dendrochronology gives the Sweet Track's ash planks as felled in the winter of 3807/3806 BC — not a century, not a decade, **a single season, five thousand eight hundred years ago** — and the Post Track beneath it is thirty years older again. Two kilometres of plank walkway on crossed pegs across a reed swamp, built by people who had farming and no metal, and who did it in what looks like a few months as one organised job. It was drowned within about ten years and the peat kept it perfectly. **And there is a jade axe beside it.** Polished jadeite, never used, never sharpened — votive — and it came from MONT VISO in the Alps, sixteen hundred kilometres away, which is AW-301. So a Neolithic farmer walked out onto a bog road in Somerset in 3800 BC carrying a green stone from Italy and put it in the water on purpose. Tier A: excavated plank by plank and dated to the year.

routes.name: The Lapis Lazuli Road (Sar-i-Sang–Ur)
routes.era: **c.4000 BC to now** — the same mine, six thousand years
routes.note: **THE MOTAGUA STORY AGAIN, ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE WORLD.** There is exactly ONE source of lapis lazuli in the ancient world — Sar-i-Sang, a valley in Badakhshan reached by a gorge — and everything is from there. The Standard of Ur. The Royal Cemetery's beads. **Tutankhamun's mask, the inlay round his eyes.** The lapis in a Sumerian queen's headdress and the lapis on a pharaoh's face were dug from the same Afghan hillside by people neither of them ever heard of, and it was already old when they got it. The mine has been worked for six thousand years and is being worked now. SHORTUGHAI on this road is the tell: a HARAPPAN colony, complete with Indus bricks and Indus seals, planted a thousand kilometres from the Indus — the Indus people did not trade for lapis, they went and sat on it. Tier C — the source, the workshops and the destinations are certain from geochemistry and excavation; the line between is inference, which is the honest situation for a road that left jewellery instead of a surface. Junctions AW-207 the Royal Road at Susa.

routes.name: Wadi Hammamat (Coptos–the Red Sea)
routes.era: predynastic to the Islamic period — five thousand years of graffiti
routes.note: **THEY CARRIED THE SHIPS ACROSS THE DESERT IN PIECES.** This is the shortest line from the Nile to the Red Sea and it has been walked since before Egypt was Egypt — there are PREDYNASTIC BOAT CARVINGS on the rock here, a hundred kilometres from any water, cut by people who lived on a river and were thinking about the sea. And then they did it: the Punt expeditions went down this wadi carrying **disassembled ships**, put them together at Mersa Gawasis on the coast, sailed to Punt for incense and ebony and myrrh, came back, TOOK THE SHIPS APART AGAIN, and stored the timbers in caves cut in the cliff for next time. The timbers are still there — excavated in the 2000s, cedar, four thousand years old, with the mortices still fitting. The wadi is also a quarry (bekhen greywacke) and a visitors' book: five thousand years of inscriptions, pharaonic, Ptolemaic, Roman, Coptic, Arab, all on the same rocks, all saying some version of I was here.

routes.name: The Mont Viso Jade Road (the Alps–the Channel)
routes.note: **THE AXE ON THE SWEET TRACK CAME FROM HERE, AND HANNIBAL'S PASS IS THREE KILOMETRES AWAY.** High on Mont Viso there are jadeite outcrops, and between about 5000 and 3500 BC people climbed to two thousand metres to quarry them and polished the stone into axes that were never meant to cut anything — and those axes are found across Europe: Brittany, Bulgaria, Ireland, and one lying beside a bog walkway in Somerset in 3807 BC (AW-298). Around 1,800 are known and they nearly all come from this one mountain. **And now the coincidence.** The Col de la Traversette, the best physical candidate for Hannibal's crossing — Mahaney's team found a churned layer with horse-gut microbes dated to ~218 BC — sits **3.7 km** from the quarries. Same mountain, thirty-six centuries apart, and neither knew about the other. **HANNIBAL IS NOT DRAWN IN THIS LAYER AND SHOULD NOT BE:** his crossing was a journey, not a road, and the same rule excludes Bashō and Orellana. The passes were already ancient — Ötzi died on one in 3300 BC — and what was remarkable was never the route. It was the elephants, in October. Tier C: the source and the finds are certain; the corridor is inferred from where the axes end up, per the AW-090 standard.

routes.name: The Kozushima Obsidian Route (Kozushima–Honshu)
routes.era: **c.38,000 BP** — the oldest route in this layer, by a margin nothing else approaches
routes.note: **THIS DISPLACES MELOS BY TWENTY-SEVEN THOUSAND YEARS.** Kozushima is a volcanic island fifty kilometres off Honshu across the Sagami Trough, which is a thousand metres deep — it has NEVER been joined to the mainland at any sea level, ever. And its obsidian, which is geochemically unmistakable, turns up at Upper Palaeolithic sites all over central Honshu **from about 38,000 years ago**. Not one piece. Hundreds of sites. Which means people in the Japanese Palaeolithic — no agriculture, no pottery, thirty thousand years before the Jomon — were **crossing fifty kilometres of open ocean, finding a specific island, and coming back with cargo, routinely, for twenty thousand years.** It is the oldest evidence of seafaring on Earth that is also evidence of a ROUTE: Australia was reached earlier, around 65,000 BP, but that was a dispersal — one way — and this layer excludes dispersals, which is why Lapita and Rapa Nui are not drawn. **This is two-way, and it is the oldest thing here.** We do not know what the boats were. We have never found one. Tier C: both ends are certain from geochemistry, and everything in between is water.

routes.name: The Bluestone Road (Preseli–Stonehenge)
routes.era: c.3000 BC; the Altar Stone's source found in 2024
routes.note: **THEY MAY HAVE MOVED A WHOLE MONUMENT, AND THE ALTAR STONE CAME FROM SCOTLAND.** Eighty bluestones, two to four tonnes each, came to Salisbury Plain from the Preseli hills in Wales — 250 km — around 3000 BC, and geologists have narrowed it to specific outcrops: Carn Goedog, Craig Rhos-y-Felin. Then Waun Mawn: a dismantled stone circle in Preseli with an empty socket whose cross-section matches a Stonehenge bluestone. **They took a stone circle down and carried it to England.** And in 2024 the Altar Stone — six tonnes, the one everything else is arranged around — was traced by zircon dating not to Wales at all but to the **Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland**, seven hundred and fifty kilometres away, almost certainly by sea. Nobody expected that; it was published two years ago. **The most studied monument on Earth was still hiding where its centrepiece came from until the day before yesterday.** Junctions AW-099 the Harrow Way at Stonehenge — which crosses the plain and predates the stones.

nodes.n: Waun Mawn (the circle they took down)

routes.name: The Spondylus Road (Ecuador–Cusco)
routes.era: c.3000 BC onward; the Chincha rafts to 1532
routes.note: **A RAFT CARRYING THIS SHELL IS WHY EUROPE KNEW PERU EXISTED.** Spondylus — mullu — is a thorny oyster that only lives in warm water, so it grows off Ecuador and nowhere south, and the Andes wanted it more than gold: it was ground and scattered at every huaca, buried with the dead, fed to the mountains. **The holiest substance in the Inca world could not be got in the Inca world.** So it came three thousand kilometres down the coast, and the carriers were the Chincha — six thousand merchants sailing balsa rafts with cotton sails, whose lord rode in a litter next to Atahualpa because that is what controlling this trade was worth. And in 1526 Pizarro's pilot Bartolomé Ruiz intercepted one of those rafts off Ecuador: twenty tonnes of textiles, silver, gold and spondylus, crewed by people wearing better cloth than he was. **He turned round and reported it, and that raft is the reason the invasion happened.** Junctions AW-046 at Chincha and AW-045 at Cusco. Tier C — the source and the destinations are certain, the sea road is inferred.

routes.name: The Old Copper Road (Isle Royale–Poverty Point)
routes.era: c.6000–3000 BC — among the oldest metalworking anywhere
routes.note: **NORTH AMERICA HAD A METAL TRADE SIX THOUSAND YEARS AGO AND ALMOST NOBODY MENTIONS IT.** Lake Superior has NATIVE copper — pure metal, lying in the rock, needing no smelting at all, just heat and hammering — and from about 6000 BC people dug it out of Isle Royale and the Keweenaw in thousands of pits with stone mauls and fire. The Old Copper Complex is contemporary with the earliest metalworking in the Old World and predates most of it. **And the copper travelled.** It is in graves from Manitoba to New York, and it is at POVERTY POINT in Louisiana — an earthwork of concentric ridges raised around 1700 BC by people who were not farmers, holding copper from two thousand kilometres north, galena from Missouri, and soapstone from Alabama. A hunter-gatherer city with an import list. Then the copper trade faded, and Europeans arrived to find people who did not work metal and concluded they never had. Tier C, per the AW-090 standard: the mine and the finds are certain, the corridor is inferred from where the metal ends up. Junctions AW-253 the Mississippi at Vicksburg.

routes.name: The Cappadocian Obsidian Road (Göllü Dağ–Jericho)
routes.era: c.9000–6000 BC — the Neolithic's toolkit
routes.note: **THE NEOLITHIC REVOLUTION RAN ON TWO VOLCANOES.** Göllü Dağ and Nenezi Dağ in Cappadocia produced obsidian good enough to be the best cutting edge on Earth until steel, and it is found at JERICHO — seven hundred kilometres away, in the eighth millennium BC. It is at Göbekli Tepe, whose builders were raising carved megaliths in 9500 BC before anybody farmed anything. It is all over ÇATALHÖYÜK, which had no streets — you walked across the roofs and dropped into your house through a hole — and which had obsidian from these hills, shells from the Mediterranean and flint from Syria, in 7000 BC. **And it reached CYPRUS**, which needs a boat, which is the same point Melos and Kozushima make in three different seas. This is the trade that the first farming villages were embedded in before they were villages: **the network came first, and the towns grew on it.** Tier C, and the honest situation for a road proved by geochemistry. Junctions AW-207 at the Cilician Gates.

routes.name: The Kola Road (Begho–Kumasi–Elmina)
routes.era: Dyula kola trade from c.1400; the Asante great roads mapped 1817
routes.note: **THE FOREST LEG OF AW-043, AND THE ANSWER TO A QUESTION ABOUT CHOCOLATE.** The Wangara Gold Road already runs Timbuktu–Djenné–Bobo-Dioulasso–Kong–Bondoukou–Begho. This is what it was reaching FOR: kola. Cola nitida grows only in this forest, and it was the one stimulant permitted in Muslim West Africa — chewed, shared, given at weddings, indispensable — so it went north up the Dyula roads for six centuries while salt and cloth came south. The Asante ran eight GREAT ROADS out of Kumasi, swept and maintained with rest-houses, and Bowdich mapped them in 1817. **The roads went both ways and so did the people sold on them:** Asante sold captives SOUTH to the Atlantic forts — Elmina, 1482, the oldest European building south of the Sahara and a slave castle — and NORTH up the Dyula roads to the Sahara. Two trades, one town, opposite directions. **THE COCOA ANSWER, honestly:** cocoa is not African — it is Amazonian, brought via São Tomé, and Tetteh Quarshie carried pods home from Fernando Po in 1876 and planted them at Mampong. Within thirty-five years the Gold Coast led the world. **So the cocoa belt IS the kola forest, replanted** — and the labour comes down this same corridor from Burkina Faso and Mali, through Bobo-Dioulasso, which is a node on AW-043 already. The honest scale: the NORC survey of 2020 found about 1.56 million children in hazardous work in Ivorian and Ghanaian cocoa — overwhelmingly family labour on smallholdings, driven by a farmgate price that leaves growers a few percent of a chocolate bar. **Trafficking is real, documented and much smaller, and conflating the two helps nobody.** The corridor is old; what moves on it now is poverty, and sometimes it is worse than that.

routes.name: The Kwango Road (Kasanje–Luanda)
routes.era: Luanda founded 1576; the trade ran to the 1860s
routes.note: **THE LARGEST ARTERY OF THE ATLANTIC SLAVE TRADE, AND IT WAS MISSING FROM THIS LAYER ENTIRELY.** West Central Africa — Angola and the Congo — sent roughly **5.7 million people** across the Atlantic: about forty-five per cent of the whole trade, more than West Africa and the Bight of Benin and the Bight of Biafra put together. If the trade has a main road, it is this one. Captives came down the Kwango corridor from Lunda and the interior to KASANJE, an Imbangala market-state that existed to broker them, and on to Luanda, where the Portuguese loaded them for BRAZIL — which took about eighty-five per cent of Angola's captives. **So this road is the other end of AW-217 and AW-232.** The Estrada Real's gold was carried by people who came down this line; the São Francisco's cattle fed them. The two ends of that were already both on the map and the middle was not. Njinga Mbande fought Portugal for thirty years from Matamba on this road and also sold captives along it, and both of those are true. The 19th-century Benguela road further south, run by the Ovimbundu, is its successor. Tier C: the corridor is documented in the Portuguese records, the line is inferred.

routes.name: The Dahomey Road (Abomey–Ouidah)
routes.era: Dahomey took Ouidah in 1727; the trade ran to the 1860s
routes.note: **A HUNDRED KILOMETRES, AND THERE ARE TWO TREES ON IT.** Dahomey was a state whose economy was raiding: the army went out each dry season, brought captives back to Abomey, and walked them down this road to Ouidah, through which perhaps a million people passed. The Agojie — the women's regiments, several thousand strong — did much of the taking. And at Ouidah the road has a ritual that is the most efficient piece of psychological engineering I have found anywhere in this layer. **The Tree of Forgetting:** captives were made to circle it, men nine times, women seven, so that they would forget their homes and their names and not return as vengeful spirits. **The Tree of Return**, three kilometres on: circled three times, so that the SPIRIT could come home even though the body never would. One ritual to erase the person, and then one to let the ghost go back. Both administered by the people selling them. The Door of No Return stands on the beach at the end. Junctions nothing — it did not need to join anything, because it only had to be a hundred kilometres long.

nodes.n: Ouidah — the Door of No Return

routes.name: The Aro Network (Arochukwu–Bonny)
routes.era: 17th c. to 1902, when the British blew up the oracle
routes.note: **AN ORACLE THAT ATE PEOPLE, AND IT WAS A WAREHOUSE.** The Aro of Arochukwu kept Ibini Ukpabi — the Long Juju — an oracle of enormous authority across Igboland: you brought your dispute to it and it judged, and the guilty were **swallowed**. They were led into a gorge, into a cave, and never came out, and a red dye ran out downstream so the waiting relatives could see the blood. There was no blood. They were walked out the back and sold, and the network of Aro settlements and the great market at Bende moved them to Bonny and Calabar, where perhaps **1.5 million people** left the Bight of Biafra. The genius of it, if that is the word, is that it needed no army: the supply came to the oracle voluntarily, brought by its own neighbours, seeking justice. The British destroyed Arochukwu in 1901–02 and dynamited the shrine. **Olaudah Equiano was Igbo and was taken as a child, and his book is the reason a great many Britons first understood what they were buying.** Tier C — the network is documented, the routes are corridors.

routes.name: The Coffle Road (Alexandria–Natchez)
routes.era: 1790–1860 — the Second Middle Passage
routes.note: **THIS RAN ON ROADS THIS LAYER ALREADY HAD, AND NONE OF THEIR NOTES SAID SO. THAT IS MY OMISSION AND THIS FIXES IT.** Between 1790 and 1860 about **one million people** were forcibly moved from the Upper South to the cotton frontier — **more than twice the number the United States ever imported across the Atlantic**. It is called the Second Middle Passage and it happened after the trade was 'abolished': Virginia and Maryland sold their people south, and roughly a third of enslaved children in the Upper South were separated from a parent. Franklin & Armfield of Alexandria ran the biggest firm and their building is still standing on Duke Street. The coffles walked: chained in pairs, twenty to forty miles a day, five to eight weeks, a thousand miles — down the Great Valley, through the Cumberland Gap, to Nashville, and then **down the Natchez Trace**, which is AW-048, whose note I wrote about boatmen walking home. Both are true. The Trace carried Kaintucks north and coffles south **at the same time, on the same surface**. Forks of the Road at Natchez was the second-largest market in the South. Junctions AW-195 at Alexandria, AW-084 at the Great Valley, AW-048 at Nashville and Natchez, AW-253 at New Orleans.

nodes.n: Natchez (Forks of the Road) — junction AW-048

routes.name: The Ganges (Gangotri–Ganga Sagar)
routes.era: millennia; the road and the goddess are the same thing
routes.note: **THE ROAD AND THE RIVER ARE THE SAME CORRIDOR, AND THE LAYER ALREADY HAD ONE OF THEM.** AW-015 the Grand Trunk Road runs beside this water for a thousand kilometres — Varanasi and Patna are nodes on both — because the Gangetic plain has exactly one axis and everything uses it. But the river is not infrastructure here, it is a DEITY: you do not travel on Ganga, you travel *in* her, and the traffic nobody counts is ashes. PRAYAGRAJ on this line is where the Ganga meets the Yamuna and, by belief, the vanished Saraswati, and the Kumbh Mela held there is **the largest gathering of human beings on Earth** — something like 240 million people over fifty days in 2019, walking to a confluence. VARANASI has been lived in since about 1200 BC; Mark Twain said it looked older than history, older than tradition, older even than legend. Junctions AW-015 at Varanasi and Kolkata, AW-016 at Pataliputra.

routes.name: The Indus & the Harappan Roads
routes.era: **2600–1900 BC** — and this layer did not have it at all
routes.note: **ONE OF THE THREE ORIGINAL URBAN CIVILISATIONS, AND IT WAS MISSING FROM THIS MAP.** Egypt is here, Mesopotamia is here, and the Indus — the largest of the three by area, five million people, cities of forty thousand — was not. It is the quietest of them and that is the whole point: **no palaces. No temples anybody can identify. No royal tombs. No kings.** What there is instead is standardisation — bricks in a 4:2:1 ratio from Gujarat to the Punjab, weights accurate across a thousand kilometres, streets on a grid, and covered drains in ordinary houses at a date when Ur's kings were being buried with their servants. DHOLAVIRA has a SIGNBOARD: ten characters, each over a metre, mounted above a gate five thousand years ago — the oldest signboard in the world, and **nobody can read it.** Four thousand inscriptions survive, averaging five signs, and the script has defeated everyone. LOTHAL has a tidal dock from 2400 BC. And AW-299 already carried the link: Shortughai, the Harappan colony at the lapis mine — they did not trade for the stone, they went and sat on it. Tier C: the sites are certain, the roads between them are inferred from the standardisation, which is itself the argument that there were roads.

routes.name: The Char Dham (the four abodes)
routes.era: attributed to Adi Shankara, c.800 AD
routes.note: **A MAN DREW A SUBCONTINENT BY WALKING ROUND IT.** Adi Shankara is said to have travelled India in the 8th century and set a matha at each of the four corners — Badrinath in the Himalaya, Puri on the Bay of Bengal, Rameswaram at the southern tip, Dwarka on the Arabian Sea — and the Char Dham yatra is the circuit of them. Whatever the history (he may have died at thirty-two, and the attribution is later), the EFFECT is not in doubt: it made a single sacred geography out of a landmass that had never been one polity, and it did it by defining a shape people walk. Some six thousand kilometres, and pilgrims do it clockwise. **The ninth closed ring in this layer**, and by far the largest: the others are a mountain, a lake, a forest or a province. This one is a country. Junctions AW-283 at Puri. **SELF-CAUGHT: the first draft cut 969 km across the Arabian Sea.** The water rule failed it — my 'clockwise round India' shaping nodes were in the ocean off Goa and in the Gulf of Khambhat. A yatra is WALKED; the coast is a shape, not a chord. Rebuilt through the real pilgrim towns, and it picks up Kanchipuram, Nashik and Ajmer on the way, which is what a road round India would do.

routes.name: The Brahmaputra (Sadiya–the Bay)
routes.era: millennia; the Ahom came over the Patkai in 1228 and stayed 600 years
routes.note: **THE MUGHALS TOOK EVERYTHING FROM KABUL TO BENGAL AND COULD NOT TAKE ASSAM, AND THEY LOST ON THIS RIVER.** The Ahom — a Tai people who walked over the Patkai from Burma in 1228 — ruled the Brahmaputra valley for six hundred years and beat the Mughal empire **seventeen times.** The last one was decisive and it was naval: at SARAIGHAT in 1671 Lachit Borphukan fought a fleet battle in the river, dying of fever, and destroyed the Mughal navy so completely that they never came back. An empire that took the Deccan was stopped by a river and a man too ill to stand. Upstream the water is the Yarlung Tsangpo, running east across Tibet for 1,700 km before it hits Namcha Barwa, turns a corner, and drops two thousand metres through the deepest gorge on Earth — which is why nobody worked out until 1913 that the Tsangpo and the Brahmaputra were the same river. Junctions AW-312 the Ganges at the delta. **JUNCTION CLAIM RETRACTED, PRE-SHIP.** The first draft claimed this meets AW-312 at the Padma. It does not: the Ganges splits at Farakka, AW-312 follows the Hooghly branch to Kolkata, and the Brahmaputra joins the PADMA — the other distributary, which this layer does not draw. **Two rivers that do meet in the world do not meet on this map**, and saying they did would have been a claim the coordinates refuse. The sweep caught it.

routes.name: The Horse Road (Goa–Vijayanagara)
routes.era: 14th–16th c.; Vijayanagara destroyed 1565
routes.note: **AN EMPIRE THAT HAD TO BUY ITS CAVALRY FROM OVERSEAS, AND THE PORTUGUESE WORKED OUT THAT THIS WAS THE LEVER.** India cannot breed warhorses well — the climate, the fodder, the diseases — so every Indian power that wanted cavalry had to import it, and Vijayanagara bought something like **thirteen thousand Arabian horses a year**, landed at Goa and walked inland. Nuniz and Paes, who lived there, describe a city of half a million with an army built on animals it could not produce. **Albuquerque took Goa in 1510 knowing exactly what he had taken:** whoever held the horse trade held the Deccan, and he told the Portuguese crown so. Then in 1565 the Deccan sultanates combined at Talikota, Vijayanagara's army broke, and the greatest city in India was systematically demolished over some months. The ruins at Hampi run for twenty-six square kilometres. **A structural dependency, in a country's own note, is worth more than a battle:** they lost because of what they had to buy. Tier C — the trade is thoroughly documented, the road is a corridor.

routes.name: The Black Hills Circuit (Ȟe Sápa)
routes.era: pre-contact; the 1868 treaty; the 1877 taking; the money still refused
routes.note: **DEVILS TOWER'S ANSWER IS NOT A TRAIL. IT IS A CIRCUIT, AND IT MAY BE A STAR MAP.** Mato Tipila — Bear Lodge, and 'Devils Tower' is a mistranslation that stuck — is sacred to twenty or more nations, and it is one station on a ceremonial round of Ȟe Sápa: Mato Paha, Pe Sla, Ȟiŋháŋ Káǥa, Washun Niya. Goodman's Lakota Star Knowledge argues the spring circuit MIRRORS THE CONSTELLATIONS — you walk the Hills as the sun walks the sky, arriving at each place as its star rises — which is contested and is also the kind of claim that is worth stating and flagging rather than omitting. **WASHUN NIYA is the fact I cannot get past.** It is the emergence place: the Lakota came out of the earth there. And Wind Cave BREATHES — it exhales and inhales, audibly, as the barometric pressure changes, which is why it is called the breathing hole. An origin story sited on a hole in the ground that respires. **AND THE ENDING.** The 1868 treaty gave the Hills to the Lakota forever; Custer found gold in 1874; the US took them in 1877. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Sioux Nation that the taking was illegal and awarded compensation. **The Lakota refused the money.** It has sat in trust for forty-five years, now over two billion dollars, uncollected — because cashing it would agree that the Hills were for sale. Tier C: the sites are public and certain, the circuit between them is ceremony, not a surveyed line. Flagged `sensitive`.

nodes.n: Pe Sla (the Heart of Everything That Is)

routes.name: The Snake River Road (Jackson–the Columbia)
routes.era: millennia; the Oregon Trail followed it after 1840
routes.note: **BOISE'S ANSWER — AND A WATERFALL DECIDES WHO EATS WHAT FOR SIX HUNDRED KILOMETRES.** Shoshone Falls is sixty-five metres high, taller than Niagara, and **salmon cannot climb it.** So the Snake plain is cut in two: below the falls the salmon run and people fish; above them they never came, and people ate other things. The Shoshone bands are named for exactly that — Agaidika, salmon eaters. Tukudeka, sheep eaters. Kamuduka, jackrabbit eaters. Yahandeka, groundhog eaters. **The names are a map of what the geography allowed**, and the falls is the line on it. The Boise valley sits below the falls, on the salmon side, which is why it was worth being there. Camas Prairie upstream is the other harvest — and the Bannock War of 1878 began when settlers' pigs rooted up the camas beds the treaty had reserved. The Oregon Trail came down this line in the 1840s because there is no other line. Junctions AW-051 the Old North Trail at Jackson Hole.

routes.name: The Lolo Trail (Weippe–the Bitterroot)
routes.era: pre-contact Nez Perce buffalo road; Lewis and Clark 1805; the flight of 1877
routes.note: **THE ROAD THE NEZ PERCE SAVED THE AMERICANS ON IS THE ROAD THEY FLED DOWN.** It runs the RIDGE, not the valleys, because the Bitterroot canyons are impassable — which means no water and no game for a hundred kilometres, and in September 1805 the Corps of Discovery took eleven days on it, ate their candles and three of their horses, and came off it starving onto Weippe Prairie. The Nez Perce there discussed killing them and taking the guns. **They were talked out of it by an old woman.** Watkuweis had been captured years before, taken east, treated decently by white traders, and returned; she said of them, do them no hurt. The expedition survived because of one woman's memory of a kindness. Seventy-two years later the Nez Perce came back over this trail going the other way, fleeing the army that had come to take their land, 1,900 km with their families, and surrendered sixty-five kilometres from Canada. Junctions AW-318 the Snake at the Clearwater's reach — not claimed; the note says so.

routes.name: Nunna daul Tsuny (the Trail of Tears — the Northern Route)
routes.note: **THE SUPREME COURT SAID THEY COULD STAY.** Worcester v. Georgia, 1832: the Cherokee Nation is a distinct community in which the laws of Georgia have no force. Jackson's administration did not comply, and in 1838 the army removed about sixteen thousand people at bayonet point from stockades and walked them two thousand two hundred kilometres. Around four thousand died. They call it Nunna daul Tsuny — the trail where they cried. **The detail that stays with me is the ICE.** At the Ohio crossing they were held for weeks in the winter of 1838–39 because the river was choked with floes: not frozen enough to walk on, too full to ferry. They waited on the bank, in December, and people died waiting for a river to make up its mind. And the Cherokee were not a people without institutions to appeal to: they had **Sequoyah's syllabary** — one man invented a writing system from nothing in about twelve years, and within a decade the nation was more literate than the states around it — a newspaper, a constitution, and a Supreme Court judgment in their favour. **None of it mattered.** Junctions AW-084 at New Echota, AW-048 and AW-311 at Nashville, AW-253 at Cape Girardeau.

routes.name: The Mississippian Exchange (Spiro–Cahokia–Etowah)
routes.note: **THE MOST IMPORTANT ARCHAEOLOGICAL FIND IN NORTH AMERICA WAS STRIP-MINED BY A COMMERCIAL COMPANY AND THEN DYNAMITED.** At Spiro the Craig Mound had a sealed hollow chamber — an air pocket, which is why the organics survived — packed with textiles, feathers, copper plates, pearls, engraved shell. In 1933 a company leased the mound, tunnelled in, and sold the contents by the basket for four years. **Then they blew up what was left with dynamite** on their way out. Almost everything we know about it is reconstructed from what collectors happened to keep. And what was in there is this route: **copper from Lake Superior** (AW-305), whelk shell from the Gulf, obsidian from the Rockies, flint from Illinois, all in one Oklahoma mound. The Southeastern Ceremonial Complex ran the same iconography from Oklahoma to Georgia — the same falcon-man, the same bi-lobed arrow, the same forked eye — across a thousand miles of chiefdoms that never had a single ruler. Tier C by the AW-090 standard: inferred from where the goods end up. Junctions AW-265 at the Arkansas, AW-253 at Cahokia.

routes.name: The Lower Creek Trading Path (Charleston–Coweta)
routes.era: the deerskin trade, c.1680–1760
routes.note: **FIFTY THOUSAND DEERSKINS A YEAR WALKED UP THIS ROAD, AND THE DEBT THEY WERE BOUGHT WITH STARTED A WAR.** Charleston's economy in the early 1700s was deerskin, and the mechanism was credit: traders advanced guns and cloth against next season's hides, the Creek and Yamasee hunted to pay it, the deer thinned, the debt grew, and the traders began taking people instead — seizing wives and children against arrears and selling them. **In 1715 the Yamasee War began by killing the traders**, in one coordinated morning across the whole frontier, and it nearly ended South Carolina as a colony. The road is older than the trade: Ocmulgee on it is a Mississippian mound centre from AW-321, then a Creek town, then a trading post, all on the same ground. Junctions AW-085 the Occaneechi Path at Augusta and AW-321 at Ocmulgee.

routes.name: El Camino Real de Florida (St. Augustine–Apalachee)
routes.era: the mission chain, c.1600–1704 — destroyed in two years
routes.note: **A ROAD OF A HUNDRED MISSIONS, AND IT WAS ERASED IN TWENTY-FOUR MONTHS.** The Spanish strung missions across northern Florida on the old Timucua and Apalachee paths — four hundred kilometres, some hundred stations, tens of thousands of people living in them by 1650. Then in 1702–04 James Moore came down from Carolina with a few dozen Englishmen and a thousand or more Creek allies and destroyed the lot: burned the missions, killed and enslaved perhaps ten or twelve thousand people, and carried the survivors north to sell. **The Timucua ceased to exist.** Not declined — ceased: a language and a people with a written grammar (a Spanish friar published one in 1614, the first grammar of any indigenous language of what is now the United States) were gone inside a generation. Some Apalachee walked to Louisiana and their descendants are still there, which is the only thread of it left. Tier C: the mission sites are excavated, the road between them is corridor. Flagged `sensitive`.

routes.name: The Nuxalk-Carrier Grease Trail (Bella Coola–the Fraser)
routes.era: pre-contact; Mackenzie walked it in 1793
routes.note: **A ROAD NAMED AFTER ITS TOURIST.** This is the grease trail proper — AW-088's note calls the Chilkoot one and this is its southern cousin, and the commodity is the same: EULACHON, a smelt so oily you can dry one, put a wick in it, and burn it as a candle. It runs up these rivers in spring in numbers that turn the water black, and the coastal nations rendered the oil and traded it inland, in boxes, along fixed routes with owners and tolls. Grease was the Pacific Northwest's currency and its butter. **And in July 1793 Alexander Mackenzie walked this trail to the Pacific and became the first European to cross North America north of Mexico — twelve years before Lewis and Clark — guided the entire way, on a road with a name, camps, protocols and a price.** He wrote on a rock at the end: *Alexander Mackenzie, from Canada, by land, the twenty-second of July, one thousand seven hundred and ninety-three.* The rock is still there. **The trail is now officially the Alexander Mackenzie Heritage Trail.** Junctions nothing — it is its own country's road, and it did not need to.

routes.name: The Frankincense Road of Dhofar (Salalah–Shabwa)
routes.era: c.1000 BC – 3rd c. AD; Ubar found by satellite in 1992
routes.note: **THE LEGEND SAID THE CITY WAS SWALLOWED BY THE EARTH. IT WAS — INTO A SINKHOLE.** Boswellia sacra grows properly in one place on Earth: the Nejd behind the Dhofar mountains, where the monsoon dies and the desert starts. Rome burned the resin by the tonne — Pliny reckoned Arabia's incense trade at a hundred million sesterces a year and complained about it, as he complained about the pepper — and this is the road it left on, north across the sand to Shabwa, where AW-019 the Incense Road takes it to Gaza. UBAR is the story. The Quran has Iram of the Pillars, a city destroyed for its arrogance and buried; Thomas heard of it, Thesiger looked for it, Lawrence called it the Atlantis of the Sands. In 1992 Nicholas Clapp's team used **satellite radar to trace the caravan tracks** — thousands of years of camel traffic compacts the sand and it shows on the image — and watched them converge on a spot at Shisr. They dug, and found a fort that had **collapsed into a limestone cavern beneath it.** Tier C: the identification with Ubar is argued and the site is certainly a caravan stop. Junctions AW-019 at Shabwa.

routes.name: The Comoros Route (Kilwa–Madagascar)
routes.era: Austronesian arrival c.500 AD; the Swahili trade after
routes.note: **MADAGASCAR SPEAKS BORNEO, AND NOBODY IS ENTIRELY SURE HOW.** Malagasy is an AUSTRONESIAN language — its closest relative is Ma'anyan, spoken along the Barito river in southern BORNEO, seven thousand kilometres east across the whole Indian Ocean — and the people who brought it arrived around 500 AD with rice, bananas, outriggers and the xylophone. That crossing is a DISPERSAL and this layer does not draw those; what it draws is what came after, which is this: the Comoros stepping-stones between the Swahili coast and Madagascar, and eight hundred years of two-way trade along them — rice and gum and cattle and enslaved people west, cloth and beads and Islam east. The Comoros are the hinge, half Bantu and half Malagasy and wholly Swahili, and they exist as a place because they sit in the gap. Junctions AW-072 at Kilwa. Tier C — the trade is certain, the sailing line is inference.

routes.name: The Mataram Road (Borobudur–Gresik)
routes.era: Sailendra and Mataram, 8th–10th c.; the court moved east c.929 and nobody knows why
routes.note: **THEY BUILT THE LARGEST BUDDHIST MONUMENT ON EARTH AND THEN WALKED AWAY FROM IT.** Borobudur is two million blocks, a stone mandala you climb through in a spiral past sixteen hundred metres of carved narrative, finished around 825. Prambanan, Hindu, enormous, is **seventeen kilometres away and the same generation** — two of the greatest religious buildings in Asia, different faiths, one plain, built by neighbours in the same lifetime, which is either tolerance or competition and the inscriptions do not say. And then, around 929, the whole court simply MOVED — east, to the Brantas — and the Kedu plain was abandoned. Volcano, plague, politics, trade: nobody knows. Borobudur went under ash and jungle and was forgotten so completely that Raffles had to be told it existed in 1814 by locals who had always known. Junctions AW-054 the Maritime Spice Route at Gresik. Tier C: the sites are certain, the road is corridor.

routes.name: The Chicago Portage (Lake Michigan–the Illinois)
routes.era: pre-contact; Jolliet saw what it was in 1673; the river reversed in 1900
routes.note: **JOLLIET SAW IT IN 1673 AND SAID IT OUT LOUD: DIG HALF A LEAGUE HERE AND YOU JOIN THE LAKES TO THE GULF.** This is the shortest and most consequential carry in North America — a couple of kilometres of wet ground between the Chicago River, which reaches the Atlantic, and the Des Plaines, which reaches the Gulf. In a wet spring you paddled straight over it. In a dry one you waded MUD LAKE, which every account describes with loathing: leeches, mud to the waist, and men dragging canoes through it for a day. **Then they did what Jolliet said.** The Illinois & Michigan Canal opened in 1848, and Chicago went from a village to the second city of a continent in one generation. And in 1900 they went further and **REVERSED THE CHICAGO RIVER** — it now flows AWAY from Lake Michigan, because the city was drinking its own sewage and the cheapest fix was to make the water run the other way. So the Great Lakes now drain to the Gulf through a ditch. **And the ditch is a biological corridor between two watersheds that had been separate since the ice** — which is why there is an electric barrier in it now, humming, to stop carp using the road Jolliet described. Junctions AW-086 the Sauk Trail and AW-329 at Chicago.

routes.name: The Lake Michigan Shore Trail (Green Bay–Chicago)
routes.era: pre-contact Potawatomi, Menominee and Ho-Chunk route
routes.note: **MILWAUKEE'S ANSWER, AND THE NAME IS THE ARGUMENT.** Millioke — the good land, or the gathering place by the waters, depending on which Algonquian reading you take, and both fit: THREE RIVERS meet there, the Milwaukee, the Menomonee and the Kinnickinnic, and people gathered where they met, which is what a confluence does. This is the west-shore trail joining two things this layer already had: the Fox–Wisconsin portage at Green Bay, which is the door between two oceans, and Chicago, which is the other door. So the lake's west shore is the strip of land between two continental gateways, and Milwaukee is halfway along it. Potawatomi, Menominee, Ho-Chunk and Ojibwe all used it and none of them owned it exclusively. Junctions AW-143 at Green Bay and AW-086/AW-328 at Chicago.

routes.name: The Grand River Trail (Detroit–Grand Haven)
routes.era: pre-contact Odawa route; Hopewell mounds at the rapids
routes.note: **GRAND RAPIDS'S ANSWER IS THE RAPIDS, AND PEOPLE WERE BURYING THEIR DEAD BESIDE THEM TWO THOUSAND YEARS AGO.** Michigan's lower peninsula has two Indigenous trunk roads across it: AW-086 the Sauk Trail in the south, and this one through the middle, following the Grand — the state's longest river — from Detroit to Lake Michigan. The rapids are the reason for the town: a fall of about five metres over a couple of kilometres, which stops boats and concentrates fish, and the STURGEON ran there, which are enormous and were worth a season's work. The **Norton Mounds** beside them are Hopewell, roughly 200 BC to 400 AD — so this is not a fur-trade site with a deep past, it is a ceremonial centre with a fur trade laid on top, and the mounds are the older claim. Junctions AW-086 at Detroit.

routes.name: The Great Hopewell Road (Newark–Chillicothe)
routes.note: **NINETY KILOMETRES, DEAD STRAIGHT, BETWEEN TWO PARALLEL WALLS — AND THE THING AT ITS END WAS A GOLF COURSE UNTIL 2024.** The Newark Earthworks are the largest geometric earthworks on the planet: the Octagon alone encloses twenty hectares, enough for four Colosseums, and Hively and Horn showed in 1982 that it is a **LUNAR OBSERVATORY** — all eight alignments of the 18.6-year lunar standstill cycle, built into the walls, by people with no writing and no metal. From it, Lepper argued, ran this: a walled avenue sixty metres wide, ruler-straight, to Chillicothe. Segments show in aerial survey and LiDAR; the full run is inferred, which is why this is tier C. **A road that does not go anywhere useful.** It connects two ceremonial centres and ignores the terrain, so it is not transport — it is procession, and the straightness is the message. And the ending: the Octagon was leased to **Moundbuilders Country Club** and played as a golf course for a century. Ohio took it back by eminent domain, the state Supreme Court upheld it in 2022, UNESCO listed it in 2023, and the golfers finally left in 2024. Junctions AW-087 at the Great Miami reach — not claimed; the note says so.

routes.name: The Hopewell Interaction Sphere (Obsidian Cliff–Newark)
routes.note: **A HUNDRED AND FORTY KILOGRAMS OF YELLOWSTONE OBSIDIAN, TWO THOUSAND FOUR HUNDRED KILOMETRES FROM YELLOWSTONE, AND NO STATE ANYWHERE IN THE STORY.** The Hopewell Mound Group in Ohio held obsidian that isotope work traces to **Obsidian Cliff** specifically — a single outcrop in what is now Yellowstone, which AW-051 the Old North Trail already passes within eighteen kilometres of. Somebody went and got it. Not traded down a chain, probably: the quantity and the un-worked cores argue for expeditions. And it is not alone — the same mounds hold **grizzly teeth from the Rockies, mica from North Carolina, copper from Lake Superior** (AW-305), **shark teeth and whelk from the Gulf, and meteoric iron.** All of it worked into ceremonial objects, most never used, much of it deliberately broken and buried. **There was no Hopewell empire.** No cities, no kings, no armies, no writing — archaeologists call it an interaction sphere because they cannot call it a state. A continent's worth of material moved for two thousand years, on foot, with no wheel and no pack animal, for ritual. Tier C by the AW-090 standard.

routes.name: The Hayes River Route (York Factory–Fort Garry)
routes.era: Cree route; the HBC's main line from 1684
routes.note: **THEY SAT STILL FOR NINETY YEARS AND IT WORKED UNTIL SOMEBODY ELSE MOVED.** The Hudson's Bay Company's whole strategy was this river backwards: plant a warehouse at York Factory on the edge of an inland sea, and let the Cree bring the furs OUT to you. It is a stupendously lazy business model and it was brilliant — the Cree became the middlemen, ran the interior trade themselves, and the Company never had to leave the beach. Joseph Robson published the line that stuck in 1752: the HBC had **'slept at the edge of a frozen sea'** for eighty years. Then the Montreal pedlars — the North West Company — went inland and simply intercepted the canoes before they got to the bay, and the model collapsed. The HBC had to move: Cumberland House, 1774, its first inland post, ninety years after the charter. The route itself is the Cree's: up the Hayes, over the height of land, down to Lake Winnipeg and the Red. Junctions AW-063/AW-065/AW-256 at Fort Garry — which makes that node the hub of four cart roads and a river.

nodes.n: York Factory (the warehouse on the beach)

routes.name: The Wabanaki Coast Path (Shawmut–Cushnoc)
routes.era: millennia; the Great Dying 1616–19
routes.note: **THIS CORRECTS ME.** I wrote in B25 that Portland was honestly off the map because 'a harbour is where roads END' — and that is a walker's assumption, and specifically a settler's. **For the Wabanaki the coast IS the road.** You go by canoe, inside the islands, on protected water the whole way from Massachusetts Bay to the Kennebec; Casco Bay alone has some two hundred islands and you can reach Machigonne — the Portland peninsula — without ever crossing open sea. A harbour is not a terminus on this road. It is a node. Portland is on the map now because I was measuring the wrong thing. **And the road's darkest fact is what was NOT on it.** Between 1616 and 1619 an epidemic — the pathogen is still argued — killed perhaps three-quarters to nine-tenths of the coastal Wabanaki, **before the Mayflower.** The Pilgrims landed in 1620 into an emptied country, took a village site called Patuxet whose people had died three years earlier, and farmed their cleared fields. Squanto was a Patuxet: he had been kidnapped, taken to Europe, and came home to find that everyone he knew was dead. **That is why he spoke English, and why there was room.** Junctions AW-213/AW-216 at Boston and AW-144 at Cushnoc.

routes.name: The Merrimack (Newburyport–Franconia)
routes.era: Pennacook fish weirs; Lowell 1823; Manchester 1838
routes.note: **THE AMERICAN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION BEGAN BY DAMMING THE FISH WEIRS, AND IT IS NAMED AFTER THEM.** The Pennacook's river ran salmon, shad and alewives in numbers that supported permanent villages at the falls — and the great falls are called **AMOSKEAG**, which is a Pennacook word meaning roughly *place of many fish*. Then Lowell was built on Pawtucket Falls in 1823 and Manchester on Amoskeag in 1838, and the **Amoskeag Millyard became the largest cotton-mill complex on Earth** — a mile and a half of brick, thirty thousand workers — sitting on top of the weir it is named for, with the fish gone. Passaconaway, the Pennacook sachem, kept the peace for forty years and told his people at the end of his life not to fight the English because they could not win, which was correct and did not help. Junctions AW-334 at the mouth.

routes.name: The Penobscot (the Bay–Katahdin)
routes.era: millennia; Panawahpskek continuously inhabited; the river's status litigated to 2021
routes.note: **A NATION NAMED AFTER A RIVER WAS TOLD THE RIVER IS NOT THEIRS.** The Penobscot Nation has lived at Panawahpskek — Indian Island — without a break for as long as anyone can establish, and their name, their identity and their reservation are all the river. In 2012 they went to court over what the reservation actually is; in 2021 the First Circuit ruled en banc that it is **the islands only — not the water between them.** They are a river people whose reservation legally stops at the waterline. KATAHDIN is at the head of it: *the greatest mountain*, where Pamola lives, and the Penobscot did not climb it, which is not superstition but a different idea about what a summit is for. Thoreau went up in 1846 and came down badly shaken, and wrote the passage about matter, vast, titanic — *Contact! Contact! Who are we? where are we?* — which is the closest that literature gets to admitting the mountain was not impressed.

routes.name: The Four Lakes Trail (Portage–Teejop–Aztalan)
routes.era: effigy mounds 700–1200 AD; Aztalan c.1100
routes.note: **MADISON WAS MY ERROR AND THIS FIXES IT.** I wrote in B21 that Madison sits on no ancient road because it is 'an 1836 planned capital'. That is true about the CITY and it is not a statement about the PLACE. The Ho-Chunk call it **TEEJOP** — four lakes — and the isthmus between Mendota and Monona carries one of the densest concentrations of EFFIGY MOUNDS anywhere: bird, bear, panther and water-spirit shapes, built between about 700 and 1200 AD, in the hundreds. **The University of Wisconsin is standing on some of them.** Wisconsin had perhaps fifteen to twenty thousand mounds and something like eighty per cent were ploughed out; the survivors are mostly here, on the lakes. This trail is the corridor they sit on — from the Fox–Wisconsin portage down the Yahara chain to the Rock, and AZTALAN at the far end is a **Mississippian** town with a stockade and platform mounds, a northern outpost of the Cahokia world (AW-321) sitting in effigy-mound country. Tier C: the mounds and the towns are certain, the line between them is inferred. **The lesson is the one Portland taught and I did not generalise: a late colonial founding says nothing about the ground.** Junctions AW-143 at Portage.

routes.name: The Opimihaw Road (Wanuskewin–the South Saskatchewan)
routes.era: **c.4000 BC – the present** — six thousand years without a break
routes.note: **SASKATOON WAS MY ERROR TOO.** I wrote in B49 that Saskatoon is 'an 1883 temperance colony, younger than the trail and beside it, not on it.' True, irrelevant, and I should have looked six kilometres north. **WANUSKEWIN** — Cree, roughly *seeking peace of mind* — has been in continuous use for about **six thousand years**: nineteen sites in one coulee, bison jumps, pounds, tipi rings, boiling pits, and a MEDICINE WHEEL, used by Cree, Assiniboine, Blackfoot, Atsina and Dakota, none of whom owned it and all of whom came. It is longer-occupied than Stonehenge, than the Pyramids, than anything in Britain — and it sits on the edge of a city whose founding date I quoted as if that settled the matter. In 2019 the bison came back after a hundred and fifty years, and within two years they had exposed **petroglyphs nobody knew were there** by rubbing on the rocks the way bison do. **The animals found the archaeology.** Tier C: the sites are excavated and certain, the corridor is the coulee and the river. Junctions AW-256 the Carlton Trail at Clarke's Crossing.

routes.name: The Nisenan Trans-Sierra Trail (the Valley–the Washoe)
routes.era: pre-contact; the emigrant road and the railway followed it
routes.note: **ROSEVILLE AND DAVIS: MY ERROR, TWICE.** I wrote in B25 that they are 'railroad towns, 1864 and 1868, and sit on no ancient road', and again that was a fact about the townsite deed and not about the country. The valley floor between the Sacramento and the Sierra foothills was **Nisenan** and **Patwin** and it was not empty: it was one of the most densely populated non-agricultural landscapes on Earth, living on acorns — which is farming by another route, since an oak grove is a crop you tend and do not plant. This is the road they used east: up the American and the Bear to the crest and over to the **WASHOE** of the Great Basin, trading acorns and shell for pinenuts and obsidian, both ways, every year. The emigrant trail took it in the 1840s, the railroad took it in 1868, and Roseville is a junction on the railway that is on the trail. **The road was there. The town is what arrived.** Junctions AW-161 the Siskiyou Trail at Sacramento. Tier C by the AW-090 standard.

routes.name: The Bengaluru Road (Mysore–Bengaluru–Kanchipuram)
routes.era: **the Begur inscription names Bengaluru c.890 AD** — six centuries before the fort
routes.note: **BANGALORE: MY ERROR, AND THE EVIDENCE IS CARVED IN STONE.** I said twice that Bangalore is 'a 1537 foundation' and left it off. Kempe Gowda built his mud fort in 1537; the NAME is six hundred years older. The **Begur inscription** — a hero-stone at the Nageshwara temple in what is now south Bengaluru — records a battle and calls the place **Bengaluru**, in Hallegannada, around 890 AD. It is sitting in the city. This road is the corridor it sits on: from **Talakad**, the Western Ganga capital on the Kaveri, up through the Bengaluru plateau to **KOLAR**, whose gold has been dug since antiquity and which is one of the deepest mines ever worked — the Champion Reef went past three kilometres and was so deep and hot that they used it to hunt neutrinos, because the rock overhead screens cosmic rays. **A road between a dead capital and a gold mine that became a physics laboratory.** Tier C: the corridor is real and the alignment is inferred. Junctions AW-314 the Char Dham at its Mysore reach — not claimed; the note says so. **EXTENDED, BECAUSE THE FIRST DRAFT WAS AN ISOLATE.** I fixed the 'Bangalore is a 1537 foundation' error and replaced it with a road that touched nothing — a dead capital to a gold mine, connected to no other route in the layer, which is its own kind of wrong: a place that trades with nowhere is not a place. It now runs west to MYSORE on AW-314 the Char Dham and east to KANCHIPURAM on AW-204, which is the real geography: Kolar's gold went to the Tamil country — **Rajendra Chola took these fields in the 11th century** and the Cholas did not march 300 km uphill for the scenery. Bengaluru sits on the road between a Ganga capital and a Pallava one, which is why there was a battle there worth carving into a stone in 890 AD.

nodes.n: Bengaluru (the name is older than the fort)

routes.name: The South Saskatchewan (the Forks–Wanuskewin–the North Branch)
routes.era: millennia; Wanuskewin from c.4000 BC; Batoche 1885
routes.note: **WANUSKEWIN NEEDED THIS AND I HAD NOT DRAWN IT.** B67 put Wanuskewin on the map and left it on ONE road, which is wrong for a place five nations came to — Cree, Assiniboine, Blackfoot, Atsina, Dakota — for six thousand years. A gathering place is a CROSSROADS by definition, and the other road is the water: the South Saskatchewan runs past the coulee, and the coulee is there **because** the river is. That is the whole logic of a bison jump: you need a river for water, a coulee for shelter, and a cliff for the drop, and Opimihaw has all three within a kilometre. The river also carries the ending. **BATOCHE** is on it — the Métis village where the 1885 resistance was broken, on the same water, forty kilometres from a place people had been coming to since before the Pyramids. Junctions AW-256 the Carlton Trail at Clarke's Crossing and Batoche, and AW-338 at Wanuskewin — which makes Wanuskewin a two-route node, and it should be.

routes.name: The Rock River (Aztalan–the Mississippi)
routes.era: Mississippian at Aztalan c.1100; Sauk at Saukenuk to 1832
routes.note: **THIS IS WHY AZTALAN IS WHERE IT IS.** A Mississippian stockaded town with platform mounds, three hundred kilometres north of Cahokia in effigy-mound country, makes no sense until you draw the water: the Rock runs from Aztalan's doorstep to the Mississippi at Rock Island, and Cahokia is downstream from there. **Aztalan is not an outpost in the wilderness. It is a port.** And the river's other end carries the ending: **SAUKENUK**, the Sauk town at the mouth, was one of the largest settlements in North America in 1800 — several thousand people, hundreds of lodges, fields worked for generations — and in 1832 Black Hawk came back across the Mississippi to plant corn in it and was pursued for four months, up the Rock, past Teejop, to the Bad Axe, where the fleeing survivors were shot in the water while trying to surrender. **The road home was the road they were destroyed on.** Junctions AW-337 at Aztalan and AW-253 at Rock Island.

routes.name: The Humboldt (the Carson Sink–Fort Hall)
routes.era: Northern Paiute and Shoshone; the California Trail 1841–69
routes.note: **THE ONLY RIVER THAT CROSSES THE GREAT BASIN, AND IT GOES NOWHERE.** The Humboldt runs west for five hundred kilometres and then simply stops — evaporating into the HUMBOLDT SINK, a marsh in a desert with no outlet to anywhere. There is nothing else: it is the one through-line across six hundred kilometres of basin and range, which is why AW-339's Sierra road had nothing to connect to until now. The emigrants called it **the most hated river in the West** — alkaline, shrinking, undrinkable by the end — and then it delivered them to the FORTY MILE DESERT, the stretch from the Sink to the Carson with no water at all. One 1850 tally of that stretch counted **1,061 dead mules, 5,000 dead horses, 3,750 dead oxen and 953 graves**, in forty miles. **And the Northern Paiute lived there and were fine.** LOVELOCK CAVE on this line gave up a bundle of DUCK DECOYS — tule reed, feathered, painted, about two thousand years old, the oldest decoys known anywhere — left in a cave by people who hunted a marsh that emigrants would later die beside. The road was never the problem. Knowing it was the whole thing. Junctions AW-339 at the Carson valley and AW-318 the Snake at Fort Hall.

nodes.n: The Raft River (the parting of the ways)

routes.name: The Clamshell Bead Road (Bodega–the Sierra)
routes.era: pre-contact; the currency of central California
routes.note: **CALIFORNIA HAD A CURRENCY, A MINT AND A STANDARD, AND NO STATE ANYWHERE.** Clamshell disk beads — Saxidomus, from the beds at Bodega and Tomales — were MONEY across central California: drilled, ground round on a slab, strung, and valued by the length of the string against a man's arm or hand. The **Pomo made them**, and made them to a standard — diameter, thickness, bore — because a currency that is not standard is not a currency. They also held the high-value issue: **MAGNESITE** from one source near Clear Lake, baked until it turns orange-red, cut into cylinders, and worth many strings of clam. Call it what it is: a mint, a reserve commodity, and a monetary policy, run by people with no king, no writing and no agriculture. The road ran the beads inland and brought back obsidian, acorns, salt and salmon — which is why AW-339's Nisenan could reach the Washoe with something worth having. Kroeber thought this the densest non-farming population in North America and it ran on shells. Tier C by the AW-090 standard: the beds, the sources and the finds are certain; the corridor is inferred from where the money ends up. Junctions AW-161/AW-339 at Sacramento.

routes.name: The North Saskatchewan (Fort Edmonton–Lake Winnipeg)
routes.era: Cree route; Cumberland House 1774 — the HBC's first inland post
routes.note: **THE FUR TRADE RAN ON PEMMICAN, WHICH MEANS THE BUFFALO FED THE CANOES.** A brigade cannot hunt and paddle at the same time, so the whole northern trade was fuelled by dried meat and fat pounded together on the plains and shipped down this river in bags — and the moment you see that, the Prairies stop being a place the fur trade crossed and start being its engine room. It got ugly exactly as you would expect: in 1814 Red River banned pemmican exports, the North West Company took that as a declaration of war on their food supply, and the **Pemmican War** followed. **CUMBERLAND HOUSE on this line is where AW-333's story ends.** The HBC slept at the edge of a frozen sea for ninety years, letting the Cree bring furs out to the bay — until the Montreal pedlars started intercepting them upstream, and in 1774 Samuel Hearne came inland and built this. The first post. Ninety years after the charter. **It is still inhabited, and it is the oldest continuously occupied settlement in Saskatchewan.** Junctions AW-256 at Fort Edmonton, AW-341 at the Forks, AW-333 at Norway House.

nodes.n: The Forks (the branches join) — junction AW-341

routes.name: The Milwaukee–Teejop Trail
routes.era: pre-contact Potawatomi and Ho-Chunk route
routes.note: **THREE WORLDS ON ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY KILOMETRES.** It starts at MILLIOKE, where three rivers meet on Lake Michigan; it passes AZTALAN, a stockaded Mississippian town that is a northern port of the Cahokia world; and it ends at TEEJOP, an isthmus covered in effigy mounds. Lake nation, Mississippian town, effigy-mound country — three quite different ideas about how to live, strung on a walk of a few days, and the road is the only reason we can say they knew about each other. WAUKESHA on it is a small joke at the Chicago Portage's expense: the Fox rises there and runs south to the Illinois and the Mississippi, so this is a **third door** between the Atlantic and Gulf drainages — a bad one, which is why nobody used it and everybody used AW-328. Junctions AW-329 at Milwaukee, AW-337/AW-342 at Aztalan, AW-337 at Teejop.

nodes.n: Waukesha (the Fox rises — the third door)

routes.name: The Connecticut (Saybrook–the Fourth Lake)
routes.era: millennia; the Deerfield captives walked up it in 1704
routes.note: **FOUR ROUTES IN THIS LAYER TOUCHED THIS RIVER AND NONE OF THEM WAS THIS RIVER.** AW-216 ends at Saybrook, AW-213 ends at Hartford, AW-214 ends at Springfield, AW-215 starts at Deerfield — four roads arriving at one water from four directions, and the water undrawn. Same error as the Mississippi and the Ganges and the Yangzi: I keep drawing the roads that meet a river and forgetting the river is the reason they meet. Quinnehtukqut, the long tidal river, is New England's spine. **BELLOWS FALLS has faces cut into the rock at the water** — Abenaki petroglyphs, undated, staring up from beside a salmon leap. **And the road runs both ways.** In February 1704 a French and Abenaki party took Deerfield and walked 112 captives up this frozen river to Canada; those who could not keep up were killed on the ice. Eunice Williams was seven. She was adopted, became Kanenstenhawi, married a Mohawk, and when her father came to redeem her **she would not go home** — and visited him later, in Mohawk dress, with her husband, and went back. Junctions AW-216 at Saybrook, AW-213 at Hartford, AW-214 at Springfield, AW-215 at Deerfield.

routes.name: The Mi'kmaq Coast (Passamaquoddy–Unama'ki)
routes.era: millennia; Basque contact from c.1500
routes.note: **THERE WAS A BASQUE–ALGONQUIAN PIDGIN BEFORE THERE WAS A COLONY.** Basque and Breton fishermen were working these waters from about 1500 — before Cartier, before any settlement — and they came back every summer for cod and whales, and they and the Mi'kmaq built a **trade language** out of it: a Basque-Algonquian pidgin, recorded in the 1500s and 1600s, with Basque words in Mi'kmaq mouths and Mi'kmaq grammar underneath. First contact in North America was not conquest. It was two groups of people who needed a vocabulary and made one. Mi'kma'ki is seven districts and Unama'ki (Cape Breton) is one; Kjipuktuk, the great harbour, is Halifax. The Bay of Fundy on this line has **the highest tides on Earth** — sixteen metres at Minas, which turns the shore into a road twice a day, and is a fact this layer already has a segment kind for. **And the treaties did not cede the land.** The Peace and Friendship Treaties of 1725–1779 are agreements not to fight; they contain no surrender. Canada's own Supreme Court said so in Marshall in 1999, and the fishery argument is still running. Tier C — the districts and the sites are certain, the coastal line is a corridor.

routes.name: The Wolastoq (the Bay of Fundy–the St. Lawrence)
routes.era: millennia; the Témiscouata portage; the Aroostook War 1838–39
routes.note: **A PEOPLE NAMED AFTER A RIVER, AND THE NAME MEANS BEAUTIFUL.** Wolastoq — the beautiful river — and the Wolastoqiyik are the people of it, which is the same construction as the Penobscot on AW-336 and a good deal more cheerful. It is also a THROUGH-ROAD, which is why it mattered to everyone else: up the Wolastoq to Madawaska, over the Témiscouata carry, and down to the St. Lawrence — so this is the inland route between the Atlantic seaboard and Quebec that does not touch the sea, and Britain spent the 1830s in a cold panic about who owned it. The **AROOSTOOK WAR** of 1838–39 was fought over exactly this corridor: two nations mobilised, a general was sent, nobody was killed, and it was settled by a line on a map — the only war in this layer whose casualty figure is zero. Grand Falls in the middle is twenty-three metres and stops everything, which is why there is a town there. Junctions AW-348 at Saint John and AW-264 at Rivière-du-Loup.

routes.name: The Turquoise & Macaw Road (Chaco–Cerrillos–Paquimé)
routes.era: c.900–1150 AD (Chaco); Paquimé's floruit 13th–14th c.
routes.note: **CHACO DRANK CHOCOLATE, AND THAT IS NOT A METAPHOR.** In 2009 Crown and Hurst tested the residue in Pueblo Bonito's cylinder jars and found **theobromine** — cacao, which grows two thousand kilometres south and cannot grow anywhere near New Mexico. Chaco also had scarlet MACAWS, which are Mesoamerican birds, and copper bells, which are Mesoamerican castings. Something was coming north. And something was going south: **CERRILLOS**, on this road, is the turquoise. Mt Chalchihuitl there is an open pit sixty metres across dug out with stone hammers, and Pueblo Bonito held perhaps two hundred thousand pieces of turquoise, nearly all of it from that hole. **PAQUIMÉ at the far end is the mechanism.** Casas Grandes has macaw PENS — adobe boxes with stone plug doors, and the skeletons of hundreds of birds — so somebody was breeding tropical parrots in the Chihuahuan desert and selling them north. Not a trickle down a chain: a business, with an aviary. Tier C by the AW-090 standard — the cacao, the birds, the bells and the turquoise are all certain, and the road between them is inferred from where they end up. Junctions AW-049 the Great North Road at Chaco and AW-047 at Albuquerque.

routes.name: The Comanchero Trail (Santa Fe–the Llano–the Three Forks)
routes.era: c.1750–1875; ended when the horses were shot
routes.note: **THE LLANO ESTACADO IS CALLED THE STAKED PLAIN BECAUSE COR0NADO'S MEN HAD TO DRIVE STAKES INTO IT TO FIND THEIR WAY BACK.** Eighty thousand square kilometres of grass so flat and featureless that a party could lose itself in a day; they navigated it by compass and by leaving markers, like sailors. And the people who owned it made an empire out of it. **Comanchería** ran the southern plains for a century and a half and forced Spain, Mexico, France and the United States to negotiate rather than conquer — and this is its trade road: COMANCHEROS, New Mexican Hispano and Pueblo traders, crossed the Llano with bread, tobacco and iron and came back with horses, hides and captives, which is the part nobody puts on the historical marker. It ran to the Wichita grass-house towns and on to the Three Forks. **And the ending is exact.** In September 1874 Mackenzie found the Comanche horse herd in PALO DURO — the one canyon in the Llano, their winter refuge — and shot **more than a thousand horses**. Not the people: the horses. They walked in to Fort Sill that winter. Tier C: the corridor is documented and the line is inferred. Junctions AW-047 at Santa Fe, AW-258/AW-265 at the Three Forks.

routes.name: The Columbia (Kettle Falls–Astoria)
routes.era: Wyam fished for 11,000+ years; drowned 10 March 1957
routes.note: **ELEVEN THOUSAND YEARS, DROWNED IN AN AFTERNOON, AND IT IS STILL DOWN THERE.** WYAM — Celilo Falls, the echo of falling water — was one of the longest continuously inhabited places in North America: people dipnetted salmon from wooden platforms slung out over the water, roped on so the current could not take them, for something over a hundred centuries. It was also the great MARKET of the Northwest — dentalia up from Vancouver Island, buffalo robes down from the plains, obsidian, baskets, slaves — the place the whole region came to. On **10 March 1957** The Dalles Dam closed its gates and the reservoir rose over it in about **four to six hours.** People stood on the banks and watched. The tribes were paid about $26.8 million. **The falls are intact under the water.** And it happened twice: KETTLE FALLS upstream, the other great fishery, went under Grand Coulee in 1940 — they held a three-day Ceremony of Tears — and Grand Coulee has **no fish ladder at all**, so it did not drown a fishery, it ended eighteen hundred kilometres of salmon river permanently. The Cascades on this line are a landslide that dammed the Columbia around 1450 AD, and the Klickitat kept the story: the Bridge of the Gods. Junctions AW-318 at the Snake confluence, AW-091 at Wallula Gap, AW-161 at Fort Vancouver.

nodes.n: The Cascades (the Bridge of the Gods)

routes.name: The Fraser (Mt Robson–the delta)
routes.era: millennia; Simon Fraser 1808; the Hells Gate slide 1913
routes.note: **A RAILWAY CREW TIPPED A HILLSIDE INTO IT IN 1913 AND THE SALMON HAVE NOT COME BACK.** Hells Gate is where the Fraser squeezes to about thirty-five metres and goes through at a speed that Simon Fraser, who ran it in 1808, described as something no man should ever attempt again — and the sockeye went up it anyway, in their millions, for as long as anyone can measure. Then in 1913 the Canadian Northern Railway blasted a cut above the canyon, dumped the spoil into the gorge, and **blocked the run.** The 1913 and 1914 returns collapsed and the Fraser sockeye has never recovered to what it was; fishways were finally built in the 1940s. LILLOOET upstream is the reason people were there: the canyon is a dry belt, the wind funnels through it, and you can **wind-dry salmon** there without smoke or salt — a natural food factory, which is why the Fraser Canyon held one of the densest populations north of Mexico. Junctions AW-324 the grease trail at Alexandria.

routes.name: The Nass & Skeena Grease Trails
routes.era: millennia; Delgamuukw 1997
routes.note: **THE ROADS ARE THE EVIDENCE, AND A COURT SAID SO.** These are the northern grease trails — eulachon oil from the Nass, the great spring fishery, carried inland by the Nisga'a, Gitxsan and Wet'suwet'en along fixed routes with owners, names and tolls, exactly as AW-088 and AW-324 describe further north and south. What makes this one different is what happened in a courtroom. In **Delgamuukw v. British Columbia (1997)** the Gitxsan and Wet'suwet'en brought their **adaawk** and **kungax** — formal oral histories, held and recited by named house groups, which describe the territories and the trails — and the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that **oral history is admissible evidence of title**, and must be given equal weight with written records. A trial judge had refused it. The Court said that was wrong. **The road here is not just a road: it is testimony**, and it is why the Nisga'a Treaty of 2000 exists. Tier C: the trails are described in the adaawk and mapped in outline; the surveyed line is not mine to draw.

routes.name: The Haida Canoe Road (SGang Gwaay–the Nass)
routes.era: millennia; the 1862 smallpox; Athlii Gwaii 1985
routes.note: **THE CANOE WAS THE EXPORT.** A Haida canoe is one red cedar log — felled, hollowed, then FILLED WITH WATER AND HOT ROCKS until the wood steams soft enough to spread the sides apart with thwarts, so the finished hull is wider than the tree it came from. Up to twenty metres, sixty people. The Haida sold them up and down the coast; the mainland nations bought Haida hulls the way you would buy a ship. It let them cross HECATE STRAIT — shallow enough in places that when wind opposes tide the sea stands straight up, and one of the genuinely dangerous stretches of water on Earth — to the Nass for eulachon grease, which is why this road ends where AW-354 begins. **SGang Gwaay's poles are being allowed to rot on purpose.** UNESCO listed the village; the Haida decided the mortuary poles should return to the ground as poles do, and refused to preserve them. A World Heritage Site is decaying by design because the people whose site it is said so. **And the 1862 horror is administrative.** Smallpox reached Victoria; the colonial authorities cleared the Indigenous camps at gunpoint and sent people home up the coast **while they were infectious.** Perhaps two-thirds of the Haida died. In 1985 at ATHLII GWAII the elders put themselves on a logging road on Lyell Island and were arrested one by one, oldest first, and that is why Gwaii Haanas exists. Tier C — the villages are certain and the sea lanes are inference. Flagged `sensitive`.

routes.name: The Salish Sea (Puget Sound–the Fraser)
routes.era: millennia; the reef nets; Boldt 1974
routes.note: **THEY BUILT AN ARTIFICIAL REEF OUT OF ROPE TO FOOL THE FISH INTO SWIMMING UP IT.** The Lummi reef net — sxwoʿleʼ — is unique on Earth: two canoes anchored abreast in a tidal channel with a net slung between them, and running out in front of it, **two long tapering lines hung with grass and cedar strips** that the salmon read as a rising sea floor. They follow the false bottom up, over the lip, into the net, and the crew lifts. It is not a trap and not a weir; it is a **hallucination**, engineered, and the sites were owned and inherited like farmland. Then in 1894 fish traps and canneries took the channels, the reef net grounds were bought out from under the families who held them, and by the 1930s it was nearly gone. **Boldt put it back.** In 1974 Judge George Boldt read the treaties — which reserve the right of taking fish 'in common with' the settlers — and ruled that in common with means **half**, and that the tribes are co-managers of the fishery. It was so unpopular the Ninth Circuit compared the backlash to Southern school desegregation. It stands. Junctions AW-091 at Puget Sound and AW-353 at the Fraser delta.

routes.name: The Yellowstone (Gardiner–Fort Union)
routes.era: millennia; Clark came down it in 1806
