routes.note: **THE LONGEST UNDAMMED RIVER IN THE LOWER FORTY-EIGHT — ELEVEN HUNDRED KILOMETRES, NOT ONE DAM.** Every other big American river in this layer has been stopped somewhere: the Columbia at Grand Coulee, the Missouri six times, the Chicago reversed outright. This one runs. And the best description of a country in this entire layer is about it — **ARAPOOISH** of the Crow, around 1830, and it is not poetry, it is a geography lecture: *The Crow country is a good country. The Great Spirit has put it exactly in the right place; while you are in it you fare well; whenever you go out of it, whichever way you travel, you fare worse.* Then he explains each direction — south is too hot, north too cold, east the water is bad, west the salmon are poor — and concludes that the Crow country is exactly in the right place. **He is describing a river valley as an argument.** POMPEYS PILLAR on it carries Clark's signature, cut in 1806, which is the only physical mark the expedition left on the landscape that is still there. Junctions AW-254 the Missouri at Fort Union, AW-051 at Livingston, AW-358 at Livingston.

routes.name: The Bozeman Trail (Fort Laramie–Virginia City)
routes.era: 1863–68; closed by treaty
routes.note: **THE ONLY WAR THE UNITED STATES LOST TO NATIVE AMERICANS, AND THIS ROAD IS WHAT IT WAS ABOUT.** Bozeman cut it in 1863 straight through the Powder River country — the best hunting ground the Lakota and Cheyenne had, guaranteed to them by treaty — to reach the Montana gold. The army built three forts to hold it. **Red Cloud closed it.** For two years nothing moved on it without being attacked; on 21 December 1866 Fetterman took eighty men out after a decoy and **not one came back**, the worst American defeat on the plains until the Little Bighorn ten years later. And in 1868 at Fort Laramie the United States **signed a treaty conceding**: abandon the forts, close the road, the Powder River country is unceded Indian territory. They did it. **As the garrisons marched out, the Lakota burned Forts Reno, Phil Kearny and C.F. Smith behind them** — the columns could see the smoke. Six years later Custer went into the Black Hills, found gold, and the same treaty was worth nothing (AW-317). **They won, in writing, and it lasted eight years.** Junctions AW-067 at Fort Laramie and AW-357 at Livingston.

routes.name: The Platte Road (the Forks–South Pass–Fort Hall)
routes.era: Pawnee earth-lodge country; ~400,000 emigrants 1841–69
routes.note: **THE WHOLE AMERICAN WEST OPENED BECAUSE OF ONE GENTLE SLOPE.** SOUTH PASS is the only place a wagon can cross the Continental Divide, and the astonishing thing about it is that **you cannot tell you are doing it** — a thirty-kilometre ramp of sagebrush so shallow that emigrants asked when they would reach the pass and were told they had crossed it that morning. Four hundred thousand people walked over the spine of a continent without noticing. The road to it is the Platte, which Twain's contemporaries called a mile wide and an inch deep, too thin to plough and too thick to drink — and which was the PAWNEE's river first, lined with earth-lodge towns. INDEPENDENCE ROCK is the register: five thousand names cut into a granite whaleback, and if you were not there by the Fourth of July you would meet snow. **The cholera is the part that gets left out.** In 1849–52 it ran up this road with the wagons and killed something like twenty thousand people; there are stretches where the graves average one to the mile. And the Pawnee, who lived on it, got the disease, lost the game to the traffic, were pushed by the Lakota from the north, and were removed to Indian Territory by 1875. Junctions AW-067/AW-358 at Fort Laramie, AW-318/AW-343 at Fort Hall.

routes.name: The Seaweed Road (the Chilean coast–Monte Verde)
routes.era: **c.14,500 BP** — the oldest route in the Americas by eight thousand years
routes.note: **THIS IS THE OLDEST ROAD IN THE AMERICAS AND IT IS MADE OF SEAWEED.** A peat bog at Monte Verde in southern Chile preserved what almost no site anywhere preserves — wood, cordage, hide, tent stakes, a child's footprint — and, in the hearths and chewed into quids, **NINE SPECIES OF SEAWEED.** They come from different shore habitats: open beach, rocky intertidal, estuary, some of them fifty to ninety kilometres away. That is not one lucky trip. That is somebody going to the coast, knowing which weed grows where, and coming back, routinely, **fourteen and a half thousand years ago.** Monte Verde is the site that killed Clovis-first: in 1997 a panel including the doctrine's fiercest defenders flew down, looked, and conceded, which is a rarer event in archaeology than a new date. Everything else in this layer's Americas is younger than this by a minimum of eight thousand years — AW-305's copper is 6000 BC, AW-338's Wanuskewin is 4000 BC. Tier C by the AW-090 standard, and it is the purest example of it: the road is inferred **entirely** from where the goods ended up, because the goods are algae and the road is gone.

routes.name: The Chavín Obsidian Road (Quispisisa–Chavín)
routes.note: **A TEMPLE BUILT AS A DISORIENTATION MACHINE, AND ITS SUPPLY LIST PROVES THE ROADS.** Chavín de Huántar is the first thing that was ever pan-Andean — not an empire, a CULT, drawing people from everywhere long before anyone conquered anything — and you can read its reach off the shelves. The obsidian is **QUISPISISA, five hundred kilometres south.** The Spondylus and Strombus are Ecuadorian, **fifteen hundred kilometres north** (AW-304). The cinnabar is Huancavelica. And what they came for is still there: underground galleries, no natural light, water channelled through the walls so the rock roars, ventilation shafts that carry sound the wrong way — and **conch trumpets found inside them**, tuned, whose acoustics in those corridors will not tell you where the sound is coming from. Add the San Pedro cactus carved on the walls, which is mescaline, and the whole building reads as **engineered**: darkness, noise you cannot locate, a drug, and at the centre the Lanzón, four metres of snarling granite you meet in the dark. Tier C — the sources are certain from geochemistry, the road between them is inference.

routes.name: The Watson Brake Road (Watson Brake–Poverty Point)
routes.era: **Watson Brake 3500 BC** — nineteen centuries before Poverty Point
routes.note: **THE OLDEST MONUMENTS IN THE AMERICAS WERE BUILT BY PEOPLE WITH NO CHIEFS, NO CROPS AND NO POTS.** Watson Brake is eleven mounds in an oval joined by a ridge, raised in Louisiana around **3500 BC** — older than Stonehenge, older than the Pyramids of Giza, and nineteen hundred years older than Poverty Point down the road at AW-305. And it breaks the rule it was supposed to obey. Monumental architecture was held to require agriculture, surplus and hierarchy; Watson Brake has **none of the three.** The builders were hunter-gatherers who came seasonally for fish and nuts, had no pottery, left no elite burials, and put up eleven mounds over roughly five centuries, a basket at a time, apparently because they wanted to. Nobody made them. There is no evidence anybody could have. Tier C: the two sites are excavated and certain, the road between them is the corridor. Junctions AW-305 at Poverty Point.

routes.name: The Green Obsidian Road (Pachuca–Teotihuacan–Kaminaljuyú)
routes.era: Teotihuacan, c.100–550 AD
routes.note: **YOU CAN TRACE AN EMPIRE BY THE COLOUR OF ITS GLASS.** Pachuca obsidian is golden-green — not grey, not black, GREEN — and it comes from one range, the Sierra de las Navajas, and Teotihuacan owned it. Something like nine tenths of the obsidian in that city is Pachuca, worked in workshops by the hundred. Which means that wherever a green blade turns up, Teotihuacan's hand was in it: at Kaminaljuyú, at Copán, and at **TIKAL**, a thousand kilometres away — where in **January 378 AD** a man named Siyaj K'ak' arrived from the west, and Tikal's king **died the same day**, and the next king was a boy whose father is named on the monuments as a lord of Teotihuacan. The stelae say it flatly and the archaeology agrees: green obsidian, Teotihuacan-style architecture, and a new dynasty, all at once. **A coup, dated to the day, visible in the rubbish.** Tier C by the AW-090 standard. Junctions AW-047/AW-236 at Tenochtitlan and AW-240/AW-242/AW-243/AW-244 at Kaminaljuyú.

routes.name: The Tiwanaku Caravan Road (Alca–Chivay–Tiwanaku)
routes.era: obsidian from c.3000 BC; Tiwanaku c.500–1000 AD
routes.note: **THE ANDEAN ANSWER TO TRADE WAS NOT TO TRADE. IT WAS TO OWN A PIECE OF EVERY ALTITUDE.** John Murra called it the VERTICAL ARCHIPELAGO and it is the most useful idea anyone has had about this continent: an Andean polity did not buy coastal fish and jungle coca and highland potatoes from strangers — it planted **colonies** at each altitude and staffed them with its own people, so a single community held land on the puna, in the valleys, on the coast and in the yungas, days apart, and moved goods between its own limbs. Not a market. **A supply chain with no counterparty.** So the roads here are internal, which is why this one runs llamas and not merchants: obsidian from ALCA and CHIVAY — Chivay's from a canyon twice the depth of the Grand Canyon — down to the Titicaca basin, in caravans of animals that carry thirty kilos each and will simply sit down if you load thirty-five. And COPACABANA at the end is the other half of the argument: Tiwanaku's andesite, in blocks over a hundred tonnes, came from there — **across the lake.** They moved them on reed boats, or by rafting them, ninety kilometres of open water at four thousand metres. Tier C by the AW-090 standard. Junctions AW-045 at Puno and Tiwanaku.

routes.name: The Baetis (Corduba–Sanlúcar)
routes.era: Tartessian metal trade from c. 1000 BC; the Roman oil road at industrial scale 1st–3rd c. AD
routes.note: WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: because Rome ate. The Via Augusta already touched Corduba, Hispalis and Gades and the layer drew all three as ROAD towns, which was the sixth version of the mistake recorded at _meta.water_rule — if several roads meet at a water, the water is why. The Baetis was the artery and the road was the tributary. Baetican olive oil moved in Dressel 20 amphorae on lyntres, shallow skiffs that could work the river and be walked on tow-ropes at low water, and the sailing season fell February–April on the high water behind the December–February harvest. The attested stops between Corduba and Hispalis are eight on the right bank and four on the left, and the ones drawn here are the ones securely located. THE FINDING IS AT THE OTHER END AND IT IS NOT IN SPAIN: Monte Testaccio in Rome, a hill just over 40 m high covering 2.2 hectares, is made of the broken packaging — Dressel 20s that could not be reused because the walls were too thick and each carried its own shipping record painted on. A road is usually known by its roadbed. This one is known by a mountain of its own empties, 1,800 km away, and that mountain is why we can read the traffic year by year. Nodes marked v are Roman place-names attached to modern towns on scholarly attribution rather than epigraphy in situ; the coordinate is the modern town's. The river ends at Sanlúcar because the bar is where the river ends — the sea leg to Gades and on to Ostia is a different kind of road and is not drawn here.

routes.name: The Ebro (Logroño–the delta)
routes.era: Iberian, then Roman from the 2nd c. BC; rafts and barges working into the 20th c.
routes.note: WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: it is the only through-route across the northeast, and the mountains on both sides guarantee it. Pliny is unusually specific and the figure is the reason this route is tier B rather than C — the Ebro runs 450 miles and is navigable for ships for 260 of them, upstream from the town of Vareia. That fixes the head of navigation at Varea, now a district of Logroño, and everything below it is a road. Caesaraugusta was the redistribution hinge in the middle: grain, timber, iron, hides and linen coming down from the interior, wine, salt fish, ceramics, marble and jewellery coming up from the coast, with the port works running along the calm right bank beside the forum. Dertosa held the seam where the river met the Via Augusta and became a maritime-and-fluvial port in one. AND THE FINDING IS THE NAME: Pliny says it in the same sentence — because of this river the Greeks called the whole of Spain Iberia. Iberus, Hiber, Iberia. A peninsula named after a road. TWO DELIBERATE ABSTENTIONS. Varea and Logroño are drawn as separate nodes 2.7 km apart, not merged: Varea is the Roman river port and Logroño is the medieval bridge town, and collapsing them would fake a continuity nobody has shown. And the route stops at Amposta rather than running out through the delta, because the Ebro delta has prograded several kilometres seaward since Roman times and the ancient mouth is not the modern one — an unearned coordinate is worse than a short line.

nodes.n: Logroño (the Puente de Piedra) — junction AW-002
Celsa (Velilla de Ebro — the first stone bridge)
Mequinenza (the Segre and Cinca come in)

routes.name: Camino Primitivo (Oviedo–Lugo–Melide)
routes.era: from c. 814, when Alfonso II walked it; the busiest road to Santiago until the 11th c.
routes.note: THE ORIGINAL, AND THE LAYER DID NOT HAVE IT. Five caminos were drawn — Francés, Norte, Portugués, Vía de la Plata, Madrid — and the one Alfonso II actually walked was missing. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS, AND IT IS A MILITARY ANSWER RATHER THAN A DEVOUT ONE: in the early 9th century the mountains were the only ground in Christian hands. The obvious line from Oviedo to Compostela is the coast, and the coast was indefensible, so the first pilgrimage in Europe went over the Puerto del Palo at 1,146 m because the flat way was not safe. Every later camino is easier than the first one, which is the reverse of how these things usually go. Alfonso II was raised at the monastery of Samos in Lugo and followed Beatus of Liébana; when the tomb was reported he went to see for himself, confirmed it, built the first basilica and founded Antealtares — so the road is the verification trip that created the destination. His successor Alfonso III walked it twice. It stayed the main road for two centuries, until the capital moved to León and the crown began promoting the Francés instead. DRAWN TO MELIDE, NOT TO SANTIAGO: from Melide the Primitivo is the Francés, and drawing the last 54 km again would put two routes on one road and manufacture a junction out of an identity. Tier B not A — the stage towns are the historic ones and Hospital de Montouto was the chief mountain pilgrim hospital in Galicia, but this is not the node-by-node attested roster that tier A requires under _meta.tier_density_rule.

routes.name: Camino Inglés (Ferrol & A Coruña–Santiago)
routes.era: 12th–16th c.; heaviest before the Reformation closed the English traffic
routes.note: WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: because for an Englishman, a Scot, an Irishman or a Scandinavian the Pyrenees were the long way round and the Bay of Biscay was the short one. This is the landward tail of a SEA road — pilgrims sailed to Ferrol or A Coruña and walked the last hundred-odd kilometres, and the Tower of Hercules, still lit, is the Roman lighthouse that brought them in. TIER A, AND THE ATTESTATION IS A CHAIN OF HOSPITALS RATHER THAN A CHAIN OF MILESTONES: the hospitallers of Sancti Spiritus held houses at Ferrol, Neda, Miño, Paderne and Betanzos; the Franciscans opened at Pontedeume and Betanzos in the 14th century under Fernán Pérez de Andrade 'O Bo'; San Lorenzo at Bruma was founded in 1140 and absorbed into the Hospital of Santiago in 1175; the A Coruña arm had houses at Sigrás and Poulo. Under _meta.tier_density_rule tier A means every node attested, not a fixed spacing, and a pilgrim hospital is an attestation of a NIGHT — the spacing here is a day's walk because that is what built it. In 1147 a squadron of crusaders bound for the Holy Land put in and walked it. TWO ARMS, ONE ROUTE, joining at Hospital de Bruma, which is why a hospital stood there: it is where two roads become one and the traffic doubles.

nodes.n: Santiago de Compostela — junction AW-002, AW-023, AW-024

routes.name: Via Nova — Via XVIII, the Geira (Bracara Augusta–Asturica Augusta)
routes.era: built AD 79–80 under Vespasian and Titus; restored under Maximinus Thrax
routes.note: WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: gold. It links the two conventus capitals of the northwest, Bracara Augusta and Asturica Augusta, across 210 Roman miles of the worst country available, and it was cut in about a year by the legate C. Calpetanus Rantius Quirinalis Valerius Festus under Vespasian and Titus. The reason to take a road over the Serra do Gerês instead of round it is that Asturica sat at the head of the Las Médulas gold workings and Rome wanted the metal out. THE FINDING IS THE MILESTONES, AND IT IS AN ARGUMENT ABOUT ADVERTISING: the Via Nova carries one of the densest concentrations of milestones anywhere in the empire — hundreds of them, on a road with no Augustan pedigree at all. A road that new does not accumulate that many markers by accident. Milestones are imperial signature, and the emperor who has just taken power by civil war signs the most. Miles XXVII–XXXIV survive nearly intact inside the Peneda-Gerês national park with bridges and walls, and one at Campo do Gerês carries Domitian's name struck out under damnatio memoriae — the empire correcting its own road signs. ELEVEN MANSIONES are named in the Antonine Itinerary: Salaniana, Aquis Originis, Aquis Querquennis, Geminas, Salientibus, Praesidium, Nemetobriga, Foro, Gemestario, Bergidum, Interamnium Flavium. Only some are securely located; those are drawn, the rest are represented by the modern towns on their reach and flagged v. PONFERRADA IS DELIBERATELY NOT ON THIS ROUTE even though it sits in the middle of the Bierzo and is already a node on AW-002 — it takes its name from the iron bridge of 1082 and did not exist when this road was cut. Claiming that junction would have been a founding-date error running the other way: not a modern date hiding an ancient site, but a modern site borrowing an ancient road.

nodes.n: Vilar da Veiga (the Geira in the Gerês)
Aquis Querquennis (Baños de Bande — the mansio and camp)
A Rúa (the Foro reach, on the Sil)
Puente de Domingo Flórez (the Gemestario reach)

routes.name: Cañada Real Conquense (Sierra Morena–the Montes Universales)
routes.era: under the Mesta from 1273; still walked twice a year
routes.note: WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: grass ripens at different times at different altitudes, and a sheep cannot wait. The Montes Universales feed a flock in summer and bury it in November; Sierra Morena feeds it in winter and burns it dry in June. The cañada is the seam between two climates and the flock is the stitch. It runs about 400–450 km from the dehesas of Andújar and Linares in the Guadalquivir valley up over Sierra Morena and across La Mancha into the Serranía de Cuenca and the Sierra de Albarracín, and it is TODAY THE MOST WALKED DROVE ROAD IN SPAIN — the Belenchón family still take some three thousand sheep and two hundred cattle up and down it, roughly a month each way, twice a year. THE LAYER HAD ONE CAÑADA OUT OF NINE. That is the gap this fills, and it is not filled: seven more are still not drawn. TWO BRANCHES, ONE DESTINATION — at Castellar de Santiago the road forks to cross Sierra Morena, the western arm 'de los Serranos' by Villanueva de la Fuente and El Picazo, the eastern 'de los Chorros' by Alhambra and the Ruidera lagoons, and they knit back together at Tragacete. THE SEASONAL DIRECTION IS RECORDED HERE AND NOT IN THE SCHEMA, per _meta.bidirectionality_rule as ruled at v80-B80: this road runs north in June and south in November and it is one road. THE HONEST CAVEATS, THREE. Sources disagree on length, 400, 450 and 532 km, because a cañada is legally 90 varas (about 75 m) wide and braids around obstacles — it is a corridor, not a line, and the polyline here is its spine, not its edge. Sources also disagree on the name: some call the whole road 'de los Serranos', others reserve that for the western arm only, which is the naming collision that _meta.id_rule exists to survive. And it is tier B rather than A because the modern walked line is documented while the medieval one is not — the Mesta chartered a corridor, not a route. ONE NODE NEEDS ITS DATE SAYING OUT LOUD: La Carolina was founded in 1767, a Carlos III Enlightenment colony planted on Sierra Morena by Pablo de Olavide, and it is five centuries younger than the Mesta charter. It is drawn anyway, and _meta.founding_date_rule is why — the rule cuts both ways. A colonial founding date is not a statement about a site, and the site here is the Despeñaperros approach, which flocks were crossing long before anyone surveyed a grid town onto it. The town was planted ON the road. What would be wrong is to read La Carolina's date as evidence of the road's, in either direction.

nodes.n: Guadalaviar (the Tajo crossed near its source)

routes.name: The Douro (Barca de Alva–Porto)
routes.era: the wine trade from the 17th c.; demarcated 1756; rabelos worked it until the dams of the 1960s–70s
routes.note: WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: the wine is made where nothing else grows and drunk where it cannot be made. The upper Douro is schist, forty degrees in August, terraced by hand into a gorge — and the only way out was down the river, in a rabelo, a flat-bottomed boat with a huge stern sweep worked from a raised platform, carrying pipes of wine to the lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia. Gaia is where the wine ages because the estuary is cool and damp and the gorge is not; the region and its warehouse are two climates a hundred and fifty kilometres apart and the river is the ligament. THE FINDING IS A LAW: in 1756 the Marquês de Pombal drew a boundary around this valley and set up the Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro, marking the vineyards with 335 stone posts, the feitorias. That makes this the oldest demarcated and regulated wine region in the world — and the demarcation exists because the English merchants who bought the wine were being sold wine from elsewhere, so the boundary is a fraud-control measure that turned into a place. AND THE HAZARD IS DRAWN: the Cachão da Valeira, a rock choke below São João da Pesqueira that wrecked rabelos and killed crews, so cargo was carried round it until it was blasted open in the 1780s — after which the river above it became a road for the first time. It is a portage that stopped being one, which is the only node of its kind in the layer. Tier B: the ports are certain, the rabelo line is reconstructed from the wine trade rather than surveyed, and the dams have since drowned the working river.

nodes.n: Barca de Alva (the head of the rabelo run)
Cachão da Valeira (the choke, blasted in the 1780s)

routes.name: Camino Lebaniego (San Vicente de la Barquera–Santo Toribio)
routes.era: relics arrive 8th c. fleeing al-Andalus; jubilee privilege granted 1512; walked continuously
routes.note: FOUND BY ENUMERATION, NOT BY PROBING, AND THAT IS THE POINT. The Catholic Church recognises FIVE jubilee cities in the world — Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela, Santo Toribio de Liébana and Caravaca de la Cruz — and until this batch this layer had roads to Santiago and to nowhere else on that list. Santo Toribio probed at 30.8 km and looked nearly covered, but the nearest node was Llanes on the Camino del Norte, which passes along the coast above it on its way somewhere else. A DESTINATION IS NOT A ROAD. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: the monastery holds the Lignum Crucis, the largest surviving fragment of the True Cross, carried west out of Jerusalem by way of Astorga and hidden in the Picos de Europa when al-Andalus took the peninsula — the same mountains, and very nearly the same reason, that put the Camino Primitivo over the Puerto del Palo. The relic went where the armies could not follow. UNESCO inscribed this in 2015 as one of the four Routes of Northern Spain, and the layer had two of those four: Coastal and Primitivo. This is the third. It is 72.7 km from salt water to a mountain monastery and it runs SOUTH, off the Santiago road and away from it — pilgrims split from the Compostela traffic at Muñorrodero, yellow arrows one way and red the other. Tier A: every node here is a village on the waymarked historic line, and the two churches that matter are on it — Santa María de Lebeña, a 10th-century Mozarabic church built by Count Alfonso of Liébana, and Santo Toribio itself.

nodes.n: San Vicente de la Barquera — junction AW-023
Muñorrodero (the red arrows leave the yellow)
Santo Toribio de Liébana (the Lignum Crucis)

routes.name: Camino Vasco del Interior (Irún–Santo Domingo de la Calzada)
routes.era: pre-Roman pass, Jacobean from the 11th c.; grew after Alfonso VIII took Gipuzkoa c. 1200
routes.note: THE FOURTH UNESCO NORTHERN ROUTE, and the layer's last missing one. Also the Camino del Túnel de San Adrián, and the tunnel is the whole reason it exists. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: the Sierra de Aizkorri is a wall, and there is a hole in it. San Adrián is a natural cavern driven clean through the rock with a medieval calzada paved through it and a hermitage inside, and traders were using it two thousand years before any pilgrim did. Pilgrims called it the mouth of hell for its darkness, and one of them wrote that it was the highest point in the world, which it is not — but a man who has just climbed 835 m out of Zegama in the rain is entitled to his opinion, and the layer keeps it because an exaggeration recorded at the time is evidence about the walking. THE COASTAL ROUTE CAME FIRST AND THIS ONE TOOK THE TRAFFIC: when Gipuzkoa passed to Castile under Alfonso VIII around 1200 the crown planted fortified towns down the Oria — Tolosa, Ordizia, Segura — and the walled villas of the Llanada beyond, and a road with garrisons on it beat a road with pirates on it. Tier A, and the attestation is dense: the pilgrim hospital of Sancho de Urdanibia at Irún, San Juan Bautista at Oiartzun, San Martín de Tours at Zegama, the hermitage of San Julián y Santa Basilisa de Aistra at Zalduondo, Santa María at Vitoria, the humilladero at Briñas, Nuestra Señora de la Vega at Haro, the Santa Cruz hermitage at Bañares. A FORK IS RECORDED IN THE NOTE AND NOT DRAWN: at Estavillo the Vía de Bayona separates for Miranda de Ebro and Burgos and never rejoins. This route takes the Rioja arm through Haro to Santo Domingo, because that is the arm UNESCO inscribed and the arm the name belongs to. The Burgos arm is a real road and belongs in the queue as its own line, not as a phantom limb on this one.

nodes.n: Túnel de San Adrián (the hole in the wall)
Zalduondo (San Julián y Santa Basilisa de Aistra)
Santo Domingo de la Calzada — junction AW-002

routes.name: Camino de San Salvador (León–Oviedo)
routes.era: 9th c. onward, once Alfonso II's relic collection made Oviedo a destination in its own right
routes.note: THE ROAD THAT EXISTS BECAUSE OF A PROVERB. Medieval pilgrims said that whoever goes to Santiago and not to the Saviour visits the servant and forgets the Lord — quien va a Santiago y no al Salvador, visita al criado y olvida al Señor — and so a great many of them turned north off the Camino Francés at León, crossed the Cantabrian range, venerated the relics in the Cámara Santa at Oviedo, and came back down or carried on along the Primitivo. IT IS THE ONLY ROUTE IN THIS NETWORK THAT IS A DETOUR BY DESIGN. Everything else here is going somewhere; this one exists to make a longer road out of a shorter one, on theological grounds, and roughly 120 km and the Puerto de Pajares at 1,379 m is the price of not offending the Lord. It closes a triangle the layer could not previously close: AW-002 comes into León, AW-367 leaves Oviedo, and until now nothing joined them, which made the Primitivo look like it started from nowhere. Tier B rather than A — the corridor and the stage towns are secure and Pajares has been the crossing since Roman times, but this is not the node-by-node hospital roster that carried the Camino Inglés to tier A under _meta.tier_density_rule.

routes.name: Camino de Fisterra-Muxía (Santiago–the end of the land)
routes.era: pre-Christian sun-cult ground; Jacobean epilogue attested from the 12th c.
routes.note: THE ONLY CAMINO THAT RUNS AWAY FROM SANTIAGO, and the layer had every road in and none out. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS, AND THE HONEST ANSWER IS OLDER THAN THE CHURCH: Finisterre is finis terrae, the end of the earth, and people were walking out to watch the sun drown there long before anyone was buried at Compostela. The Ara Solis stood somewhere on that headland. The medieval pilgrim who kept walking west after the cathedral was finishing a journey the cathedral had been built across, not extending one — and the burning of clothes and the sea-bathing at the cape are the parts of the ritual that no one can find a Christian source for. THE LAYER'S OWN LOGIC DEMANDED THIS ONE: AW-002, AW-023, AW-024 and AW-368 all terminate at Santiago, four roads arriving and nothing leaving, which is the shape of a place that is only ever a destination. It is not one. TWO ARMS, DRAWN AS TWO SEGMENTS: the split at Hospital sends one line to Fisterra and the cape, the other north to Muxía and the Virxe da Barca, whose stone boat is said to be the one the Virgin sailed in — a shrine that is a boat, on the shore, at the end of a road. Many walk both, in either order, which is why the join is at Hospital and not at either end. Tier B: the waymarked line is certain and the stage towns are the historic ones, but the medieval alignment beyond Negreira rests on tradition more than on hospitals.

nodes.n: Santiago de Compostela — junction AW-002, AW-023, AW-024, AW-368
Cabo Fisterra (the Ara Solis, the burning of clothes)
Muxía (Virxe da Barca — the stone boat)

routes.name: El Camino de Sevilla al Rocío (the Romería)
routes.era: shrine attested from the 15th c.; the brotherhood road walked annually, now by roughly a million
routes.note: THE LARGEST PILGRIMAGE IN SPAIN AND THE LAYER HAD NO IDEA IT EXISTED. Found by enumeration; a probe would never have reached it, because El Rocío sits 41 km from the nearest node and that node is a river port on the Baetis. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: an image of the Virgin in a marsh, and the fact that getting to her is the point. Almonte's brotherhoods walk to the aldea at Pentecost with ox-drawn carts, and the road is not incidental to the devotion — it IS the devotion, which is why they walk it rather than drive the hour it would take. This is the Sevilla road, best known of the several, and the layer draws its spine: out of Triana, over the Aljarafe, across the Guadiamar at the Vado del Quema, into Villamanrique to salute the oldest brotherhood at the Magdalena, then along the Raya Real through the Coto del Rey and over the Ajolí, which the romeros call the gate of heaven. IT IS A CORRIDOR, NOT A LINE — the same problem as the Cañada Real Conquense at AW-370, and for the same reason. Different hermandades take different tracks across the Aljarafe and the Doñana pinewoods; the sources say plainly that the entry at the Ajolí is the ONLY point common to all of them. So the drawn line is the Sevilla hermandad's route and the note says so. THE ROAD RUNS ON PASTORAL RIGHTS-OF-WAY: the Cordel de Triana and the Cañada Real de los Isleños are drove roads, chartered for sheep, and the romería uses them because in Spain a vía pecuaria is public in perpetuity. A pilgrimage kept alive by grazing law. Tier B: the crossings and the towns are certain, the tracks between them are plural.

nodes.n: Ermita de Cuatrovitas (Bollullos de la Mitación)
Villamanrique de la Condesa (la Primera y Más Antigua)
Palacio del Rey (the Coto del Rey)
Puente del Ajolí (the gate of heaven)

routes.name: Camino de la Cruz (Orihuela–Caravaca de la Cruz)
routes.era: the Vera Cruz relic attested at Caravaca from 1231; jubilee granted in perpetuity 1998
routes.note: THE FIFTH JUBILEE CITY, AND THE LAST ONE THIS LAYER COULD NOT REACH. Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela, Santo Toribio de Liébana, Caravaca de la Cruz — five places in the world where the Church grants a Holy Year in perpetuity, and before B81 this layer had roads to exactly one of them. Santo Toribio was closed at AW-372. This closes Caravaca. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: a double-armed cross, said to have been brought by angels in 1231 so that a captive priest could say Mass before the Moorish lord Abu Zeyt, who converted on the spot. The relic is a fragment of the True Cross, as at Liébana, and the two Spanish jubilee cities therefore hold pieces of the same object at opposite ends of the peninsula — one in the Picos de Europa, one in the Murcian sierra, both put where armies would not easily come. THE ROUTE DRAWN IS THE PRINCIPAL ONE: roughly 120 km from Orihuela, following the Segura upstream and then turning northwest onto the old railway alignment through Mula and Bullas into the high country. Several other caminos converge on Caravaca and are NOT drawn here: a route from Cartagena and Mazarrón, one of about 60 km from Vélez Blanco past the sanctuary complex at La Encarnación, the 160 km Camino de San Juan de la Cruz over the Sierra de Segura, and a Templar road of nearly 900 km linking former Templar holdings through Pamplona, Artajona, Daroca, Teruel, Alcalá del Júcar and Jumilla. Each is its own line and each belongs in the queue. Drawing them as branches of this one would fake a network the sources do not describe. Tier B: the endpoints and the corridor are certain, the medieval alignment is not.

nodes.n: Caravaca de la Cruz (the Vera Cruz)

routes.name: Camino de Guadalupe (Toledo–the Real Monasterio)
routes.era: image venerated from 1340; royal patronage under Alfonso XI after Salado, 1340
routes.note: THE DESTINATION WAS ALREADY ON THE MAP AND THE ROAD WAS NOT — the false-negative pattern in its purest form. Guadalupe probed at 0.4 km and looked covered; the node was AW-037, the Cañada Real Soriana Occidental, a SHEEP ROAD that happens to pass the monastery on its way to Extremaduran winter pasture. See _meta.false_negative_rule. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: Spain's most venerated Marian shrine before Compostela's rival ever rose in the south, and a monastery that became the crown's own. Columbus came here to give thanks and named an island for it; the devotion crossed the Atlantic and the Virgin of Guadalupe at Tepeyac in Mexico takes her name from this one. That transmission is why this route matters to a layer that also intends to draw the Tepeyacac causeway: the same name at both ends of an ocean, carried by people who walked. TIER C, AND THE REASON IS HONEST: pilgrims came to Guadalupe from every direction and the caminos are today a signposted modern network rather than a single attested medieval line. What IS certain is that the shrine drew traffic off the Toledo road and that the approach ran through the Puerto de San Vicente into the Sierra de Villuercas. Anchors and the pass are drawn; the rest is not, on the same principle that stripped the shaping nodes off the King's Road at AW-062. If a documented medieval alignment turns up, this becomes tier B and gains nodes.

routes.name: Camino Sanabrés (Granja de Moreruela–Santiago)
routes.era: Mozarabic monastic foundations from the 10th c.; the Cistercians arrive 1143
routes.note: THE FORK IN THE VÍA DE LA PLATA THAT THE LAYER NEVER DREW. AW-025 came up from Mérida and ran on to Astorga to meet the Francés, and that is only half of what pilgrims did: at Granja de Moreruela the road splits, and the western arm cuts across Sanabria and the Galician sierras straight to Santiago, about 365 km, without ever touching the Francés at all. The layer had the junction town as a node and no second road leaving it. WHY THIS FORK EXISTS: the eastern arm is easier and joins the busiest road in Europe; the western arm is harder and stays alone, and people chose it anyway, which tells you the crowd was not always the attraction. THE ATTESTATION IS MONASTIC AND UNUSUALLY GOOD: Santa María de Moreruela at the fork is the oldest Cistercian house in Spain and was originally called SANTIAGO de Moruela; Tábara had a Mozarabic monastery of San Salvador and its scriptorium produced the Beato de Tábara, whose famous miniature of the tower is the earliest picture of a Spanish scriptorium at work; Santa Marta de Tera grew around its abbey and holds the earliest known sculpture of Santiago dressed as a pilgrim — the iconography of the road, carved on the road; and at Rionegro del Puente the Cofradía de los Falifos was founded in the 14th century at the sanctuary of the Virgen de la Carballeda, a confraternity whose business was bridges and pilgrims. IT REJOINS THE ROMAN ROAD WITHOUT MEANING TO: at Xunqueira de Ambía this camino stands on AW-369, the Via Nova, eleven centuries after Vespasian's legate cut it. TWO ENTRANCES TO GALICIA are attested, by A Gudiña and Laza, or the longer way by Verín. The Laza line is drawn because it is the shorter and the more walked; Verín is real and is not a branch of this route's geometry. Tier B: stage towns and monasteries are secure, the intervening line is the modern waymarking.

nodes.n: Santa Marta de Tera (Santiago as pilgrim, carved)
Rionegro del Puente (the Cofradía de los Falifos)
Ourense (the hot springs and the Roman bridge)
Santiago de Compostela — junction AW-002, AW-023, AW-024, AW-368, AW-375

routes.name: Camino de Invierno (Ponferrada–Silleda)
routes.era: medieval; the winter alternative to O Cebreiro, and probably older than the pass road
routes.note: THE ROAD THAT EXISTS BECAUSE OF SNOW. At Ponferrada the Camino Francés turns west and climbs O Cebreiro at 1,300 m, which from November to March is a way to die. So pilgrims went down the Sil instead — round the mountains rather than over them, along the river gorge into Valdeorras and Lemos and up to Lalín, and the road is called the Winter Way because that is when you took it. It is the only Jacobean route in this layer NAMED FOR A SEASON, and it is a straightforward argument about weather made with feet. THE FINDING IS THAT IT IS PROBABLY THE OLDER ROAD: it follows the Sil, and the Sil is where Rome went. This camino stands on AW-369, the Via Nova, at THREE separate nodes — Puente de Domingo Flórez, O Barco de Valdeorras and A Rúa — because a river gorge has one floor and everyone who ever needed to cross that country used it. It also passes Las Médulas, the ruined mountain Rome washed apart with aqueduct water to get the gold out, which is the reason the Via Nova was cut in the first place. A pilgrim road running through an industrial casualty of the empire whose road it is borrowing. DRAWN TO SILLEDA, NOT TO SANTIAGO: the Invierno merges into the Sanabrés at A Laxe just short of Silleda, and from there the two are one road. Same ruling as the Primitivo at AW-367 — drawing the shared tail twice would manufacture a junction out of an identity. Tier B.

nodes.n: Las Médulas (the mountain Rome washed away)
Puente de Domingo Flórez — junction AW-369
O Barco de Valdeorras — junction AW-369

routes.name: Camino Mozárabe (Almería & Málaga–Córdoba–Mérida)
routes.era: from the 9th–10th c., walked by Christians living under Muslim rule; revived in the 20th c.
routes.note: HELD BACK FROM B80 BECAUSE IT WAS UNRESEARCHED, AND DRAWN NOW BECAUSE IT IS NOT. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS, AND IT IS THE MOST POLITICALLY LOADED ANSWER IN THE NETWORK: the mozárabes were Christians living under Islamic rule in al-Andalus, and this is the road they took north to Compostela — out of Córdoba, the greatest city in Europe at the time, toward a shrine in the small Christian kingdom that was the ideological engine of the war against their own rulers. They walked from the caliphate to the thing that would eventually destroy it. Whether that is loyalty, dissent, tourism or all three at once is not something a polyline can settle, and the layer does not try; it records that people did it and that both ends are real. THE STRUCTURE IS A DELTA, NOT A LINE. Arms come up from Almería, from Málaga, from Granada and from Jaén, converge in the Subbética around Baena, reach Córdoba, and run north-west over the Sierra Morena to Mérida, where the road joins AW-025 and becomes the Vía de la Plata. Two arms are drawn here — Almería and Málaga — and the Jaén arm is not, because its line is contested and drawing it would be asserting. IT IS ALSO THE OTHER HALF OF AN ARGUMENT THIS LAYER ALREADY MADE: AW-133 carries the coastal trade line through Urci and Malaca, and both of those ports now have a road going inland from them for a reason that is not trade. Tier B: the endpoint cities and the Subbética towns are secure, the medieval alignment between them is reconstructed. MISSED-JUNCTION SWEEP CAUGHT ONE, v83-B83: this route's 'Guadix' was drawn 456 m from AW-069's 'Acci (Guadix)' — the same town under its Roman and its modern name, and therefore an unclaimed junction rather than two places. The node now carries AW-069's frozen coordinate. This is exactly the failure _meta.missed_junction_rule was written for, and it is worth noting that A NAME CHANGE IS THE CLASSIC CONCEALMENT: nothing in either string tells you they are one place, so only the geometry could find it. Run nearmiss.py on every batch, without exception.

routes.name: Camí de Sant Jaume (Montserrat–Lleida–Logroño)
routes.era: medieval; Montserrat's Black Madonna venerated from the 12th c.
routes.note: THE CATALAN ROAD, AND IT SOLVES A PROBLEM THE LAYER HAD WITHOUT NOTICING: Montserrat probed at 36 km from anything and the nearest node was Barcelona on the Via Augusta — a Roman road passing a mountain that did not matter yet. La Moreneta, the Black Madonna, has drawn Catalans up that serrated rock since the 12th century, and the pilgrims who then continued to Compostela went west by the Ebro basin. This route gives Montserrat its road. WHY IT RUNS THIS WAY: Catalonia's exit to the west is the Ebro valley and there is no second option — the Pyrenees close the north and the Maestrat closes the south. So the camino follows the same corridor as AW-366, the river, for the same reason the river is there. It meets the Camino Francés at Logroño, where the Ebro and the pilgrim road cross at the Puente de Piedra, and the layer now has three separate routes standing on that bridge. Tier B: the terminal cities and the Ebro corridor are certain, the intervening alignment is the modern waymarked line rather than a documented medieval one.

routes.name: Camino de Levante (Valencia–Toledo–Zamora)
routes.era: medieval; the road from the Mediterranean kingdoms to the Vía de la Plata
routes.note: THE LONGEST SPANISH CAMINO NOBODY MENTIONS — roughly 1,000 km from the Mediterranean to Zamora, where it joins the Vía de la Plata and becomes AW-025. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: Valencia is a great city with no easy way north, because the Iberian System stands in the way and the coastal road runs to France rather than to Galicia. So pilgrims from the Levante went WEST first, across La Mancha to Toledo, and only then turned north — a road shaped entirely by a mountain range it declines to cross. It is the mirror image of the Ruta de la Lana, which does cross it. TIER C, AND THE HONEST REASON: this is a long modern reconstruction across country where the medieval traffic is poorly documented, and the anchor cities are far more certain than the line between them. The layer draws the cities it can defend — Valencia, Albacete, Toledo, Ávila, Medina del Campo, Zamora — with the intermediate towns kept sparse rather than padded. This is the AW-062 principle applied at scale: where the alignment is not known, do not draw a confident line through it, and do not add shaping nodes to make the geometry look surveyed. See _meta.densify_warrant_rule.

routes.name: Ruta de la Lana (Alicante–Cuenca–Burgos)
routes.era: the wool trade from the 13th c. under the Mesta; Jacobean use attested from 1624
routes.note: A TRADE ROAD THAT BECAME A PILGRIM ROAD, WHICH IS THE ORDER THESE THINGS USUALLY HAPPEN IN. The Wool Route carried Castilian merino north from the Levante and the Serranía de Cuenca to the Burgos wool market and the Cantabrian ports, and pilgrims used it because it was already there, already provisioned, and already patrolled. The name is the giveaway: it is not called the Camino de anything. THE LAYER CAN NOW SHOW THE OVERLAP: it crosses the same Iberian System country as AW-370, the Cañada Real Conquense, because sheep and pilgrims want identical things from a landscape — water at intervals, a pass that is open, and somebody who will sell you food. The wool went one way and the walkers went the other, and per _meta.bidirectionality_rule that is a note, not a schema field. THE JACOBEAN ATTESTATION IS UNUSUALLY PRECISE: a pilgrim from Monteagudo de las Salinas left a written account of walking to Compostela this way in 1624, which is a rare thing — a specific person on a specific road in a specific year. Tier C: the corridor is certain and the trade is thoroughly documented, but the pilgrim alignment rests on that one account and a modern reconstruction. SECOND MISSED JUNCTION CAUGHT BY THE SWEEP, v84-B84: Sigüenza was drawn 275 m from AW-037, the Cañada Real Soriana Occidental. It is the same town and now carries AW-037's frozen coordinate. THE COINCIDENCE IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS ROUTE — a wool road and a drove road meeting at Sigüenza is not an accident of drawing, it is the reason both roads are there. The sweep found the thing the note was already arguing for.

nodes.n: Villalba de la Sierra — junction AW-370

routes.name: Camino Baztanés (Bayonne–Pamplona)
routes.era: medieval; the low-pass alternative to Roncesvalles
routes.note: THE PYRENEAN BACK DOOR. Everyone knows Roncesvalles, where the Camino Francés crosses at 1,057 m and where Roland is supposed to have died. This is the other way: up the Nive from Bayonne, over the Otsondo at 602 m into the Baztán valley, and down the Bidasoa country to Pamplona — about 110 km, and roughly half the climb. IT EXISTS FOR THE SAME REASON THE CAMINO DE INVIERNO EXISTS, one range further east: when the high pass is shut or dangerous, the traffic goes round. Two routes in this layer are now named alternatives to a mountain, which is a pattern worth watching for elsewhere — a famous pass usually has a humbler twin that carried more people in bad weather and got less poetry. It was also the smugglers' country, and later the road out for refugees crossing in both directions in 1936 and 1940, though that is not what the layer is drawing. Tier B: the corridor, the pass and the valley towns are certain; the medieval alignment through the Baztán is reconstructed from the modern waymarking.

routes.name: Camino Ignaciano (Loyola–Manresa)
routes.era: walked once, by one man, in 1522; retraced as a route from 2012
routes.note: THE ONLY ROUTE IN THIS LAYER THAT IS ONE MAN'S ITINERARY, AND IT IS DRAWN WITH A CAVEAT ATTACHED. In 1522 Íñigo López de Loyola, convalescing from a cannonball at Pamplona, left his family house and walked roughly 650 km east — to Montserrat, where he laid down his sword before the Black Madonna and swapped clothes with a beggar, and then to a cave at Manresa, where he stayed eleven months and drafted the Spiritual Exercises. THE ROAD TEST IS THE PROBLEM AND THE NOTE SAYS SO PLAINLY: the layer's standing discipline is that JOURNEYS ARE NOT ROADS. Hannibal is excluded, Lewis and Clark are excluded, the peopling of the Americas is excluded — a single passage, however consequential, is not a road. By that rule this should not be here. It is here on a narrow and arguable ground: the itinerary was reconstructed in 2012 and has been walked continuously since by pilgrims in both directions, so a one-man journey has, five hundred years late, become a two-way road. THAT IS A RULING, NOT A FACT, and it is Laurie's to reverse — see the queue's standing question on living pilgrimages of recent date. If it is reversed, this route comes out and the precedent stands: a modern revival does not retroactively make a historical journey into a historical road. Tier C throughout, because the 1522 line is inferred from an autobiography written thirty years afterwards by a man who was not keeping a map.

routes.name: Ruta Teresiana — de la cuna al sepulcro (Ávila–Alba de Tormes)
routes.era: the ground Teresa of Ávila covered 1515–1582; waymarked as a route in the modern era
routes.note: FROM THE CRADLE TO THE GRAVE, and the layer has nothing else shaped like it: a route defined by the two ends of one life. Teresa of Ávila was born inside these walls in 1515 and died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582, and the 115 km between is walked because she is at both ends of it. WHY IT IS A ROAD AND NOT A JOURNEY — the test AW-386 nearly failed: Teresa did not walk this once. She spent twenty years founding convents and crossing and recrossing this exact country by cart and on foot, and the route strings together the places that recur — Gotarrendura where her parents married and she spent part of her childhood, Fontiveros where John of the Cross was born, Duruelo where he and Antonio de Jesús founded the first discalced Carmelite house at her instruction, Mancera where that foundation moved. This is habitual ground, not a single passage. IT SHARES ITS FIRST LEG WITH THE CAMINO DE SANTIAGO and the sources are precise about where they part: from Ávila to Gotarrendura the yellow Jacobean arrow and the red Teresian arrow run together on the same waymarks, and beside the parish church at Gotarrendura the Camino turns off for Arévalo and Medina del Campo and only the red arrow goes on. TWO ARMS FROM MANCERA DE ABAJO, both signposted and both drawn: the southern by Macotera, about 30 km, and the northern by Peñaranda de Bracamonte, about 40. They rejoin at Garcihernández. Tier B: the towns are certain and the Teresian sites are documented, but the line between them is modern waymarking over ground she crossed by many routes.

nodes.n: Ávila (Iglesia de La Santa) — junction AW-383
Gotarrendura (the yellow arrow leaves the red)
Fontiveros (San Juan de la Cruz born)

routes.name: Vía de Bayona (Estavillo–Burgos)
routes.era: medieval; the Castilian arm of the Bayonne road
routes.note: THE OTHER ARM OF AW-373, DRAWN AS ITS OWN LINE RATHER THAN AS A PHANTOM LIMB. The Camino Vasco del Interior and the Vía de Bayona share their whole course from Irún to Estavillo and then part for good: the Vasco turns southwest through Haro to meet the Francés at Santo Domingo de la Calzada, the Bayona keeps south to Miranda de Ebro and drives on to Burgos. AW-373's note recorded the fork and declined to draw it, on the grounds that a route which shares 200 km with another and then diverges is a second road, not a branch. This is that second road. WHY BOTH EXIST: they answer the same question — how does a pilgrim landing at Bayonne reach the Camino Francés without the Pyrenees — and they answer it at different points on the Francés. Santo Domingo is 60 km short of Burgos, so the Vasco arm saves a day and the Bayona arm reaches a cathedral city with a market, a mint and the Las Huelgas and Miraflores foundations. One is faster and one is better provisioned, which is most of what a medieval routing decision ever came down to. It runs through Pancorbo, a gorge so narrow it has been the strategic gate into Castile since the Romans held it and the Muslims fortified it. Tier B: the corridor and the towns are certain, the alignment is the modern waymarking.

routes.name: Camino del Sureste (Alicante–Albacete)
routes.era: medieval; the southeastern feeder to the Levante road
routes.note: A FEEDER, DRAWN ONLY AS FAR AS THE ROAD IT FEEDS. From Alicante the pilgrim traffic ran inland through Villena and Almansa to Albacete, and there it joined the Camino de Levante and became it; from Albacete to Zamora the two are one road, which is AW-383. So this route stops at Albacete. Same ruling as the Camino Primitivo at Melide, the Camino de Invierno at Silleda and the Camino Mozárabe's Málaga arm at Baena: DRAWING A SHARED TAIL TWICE MANUFACTURES A JUNCTION OUT OF AN IDENTITY, and this layer now has four routes obeying that rule, which makes it a convention rather than a judgement call. WHY THIS ROAD EXISTS: it is the last of the peninsula's four compass approaches to be drawn. Pilgrims reached Compostela from the north by the Norte and the Primitivo, from the east by the Catalan road and the Ebro, from the south by the Mozárabe and the Vía de la Plata — and from the southeast corner, the driest and least-travelled quarter, by this. Villena and Almansa are the gates between the coastal huerta and the meseta, which is why both are also on AW-384, the Ruta de la Lana: wool going one way, pilgrims the other, on the only viable line through. Tier C: the corridor is certain and the towns are unambiguous, but the medieval pilgrim traffic here is thinly documented and the route is largely a modern reconstruction.

routes.name: Camino Olvidado (Bilbao–Villafranca del Bierzo)
routes.era: 9th–13th c., heavily used; abandoned as the Reconquista moved south; recovered from 1993
routes.note: THE FORGOTTEN WAY, AND THE REASON IT WAS FORGOTTEN IS THE BEST FINDING IN THE SPANISH SET. Also the Viejo Camino and the Camino de la Montaña. Between the 9th and 13th centuries this was one of the most-used roads to Compostela, and it exists because of a specific fear: the aceifas, the Muslim summer raiding columns that swept the meseta. Pilgrims would not cross open Castile while those were running, and the coast was too broken to walk, so they threaded the foot of the Cantabrian range — 508 km along the mountain skirt where the raiders did not come. THEN THE DANGER WENT AWAY AND THE ROAD DIED. As the frontier moved south the meseta became safe, the Camino Francés was shorter and better provisioned, and traffic drained off this line until it was forgotten so completely that it had to be RECOVERED, from 1993, by an association in Bizkaia working from Roman and medieval roadbed, bridges and Romanesque churches with Jacobean iconography. THIS IS THE OPPOSITE CASE TO THE CAMINO DE INVIERNO AT AW-380, and the pair make an argument together. The Invierno exists because of snow, which is permanent, so the Invierno is still walked. The Olvidado existed because of raiders, which was temporary, so the Olvidado died. A ROAD OUTLIVES ITS REASON ONLY IF ITS REASON OUTLIVES ITS CENTURY. It is the layer's clearest case of a road killed by peace. IT IS ALSO A JUNCTION MACHINE: pilgrims left it at Cistierna for Santo Toribio by the Vadiniense, at La Robla for Oviedo by the Camino del Salvador, and at Valdorria to venerate San Froilán — three of those four routes are now in this layer and meet it on its own nodes. Sources give 18, 20, 21 or 22 stages depending on which variants are counted; the two-arm choices at Güeñes and at Boñar are recorded here and only the main line is drawn. Tier B: the stage towns are certain and the recovered line is well signposted, but the medieval alignment between them is reconstruction.

nodes.n: Espinosa de los Monteros (the Velasco tower)

routes.name: Ruta Vadiniense (Santo Toribio de Liébana–Mansilla de las Mulas)
routes.era: medieval; the way on from Liébana once the Lignum Crucis had been venerated
routes.note: THE SECOND HALF OF A JOURNEY THIS LAYER HAD ONLY HALF OF. AW-372, the Camino Lebaniego, brings the pilgrim 73 km up from the sea to Santo Toribio, and at B81 the road simply stopped there, as though everyone who reached the Lignum Crucis went home. They did not. The Vadiniense carries on 145 km south over the Picos de Europa to rejoin the Camino Francés at Mansilla de las Mulas, and the two together are one continuous act: sea, relic, and on to Compostela. WHY IT RUNS SOUTH THROUGH THE WORST OF THE MOUNTAINS: because Liébana is a hole in the Picos with only two ways out, and the northern one is where you came from. The route takes the Puerto de San Glorio and drops into the Esla headwaters, which is why the crossing is the highest thing in this network outside the Pyrenees. THE NAME IS ARCHAEOLOGY: the Vadinienses were a Cantabrian people whose funerary stelae, inscribed in Latin with horse and warrior motifs, are found through exactly this valley system. The road is named for the people whose gravestones mark its course, which is a colder version of the same reasoning as the Baetis being known by a hill of its own broken amphorae. IT CROSSES THE OLVIDADO AT CISTIERNA, and both are now drawn, so the layer can show what a pilgrim actually had: arrive at Cistierna from Bilbao on the Olvidado, turn north for the relic, come back, carry on. Tier B: six stages, the towns are certain, the alignment is the recovered modern line.

nodes.n: Santo Toribio de Liébana (the Lignum Crucis) — junction AW-372
Mansilla de las Mulas — junction AW-002

routes.name: Camino de San Juan de la Cruz (Beas de Segura–Caravaca)
routes.era: the ground John of the Cross worked from 1578; established as a route by the Discalced Carmelites
routes.note: THE THIRD ROAD IN THIS LAYER BELONGING TO THE SAME TWO PEOPLE. AW-387, the Ruta Teresiana, passes Fontiveros where John of the Cross was born and Duruelo where he and Antonio de Jesús founded the first discalced house at Teresa's instruction. This is his own country, 160 km over the Sierra de Segura from Beas de Segura — where he was confessor to the Carmelite nuns — to Caravaca, where Teresa founded a convent in 1576 and where he went to help establish it. THE ROUTE THEREFORE DOES TWO JOBS AT ONCE: it is a road to a jubilee city, and it is the mountain leg of a reform that reshaped Spanish religious life. It was established by the Discalced Carmelites of Caravaca and of Beas de Segura together with the association of towns along it, which is to say by the successors of the people who walked it. TIER C AND ANCHORS ONLY. The endpoints and the Sierra de Segura corridor are certain; the sixteenth-century line across that range is not, and the modern waymarking is a hiking route. Drawn on the AW-062 principle — where the alignment is not known, do not draw a confident line through it. See _meta.densify_warrant_rule.

nodes.n: Caravaca de la Cruz (the Vera Cruz) — junction AW-377

routes.name: Camino de la Vera Cruz (Vélez Blanco–Caravaca)
routes.era: historic approach from the Almerían altiplano; the Vera Cruz venerated at Caravaca from 1231
routes.note: THE SHORT ARM, AND IT IS DRAWN CHIEFLY TO MAKE A POINT ABOUT SHAPE. Caravaca is a jubilee city and jubilee cities do not have A road, they have a DELTA — six approaches are attested here, and drawing one and calling it the camino would misrepresent how pilgrimage geography actually works. AW-377 draws the principal 120 km line from Orihuela; AW-392 draws the Carmelite road over the Sierra de Segura; this draws the 60 km approach from Vélez Blanco across the cereal altiplano. THREE MORE REMAIN UNDRAWN and are named here so nobody thinks the set is closed: the route from Cartagena and Mazarrón, and a Templar road of nearly 900 km linking former Templar holdings through Pamplona, Artajona, Daroca, Teruel, Alcalá del Júcar and Jumilla. That last one is the longest road to any Spanish shrine and it is being re-signposted; it wants a batch of its own and proper research, not a guess. THE ROAD PASSES LA ENCARNACIÓN, a sanctuary built over a Roman temple built over an Iberian sanctuary — three religions stacked on one hillside, on the way to a fourth thing. Tier C, anchors only: the endpoints are certain and the intervening line is not.

nodes.n: Caravaca de la Cruz (the Vera Cruz) — junction AW-377

routes.name: Ruta do Mar de Arousa e Río Ulla (the Traslatio)
routes.era: the Traslatio placed by tradition in AD 44; sailed as a pilgrimage since 1965
routes.note: THE ROAD THE DESTINATION ARRIVED BY, AND THE ONLY ONE IN THE NETWORK THAT RUNS THE WRONG WAY DOWN TIME. Every other camino in this layer was made by people going TO Santiago. This one traces the journey that made Santiago exist: by tradition the disciples brought the Apostle's body by sea from Jaffa, entered the Ría de Arousa, went up the Ulla and landed at Iria Flavia, and the stone they moored to — the Pedrón — is still in the church at Padrón and gave the town its name. Forty miles of water, then twenty-five kilometres on foot. THE LAYER HAD NO MARITIME CAMINO AT ALL, which was a real hole: the Spanish federation records THIRTY maritime routes to Santiago alongside the land ones, and this layer, which draws the Kula Ring and the Chontal canoe road and the Nicaragua Transit, had drawn none of them. The Camino Inglés at AW-368 is the landward tail of a sea road whose sea leg is still missing. This is the first. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE MYTH: the water route is why the shrine is where it is. Iria Flavia was the episcopal see and a working port; Compostela is inland and had nothing until a tomb was reported there. The Ría de Arousa is the deepest navigable penetration of this coast, and a body arriving from the Levant would arrive exactly here or not at all. Whatever one makes of the tradition, the GEOGRAPHY of it is sound, which is the most a layer like this can say and more than it can usually say. IT IS ALSO THE ONLY MARITIME VIA CRUCIS IN THE WORLD — seventeen stone calvaries set on the banks and islands of the ría since 1965. TIER C AND THE REASON IS EXPLICIT: the AD 44 voyage is tradition, not record, and the modern pilgrimage dates from 1965. What is drawn is the WATER ITSELF and the ports on it, all of which are real and all of which are old; the claim is that this is the route, not that the voyage happened. Segments are kind sea and river per _meta.water_rule and render dashed.

nodes.n: Pedras Negras (O Grove — the outer entry)
Catoira (Torres de Oeste — key and seal of Galicia)
Pontecesures (the Roman bridge and O Alfolí)
Padrón (the Pedrón — Iria Flavia) — junction AW-024

routes.name: Variante Espiritual (Pontevedra–Armenteira–Vilanova de Arousa)
routes.era: the Armenteira house founded 1162; walked as the Padre Sarmiento route from 1745
routes.note: THE LAND LEG THAT PUTS PILGRIMS ON THE BOAT. The Traslatio at AW-394 is a water road, and a walker coming up the Camino Portugués needs a way to reach the water — this is it. It leaves AW-024 at Pontevedra, climbs to the Cistercian monastery of Armenteira, drops down the Ruta da Pedra e da Auga beside the mill-streams of the Armenteira river, and reaches tidewater at Vilanova de Arousa, where AW-394 begins. THE THREE ROUTES NOW INTERLOCK PROPERLY: Portugués in, Espiritual across, Traslatio up the ría, and back onto the Portugués at Padrón for the last day into Santiago. That is a real pilgrim's itinerary and until this batch the layer could not represent it, because the middle two legs did not exist. IT IS ALSO A DOCUMENTED PILGRIMAGE, WHICH THE TRASLATIO ISN'T: Father Martín Sarmiento walked this way in the Holy Year of 1745 and the route carries his name for that reason, so the land leg has a specific person on a specific date behind it while the sea leg has only tradition. That is worth saying out loud, because the two are usually sold together and they rest on very different evidence. Tier C: three stages, the monastery and the endpoints are certain, the alignment is modern waymarking.

nodes.n: Ruta da Pedra e da Auga (the mill streams)

routes.name: The Allegheny Path (Philadelphia–Paxtang)
routes.era: pre-contact; a bridle path within a few years of Penn's arrival; wagon road by the Revolution
routes.note: WALLACE No. 1, AND THE OLDEST ROAD IN PENNSYLVANIA. John T. Faris called the Philadelphia–Harrisburg section the oldest road in the state passing between the Delaware and the Susquehanna, and it was in use by Indians and white men from the earliest colonial days. THE NAME SURVIVED THE ROAD: Allegheny Avenue in Philadelphia runs on it, Alleghenyville and Allegheny Creek in Berks County sit on it, and Allegheny Street in Hollidaysburg is the far end — a road that dissolved into street names across three hundred miles. A 1684 survey of Swan Swanson's land near the falls of the Schuylkill already marks 'One Inden Road to Netopcomb' crossing 'Vacant Indian Feilds'. THE FINDING IS A DECISION ABOUT WET GROUND, and it is the clearest illustration of Wallace's three words for Indian path-making — DRY, LEVEL, DIRECT. Between Blainsport and Myerstown the path climbs over South Mountain through the ravine called die Kluft instead of going round by Newmanstown as the modern road does, which looks perverse until you learn that the southern slope is all springs and marsh and is still locally called the Upper and Lower Swamp, with a Union church at Blainsport still called the Swamp Church. The north side was dry. THEY WENT OVER THE MOUNTAIN TO KEEP THEIR MOCCASINS DRY. Wallace's general point lands here too: the frost-heaved discomfort of driving modern roads that left the Indian's dry ridge routes is a reminder of how good a road engineer the Indian was. Drawn Philadelphia to Paxtang; west of Harrisburg the traffic split among the Frankstown, Raystown, New and Kittanning paths, all of which are or will be their own lines. Tier B: Wallace's own reconstruction, dense with named landmarks, but the line rests on tradition and terrain as much as survey.

nodes.n: Robin Hood's Ford (below the Falls of the Schuylkill)
die Kluft (over South Mountain, to keep dry)

routes.name: The Frankstown Path (Harris's Ferry–Frankstown)
routes.era: pre-contact; the traders' favoured road west through the first half of the 18th c.
routes.note: WALLACE No. 26, AND THE ONE THE TRADERS PREFERRED. West of Harrisburg a traveller bound for the Allegheny could take the Frankstown Path, the New Path, the Raystown Path or the Kittanning Path, and Wallace is explicit that the Frankstown was the one most favoured by early Indian traders. It runs from Harris's Ferry through the ridge-and-valley country to Frankstown on the Juniata, where it hands over to AW-179, the Kittanning Path, for the crossing of the Allegheny Front. THE NAME IS A TRADER'S NAME: Frankstown is Frank Stevens's trading post, and Wallace notes the path could equally have been named from any other stopping point along it — which is why this domain has as many Kittanning and Venango paths as there were people walking toward those places. WHAT THE PATH DID TO AVOID A CLIMB: west of McAllister's Gap at Roxbury it TURNS ON ITSELF rather than take the steep rocky ascent, one of the few places where Wallace records a path deliberately going backwards to go forwards. IT ALSO CARRIES A SHADES OF DEATH. Wallace records two stretches of that name in Pennsylvania, and one of them is on this path at Shade Gap — not swamp in the modern sense but mountain land so overgrown with laurel, hemlock and white pine that it was the blackness above rather than the wet below that troubled travellers. Tier B.

nodes.n: McAllister's Gap (Roxbury — the path turns on itself)

routes.name: The Bald Eagle Creek Path (Great Island–Frankstown)
routes.era: pre-contact; a warriors path linking the Six Nations country to Virginia and the Carolinas
routes.note: WALLACE No. 2, AND IT IS A LINK RATHER THAN A DESTINATION. This is the middle section of a warriors path running from the Six Nations country south through Bedford and Wills Creek into Virginia and the Carolinas — the northern end of the same system as AW-084, the Great Warriors Path. Wallace's own framing is the useful one: THE BALD EAGLE PATH WAS A LINK BETWEEN TWO IMPORTANT TRAIL COMPLEXES. At the Great Island, paths converged from the Six Nations country — the Sinnemahoning, the Pine Creek, the Sheshequin. At Frankstown, paths converged from the Catawba and Cherokee country to the south and from Kittanning, Chartier's Landing and the Forks of the Ohio to the west. This road is the eighty-odd miles that made those two knots one system. IT IS NAMED FOR A MAN AND HIS VILLAGE: the Munsee Delaware chief Bald Eagle, whose town Bald Eagle's Nest stood at Milesburg. THE ROAD IS SIGNPOSTED IN ITS OWN NOMENCLATURE — the Warriors Mark and the Warriors Sleeping Place are both nodes on it, place names that survived because the warriors did. Tier B.

routes.name: The Venango Path (Forks of the Ohio–Presque Isle)
routes.era: pre-contact; improved as a French military road 1753–58
routes.note: WALLACE No. 117, AND THE ROAD THE SEVEN YEARS' WAR CAME DOWN. The layer has drawn both ends of this for years — Presque Isle on AW-200, the Forks of the Ohio on AW-137 and AW-138 — and never the road between them, which is the water_rule failure in a dry costume: two named places connected in every eighteenth-century document and no line joining them. WHY IT EXISTS: it is a PORTAGE, in Wallace's sense, between two water systems — Lake Erie and the Ohio — and it is named for the Lenape town of Venango at the meeting of French Creek and the Allegheny, now Franklin. Whoever held this line held the connection between New France on the lakes and the Ohio country, which is why the French built forts along it in 1753 and why a 21-year-old Virginia militia major named George Washington walked up it that December with Christopher Gist to tell them to leave. They did not leave. Wallace gives Washington's route its own appendix. THE PATH IS ALSO WHERE HE RECORDS THE WORST GOING IN THE BOOK: John Heckewelder's party in 1800 in the beech swamp northeast of Meadville, deep marsh and surface roots that trapped the horses' legs; and in the portage area between Presque Isle and French Creek, Wallace's remark that a trail graphed decade by decade would show a blurred band A MILE OR MORE WIDE. That is the corridor-not-a-line finding again, from AW-370 and AW-376, stated by a different discipline about different ground. Tier B.

routes.name: The Logstown Path (Logstown–Venango)
routes.era: pre-contact; the preferred northern route BEFORE the forts were built at the Forks
routes.note: WALLACE No. 56, AND IT CARRIES THE BEST GEOLOGICAL FINDING IN THE PENNSYLVANIA SET. Wallace: the Logstown Path offered an all-weather highway with an excellent ford of Muddy Creek in Butler County, PROVIDED BY REMAINS OF THE TERMINAL MORAINE OF THE WISCONSIN GLACIER. A pilgrim road in Spain runs on a drove road because grazing law made it permanent; this road runs where it does because an ice sheet stopped there and dumped its load in the right place. The moraine is the ford; the ford is the road; the road is why Logstown mattered. Deep time as roadbed. IT ALSO CORRECTS AN ASSUMPTION THE LAYER WAS MAKING. AW-399, the Venango Path, runs north from the Forks of the Ohio — but Wallace is explicit that BEFORE white men occupied the Forks and built Fort Duquesne and Fort Pitt, the preferred Indian route from that vicinity to Venango and Lake Erie was by way of Logstown, eighteen miles down the Ohio. So the older road is this one, and the Venango Path's dominance is an artefact of the forts. The layer now shows both, and the pair record a change of route caused by a change of politics — the same shape as the Camino Olvidado dying when the meseta became safe. Logstown itself was the diplomatic capital of the Ohio Country and sat at Legionville, about two and a half miles north of Ambridge. Tier B.

nodes.n: The Muddy Creek ford (on the Wisconsin terminal moraine)

routes.name: The Sheshequin Path (Otstonwakin–Sheshequin)
routes.era: pre-contact; Conrad Weiser's road to Onondaga through the 1730s and 1740s
routes.note: WALLACE No. 103, AND IT IS DRAWN BECAUSE OF A CHOICE ONE MAN MADE OVER AND OVER. A traveller leaving Shamokin for Tioga had three main paths and arguably a fourth: the Great Warriors Path, the Towanda Path, the Sheshequin Path, and the Wyalusing. Conrad Weiser, on his ambassadorial journeys to Onondaga, ALWAYS TOOK THIS ONE — and Wallace's account of why is the most human piece of routing analysis in the book. The Great Warriors Path was easier, lower and better provisioned, running through a succession of Delaware, Shawnee, Mahican and Nanticoke villages where food and shelter were everywhere. Weiser avoided it. Wallace's guess: it was the CERTAINTY OF TOO MUCH COMPANY that put him off, because Indian etiquette required him to stop and share his message with the chief men of every village he passed. A diplomat chose the harder road to avoid having to do diplomacy on it. WHAT THE ROAD COST HIM: the Lycoming valley is flat and narrow with steep abrupt sides, floods easily, submerges the path and forces travellers onto the cliffs. Bohemia Mountain at the head of the creek had so bad a reputation for gathering storms that the Indians said an OTKAN, an evil spirit, lived there. Beyond it the soil is thin, the trees weakly rooted, and windstorms littered the ground — modern maps still mark a place called Windfall. Bishop Spangenberg came through in 1745 and called it a wilderness where one does not see the sun all day long, the woods so thickly grown that sometimes one can hardly see twenty paces ahead. Tier B. DIRECT PRIMARY-SOURCE CONFIRMATION FOUND v158-B158. Beauchamp's edited 'Moravian Journals Relating to Central New York, 1745-66' preserves Bishop Spangenberg's own diary of the June 1745 journey Wallace's note describes in the abstract — this is literally one of the times Weiser took this path, recorded as it happened rather than reconstructed after the fact. From Shamokin the party (Spangenberg, Weiser, John Joseph, Zeisberger, Shikellamy, his son Andrew, and Andrew Sattelihu) went up the West Branch past Shawnee Creek and Shikellamy's former town to a 'Warrior's Camp,' then to Otstonwaken (this route's own terminus) on 8 June. From there the diary names camps this route's node list doesn't: 'the Ant Hills' (the Towanda Creek valley's peaked hills, so named because they resembled anthills), the 'Coffee House' camp, a salt-lick where two Flathead prisoners killed a Mohawk guard and were themselves killed (the tomahawk scars still visible on the trees, per the diary), and 'Bear's Claws,' named for a bear's claws the Indians nailed to a tree there. They crossed Osgochgo Creek to reach the North Branch, then followed 'the narrow path on the mountain by the river' up to Tioga — arriving at a Mohican town 180 miles from Shamokin by the diary's own reckoning, twelve days out. Shikellamy and Sattelihu renamed the missionaries on the road, saying their own names were too hard to pronounce: Spangenberg became T'gerhitonti ('a row of trees'), John Joseph became Hajingonis ('one who twists tobacco'), Zeisberger became Ganousseracheri ('on the pumpkin').

routes.name: The Towanda Path — the Genesee Road (Muncy–Tioga)
routes.era: pre-contact; possibly a Susquehannock runners' road; a settlers' road by 1790
routes.note: WALLACE No. 112, THE SHORTEST WAY FROM THE WEST BRANCH TO TIOGA, AND IT CARRIES THE PAINTED LINE. Where this path came down off the Burnet Hills along Millstone Creek it was known to the early settlers — and is still known among their descendants of the fourth generation — as THE PAINTED LINE, for the succession of painted trees found along it. It was an Indian custom to strip a ring of bark from a tree and paint the news of the day on the exposed wood in red ochre and charcoal, and these paintings stayed legible for as long as FIFTY YEARS. All the Indians of Pennsylvania could read them whatever their spoken language. Wallace prints Abraham Steiner's 1789 reading of one such tree: seven muskets stacked meant seven warriors went to war from there; a turkey meant their leader was of the turkey clan; eight diagonal lines meant eight raids; arrows through a line counted the killed and arrows short of it the wounded; a mark joining two lines meant he had turned back and gone straight out again without going home; and six men lying feet-higher-than-heads meant six white people dead. A ROAD WITH ITS OWN NEWSPAPER, WRITTEN ON THE TREES BESIDE IT, IN A SCRIPT EVERYONE COULD READ AND NOBODY SPOKE. Wallace calls this by far the shortest path from Muncy to Tioga — about eight or nine miles shorter than the modern roads — and wonders why Weiser never used it, guessing the hills, or the dangerous ford of the Loyalsock at Hillsgrove where Baron Charles Boulogne, land agent for the Asylum colony, was later drowned. Tier B.

routes.name: The Wyalusing Path (Friedenshütten–Muncy)
routes.era: pre-contact; Friedenshütten 1765–72
routes.note: WALLACE No. 129. UPGRADED v108-B108, AND THE NORTHERN TERMINUS MOVED. At B89 I drew this from Wyalusing; Wallace starts it at Friedenshütten, the Moravian Indian village TWO MILES DOWN THE RIVER from present Wyalusing at the mouth of Wyalusing Creek. It crosses the Susquehanna to the mouth of Sugar Run, climbs Bartlett Mountain, and ENTERS THE WILDERNESS ON DUTCH MOUNTAIN, holding a course between the swamps at the head of Loyalsock Creek to the west and Mehoopany Creek to the east — a path defined by the two bogs it is threading between. THE BEST NODE NAME IN THE PENNSYLVANIA SET IS ON THIS ROAD. About twelve miles from the Susquehanna there was a favourite stopping place known as THE SIGN OF THE GOOSE — an inn-name, on a footpath, in country with no inns. Wallace thinks it was the Moravian Cabbin referred to in Northumberland County Warrant F 86, which is a land deed being used to locate a nickname. It joins Cock Eye's Cabin, Toby's Cabins and the Warriors Spring in _meta.old_town_rule: SHELTERS EVERY TEN OR TWELVE MILES, named by the people who slept in them. AND THE THIRTY-SIX FORDS STILL STAND. Ettwein's count is why this road was a summer road only, and it remains the layer's most precise seasonal rating. Tier B now that the line is Wallace's rather than mine.
