routes.name: The Mingo Path (Mingo Town–Kuskuskies)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Beaver valley road between the Ohio and the Kuskuskies towns
routes.note: WALLACE No. 64, AND IT IS THE ROAD THAT ANSWERS THE QUESTION 'WHAT DID THE FOREST ACTUALLY LOOK LIKE'. Wallace uses this path to demolish the trackless-wilderness myth, quoting the Rev. David McClure walking it on 7 September 1772 from the Mingo Town at the mouth of the Beaver to Kuskuskies at its head: for a wilderness the travelling was pleasant, as there was no underbrush and the trees did not grow very closely together. Johann Schoepf said the same in 1788 — the woods for the most part entirely free from undergrowth, very convenient for both hunter and traveller. THE OPEN FOREST IS THE PRECONDITION FOR THE WHOLE NETWORK. Pennsylvania has no birch for canoes and its rivers are shallow, swift and broken by mountains, so nearly all early travel was BY LAND — and land travel at that scale only works because the woods were walkable. Wallace's point is structural: the reason this state has a hundred and thirty paths and not a hundred and thirty canoe routes is a fact about trees. Kuskuskies stood at New Castle where the Shenango and Mahoning make the Beaver; Mingo Town is now Rochester. Tier B.

nodes.n: Kuskuskies (New Castle — the Shenango and Mahoning)

routes.name: The Mahoning Path (Kuskuskies–the Tuscarawas)
routes.era: pre-contact; the eastern end of the Great Trail to Detroit
routes.note: WALLACE No. 61, AND IT IS THE LAYER'S CLEANEST EXAMPLE OF WHY FROZEN IDS EXIST. Wallace: the Mahoning Path west of Kuskuskies was ALSO KNOWN AS the Salt Lick Path, the Tuscarawas Path, the Sandusky Path, the Detroit Path — or by the name of any other place it may have led to. FIVE NAMES FOR ONE ROAD, none of them wrong, each of them belonging to whoever was standing at a different point on it. Wallace calls this haphazard system of nomenclature a danger to the geographer, and it is exactly the hazard _meta.id_rule was written against: a layer that keyed on names would either duplicate this road five times or silently merge five different roads. AW-405 is the road. The names are notes. WHERE IT GOES: west out of Kuskuskies past the Salt Spring — Abraham Steiner and John Heckewelder came back along it from Pettquotting in 1789, and it was on this path that Steiner recorded the painted warrior tree — and on to the Tuscarawas, where it meets AW-156 at the Cuyahoga portage and continues as the Great Trail toward Detroit. Only the Pennsylvania-to-Tuscarawas reach is drawn; the continuation west is Ohio country and wants an Ohio roster. Tier B.

routes.name: The Kuskusky–Ohio Forks Path (Pittsburgh–New Castle)
routes.era: pre-contact; heavily used by traders and land agents in the 1750s
routes.note: WALLACE No. 48. UPGRADED v100-B100 FROM ANCHORS-ONLY TO WALLACE'S OWN LINE, now that his text is on disk — see _meta.wallace_text_on_disk. THE ROUTE IS NOT WHAT I GUESSED. At B90 this was drawn Pittsburgh to New Castle via Franklin Park on a documented alignment fragment, three nodes and a straight line. Wallace's actual reconstruction is that the path crossed the Allegheny at the Forks and then RAN ON THE VENANGO PATH through West View and Perrysville as far as the head of Girty Run, where it left the other road and took a north-northwest course — crossing Brush Creek a mile southwest of Ogle, Connoquenessing Creek a few miles west of Zelienople, and Slippery Rock Creek near Wurtemberg, to reach the Beaver at Chewton. TWO ROADS SHARING THEIR FIRST TWENTY KILOMETRES AND THEN PARTING AT A CREEK-HEAD is a thing anchors-only drawing cannot show at all, and it is the commonest shape in this network. EAST MORAVIA IS NAMED FOR A TOWN ACROSS THE RIVER. Friedensstadt, the City of Peace, was the Moravian Indian settlement Bishop Ettwein's Hegira of 1772 was walking toward when it came through the windfall on AW-403's country — the same journey, the far end. Tier B.

The head of Girty Run (the paths part)

routes.name: The Kuskusky–Venango Path (New Castle–Harrisville)
routes.era: pre-contact; walked by George Washington in December 1753
routes.note: WALLACE No. 49. UPGRADED v100-B100 FROM TWO NODES TO SEVEN. At B90 this was drawn as a bare pair, New Castle to Harrisville, because only the termini were known from the name. Wallace gives the whole line: east from Kuskuskies on much the course of U.S. 422, passing about a mile southeast of Rose Point and a quarter-mile north of McConnells Mills, crossing SLIPPERY ROCK CREEK AT ALLENS MILL and MUDDY CREEK AT PORTERSVILLE STATION, then through West Liberty and Redmond to Harrisville. THE MEASUREMENTS ARE THE POINT. 'A mile southeast', 'a quarter of a mile north' — that is a man who walked it with a map, and it is the difference between a route and a guess. AND FROM PORTERSVILLE ONWARD IT IS WASHINGTON'S ROAD. Wallace states that from that crossing the path followed the line George Washington took in 1753 on his journey from Logstown to Fort Le Boeuf — the ultimatum ride that started the Seven Years' War, and the subject of his fifth appendix. This layer already draws the two ends of that journey at AW-400 and AW-399; this is the middle. Still drawn to Harrisville under _meta.shared_tail_rule, where it joins the Venango Path proper. Tier B.

routes.name: The Kuskusky–Kittanning Path (Kittanning–New Castle)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Delaware towns at both ends destroyed within a decade of each other
routes.note: WALLACE No. 47. CORRECTED v100-B100, AND THE CORRECTION MATTERS. At B90 I drew this via Slippery Rock, inferring a line from the map. Wallace says it ran PAST WHAT IS NOW THE COURTHOUSE IN THE CITY OF BUTLER — thirty kilometres south of where I put it. The node is fixed. He also says the path was A PROJECTION OF THE GREAT SHAMOKIN PATH and that it MERGED WITH PATHS FROM CHARTIER'S TOWN AND PITTSBURGH on its way to Kuskuskies, which independently confirms the Butler convergence that AW-409 already showed and makes Butler a genuine four-road knot rather than a coincidence of my drawing. IT STAYS TIER C ON WALLACE'S OWN AUTHORITY. His motorist note says plainly that the course of this path has not been fully determined and offers U.S. 422 only for a general view of the country. That is the source declining to commit, and the tier follows the source rather than the length of the entry. Kittanning was the Delaware military headquarters until Armstrong's raid destroyed it in 1756; Kuskuskies took its refugees and was itself abandoned by the 1770s.

routes.name: The Kuskusky–Chartier's Town Path (Tarentum–New Castle)
routes.era: pre-contact; Chartier's Town abandoned c. 1745; Post's crossing November 1758
routes.note: WALLACE No. 45. UPGRADED v100-B100 WITH THE TWO NODES WALLACE ACTUALLY GIVES, and it remains tier C because his own source is thin in a specific and instructive way. THE EVIDENCE IS ONE MAN'S DIARY OVER FOUR DAYS. Christian Frederick Post and his party took from 13 to 16 November 1758 to get from Chartier's Town to Kuskuskies. They built rafts, dressed themselves as well as they could in Indian dress, and did not all get across the Allegheny until two in the afternoon. They passed two days through thick bushes of briars and thorns so that it was very difficult to get through. At noon on the 15th they CROSSED THE ROAD FROM VENANGO TO FORT DUQUESNE — which is AW-399, and is how we know they were east of it. On the 16th they went down a long valley, crossed the flats north of West Pittsburg, and passed through OLD KUSKUSKY, abandoned since about 1756, to reach New Castle. WALLACE'S VERDICT IS THE HONEST ONE AND I HAVE KEPT IT: Post's journal does not give sufficient detail to make clear which of several possible paths he took. A four-day itinerary with a river crossing, a road crossing and a briar thicket is not a survey, and the tier says so.

routes.name: The Kuskusky–Cussewago Path (Meadville–New Castle)
routes.era: pre-contact; walked by Robert R. Roberts in 1796
routes.note: WALLACE No. 46. UPGRADED v100-B100 FROM THREE NODES TO NINE. Wallace's line runs from Cussewago down the French Creek valley to the mouth of Conneaut Outlet, west to the head of Sandy Creek, southwest to Greenville and Clark, a little east of Sharpsville, and reaches the Shenango at West Middlesex, following it through Pulaski to New Castle. THE FINDING IS WHY WASHINGTON COULD NOT USE IT. Stevens and Kent argue this is the road the Half King meant on 25 November 1753 when he told Washington that the nearest way from Logstown to Fort Le Boeuf was NOW IMPASSABLE, BY REASON OF MANY LARGE MIRY SAVANNAS. Pymatuning Swamp stretches for miles down the Shenango valley and Conneaut Marsh runs south from the lake; after autumn rain the whole corridor drowns. So the most direct road in northwestern Pennsylvania was seasonally unusable, and the man carrying the ultimatum that began a world war had to go the long way round. THAT IS _meta.seasonal_road_rule AT ITS MOST CONSEQUENTIAL — not a comfort question but a strategic one, and it is why AW-399, the longer Venango Path, is the famous road and this one is not. Tier B.

routes.name: The Presque Isle Portage (Lake Erie–French Creek)
routes.era: pre-contact; cut into a French military road in 1753
routes.note: WALLACE No. 94H, AND IT IS THE SHORTEST ROUTE IN THIS LAYER THAT DECIDED A CONTINENT. Twenty-odd kilometres of carry between Lake Erie and the head of French Creek, and on the far side the water runs to the Allegheny, the Ohio, the Mississippi and the Gulf. WHOEVER HOLDS THIS CARRY HOLDS THE JOIN BETWEEN NEW FRANCE AND LOUISIANA. The French understood that exactly, built Fort Presque Isle at one end and Fort Le Boeuf at the other in 1753, and the whole Ohio crisis followed. A portage is the place where a water system stops being a road, and empires are shaped by where that happens. IT IS ALSO WHERE WALLACE MAKES HIS BEST METHODOLOGICAL POINT. As trees fell and the path adjusted around them, a trail moved a little each decade — and if you could graph one decade by decade you would get a broad blurred band, IN THIS PORTAGE AREA A MILE OR MORE IN BREADTH. That is the same finding as the 90-vara cañada at AW-370 and the multiple hermandad tracks at AW-376, arrived at by a third discipline on a third continent's worth of different ground. The line drawn here is the spine of a mile-wide thing. Node type is portage at both ends because that is what they are: places where you stop paddling and start carrying.

routes.name: The Chautauqua Portage (Lake Erie–the Allegheny)
routes.era: pre-contact; Céloron 1749; French military use 1754–58
routes.note: WALLACE No. 94C. UPGRADED v102-B102 WITH THE WATER LEG, which is the half that matters. The carry is only nine kilometres from Barcelona up to Mayville; from the lake's outlet at Celoron, a mile northwest of Jamestown, CANOES HAD FREE PASSAGE down the Chadakoin and the Conewango to the Belle Rivière — the Allegheny — at Conewango. Drawing the portage without the water was drawing the hinge without the door. THE FRENCH CHOSE AND THEN UN-CHOSE IT. In 1753, when France began the military occupation of the Allegheny valley, the Chautauqua Portage was REJECTED in favour of Presque Isle, because Presque Isle had the better harbour on Lake Erie. The next year they brought Chautauqua back into use and ran both throughout the campaign. A shorter carry with a worse harbour against a longer carry with a better one — they picked the harbour, then discovered they needed the capacity of both. AW-411 IS THE OTHER HALF OF THAT DECISION, a hundred kilometres west, and the two routes only make sense read together. Tier B. Segments are land then river per _meta.water_rule; the river leg includes Chautauqua Lake itself.

routes.name: The Allegheny Big Portage Path (Canoe Place–Canoe Place)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 94A, 'Allegheny Portage: Big Portage Path.' UPGRADED v127-B127 to tier B on Reading Howell's 1792 map, which shows the 23-mile portage clearly: head of navigation on the Sinnemahoning at Canoe Place (Shippen, now Emporium, at the confluence of Portage Creek and the Driftwood Branch), up Portage Creek through Gardeau, over the Big Lookout Divide at Keating Summit (1,880 ft), down Little Portage Creek to the second Canoe Place at Port Allegany, where Portage Creek meets the Allegheny. THE NAME IS THE INSTRUCTION: a Canoe Place is where the canoes stop, and there are at least three on Wallace's map — Port Allegany, Emporium and Cherry Tree — each marking the last water on one side of a height of land. THIS CARRY JOINS THE GULF OF MEXICO TO CHESAPEAKE BAY: west of the summit drains to the Mississippi, east to the Susquehanna, and about twenty miles of walking is the entire difference. GRADIENT AS DATING EVIDENCE, Wallace's own form of it here: the grades are easy and the divide comparatively low (compare Negro Mountain on the Turkeyfoot Path, 1,125 ft higher gain), which is why it has been suggested this may be the route the first Indians took across the mountains ten to fifteen thousand years ago. Certainly heavily used by settlers moving west in the early 19th century — Benjamin Burt, who settled at Burtville in 1810, made canoes out of white pine logs for settlers packing goods across from Shippen to float down the Ohio. NOW JOINS AW-508, the Little Portage Path (94B), at Keating Summit — previously undrawn because its line was not in hand; it now is.

routes.name: The Cherry Tree Portage (Canoe Place–Diamondville)
routes.era: pre-contact; the tree a survey corner of the 1768 Purchase
routes.note: WALLACE No. 94D. UPGRADED v106-B106 WITH THE MEASURED LENGTH AND THE FAR CANOE PLACE. At B91 this was two anchors and a guess at the western end. Wallace gives it exactly: TEN MILES, from the Cherry Tree or Canoe Place at the headwaters of the West Branch to DIAMONDVILLE ON TWO LICK CREEK — not Indiana, which is where I put it. And the reason Diamondville matters is what happens after: from that second canoe place they paddled down Two Lick to Blacklick, down Blacklick to the Conemaugh, then the Kiskiminetas, and finally the Allegheny at Freeport. TEN MILES OF WALKING BUYS THREE HUNDRED KILOMETRES OF WATER. WALLACE EXPLAINS THE WHOLE PENNSYLVANIA NETWORK IN HIS PORTAGE PREAMBLE and it belongs on this route: canoe travel there was harder than in Canada or New England for two reasons — the Appalachians were not pierced by her rivers, so the barrier could be surmounted only by LONG portages; and the canoe birch did not grow in Pennsylvania, so dugouts and elm bark were clumsy in water and TOO HEAVY TO BE CARRIED ANY DISTANCE OVERLAND. Hence the practice this layer should have drawn from the start: at the head of navigation they LEFT THEIR CANOES IN THE BUSHES, carried the goods on their backs over the divide, and BUILT FRESH CANOES on the other side. The boat was expendable and the cargo was not, which is why a Canoe Place is a place and not a thing. About two miles southwest of Cherry Tree the portage met the Kittanning Path and followed it past Cookport and Shawnee Cabins. Tier B.

routes.name: The Great Bend Portage (Lanesboro–Stockport)
routes.era: pre-contact; mapped as 'Portage 19ms' in 1793–94
routes.note: WALLACE No. 94G. CORRECTED v120-B120 — I HAD BOTH ENDS WRONG. At B91 this was drawn Great Bend to Deposit, which is the Susquehanna's own bend and the Delaware's West Branch. Wallace runs it from THE TUSCARORA TOWN at the mouth of Conawacta Creek — in the Great Bend at what is now LANESBORO — to STOCKPORT on the Delaware. Different towns, different creek, thirty kilometres off. TWO MAPS AND A DRAFT FIX IT. The Adlum-Wallis 'A General View of Pennsylvania' of 1793-94 labels it 'PORTAGE 19MS' and shows it running between 'Harmony', which is Lanesboro, and Stockport. Samuel Harris's draft of the Great Bend country, made in 1774, has it running up the NORTH BANK of Conawacta Creek, then over the mountains by Starrucca and Shehawkin Lake, and down to the Delaware. A NUMBER WRITTEN ON A MAP — nineteen miles — is a stronger fix than any prose in this domain, because it is the only place a carry's length is stated by someone who expected to be believed. THE CORRECTION ALSO EARNS A JUNCTION: Lanesboro is already in the layer as the Tuscarora Town on AW-424, the Lackawanna Path. The carry and the road meet, which the wrong version could not show.

routes.name: The Venango–Chinklacamoose Path (Clearfield–Franklin)
routes.era: pre-contact; a branch of the Great Shamokin Path
routes.note: WALLACE No. 118. UPGRADED v101-B101 FROM FOUR NODES TO ELEVEN. It is a BRANCH of the Great Shamokin Path, and Wallace names the place it branches: THE PARTING OF THE WAYS, a big spring near Luthersburg. From there it runs northwest through Eriton and West Liberty near Du Bois, past the old Steele School, crossing Sandy Lick Creek at Sandy Valley, up the west bank of Panther Run for a mile before crossing it, west past Snyder School and Emrickville to Brookville — where it fords Redbank Creek at the mouth of Sandy Lick and crosses the North Fork just above its mouth — then Roseville, Corsica and Strattonville, and about half a mile west of Strattonville it turns north and fords the Clarion at CLEW'S RIFFLE. THE PRECISION IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF EVIDENCE FROM THE REST OF THIS DOMAIN. 'Up the west bank of Panther Run for a mile, crossed it'; 'about half a mile west of Strattonville'; a named riffle on a named river. Those are warrantee-survey facts, not tradition, and they are why this route moves to tier B while its neighbour AW-418 does not. THE LAYER NOW HAS THREE 'PARTINGS'. Wallace's introduction gives the Parting of the Roads west of Ligonier where Forbes and later Bouquet had to choose; AW-406 leaves the Venango Path at the head of Girty Run; and this leaves the Great Shamokin at a spring. A fork with a name is a fork people argued about.

routes.name: The Venango–Conewango Path (Franklin–Warren)
routes.era: pre-contact; described by General William Irvine in 1785
routes.note: WALLACE No. 119, AND THE FIRST WORDS OF HIS ENTRY ARE A SEASONAL RATING: 'IN GOOD WEATHER there was a tolerable path along the bank of the Allegheny River from Venango to Conewango.' Tolerable, in good weather — which is the frankest description of any road in this layer. THE WITNESS IS A SURVEYOR WITH A GRIEVANCE. General William Irvine walked it in the summer of 1785 exploring the Donation Lands and reported to the Supreme Executive Council. Wallace notes drily that Irvine was faulty in estimating distances but gives a good account of conditions. The first eight miles, Venango to Oil Creek, caused no trouble. After that: from Oil Creek to Cuskakushing, an old Indian town about seventeen miles on, THE WHOLE OF THIS WAY IS BARREN, HIGH MOUNTAINS, NOT FIT FOR CULTIVATION; THE MOUNTAIN PRESSES SO CLOSE ON THE RIVER THAT IT IS ALMOST IMPASSABLE. A man sent to value land for soldiers' bounties, reporting that the land is worthless and the road nearly gone. THAT IS WHY THE ROUTE EXISTS IN THE RECORD AT ALL — not because anyone celebrated it, but because someone was obliged to assess it and could not say anything good. Upgraded v101-B101 with Cuskakushing added. Tier B.

nodes.n: Oil Creek (eight easy miles) — junction AW-533
Cuskakushing (Tionesta — where the mountain presses on the river)

routes.name: The Venango–Kittanning Path (Kittanning–Bullocks Ford)
routes.era: pre-contact; Brodhead's expedition against the Seneca, 1779
routes.note: WALLACE No. 120, AND IT STAYS TIER C BECAUSE HE SAYS IT SHOULD. His opening is unusually blunt: THAT THERE WAS AN INDIAN PATH FROM KITTANNING TO VENANGO IS ACCEPTED, BUT THERE IS NO AGREEMENT AS TO THE PRECISE COURSE IT TOOK. PERHAPS THERE WERE SEVERAL VARIANTS. He then lists them without choosing — one tradition through Rimersburg to Bullocks Ford on the Clarion near Callensburg; another through Fish Basket at Oak Ridge, at the mouth of Town Run on Redbank Creek, and over the Clarion at the same ford; others put the crossing at Canoe Ripple or at Piney. FOUR CANDIDATE FORDS ON ONE RIVER AND NO WAY TO CHOOSE. This layer draws the Fish Basket line because Fish Basket is independently attested on AW-429 and appears on Wallace's own map key, and it stops at Bullocks Ford — north of the Clarion the path ran to the vicinity of Van and joined the Frankstown road, but Van's position is not established well enough to place a junction on it, so none is claimed. COLONEL DANIEL BRODHEAD IS SAID TO HAVE USED IT in 1779 on his expedition against the Seneca — the western arm of the same campaign whose eastern arm made AW-181, the Forbidden Path, and whose northern reach burned the Seneca towns. Three routes in this layer are now connected by that single summer.

routes.name: The Punxsutawney–Venango Path (Punxsutawney–Fish Basket)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 95, CORRECTED v128-B128 AGAINST THE PRIMARY TEXT, AND THE CORRECTION MATTERS. Drawn at v92-B92, before wallace.txt was on disk (source_extraction_method wasn't solved until v95-B95), this route previously ran Punxsutawney to Brookville and claimed a junction with AW-416. THAT ENDING WAS NEVER IN WALLACE. His actual text: strong local tradition, confirmed by excellent terrain, has the path leaving Punxsutawney about where Pa. 36 does, climbing a ridge, turning at Frostburg, running another good ridge to Grange, where it FORKS — the main line continuing past Ringgold to cross Redbank Creek either at Hawthorn or at Fish Basket, while an alternate leaves at Grange via Zion Church to meet the Frankstown-Venango Path (AW-429) near McGregor. THE TWO REJOIN AT FISH BASKET, where 'the path from Frankstown to Venango came in, and the two proceeded as one' via Piney, Edenburg, Kossuth and Van to Franklin. This layer draws the main line to Fish Basket — already an attested junction node shared with AW-418 and AW-429 — and stops there per shared_tail_rule, rather than re-drawing the Frankstown-Venango leg. The alternate via Zion Church/McGregor is noted, not drawn (single_line_is_an_artefact_rule: a fork this well attested deserves acknowledgment even where only one branch is drawn). CONSEQUENCE: AW-432's Brookville node cited AW-419 there; that claim is now false and has been corrected in the same batch (junction_dependency_rule). Punxsutawney's own etymology discussion is preserved from the prior note: Punkwsutenay, roughly the town of the sandflies or gnats, a naming logic keyed to the traveller's experience of arrival rather than to settlement, alongside the Warriors Sleeping Place, Hart's Sleeping Place, Burnt Cabins, Shades of Death, Windfall and the Shades elsewhere in Wallace's index. JUNCTION CLAIM TO AW-431 REMOVED v139-B139: that claim was true only because AW-431 used to (incorrectly) end at Punxsutawney; AW-431 has since been corrected to run Ligonier–West Hickory and no longer touches this node (junction_dependency_rule again).

routes.name: The Cornplanter–Venango Path (Warren–Franklin)
routes.era: the grant to Cornplanter 1791; the town drowned by the Kinzua Dam 1965
routes.note: WALLACE No. 19. UPGRADED v113-B113, AND THE REASON IT WAS STILL WAITING IS ITSELF THE FINDING. At B101 this researcher composed an upgrade for this route and believed it had shipped. The lore store built at B113 anchored an entry to the Drake Well oil spring on AW-420 — and lore.py's integrity check snapped it 22 km to Tidioute, because THE NODE HAD NEVER EXISTED. The B101 batch file on disk contained AW-416, AW-417, AW-418 and AW-429; AW-420 was in the composition and not in the file. Guard, census and near-miss sweep were all clean throughout, because none of them can see a route that was never changed. IT TOOK A FOURTH TOOL, BUILT FOR A DIFFERENT PURPOSE, TO NOTICE. THE ROUTE ITSELF: from Warren down the NORTH bank of the Allegheny to Buckaloons, then up the north bank of Brokenstraw Creek past Youngsville and Pittsfield — inland, away from the river — and two or three miles beyond Pittsfield it turns southwest, recrosses the Brokenstraw, and follows A RIDGE to the oil spring near Titusville. Another ridge carries it to the French Creek crossing at Franklin. IT GOES BY THE OIL SPRING, AND THAT IS NOW DRAKE WELL PARK. The seep the Seneca skimmed is where Edwin Drake drilled in 1859 and started the petroleum industry. A path bent to reach a spring of something nobody yet had a use for. Wallace notes the first section, crossing the mountain from Cornplanter's Town to Warren, is AW-450's ground.

nodes.n: Venango (Franklin) — junction AW-399, AW-400, AW-416, AW-417

routes.name: The Pechoquealin Path (the Delaware Water Gap–Wyoming)
routes.era: pre-contact; carried Delaware families west after the Walking Purchase of 1737
routes.note: WALLACE No. 85, AND THE FIRST OF FOUR PATHS THIS BATCH DRAWS INTO A HUB THE LAYER DID NOT HAVE. The Wyoming Valley — Wilkes-Barre, Kingston and their neighbours — was one of the great Indian centres of Pennsylvania and there was not a single node on it. Wallace faced a naming problem here and solved it in a way worth recording: rather than have half a dozen Wyoming Paths, HE DROPPED THE NAME WYOMING ALTOGETHER and called the paths radiating into it by points on the OUTSIDE RIM — the Pechoquealin, the Wechquetank, the Wapwallopen and the Lackawanna. A hub too important to name a road after. That is a cartographer's ruling of exactly the kind _meta.id_rule exists to survive, made by hand in 1965. THIS ARM CARRIES A SHADES OF DEATH TWENTY MILES LONG in Monroe County. Wallace is careful about the word: the English swamp, like the German Schwamm, did not necessarily mean stagnant water — often it meant mountain land saturated with subsurface water and so heavily overgrown with laurel, hemlock and white pine that IT WAS THE BLACKNESS ABOVE RATHER THAN THE MOISTURE BELOW that troubled the traveller. Two tracts in Pennsylvania carry the name; this is the longer. Pechoquealin was the Delaware settlement at the Water Gap, and after the Walking Purchase of 1737 stripped the Forks of the Delaware from them, this is the road a good many of its people took west. Tier B.

nodes.n: The Shades of Death (twenty miles of it)
Wyoming (Wilkes-Barre) — junction AW-422, AW-423, AW-424, AW-425

routes.name: The Wechquetank Path (Bethlehem–Wyoming)
routes.era: the mission at Wechquetank 1760–63; the path walked by the Moravians in 1765
routes.note: WALLACE No. 128. CORRECTED v107-B107 — IT STARTS AT BETHLEHEM, NOT AT WECHQUETANK. At B93 I drew it from the mission town because the path's name is the mission's, which was exactly the mistake _meta.wallace_roster_rule warns against: THE NAME MARKS A PLACE ON THE ROAD, NOT ITS END. Wallace heads it 'From Bethlehem to Wilkes-Barre' and calls it the NEW PATH to Wyoming, sometimes DAVID'S PATH — a third name this layer would have missed. THE ROUTE IS A REFUGEE COLUMN'S ROUTE. Wechquetank was a Moravian Indian mission founded in 1760 and EVACUATED IN 1763 WHEN IT WAS THREATENED BY THE PAXTON BOYS during Pontiac's War — the same frontier mob that murdered the Conestoga at Lancaster. The converts were taken to Philadelphia for protection, and in 1765 the Moravians brought them back out along this road on the way to a new home at Wyalusing. So AW-403's Friedenshütten at the far end and this road are one story: a congregation moved twice by other people's violence, and the road is the second move. THE FORK AT NEWBURG IS DRAWN because Wallace draws it: the left fork is this path, the right went to Nazareth and the Wind Gap. Tier B.

nodes.n: Newburg (the fork — right goes to the Wind Gap)
Wyoming (Wilkes-Barre) — junction AW-421, AW-423, AW-424, AW-425

routes.name: The Wapwallopen Path (Wapwallopen–Wyoming)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 123, THE THIRD WYOMING ARM, AND IT IS ON FIRE. Martin Mack walked it on 19 April 1745 and wrote that the woods were burning all round them, the trees falling because the fire burnt so strong, and that between two great rocky mountains the flame ahead was so high they were afraid to go through it and could find no other way. His companion Christian Frölich went first and the flames closed over his head; Mack lost sight of him, called, was answered, and followed. FOREST FIRE IS THE HAZARD THIS LAYER HAS NEVER ONCE RECORDED, on any continent, in four hundred and twenty routes. Flood, snow, ice, windfall, raiders, pirates and rapids are all in here; fire is not, and it plainly belongs — the eastern woods burned regularly, and a path through burning country is a specific and survivable difficulty rather than a catastrophe, which is exactly why it shows up in a travel diary as an anecdote and not as a disaster. Wallace's own framing is the useful correction: life on the trail was neither as dangerous nor as monotonous as readers of Fenimore Cooper suppose, and the forest was A BUSY PLACE. Tier C, anchors only. UPGRADED v130-B130 to tier B on the motorist directions, which give a specific line: Pa. 29 north from Wapwallopen to the mouth of Little Wapwallopen Creek, up the valley and over Penobscot Mountain (drawn here as the attested waypoint), then via Slocum Corners, Follstown and Sheatown to Wilkes-Barre. NOT DRAWN: the same entry also describes a wholly separate 'blind path' alternate that Grube and Rundt struggled through in 1754 on the OTHER side of the Susquehanna, navigating by notched trees until even those ran out — a different route to Wyoming, not a variant of this one, and not attested well enough here to place (single_line_is_an_artefact_rule: two paths are described in one entry and only one is drawn).

routes.name: The Lackawanna Path (Wyoming–Oquaga)
routes.era: pre-contact; Oquaga a major Iroquois town until Sullivan's expedition, 1779
routes.note: WALLACE No. 50. CORRECTED v100-B100, AND THIS ONE WAS SIMPLY WRONG. At B93 I drew it Wyoming–Pittston–Carbondale–COCHECTON, sending it east to the Delaware. Wallace's entry is titled FROM PITTSTON TO WINDSOR, N.Y. — it goes NORTH up the Lackawanna and over the Bald Mountains to Oquaga on the North Branch of the Susquehanna, above the Great Bend. Wrong watershed, wrong destination, ninety kilometres out. IT IS ALSO CALLED THE OQUAGA OR ONAQUAGA PATH, which is the name that would have caught the error if I had been reading the source instead of the map. WHAT THE REAL LINE SHOWS: paths ran on BOTH banks of the Lackawanna — one from Lackawanna, or Assarughney, on the north side at the mouth, another from Adjouquay on the south side — and they converged at Old Forge about three miles up. Then Taylor, Capoose Meadows at Scranton, and north through LEGGETTS GAP in the Bald Mountains to the Tuscarora Indian Town at Lanesboro, where Starrucca Creek meets the Susquehanna in the Great Bend. A branch led to Apple Tree Town. THE SOUTHERN TERMINUS IS KEPT AT WYOMING deliberately, because Wallace's introduction lists the Lackawanna among the four paths he named from the outside rim rather than let any of them take the name Wyoming — so the valley is its true foot even though his entry heads the road at Pittston. Tier B.

routes.name: The Lehigh Path (the Forks of the Delaware–Wyoming)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Moravian road from Bethlehem to the mission towns
routes.note: WALLACE No. 53, AND THE FIFTH ROAD INTO WYOMING. It runs from the Forks of the Delaware — Lechawekink, where the Lehigh meets the Delaware at Easton — up the Lehigh past Bethlehem and Gnadenhütten and over the Broad Mountain to the Susquehanna. THE FORD IS THE STORY. Martin Mack crossed the Lehigh on foot in early April 1745 and recorded that it was so extremely cold they thought at first they could not endure it; midstream it was deep and the current so strong he expected every minute to be carried down, and his feet jammed between two great rocks. He got out by taking hold of a companion's coat. THAT IS WHAT A FORD NODE MEANS. This layer draws hundreds of them, one symbol each, and they are not equivalent — some are a wet boot and some are the place a man nearly died in April with his feet stuck. Wallace's introduction makes the general point: the most innocent ford could turn bad, a flash flood could change a rivulet into a torrent, and when John Harris's party retreated across the Susquehanna to Shamokin after the Penns Creek ambush in 1755, four or five of his men drowned at the crossing. Wallace also notes that at Easton the name Lechawekink meant the Forks, but 'the Forks of the Delaware' meant a wide territory including Nazareth, Bethlehem, Allentown and more besides — an ambivalence in Indian place names where a word is both a point and a region. Tier B.

The Lehigh ford that nearly took Mack
Wyoming (Wilkes-Barre) — junction AW-421, AW-422, AW-423, AW-424

routes.name: Logan's Path (McElhattan–Lewistown)
routes.era: pre-contact; John Logan in the Kishacoquillas Valley from about 1765
routes.note: WALLACE No. 55A. CORRECTED v107-B107 ON BOTH ENDS AND ON THE MAN. At B93 I drew this from the Great Island at Lock Haven and named it for 'the Mingo leader Logan'. Wallace runs it from the vicinity of Tishimingo on the West Branch near the mouth of Chatham Run — McElhattan, between Lock Haven and Jersey Shore — to Logan's Spring near Reedsville and on to Kishacoquillas. Both termini moved. AND THE MAN IS THE OTHER BROTHER. Wallace names him SHICKELLAMY'S SON JOHN LOGAN, 'NOT TO BE CONFUSED WITH HIS BROTHER, JAMES LOGAN', who lived a few years after 1765 in the Kishacoquillas Valley. At B99 I wrote a note on AW-434 celebrating 'one man with two roads named after him in different parts of the state'. IT WAS TWO MEN. James is on Logan Run beside the Susquehanna on the Catawissa Path; John is here, a hundred and eighty kilometres west. A FINDING BUILT ON A CONFLATION IS WORSE THAN NO FINDING, because it reads as insight and travels further than a plain error would. AW-434's note is amended in the same batch. THE ROUTE IS ALL GAPS, which is why it was famous for climbing: through the gap in Bald Eagle Mountain by Shoemaker Park and the Lock Haven Reservoir, across Chestnut Flat to Rosecrans, through the gap in Sugar Valley Mountain to Loganton, west to Booneville, south through Logan's Gap — now Kahl Gap — and then southwest over Nittany and Brush mountains. Fithian's minuet line belongs to the Seven Mile Mountain further along the same country. Tier B.

nodes.n: The gap in Bald Eagle Mountain (Shoemaker Park)

routes.name: The Raystown–Chinklacamoose Path (Bedford–Clearfield)
routes.era: pre-contact; reconnoitred, or not, in June 1758
routes.note: WALLACE No. 97. CORRECTED v108-B108 — IT GOES BY FRANKSTOWN, not by Hollidaysburg as I drew it at B94, and Wallace says the Raystown-to-Frankstown half was PART OF THE WARRIORS PATH from the Great Island. THE EVIDENCE IS A COLONEL COMPLAINING. Bouquet to Forbes, from the camp near Reas Town, 28 June 1758: the post of Shingalamuch is not so easy to reconnoitre, it is 30 miles from here to Franks Town, and 70 FROM THERE ACROSS CONTINUOUS MOUNTAINS. THE INDIANS DO NOT SEEM INCLINED TO MAKE THIS JOURNEY; I shall see if I can persuade them to make it, and give them a couple of our men. THAT IS THE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE ABOUT A ROAD IN THE WHOLE BOOK. Everything else in this layer records that a path existed; this records what people thought of walking it. The men who knew the country best did not want to go, and an officer had to bribe them and send escorts. A ROAD CAN BE REAL, KNOWN, MAPPED AND STILL UNPOPULAR, and the layer has no way to draw that except in the note. It also dates the reluctance precisely: seventy miles of continuous mountain between Frankstown and Clearfield, in the wettest campaign season of the war. Tier B. JUNCTION-DEPENDENCY FIRING AGAIN, v108-B108. This route claimed AW-429 at Frankstown and at Chinklacamoose. Both claims were true of the AW-429 I drew at B94 and FALSE OF THE ONE I CORRECTED AT B101, which now runs Cherry Tree to Franklin and touches neither place. I re-asserted them from memory of geometry I had myself already fixed, three batches earlier. THE GUARD CAUGHT IT AND THE LESSON IS SHARPER THAN AT B100: it is not enough to re-run the guard after a correction — the researcher must also stop carrying the pre-correction picture in his head. Read the route back before claiming a junction with it.

routes.name: The Frankstown–Burnt Cabins Path (Burnt Cabins–Frankstown)
routes.era: pre-contact; the cabins burned by the province in 1750
routes.note: WALLACE No. 27. CORRECTED AND UPGRADED v108-B108. At B94 I ran this by Aughwick on the Frankstown Path; Wallace runs it by FORT LITTLETON, Three Springs and Saltillo, then across THE BARRENS to the Raystown Branch of the Juniata near the mouth of Trough Creek, a mile and a half north of Marklesburg, over Tussey Mountain, west through Shelleytown on Clover Creek, over Lock Mountain west of Royer, and down to Frank Stevens' trading post at the mouth of Oldtown Creek. Nine nodes where I had three, and a different corridor. THE FORT LITTLETON CORRECTION CLOSES A TRIANGLE. AW-430 already ran Standing Stone to Fort Littleton; this route now meets it there, so the Juniata country and the Forbes corridor are joined at a 1755 provincial fort rather than at my guess. WHAT THE EVIDENCE IS, IN WALLACE'S OWN TERMS: for the stretch between the two branches of the Juniata it is A STRONG LOCAL TRADITION AT MARKLESBURG, resting on Frank Brumbaugh and the Stone Church. That is the field worker's maxim — ask the oldest inhabitant — carrying a kilometre of road. Tier B, because the tradition is specific to a building and a creek mouth rather than to a general direction. JUNCTION-DEPENDENCY FIRING AGAIN, v108-B108. This route claimed AW-429 at Frankstown and at Chinklacamoose. Both claims were true of the AW-429 I drew at B94 and FALSE OF THE ONE I CORRECTED AT B101, which now runs Cherry Tree to Franklin and touches neither place. I re-asserted them from memory of geometry I had myself already fixed, three batches earlier. THE GUARD CAUGHT IT AND THE LESSON IS SHARPER THAN AT B100: it is not enough to re-run the guard after a correction — the researcher must also stop carrying the pre-correction picture in his head. Read the route back before claiming a junction with it.

routes.name: The Frankstown–Venango Path (Cherry Tree–Franklin)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 28. CORRECTED v101-B101, AND THIS WAS THE WORST ERROR IN THE PENNSYLVANIA SET. At B94 I drew it Frankstown to Clearfield — north-east, into the West Branch country, on the reasoning that a two-terminus name gives you the ends. It does not go there. Wallace: from Frankstown to a little beyond the crossing of the West Branch a mile and a half south of Cherry Tree, THE PATH TO VENANGO WAS IDENTICAL WITH THE PATH TO KITTANNING — and at a spring on a hill about four miles as the bird flies beyond that crossing, the paths separated. From there it runs down the Little Mahoning to its mouth, crosses the Big Mahoning, and goes north-northwest to ford Redbank Creek from Oak Ridge to the Indian town of FISH BASKET at the mouth of Town Run, then over Middle Run about a mile and a quarter from its mouth and Leisure Run a mile and a quarter beyond. A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT COMPASS BEARING FROM THE ONE I GUESSED. The lesson is exact and goes in _meta: a two-terminus name tells you the ENDS, NOT THE MIDDLE, and where two roads share a long trunk the name can point at a place the road only reaches by way of somewhere else entirely. Drawn from the divergence under _meta.shared_tail_rule, since Frankstown to Cherry Tree is AW-179. Tier B.

routes.name: The Standing Stone–Fort Littleton Path (Huntingdon–Fort Littleton)
routes.era: pre-contact; Fort Littleton built 1755
routes.note: WALLACE No. 106. UPGRADED AND SHORTENED v129-B129 under shared_tail_rule. Wallace's text is short and precise: fording the Juniata at Standing Stone (Huntingdon), the path ran south up the valley of Crooked Creek, crossed the divide, and MET THE FRANKSTOWN–BURNT CABINS PATH (AW-428) about two miles northeast of Marklesburg — identified here with AW-428's existing 'North of Marklesburg (the Stone Church)' node, the nearest attested point on that route to Wallace's description, rather than manufacturing a new coordinate two miles away that a near-miss sweep would only flag as a probable duplicate. FROM THAT POINT IT FOLLOWED THE FRANKSTOWN–BURNT CABINS PATH (crossing the Raystown Branch of the Juniata at Sarah) TO FORT LITTLETON — drawn on AW-428 already, so this route stops at the merge rather than re-drawing it. The route keeps its historical name (Standing Stone–Fort Littleton) for its full logical extent, per two_terminus_selection_rule, even though the DRAWN line is shorter. The path is shown on William Scull's 1770 map of Pennsylvania, in both the English and French editions. CONSEQUENCE: AW-428's Fort Littleton node previously cited AW-430 there; that claim is now false (AW-430 no longer reaches Fort Littleton) and has been corrected in the same batch, with the AW-430 citation moved to the actual merge point (junction_dependency_rule). The Standing Stone origin story — the Oneida's carved pillar, carried away when they left Huntingdon in the 1750s, the settlers' replacement standing in its place — is preserved from the prior note. GATE NOTE: no shaping node inserted for the Crooked Creek leg — the Huntingdon–merge hop is 16 km, well under the tier-B 120 km limit, so none was gate-warranted (densify_warrant_rule). Crooked Creek is described in prose only.

routes.name: The Loyalhanna–Goschgoschink Path (Ligonier–West Hickory)
routes.era: pre-contact; Goschgoschink a Munsee town, Moravian mission 1768–70
routes.note: WALLACE No. 58, FULLY CORRECTED v139-B139 AGAINST BOTH THE PRIMARY TEXT AND AN INDEPENDENT SECONDARY SOURCE. The prior geometry (Ligonier–Saltsburg–Punxsutawney) matched NOTHING in Wallace's actual entry — Punxsutawney is never mentioned for path 58, and Saltsburg lies on a wholly different corridor. This was the same class of error as AW-419/AW-430/AW-470: drawn before wallace.txt was on disk, from a guess that turned out wrong once the text was available. WALLACE'S ACTUAL DESCRIPTION IS A THREE-LEG COMPOSITE, NOT AN INDEPENDENT ROAD: 'From Loyalhanna (Ligonier) as far as to Rayne Township in Indiana County, the path to Goschgoschink followed the Catawba Path [AW-432]. From there to Redbank Township in Jefferson County, it followed the Venango-Frankstown Path; and after that it followed the Goschgoschink Path to the Indian settlement at Goschgoschink on the upper Allegheny.' RESOLUTION OF THE FIRST TWO LEGS: AW-432 (the Catawba Path) already runs Ligonier through Homer City, Georgeville (within a few km of Rayne Township's centroid) and on through Trade City, Hamilton and Worthville to Brookville, on Redbank Creek in Jefferson County — there is no administrative 'Redbank Township' in Jefferson County (only in neighbouring Armstrong and Clarion Counties), so this is read as Wallace's loose regional name for the Redbank Creek valley stretch, not a township boundary. Wallace names this same ground 'Catawba Path' for its southern half and 'Venango-Frankstown Path' for its northern half — one more case of a single corridor carrying different names depending on who was walking it and from where, the same pattern already documented at AW-473 (the Cayahaga Path, sixth name for one road). SO THE FIRST TWO LEGS ARE DRAWN AS A SINGLE B-TIER HOP, LIGONIER TO BROOKVILLE, IDENTICAL TO AW-432'S OWN LINE AND NOT RE-DRAWN NODE BY NODE (shared_tail_rule) — the hop is 103 km, within the tier-B gate limit. THE THIRD LEG IS GENUINELY NEW GROUND. Wallace gives no routing detail for it and states plainly elsewhere in this entry that 'no adequate tracing of this path by modern roads is possible.' An independent secondary source — Wikipedia's own 'Goschgoschink Path' article, also called Mead's Path in places — corroborates the general corridor: from Brookville, 'north of Clarion, to West Hickory, Pennsylvania, in Forest County and the Allegheny River,' where the Zeisberger mission refugee towns collectively called Goschgoschink stood from 1767. This leg is drawn at C, anchors loose, on Wallace's own hedge — the corridor's existence is corroborated, its precise line is not. IMPROVED v145-B145: the third leg (Brookville to Goschgoschink) previously used an approximate, tier-C guess sourced only from path 58's brief mention. Wallace has a full dedicated entry for this ground (No. 32), now drawn separately and precisely as AW-518. This route's own drawn geometry now stops at Brookville and cites AW-518 rather than re-drawing an inferior version of the same line (shared_tail_rule).

nodes.n: Brookville (fording Redbank Creek — the loose ’Redbank Township, Jefferson County’ of Wallace’s text) — junction AW-416, AW-432, AW-518

routes.name: The Catawba Path (Ichsua–Morgantown)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Iroquois–Catawba war road, in use until the peace of 1751
routes.note: WALLACE No. 7, AND HE CALLS IT ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT INDIAN HIGHWAYS IN NORTH AMERICA. It ran from Ichsua on the upper Allegheny through Indiana and Uniontown to Morgantown and on into the Carolinas, Kentucky and Tennessee — and with its connections at each end it reached FROM CANADA TO FLORIDA and west into the Mississippi valley. Iroquois agents used it to keep an eye on the international scene; war parties of the Five Nations went south on it and Catawba and Cherokee parties came north on it, each striking at hereditary enemies. IT HAS SIX NAMES IN WALLACE'S TEXT ALONE — the Great Catawba War Path, the Iroquois Path, the Iroquois Main Road, the Cherokee Path, the Tennessee Path, the Catawba Path — which is _meta.wallace_roster_rule in its purest form and the reason frozen IDs matter here more than anywhere. THE FINDING IS A BOUNDARY. Wallace records that a western branch of this path, crossing the Monongahela and fording Dunkard Creek near Mount Morris, MARKED THE WESTERN LIMIT OF SURVEY AUTHORIZED BY THE IROQUOIS WHO ACCOMPANIED MASON AND DIXON IN 1767. The most famous line in American geography stops where an Indian war road crosses it. Two surveyors with the best instruments in the world went as far as a footpath and were told that was far enough. IT IS ALSO HARD TO TRACE PRECISELY, and Wallace says why: in early days it was little used by white men, so travellers noted it only where it crossed the better-known east-west traders' paths. The nodes drawn are his. Tier B. THIRD CASCADE, v102-B102. This node claimed a junction with AW-414, the Cherry Tree Portage, which was true only while that portage was drawn to Indiana. Wallace runs it to Diamondville on Two Lick Creek, so the claim went with the correction. THE RUNNING TALLY IS THE USEFUL PART: three junction cascades in three upgrade batches, one anticipated and two caught by the guard. Every single one was a claim made in good faith against a route that turned out to be wrong. A JUNCTION IS ONLY AS TRUE AS THE WEAKER OF THE TWO ROUTES IT JOINS, and an anchors-only route can support no junction at all except at its named ends.

nodes.n: The Clarion at the Millstone mouth
Trade City (the Great Shamokin Path crosses)
Squirrel Hill (the Conemaugh ford at New Florence)

routes.name: The Catfish Path (Waynesburg–the Forks of the Ohio)
routes.era: pre-contact; Catfish's camp established at Washington by 1769 or earlier
routes.note: WALLACE No. 9, AND IT IS NAMED FOR A MAN WHO MOVED. Catfish — Tingoocque — was an influential Delaware formerly of Kuskusky who by 1769 had set up camp where Washington now stands, at a crossroads: north to the Forks of the Ohio, south to the Warriors Branch, and the Mingo Path running east-west through it. THE CAMP MADE THE CROSSROADS FAMOUS ENOUGH TO NAME THE ROADS. Wallace has a dozen of these — Chartier's Town, Kickenapaulin's, Bald Eagle's Nest, Peholand's Town, Cornplanter's — and the pattern is consistent: in this domain A PLACE IS OFTEN JUST WHERE A PARTICULAR PERSON WAS LIVING AT THE TIME, which is why the names move when the people do (_meta.name_as_point_and_region). THE TESTIMONY IS A ONE-LINE DIARY ENTRY. The Rev. David Jones came east from Grave Creek and Wheeling in July 1772 and wrote that they set out for Fort Pitt on a small path called Catfish's road, which led through the middle of the land between the Ohio and the Monongahela; three days later he reached Fort Pitt. That is the whole attestation for a route now drawn across sixty kilometres — one clergyman, two sentences, and a name. Tier B, because the sentence is specific about the ground. GUARD CAUGHT A FALSE JUNCTION HERE, v95-B95: this node originally claimed a junction with AW-409, the Kuskusky-Chartier's Town Path, which runs New Castle to Tarentum and never comes near Washington. The claim was simply wrong and the guard refused it. WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE IT IS THE FIRST FALSE JUNCTION IN THIS RUN: 96 batches of junction claims and the guard had verified every one until this. It fails loudly and cheaply, which is exactly what it is for.

nodes.n: Forks of the Ohio (Pittsburgh) — junction AW-137, AW-138, AW-399, AW-406

routes.name: The Catawissa Path (Catawissa–Shamokin)
routes.era: pre-contact; a short cut from the Wyoming Valley to the Forks of the Susquehanna
routes.note: WALLACE No. 8, AND IT IS A SHORT CUT — the layer's first explicit one. Travellers coming down from the Wyoming Valley on the Great Warriors Path turned south at the Fishing Creek crossing, forded the Susquehanna at the mouth of Catawissa Creek, and took this path over the hills to Shamokin, saving the long river bend. A NETWORK DENSE ENOUGH TO HAVE SHORT CUTS IS A NETWORK, not a scatter of trails, and this is the evidence that Pennsylvania's was one. IT PASSES A NAMED MAN'S CABIN. Logan Run is named for Shickellamy's lame son James Logan, whose cabin stood beside the Susquehanna about half a mile west of the run's mouth — the same Logan whose family were murdered at Yellow Creek in 1774 and who gave the speech that got into every American schoolbook. CORRECTED v107-B107: this note originally said AW-426, Logan's Path, was named for the SAME man and celebrated 'one man with two roads named after him in different parts of the state'. IT WAS TWO MEN. Wallace names Logan's Path for Shickellamy's son JOHN Logan, 'not to be confused with his brother, JAMES Logan' — and it is James who lived on Logan Run here. Two brothers, two roads, a hundred and eighty kilometres apart. THE CONFLATION WAS WORSE THAN A PLAIN ERROR because it had been dressed as a finding, and a finding travels further than a mistake does. Wallace also notes the path was later used by two settler migrations, Presbyterian into Rush Township and Methodist into the Augusta area — an Indian short cut carrying denominations. Tier B.

nodes.n: Catawissa (Lapachpeton's Town, the ford) — junction AW-545

routes.name: The Brokenstraw Path (Buckaloons–Fort Le Boeuf)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 6, AND THE NAME IS A MISHEARING THAT STUCK. Buckaloons is an English corruption of the Delaware Paks-kalunska, broken straw — the Faille Coupée of the French records. THREE LANGUAGES AND THREE SPELLINGS OF ONE PLACE, and Wallace's editorial rule is to use whichever English usage has made familiar, which is why this layer's node strings should be read as conventions rather than transcriptions. Buckaloons was a centre where paths converged from Cornplanter's Town, from Goschgoschink, from Venango and from Fort Le Boeuf. THE ATTESTATION IS A CAPTIVITY NARRATIVE, and it is worth quoting the shape of it: John Hockstattler, a Swiss settler, was taken in 1755 by Delawares and Shawnees from Berks County to Fort Le Boeuf and thence to Buckaloons, escaped in the spring of 1758, and on examination described three days' travel east-south-east to the creek mouth where an Indian town stood. Wallace notes explicitly that WHAT WE KNOW OF THE WARRIORS PATHS COMES LARGELY FROM WARRANTEE SURVEYS AND THE NARRATIVES OF WHITE CAPTIVES — the early mapmakers recorded traders' paths and disregarded the rest. A whole class of road in this layer is known only because some of the people carried along it came back and were questioned. TIER C DELIBERATELY: Wallace says the western reaches are marshy, that the path was not much used there, and that ITS COURSE HAS NOT BEEN MAPPED. Drawn to Waterford on his line of towns and no further precision claimed.

nodes.n: Fort Le Boeuf (Waterford) — junction AW-399, AW-411, AW-533

routes.name: The Blue Rock Path (Phoenixville–the Blue Rock ford)
routes.era: pre-contact; the principal Susquehanna crossing before Wright's Ferry
routes.note: WALLACE No. 4, AND ITS NAMESAKE IS UNDER WATER. The Blue Rock was a rock painted blue at a Susquehanna ferry landing south of Washington Boro, and the ford beside it — usable in low water — had been known from ancient times. It was the most prominent crossing on the river before Wright's Ferry, used by the Cartledges, James Patterson, Peter Chartier and the other Indian traders, and it connected the Schuylkill valley paths with the Monocacy Path running south into Maryland and Virginia. THE BLUE ROCK IS NOW SUBMERGED BY THE WATERS OF THE SAFE HARBOR DAM. That is the THIRD drowned node in this layer — Dunwich under the North Sea, Cornplanter's Town under the Kinzua reservoir, and now the rock that named this road under a hydroelectric pool. Per _meta.drowned_node_rule the node stays, at the coordinate of the drowned thing. TWO OF THE THREE WERE DROWNED BY DAMS IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY, which is a pattern rather than a coincidence: a river crossing is exactly the place an engineer wants, so the fords that made the network are disproportionately the things impoundment destroys. Tier C: Wallace says there is little explicit evidence of Indian use and rests the line on a tradition recorded by Martin Brackbill, which is honest and is why the tier is what it is.

nodes.n: The Blue Rock ford (drowned by Safe Harbor)

routes.name: Camino de la Vera Cruz — the Templar road (Puente la Reina–Caravaca)
routes.era: the Templar commanderies dissolved 1312; Jaime II's route of 1296–1301; recovered from the 1990s
routes.note: THE LONGEST ROAD TO ANY SPANISH SHRINE — nearly 900 km in 29 to 33 stages, and the only route in this layer that is organised around A DISSOLVED MILITARY ORDER. It links the old Templar encomiendas across five autonomous communities: Navarra, Aragón, Castilla-La Mancha, Valencia and Murcia. IT BEGINS BY LEAVING THE CAMINO DE SANTIAGO. From Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port or Roncesvalles the pilgrim walks the Camino Francés, and at Puente la Reina — the town whose whole reason for existing is that the French roads converge there — the two part company for good, one bearing west for Compostela and one bearing southeast for Caravaca. THIS LAYER NOW HOLDS BOTH SIDES OF THAT FORK, which is the point of drawing it: Puente la Reina is not a stage on a road, it is a DECISION, and until this batch the layer could only show one of the two answers. Drawn from the fork under _meta.shared_tail_rule. WHAT IT RESTS ON, HONESTLY: a documented medieval road did link Puente la Reina by Estella, Los Arcos and Logroño with Tudela, and Tudela by Zaragoza with Calatayud, Daroca and Teruel — and Jaime II of Aragón used part of this itinerary between 1296 and 1301 when he took Caravaca, which then belonged to the Crown of Aragón for eight years. So the CORRIDOR is medieval and royal. The 900 km line as a single pilgrimage is a modern recovery, promoted from Murcia and still being re-signposted. Tier C for that reason, and the note says so rather than letting the length imply antiquity. Caravaca now takes some two hundred thousand pilgrims a year and half a million in a Jubilee Year, on a Holy Year granted in perpetuity.

nodes.n: Puente la Reina (the roads part) — junction AW-002
Caravaca de la Cruz (the Vera Cruz) — junction AW-377, AW-392, AW-393

routes.name: Camino del Campo de Cartagena (Cartagena–Caravaca)
routes.era: modern waymarking on old inland tracks from the Mediterranean ports
routes.note: THE ARM FROM THE SEA, 132 km in five stages. Cartagena is the deepest natural harbour on the Spanish Mediterranean and has been a port since the Carthaginians founded it; this route takes a pilgrim who arrives by water and puts him on the road inland. THE LAYER NOW HAS FOUR CARAVACA ARMS DRAWN AND CAN COUNT THE REST. Enumerating the Murcian sources properly turns up a delta far larger than the three I named at B93: besides the Orihuela road at AW-377, the Carmelite road at AW-392, the Vélez Blanco road at AW-393 and the Templar road at AW-437, there are the Camino del Altiplano (Yecla–Jumilla, 156 km, on the GR-252), the Camino del Bajo Guadalentín (Mazarrón–Totana, 132 km, GR-253), the Camino del Alto Guadalentín (Águilas–Lorca, 130 km, GR-253), the Camino Espiritual del Sur from Guadix, and two short feeders from Granja de Rocamora and from Abanilla-Ulea. ELEVEN ROADS TO ONE TOWN OF TWENTY-SIX THOUSAND PEOPLE. That is what a jubilee city looks like from the ground, and it is the same shape as Kuskuskies with five paths or Wyoming with five: a place is a hub because of what people want there, not because of its size. Tier C: the corridor is old and the waymarking is new.

nodes.n: Caravaca de la Cruz (the Vera Cruz) — junction AW-377, AW-392, AW-393, AW-437

routes.name: Camino Espiritual del Sur (Guadix–Caravaca)
routes.era: modern; on the old Altiplano tracks between Granada and Murcia
routes.note: 318 km IN FOURTEEN STAGES, from the Granadan comarca of Guadix through Baza and Huéscar on the Altiplano to the basilica at Caravaca — the longest of the southern arms and the one that crosses the emptiest country. IT SHARES A NODE WITH THE MOZÁRABE AND THAT IS THE INTERESTING PART. Guadix is Acci on the Via Augusta, it is a stage on AW-381 where Christians under Muslim rule walked NORTH to Compostela, and it is now also the head of a road running EAST to Caravaca. The same town, the same century, two pilgrim roads going opposite ways to two different relics — and the missed-junction sweep found Acci for us at B83 only because a Roman name and a modern one sat 456 m apart. THREE ROUTES NOW MEET THERE and none of them would have been visible from the others by name alone. Tier C: promoted by an association of municipalities and currently in the process of being signposted, which the note records rather than disguises. FIFTH SWEEP CATCH, v96-B96, AND IT COMPLETES A PATTERN. Baza was drawn 209 m from AW-069's 'Basti (Baza)'. Together with Acci/Guadix at B83 and Sigüenza at B84 and the two Pennsylvania catches at B92, the sweep has now found five unclaimed junctions — and THREE OF THE FIVE ARE THE SAME FAILURE: A ROMAN NAME AND A MODERN NAME FOR ONE TOWN, sitting a few hundred metres apart because two researchers rounded a coordinate differently. In Iberia the Via Augusta and the Roman viae carry Latin names and every later road carries Castilian ones, so this collision is STRUCTURAL, not accidental. Whenever a route is drawn across ground the Roman network already occupies, sweep before shipping and expect a hit.

nodes.n: Caravaca de la Cruz (the Vera Cruz) — junction AW-377, AW-392, AW-393, AW-437, AW-438

routes.name: Camino de Uclés (Madrid–Uclés)
routes.era: Uclés head of the Order of Santiago from 1174; the road waymarked in the modern era
routes.note: A PILGRIMAGE TO SANTIAGO THAT DOES NOT GO TO SANTIAGO, and it is the strangest route in the Iberian set. The Monastery of Uclés in Cuenca is the seat of the ORDER of Santiago and the second great Jacobean shrine in Spain — the apostle venerated in his own house rather than over his tomb. 144 km from Madrid across La Mancha in eleven short stages, running EAST, away from Compostela. THE WAYMARKING IS A DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE. Every other route in this network follows yellow arrows and the scallop on blue. This one follows RED arrows carrying the Cross of Santiago on white. It has its own pilgrim credential issued by its own association, and on arrival it grants its own certificate — the UCLESSIANA, its version of the Compostela. A DIFFERENT ARROW, A DIFFERENT PASSPORT, A DIFFERENT CERTIFICATE, AND THE SAME SAINT. This layer has drawn thirty-odd roads whose entire logic is that they converge on one tomb in Galicia, and here is a road built on the proposition that they need not. It is a schism rendered as infrastructure, and the fact that it is quiet and little-walked is part of the finding rather than an argument against drawing it. Tier B: the stages, the length and the destination are documented, and the monastery — Plateresque, Herrerian and Churrigueresque on a hill above the Bedija, on Muslim fortifications — is unambiguous.

routes.name: Calzada de los Blendios — the Besaya road (Suances–Herrera de Pisuerga)
routes.era: Roman, from the Cantabrian Wars of 29–19 BC; a Jacobean feeder in the medieval period
routes.note: THE ROAD ROME BUILT TO FINISH A WAR. The Calzada de los Blendios runs from Portus Blendium on the Cantabrian coast up the Besaya valley and over the divide to Pisoraca, and its purpose was to get legions and supplies into the mountains during the Cantabrian Wars — the last and hardest of Augustus's Iberian campaigns, which took ten years to subdue a people Rome had assumed would fold in one. IT IS ALSO THE BEST-PRESERVED ROMAN ROADBED IN CANTABRIA. The stretch between Bárcena de Pie de Concha and Pesquera survives with its paving and kerbs, and it is the rare case in this layer where the thing itself can still be walked on rather than inferred from towns — most of the network is known from where it went, not from what it was made of. THE LATER LIFE IS THE USUAL ONE: a Roman military road became a Jacobean feeder, carrying pilgrims landing on the Cantabrian coast inland to meet the Camino Francés on the meseta. That is the same sequence as AW-384 the Ruta de la Lana — a road built for one purpose that gets used for another because it is already there, already graded, and already provisioned. Tier B.

nodes.n: Bárcena de Pie de Concha (the surviving calzada)

routes.name: Caminho Português Interior (Viseu–Ourense)
routes.era: medieval; the inland Portuguese road, older than the coastal traffic
routes.note: THE PORTUGUESE ROAD THAT DOES NOT FOLLOW THE COAST, and it is the third and last Portuguese line this layer needed. AW-024 carries the Camino Portugués up the littoral from Lisbon through Porto; this one runs inland from Viseu through the Douro country and the Trás-os-Montes to enter Galicia at Verín and reach Ourense, where it joins AW-379, the Sanabrés, for the last stretch to Santiago. Drawn to Ourense under _meta.shared_tail_rule. IT CROSSES THE DOURO AT PESO DA RÉGUA, which means this pilgrim road and AW-371, the wine river, now stand on the same node — a camino and a rabelo route meeting at the one place in that gorge where crossing is easy. Régua is a port because the river is navigable to there and a pilgrim stage because the valley is crossable there, and those are the same fact about the same water. WHY THE INLAND ROAD IS OLDER: the Portuguese coast north of Porto is a succession of river mouths and lagoons, each needing a ferry, while the interior is hard walking but continuous. Coastal traffic became dominant only once the crossings were bridged, which is the same inversion as AW-390 the Camino Olvidado — the difficult inland road came first and the easy road took the traffic later. Tier C: the corridor and the towns are certain, the medieval alignment is reconstructed.

routes.name: Camino del Altiplano (Yecla–Jumilla)
routes.era: modern waymarking on the Murcian altiplano tracks
routes.note: 156 km IN FIVE STAGES, running on the GR-252 across the Murcian altiplano from Yecla through Jumilla to Caravaca — and drawn only as far as Jumilla, because from there it is AW-437, the Templar road, under _meta.shared_tail_rule. THIS IS THE SEVENTH APPLICATION OF THAT CONVENTION and it is now doing something the layer could not do without it: keeping ELEVEN ROADS TO ONE TOWN legible. Without the rule, six drawn Caravaca arms would each redraw the last thirty kilometres into the city, six lines stacked on one corridor, and the near-miss sweep would fire on every node of the overlap forever. THE ARMS ALL RUN ON WAYMARKED GR FOOTPATHS — this one on the GR-252, the two Guadalentín arms on the GR-253 — which is worth recording as a fact about how these roads survive. In Spain a long-distance footpath is a maintained legal object with a number, and a devotional route laid onto one inherits that maintenance. Same mechanism as AW-376, where the Romería runs on chartered drove roads because a vía pecuaria is public in perpetuity: THE PILGRIMAGE PERSISTS BY BORROWING SOMETHING ELSE'S LEGAL STATUS. Tier C.

routes.name: Camino del Bajo Guadalentín (Mazarrón–Totana)
routes.era: modern waymarking; the Guadalentín corridor in use since antiquity
routes.note: 132 km IN FOUR STAGES on the GR-253, from the Mediterranean at Mazarrón inland to Totana and on to Caravaca — drawn to Totana, where it meets AW-438 and becomes it. MAZARRÓN IS A MINING PORT AND HAS BEEN ONE SINCE CARTHAGE. Its lead and silver workings were among the richest in the western Mediterranean and were still producing under Rome; the Guadalentín corridor behind it is the natural road inland, which is why a devotional route can be laid on it now without inventing anything. THE PATTERN ACROSS THE CARAVACA DELTA IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: every one of these arms starts at a port or a frontier town — Cartagena, Mazarrón, Águilas, Orihuela, Vélez Blanco, Guadix, Yecla — and runs inland to a mountain shrine at 800 m. The roads are old because the ECONOMIC geography is old; the pilgrimage is the newest thing on them. Tier C.

routes.name: Camino del Alto Guadalentín (Águilas–Totana)
routes.era: modern waymarking; Lorca a frontier city of the Reconquista
routes.note: 130 km IN FOUR STAGES on the GR-253, from Águilas on the coast through Lorca and on toward Caravaca — drawn to Totana under _meta.shared_tail_rule. WITH THIS THE CARAVACA DELTA IS AS COMPLETE AS THIS LAYER CAN MAKE IT: nine of the eleven attested roads are now drawn, and the two that are not are short feeders — Granja de Rocamora at 36 km and Abanilla-Ulea at 28 km — whose junction point the sources disagree about, one placing them on the Campo de Cartagena road and another on the Camino de Levante. THAT DISAGREEMENT IS THE REASON THEY ARE NOT DRAWN, and recording it is more useful than picking one. LORCA IS THE POINT OF THIS ARM. For two and a half centuries it was the frontier city between Castile and Granada, walled, garrisoned and raided, and the roads behind it were kept open because a frontier has to be supplied. A pilgrim road running up a military corridor is the ordinary case in this layer rather than the exception — the Camino Olvidado, the Via Nova, the Calzada de los Blendios and the Ruta de la Lana all do it. NOTHING IS BUILT FOR PILGRIMS; PILGRIMS USE WHAT IS THERE. Tier C.

routes.name: The Delaware River Path — the Minsi Path (Philadelphia–Fort Hunter)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Mohawk war road to the southeastern seaboard
routes.note: WALLACE No. 22, AND IT IS THE LONGEST CONTINUOUS LINE IN THE PENNSYLVANIA SET — Philadelphia to the Mohawk River, four hundred kilometres, joining the Delaware estuary to the Iroquois heartland without ever leaving a river valley. It runs up the Delaware by Bethlehem, the Wind Gap, Depui's and Minisink Island, crosses at Matamoras to Port Jervis, continues by Cushetunk, Shehawken and Cookose, climbs the West Branch to Stamford, THEN CROSSES INTO THE SCHOHARIE and descends that creek to Ossernenon, the Lower Mohawk Castle, where Fort Hunter was later built. WALLACE CALLS IT THE MOHAWK WAR PATH TO THE SOUTHEASTERN SEABOARD, and Frank Lichtenthaeler's evidence is that the Schoharie Palatines drove their CATTLE down it in 1723 while their goods went down the Susquehanna on rafts — a household split between two watersheds, the possessions floating one way and the herd walking the other. THIS ROUTE STITCHES THE LAYER TOGETHER. It coordinate-matches five existing routes at Philadelphia, Bethlehem, Minisink Island, Cochecton and Deposit, which is more junctions than any other single road here — because a valley road that runs four hundred kilometres necessarily crosses everything that runs across it. Until this batch the layer held the Delaware's tributaries and portages and not the Delaware itself. Tier B. CASCADE CAUGHT BY THE GUARD, v100-B100. This node claimed a junction with AW-424, the Lackawanna Path — a claim that was only ever true because AW-424 was drawn to the WRONG DESTINATION at B93. When the upgrade pass corrected that route to run north to Oquaga instead of east to Cochecton, this junction became false and the guard refused the layer. THAT IS THE MOST VALUABLE THING THE GUARD HAS DONE IN A HUNDRED BATCHES: it did not catch a typo, it caught the DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE OF A CORRECTION. Junction claims are a dependency graph, and fixing one route can silently orphan a claim made on another. Corollary: after any route's geometry changes, re-run the guard on the WHOLE layer, never just the batch. SECOND CASCADE, v102-B102, AND THIS TIME ANTICIPATED RATHER THAN CAUGHT. The Deposit node claimed a junction with AW-415, the Great Bend Portage — which the same batch moved twenty kilometres east to run Lanesboro-to-Stockport, its true line. The claim was checked and removed BEFORE the guard ran, per _meta.junction_dependency_rule. Two of this route's five junction claims have now been withdrawn because the routes they pointed at were wrong; both were made in good faith against anchors-only drawings. THE UPGRADE PASS IS ALSO A JUNCTION AUDIT.

nodes.n: Philadelphia (the Schuylkill) — junction AW-139, AW-180, AW-396
Matamoras (the Delaware crossing to Port Jervis)
Ossernenon (Fort Hunter — the Lower Mohawk Castle)

routes.name: The Glades Path (Raystown–Catfish)
routes.era: pre-contact; opened as the Glades Road in 1772
routes.note: WALLACE No. 31, AND IT IS CALLED THE MIDDLE INDIAN TRAIL BY THE PEOPLE WHO LIVE ON IT. The Reverend E. Austin Cooper told Wallace that Highway 31 is known locally by that name — intermediate between the Raystown Path to the north and Nemacolin's Path to the south. THREE PARALLEL ROADS ACROSS THE SAME MOUNTAINS, and this layer now holds all three: AW-138, AW-137 and this. That is the real texture of the Allegheny crossing, and it is invisible if you draw only the famous two. IT IS THE ROAD AMERICA LEFT ON. In 1788 General Rufus Putnam led a body of New England settlers down it to West Newton on the Youghiogheny, where they built boats and embarked on 2 April for the journey on which they founded Marietta — the first to establish American government in the Northwest Territory. An Indian path across Pennsylvania was the on-ramp for the settlement of Ohio, and the boats were built at the point where the walking stopped and the water started, which is the whole logic of AW-413's Canoe Places restated in a different century. It crosses the Braddock Road at Mount Pleasant and the Catawba Path at Laurelville, and ends at Catfish where AW-433 begins. Tier B.

nodes.n: Somerset (the Glades of Stony Creek) — junction AW-521
West Newton (the Youghiogheny ford — Putnam's boats)

routes.name: The Conoy Path (Conoy Town–Carlisle)
routes.era: the Conoy at Conoy Town c. 1718–1743; Bezaillon's grant 1719
routes.note: WALLACE No. 17, AND IT IS ALSO CALLED THE CONEWAGO PATH, BECAUSE IT FORDED THE SUSQUEHANNA AT CONEWAGO FALLS — and Conewago means 'at the rapids'. A road named for the noise the water makes. THE NAME AT THE OTHER END IS A PEOPLE WHO WERE ONLY THERE FOR TWENTY-FIVE YEARS. The Conoy lived at Conoy Town from about 1718 to 1743, having already been pushed north out of Maryland, and moved on again afterwards — and their name stuck to the town, the creek and the road long after they had gone. This layer keeps meeting that: Chartier's Old Town, Cornplanter's, Peholand's, Catfish, Bald Eagle's Nest. A NAME IS THE SLOWEST-MOVING THING ON A ROAD. IT IS ALSO THE WESTERN END OF OLD PETER'S ROAD. Peter Bezaillon, the Indian trader, was granted seven hundred acres at Conoy Town in 1719 and his post there became the terminus of his pack trail — the same Old Peter's Road that Wallace uses in his introduction as the type specimen of good Indian routing, DRY, LEVEL AND DIRECT, running from Downingtown to the Susquehanna without a serious obstacle. The path joins the Allegheny Path at Letort's Spring in Carlisle and runs on to the Forks of the Ohio. Tier B.

nodes.n: The ford below Conewago Falls (York Haven)

routes.name: The Conemaugh Path (Raystown–Conemaugh)
routes.era: pre-contact; Conemaugh a Delaware town on the Stony Creek junction
routes.note: WALLACE No. 13, AND THE DESTINATION HAS TWO NAMES BECAUSE IT HAD TWO IDENTITIES. Conemaugh was the Delaware town at the junction of the Conemaugh River with Stony Creek, and it was sometimes called Kickey Husten's Town — a place name and a person's name for one settlement, which is _meta.name_as_point_and_region working on a single village rather than a region. It is Johnstown now. THE PATH'S WORK IS THE ALLEGHENY FRONT. From Raystown it runs north up the east side of the Juniata past Cessna and Reynoldsville at the Big Fork of Dunning Creek, and then SURMOUNTS THE FRONT — the single hardest piece of ground in Pennsylvania, the escarpment that no river breaks and that made the state a land-travel state. Wallace's introduction says it plainly: none of her rivers broke through the Allegheny Mountains, which interposed a barrier between east and west. Every road in this layer that crosses it does so by climbing, and this is one of the shorter and steeper answers. Tier B.

nodes.n: Reynoldsville (the Big Fork of Dunning Creek)

routes.name: Cornplanter's Path (Jenuchshadego–Conewango)
routes.era: 18th c.; the Seneca grant of 1791; the town drowned 1965
routes.note: WALLACE No. 18, AND IT IS THE ROUTE HIS OWN CORRESPONDENT REFUSED TO BELIEVE IN. This layer has quoted Merle Deardorff's letter twice already at AW-417 without being able to draw the ground it describes: he knew of SEVEN early ways between Cornplanter's Town and Warren and thought there were probably dozens. Wallace prints it, agrees, and then maps the one most frequently used anyway — down the Allegheny to the mouth of Hodge Run, up the run to Scandia, southwest along the summit of Quaker Ridge to Smith Corners, and there a choice of AT LEAST THREE MORE descents: Glade Run, Indian Hollow, or Hatch Run. A ROAD THAT BRANCHES THREE WAYS IN ITS LAST FIVE KILOMETRES IS NOT A LINE, and this is the layer's most honest single case of that. HODGE RUN CARRIES ITS OWN INSTRUCTIONS. The Seneca called it Dyaindon — 'where the road comes down'. A watercourse named for the fact that a path uses it, which is the reverse of the usual direction: normally the water is the older fact and the road takes its name. Here the traffic was heavy enough to name the creek. Both ends are already in this layer, Jenuchshadego at AW-420 and Conewango at AW-417, so this route closes the last unbuilt side of the upper Allegheny triangle. Tier C, deliberately: with three attested descents and dozens implied, one drawn line is a convenience and the note says so. STALE JUNCTION REMOVED v113-B113. This node claimed AW-420 at Cornplanter's Town. When AW-420 was finally upgraded — see _meta.lore_store for how its absence was discovered — Wallace's own text moved its southern head to Warren, because he says the Cornplanter's-Town-to-Warren leg IS this route's ground and not that one's. FOURTH STALE-JUNCTION FAILURE IN THIS RUN and the first caused by a route getting LONGER rather than shorter, which widens _meta.junction_dependency_rule: any change to a route's extent, in either direction, can orphan a claim made against it.

nodes.n: Scandia (up Dyaindon — where the road comes down)

routes.name: The Old Iroquois Trail (Canajoharie–Onondaga)
routes.era: the great trail of the 17th century; superseded by the Rome line in the 18th
routes.note: THE FIRST NEW YORK ROUTE, AND IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE LAYER ALREADY HELD THE WRONG ONE. AW-077, the Mohawk Trail, reproduces Lewis Henry Morgan's scheme from 'League of the Iroquois' node for node — Albany, Schenectady, Canajoharie, Little Falls, Utica, Oriskany, the Oneida Carry at Rome, Oneida Castle, Onondaga. Beauchamp's 1905 correction says that line is LATE. ROME WAS NOT AN OBJECTIVE POINT until western trade became vigorous, and there was probably little travel that way till the 18th century. WHAT THE 17TH-CENTURY ROAD ACTUALLY DID: Van Curler, going to Oneida in 1634, left the Mohawk EAST of present Canajoharie and crossed the upper waters of Oneida Creek — and Beauchamp writes that later accounts show THIS WAS LONG THE ONLY GREAT TRAIL, AND THIS FACT MORGAN OVERLOOKED. Colonel Romer's map of 1700 marks the same thing: leaving the Mohawk at the third castle, southwesterly near the head of Schuyler Lake, then west to Old Oneida. TWO MORE CORRECTIONS ARE DRAWN HERE. Modern Oneida Castle is a recent town; Gen. John S. Clark placed OLD Oneida in the southwest corner of Vernon, where Sauthier's map shows it. And Morgan's Deep Spring is unattested — no colonial traveller mentions it, one of Gansevoort's officers called it merely a sunken spring in the road in 1779, and the Onondagas told Beauchamp their favourite resting place was GREEN LAKE near Kirkville, north of Morgan's line. A resting place named by the people who rested at it beats a spring named by a surveyor. Tier B. Johnson and the Moravians put the 1756 trail a mile south of Jamesville, entering the Onondaga valley far south of the turnpike — recorded here rather than drawn, because the Moravian journals show SEVERAL trails between Oneida and Onondaga and one line cannot carry them.

nodes.n: East of Canajoharie (Van Curler leaves the Mohawk, 1634)
