routes.name: The Indian Ladder Road (Schoharie–Albany)
routes.era: pre-contact; the escarpment climb still named for its notched-log ladder
routes.note: NAMED AT LAST. This layer identified the Helderberg escarpment as a gap at the very start of the New York work — Indian Ladder probed at 18.8 km from the nearest node, with Schoharie 0.5 km away, the Mohawk valley covered to within a kilometre, and the escarpment between them empty. The route was NOT DRAWN then, deliberately, because 'roughly where the corridor runs' is not a coordinate. Beauchamp names it in one sentence: a branch turned up Foxes Creek, crossed the Helderbergs and ended at Albany — THIS WAS THE INDIAN LADDER ROAD. IT IS A BRANCH, WHICH IS THE PART I HAD WRONG. I had assumed a road from the Schoharie flats to Albany in its own right. Beauchamp makes it a limb of the great Susquehanna trail: the line comes up the Charlotte to its head, crosses to the Cobleskill, meets the Schoharie, and THERE throws off branches — one over the Helderbergs to Albany, one across Middleburgh to the Catskill and the Hudson. The escarpment road is a way OFF a through-route, not a road between two towns. THE NAME IS THE ARTEFACT. The Indian Ladder was a notched log set against the cliff, and the climb kept the name for two centuries after the log rotted — the same mechanism as Standing Stone at AW-430, where the Oneida took the stone away and the town kept the name. A ROAD REMEMBERS ITS HARDEST TEN METRES. Tier B: Beauchamp names the creek, the range and both ends; the line between Foxes Creek and the cliff is his corridor rather than his survey. CROSS-CONFIRMED v163-B163 against Judge Brown's second named foot-path (per Simms, History of Schoharie County, 1845): 'began at Albany and led over the Helleberg, down Foxes creek valley, and terminated in Schoharie. By this path the Germans traveled, who first settled Schoharie' — already this route's own Foxes Creek waypoint. Brown adds that the road existing in his own day (1845) still followed nearly the same line.

nodes.n: Fort Orange (Albany) — junction AW-077, AW-157, AW-182, AW-266

routes.name: The Susquehanna Trail (Tioga Point–Canajoharie)
routes.era: pre-contact; a principal Iroquois thoroughfare in the later wars
routes.note: THE ROAD THE INDIAN LADDER HANGS OFF. Beauchamp: trails naturally converged at Tioga Point where the Chemung united with the Susquehanna, AND THESE BECAME IMPORTANT THOROUGHFARES FOR THE IROQUOIS IN THEIR LATER WARS. Morgan named two trails up the river; this is the northern, following the north bank, crossing the Chenango at Binghamton, on to the Unadilla, and there INTERSECTING THE ONEIDA TRAIL — then up the Charlotte and by Cherry Valley creek to Canajoharie on the Mohawk. IT IS THE SPINE OF THE WHOLE EASTERN NETWORK. From it hang the Indian Ladder road over the Helderbergs at AW-452, the Catskill branch at AW-454, and the Cobleskill line into the Schoharie. Tioga Point at one end already carries four routes in this layer; Canajoharie at the other carries three. This single road connects them, and until now the layer had both knots and nothing between. WHY IT MATTERED IN THE WARS is the same reason it mattered in peace — it is the only continuous line from the Iroquois heartland to the Pennsylvania frontier that does not cross a divide, which is why Sullivan's army went up it in 1779 and why the towns on it were the ones burned. Tier B. CAVEAT ADDED v104-B104, FROM THE SAME SOURCE THAT GAVE THE ROUTE. Beauchamp states flatly that IN 1753 THERE WAS NO ROAD AT ALL ALONG THE NORTH BANK OF THE SUSQUEHANNA FROM OWEGO TO THE CHENANGO RIVER — which is precisely the stretch between this route's first two nodes. So the northern bank line is NOT continuously attested for the mid-18th century, whatever Morgan's scheme shows. The route stays drawn because Beauchamp also says trails converged at Tioga Point and became important thoroughfares in the later wars, and because he treats the corridor as real; but the Owego-Chenango reach is a documented absence sitting inside a drawn line, and the note is the only place that can live. RECORDING A SOURCE'S OWN CONTRADICTION IS BETTER THAN CHOOSING BETWEEN ITS HALVES.

nodes.n: Athens (Tioga Point) — junction AW-079, AW-181, AW-401, AW-402
Unadilla (the Oneida trail intersects) — junction AW-081, AW-198

routes.name: The Catskill Trail (Middleburgh–the Hudson)
routes.era: pre-contact; a Mahican–Iroquois contact route to the Hudson
routes.note: THE SECOND BRANCH OFF THE SCHOHARIE, and the sister of the Indian Ladder road. Beauchamp: another crossed the town of Middleburgh to the Catskill, following that stream to the Hudson. TWO WAYS DOWN OFF THE SAME PLATEAU, forty kilometres apart, and the layer now holds both — one over the escarpment to Albany, one down a creek to the river. They answer the same question differently, which is the commonest shape in this whole layer: the Presque Isle and Chautauqua portages, the Invierno and the Francés, the Great Bend and Lackawanna carries. BEAUCHAMP'S OWN CAVEAT IS THE INTERESTING PART. He writes that IT IS EVIDENT THESE TRAILS CAME FROM THE RECENT OCCUPATION OF SCHOHARIE CREEK — meaning the whole branching system here is late, a product of people moving into the Schoharie rather than an ancient pattern. So a road can be genuine and recent at once, and the layer should not read antiquity into a good line. Tier C on that basis, and because the course between Middleburgh and the creek is not given. It reaches the Hudson where AW-198 already lands at Catskill. CROSS-CONFIRMED AND NAMED v163-B163: Jeptha Simms's History of Schoharie County (1845) records this as the first of five named foot-paths Judge Brown (interviewed by Simms in 1837, then in his nineties) recalled from before white settlement — 'began at Catskill, and followed the kill of that name up to its source at the Vlaie, from whence it continued down to Middleburgh.' The unnamed shaping node previously standing in for the summit crossing is now given the name Brown himself gave it.

routes.name: The Lake Ridge Trail (Oswego–the Genesee)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Ontario shore road
routes.note: IT FILLS A GAP THIS LAYER MEASURED AND COULD NOT CLOSE. Oswego probed at 51.8 km from anything — the water road from the Oneida Carry down to Lake Ontario was absent, and so was the shore road west from it. This is the shore road. Beauchamp, following Morgan: from Oswego one followed THE LAKE RIDGE to Irondequoit bay, turned up the bay to its head, crossed the Genesee at the Rochester aqueduct, struck the ridge road at the lower falls and went west to the Tuscarora village. THE LAKE RIDGE IS A BEACH THAT IS NO LONGER ON A LAKE. It is the abandoned shoreline of glacial Lake Iroquois, a raised gravel bar running parallel to the modern Ontario shore — dry, level and continuous, which is Wallace's three words for good path country arrived at by an ice sheet. AW-400's Muddy Creek ford sits on a Wisconsin terminal moraine; this whole road sits on a Wisconsin strandline. TWO OF THE BEST ROADS IN THIS LAYER ARE THINGS A GLACIER LEFT BEHIND. Beauchamp flags the western end as a recent town, so the Tuscarora terminus is 18th-century; the ridge itself is not. Tier B.

nodes.n: Along the lake ridge (the glacial strandline)
The Genesee at the Rochester aqueduct
The lower falls (onto the ridge road)

routes.name: Van Curler's Road (Albany–Oneida, 1634)
routes.era: walked December 1634 – January 1635; the earliest traceable route west from Albany
routes.note: THE EARLIEST TRAIL THAT CAN BE TRACED WESTWARD FROM ALBANY, and it is dated to the day. Arent Van Curler walked it in the winter of 1634 when there were no white settlements west of Albany and all the Mohawk towns lay west of Schoharie creek. Beauchamp reconstructs it stage by stage from the itinerary. A UNIT PROBLEM SITS UNDER THE WHOLE ROUTE and Beauchamp solves it in one line: VAN CURLER'S RECORDED MILES ARE EACH EQUAL TO ABOUT TWO ENGLISH MILES. Every distance in the account has to be doubled before it means anything, which is why an itinerary that looks like a short walk is in fact a hundred and thirty kilometres. A ROUTE RECONSTRUCTED FROM A DIARY IS ONLY AS GOOD AS ITS UNIT CONVERSION. IT NAMES THE FOUR MOHAWK CASTLES IN ORDER — Onekagoncka, Canagere, Sohanidisse and Tenotoge — with the lesser towns between them: Canowarocle, Senatsycrosy, Osguage, Cawaoge. Canagere stands 44 miles from Albany and Tenotoge 51, east of present Canajoharie. For at least thirteen miles he followed the SOUTH bank, and like later travellers he then left the river: from Spraker's he took a westerly course, crossed Canajoharie creek but passed SOUTH of the Otsquago. That southerly swing is the thing Morgan's scheme misses, and it is why AW-451 exists. THE LAST LINE OF THE ACCOUNT IS THE BEST. They walked through the snow, AND THE MILES SEEMED LONG. Four hundred years on, that is still the most useful thing anyone has said about winter travel on this road. Tier B: Beauchamp's own placings, county by county, from a source that gives distances but not bearings.

routes.name: The Oswego Water Road (the Oneida Carry–Lake Ontario)
routes.era: pre-contact; the fur artery, fortified by both empires from the 1720s
routes.note: THE GAP THIS LAYER MEASURED IN ITS FIRST WEEK. Oswego probed at 51.8 km from anything and the diagnosis was recorded then: AW-077 stops at Onondaga, AW-182 goes north to Ticonderoga, and NOBODY DREW THE WAY WEST TO THE LAKE, WHICH IS HOW THE FUR ACTUALLY MOVED. Rivers are roads, again. THE WHOLE CONTINENT HINGES ON THE OTHER END OF IT. At the Oneida Carry a man could lift his canoe out of the Mohawk, walk it a mile or so to Wood Creek, and be on water that runs to Oneida Lake, the Oswego River, Lake Ontario and everything beyond — while the water he left runs to the Hudson and the Atlantic. That is why Fort Stanwix is where it is, why the 1768 treaty line was drawn there, and why AW-411's Presque Isle carry has an eastern twin nobody names. TWENTY MINUTES OF CARRYING SEPARATES TWO OCEANS, which is _meta.portage_rule stated for the fifth time and the first in New York. BEAUCHAMP'S OWN NOTE CLINCHES THE PRIORITY: writing of a later map he says flatly that THERE ARE NO TRAILS ON THE SUSQUEHANNA, THE RIVER BEING USED INSTEAD. Where water serves, the land road is not made — so the ABSENCE of a path is evidence of a working river, and a layer that draws only footpaths will systematically miss the busiest corridors. Three Rivers, where the Seneca and Oneida join to make the Oswego, is named on Sauthier as a trail destination in its own right. Tier B.

nodes.n: The Oneida Carry (Fort Stanwix) — junction AW-077
Three Rivers (the Seneca and Oneida make the Oswego)

routes.name: The Carrying Place Path (Oneida–the Oneida Carry)
routes.era: on Romer's map of 1700; became a thoroughfare once Oswego was a trading post
routes.note: A SPUR, AND ITS GEOMETRY IS THE FINDING. Beauchamp on Romer's 1700 map: a trail leads from Oneida to the Carrying Place and RUNS AT RIGHT ANGLES TO THE MAIN ROAD, from which it was a short day's journey. The great east-west trail did not go to the portage — the portage hung off it, perpendicular, a detour you took only if you meant to leave the Mohawk system altogether. THE LAYER HAD BEEN DRAWING THIS BACKWARDS. AW-077 sends the main trail THROUGH the Oneida Carry at Rome, because that is Morgan's scheme; Beauchamp says at that period there was little land travel along the Mohawk above Little Falls and the portage was only SOMETIMES used. The Carry became central later, and the reason is commercial: WHEN A TRADING POST WAS ESTABLISHED AT OSWEGO IT BECAME AN IMPORTANT THOROUGHFARE. A spur turns into a trunk because somebody opens a shop at the far end. THE BEST FIRST-HAND DESCRIPTION OF A ROAD IN THIS WHOLE LAYER is Romer's companions, October 1700, sent to see how the Carrying Place could be made: they hired an Indian who showed them the way, and WE CAME BY A MOST MISERABLE PATH TO THE CARRYING PLACE, which they viewed as far as Wood Creek before going on to Oneida in the evening. Two adjectives from a working surveyor beat a page of reconstruction. Tier B.

nodes.n: The Oneida Carry (Fort Stanwix) — junction AW-077, AW-457

routes.name: The Onondaga Branch Trails (Pompey–Onondaga Lake and Chittenango)
routes.era: Onondaga at Pompey c. 1677–1700; the town moved east of Onondaga creek soon after
routes.note: TWO TRAILS ONLY, AND THAT IS THE POINT. Beauchamp reads Romer's 1700 map: the trail goes from Oneida to Onondaga, and FROM THAT TOWN THE PARTY TRAVERSED TWO TRAILS ONLY — one to Onondaga lake and the other to the fishing place on Chittenango creek. A capital of the Confederacy with a through-road and exactly two local roads, going to salt water and to fish. THE HUB IS NOT WHERE THE LAYER PUTS IT. Greenhalgh in 1677 found Onondaga STILL IN POMPEY, about two miles south of Morgan's later trail — twenty kilometres southeast of the Syracuse node AW-077 and AW-451 use. Both are correct for their dates. This route therefore carries a second node called Onondaga at a different coordinate, which is _meta.name_as_point_and_region in its sharpest form: the same capital, two positions, a generation apart, and NO WAY TO DRAW BOTH WITHOUT DRAWING THE NAME TWICE. Beauchamp adds that when the town moved east of Onondaga creek a few years later, the removal HAD MOST EFFECT ON THE BRANCH TRAILS — the through-road barely moved and the local ones were remade. A CAPITAL'S LONG-DISTANCE CONNECTIONS ARE MORE STABLE THAN ITS ERRANDS. Greenhalgh's ride also records that by 1677 the four Mohawk castles and one small village were ALL ON THE NORTH SIDE of the river, where Van Curler in 1634 found them all on the south (AW-456) — a documented bank-shift inside forty-three years. Tier B.

nodes.n: The fishing place on Chittenango creek

routes.name: The Kanestio Trail (Kanestio–Ganuskago)
routes.era: on Guy Johnson's map of 1771; Kanestio destroyed 1764
routes.note: THE SOUTHERN-TIER LINK, and its western end is a town the Iroquois themselves destroyed. Beauchamp records only that KANESTIO IS CONNECTED WITH GANUSKAGO — Dansville — and that is the whole entry. Kanestio on the Canisteo river was a mixed refugee town, Delaware and Seneca and others, outside the League's discipline and notorious for raiding; in 1764 the Iroquois were required to break it up and its people scattered. A ROAD IN THIS LAYER WHOSE TERMINUS WAS DELIBERATELY ERASED BY THE POLITY THAT OWNED THE ROAD is unusual — Kittanning was burned by Armstrong, Cornplanter's Town drowned by an agency, Burnt Cabins fired by a province, but this one was cleared by its own confederacy. TWO NODES AND NOTHING BETWEEN, on Beauchamp's own brevity. It runs the Canisteo to the Genesee headwaters and completes the southern tier of the New York set, which otherwise has nothing between the Susquehanna Trail at AW-453 and the Genesee. Tier C. SIXTH SWEEP CATCH, v105-B105, AND IT EXTENDS THE PATTERN TO A NEW LANGUAGE PAIR. Kanestio was drawn 411 m from AW-181's 'Canisteo'. Three of the six catches so far have been Latin against Castilian (Acci/Guadix, Basti/Baza) or Roman against modern; this is IROQUOIS AGAINST ENGLISH. The mechanism is identical and it is structural, not accidental: this layer draws routes from sources written in different centuries and different languages, and the SAME PLACE ARRIVES UNDER DIFFERENT NAMES with independently rounded coordinates. In New York, where Beauchamp's whole other book is 'Aboriginal Place Names of New York', expect this on almost every route. Sweep before shipping, always.

routes.name: The Turkeyfoot Path (Wills Creek–Turkeyfoot)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Turkeyfoot Road opened on it in 1751
routes.note: WALLACE No. 115, AND THE NAME IS A CONFLUENCE SEEN FROM ABOVE. Turkeyfoot — now Confluence — sits where three waterways meet: the Youghiogheny, the Little Youghiogheny or Little Crossings (now the Casselman), and the North Fork of Laurel Hill Creek. Three channels spreading from one point, like a print in mud. IT IS ALSO A NAME THAT BELONGS TO SEVERAL ROADS AT ONCE. Wallace: it was at the junction of several Indian paths, EACH OF WHICH, FROM ITS TERMINAL POINT, WAS CALLED THE TURKEYFOOT PATH. That is _meta.wallace_roster_rule in its purest form — the name attaches to the destination and every approach inherits it, so 'the Turkeyfoot Path' is four roads wearing one label. This layer draws the Wills Creek arm and says so. THE 1751 ROAD IS THE EVIDENCE. Wallace's introduction uses the Turkeyfoot Road as his type case for how little was needed to turn a footpath into a highway: opening it meant NO MORE THAN CUTTING THE BRUSH AND REMOVING THE LOGS FROM AN INDIAN PATH. Many sections are still visible and a few carry modern traffic. Tier B: local tradition with documentary support, in his own phrasing.

routes.name: The Tuscarora Path (Path Valley–Shamokin)
routes.era: the Tuscarora migration north, c. 1713–1722
routes.note: WALLACE No. 116, AND IT IS A ROAD NAMED FOR A NATION IN MOTION. Path Valley — the West Branch of Conococheague and the Tuscarora Creek valley — is named for the path, and the path is named for the Tuscarora. Wallace gives two accounts of why and declines to settle it. TRADITION says it was the way the Tuscarora came during the eighteenth century to find refuge in the Iroquois country of northern Pennsylvania and upstate New York, after their war with Carolina and the fall of their last great fort, Narhantes. DONEHOO thought the Iroquois had already named it that, EARLIER, because it was the way to their Iroquoian kin whom they later adopted as the sixth nation of the Confederacy. THE TWO READINGS INVERT THE CAUSATION AND BOTH ARE PLAUSIBLE: either a people gave their name to the road they fled along, or a road already named for its destination happened to carry that people home. This layer cannot settle it either and the note records both, which is the correct treatment of a source that refuses to choose — the same as AW-418's four fords. IT IS THE LAYER'S FIRST ROAD OF REFUGE. AW-320 draws the Trail of Tears, but that was a forced march; this is a nation walking out of a lost war toward relatives, and arriving. Tier B.

nodes.n: Path Valley (the West Branch of Conococheague)
Shamokin (Sunbury) — junction AW-084, AW-178, AW-180, AW-434

routes.name: The Virginia Road (Paxtang–Winchester)
routes.era: the EARLIEST of the four Iroquois highways south; east of the Allegheny, displaced westward from the 1730s
routes.note: WALLACE No. 121, AND IT IS DRAWN TO FIX A TEMPORAL ERROR THE LAYER HAD ALREADY MADE. Wallace: in early times THE MAIN IROQUOIS HIGHWAY TO THE SOUTH LAY EAST OF THE ALLEGHENY MOUNTAIN; but after the coming of white settlers WHO INSISTED THAT THEIR CLEARINGS PRE-EMPTED THE INDIANS' RIGHT OF WAY, the Warriors Path WAS PUSHED EVER FARTHER WEST — from the Virginia Road to the Tuscarora Path, the Penns Creek Path, and finally the Catawba Path and its offshoots in western Pennsylvania. FOUR SUCCESSIVE ROADS DOING ONE JOB, EACH SHOVED WEST BY THE LAST WAVE OF FENCES. Until this batch the layer held the two LATEST members of that series — AW-432 the Catawba Path and AW-462 the Tuscarora Path — and neither of the two earlier ones. It had drawn the displaced road and not the original. THIS IS THE OLDEST. Paxtang to Letort's Spring at Carlisle, Dunning's Spring at Mount Rock, the Big Spring to Shippensburg, across the Conococheague at Scotland or Red Bridge, past the Falling Spring at Chambersburg and Greencastle to Winchester. It is a road defined by SPRINGS, which is what an east-of-the-mountain road can afford to be — the western replacements are defined by gaps and fords instead, because they were pushed into worse country. Also called the Potomac Road and sometimes the Great Trail. Tier B. SEVENTH SWEEP CATCH, v109-B109, AND IT CONFIRMS THE ROUTE'S IDENTITY. Both the Falling Spring at Chambersburg and Winchester were drawn within 150 m of nodes AW-084 already held — the Great Warriors Path. That is not a collision to be tidied away, it is EVIDENCE: Wallace lists the Virginia Road among the paths white men called a Warriors Path, and here the two roads are demonstrably standing on the same ground at both ends of the Cumberland Valley. The sweep found a relationship, not just a duplicate.

nodes.n: Paxtang (Harrisburg) — junction AW-084, AW-138, AW-396, AW-397

routes.name: The Penns Creek Path — Karondinhah (Sunbury–Frankstown)
routes.era: the THIRD of the four southern highways; in use as the earlier two were closed off
routes.note: WALLACE No. 87, THE THIRD MEMBER OF THE DISPLACED SERIES, and the layer now holds all four in sequence: AW-463 the Virginia Road east of the mountain, AW-462 the Tuscarora Path, this, and AW-432 the Catawba Path in the west. FOUR ROADS, ONE FUNCTION, A CENTURY OF BEING PUSHED. Drawing them together is the only way the layer can show what encroachment did to a network — a single line through that country would have flattened a hundred years of displacement into one route. THE IROQUOIS NAME IS ON THE RECORD: known among them as the KARONDINHAH PATH, which is worth keeping because most of this domain's names are English or Delaware and the Iroquois were the polity that maintained the road. IT COLLECTS THE OTHER PATHS AS IT GOES. Wallace has it cross the plains beyond Spring Mills intersecting Logan's Path coming in from Tishimingo — AW-426, corrected two batches ago — and the path from Bald Eagle's Nest to Kishacoquillas, before meeting the Frankstown Path at Water Street and following it in. HIS HONESTY ABOUT THE MIDDLE IS WORTH QUOTING: from the vicinity of Linden Hall ITS EXACT COURSE HAS NOT BEEN DETERMINED, but it PROBABLY ran by Boalsburg, Shingletown, Pine Grove Mills, Rockspring, Baileyville, Graysville and down Spruce Creek. Seven named villages behind the word 'probably', which is what tier B evidence looks like when the author is being careful.

Down Spruce Creek to the Little Juniata

routes.name: The Sinnemahoning Path (Great Island–Port Allegany)
routes.era: pre-contact, and possibly the oldest road in the Pennsylvania set
routes.note: WALLACE No. 104, AND IT CARRIES THE OLDEST CLAIM IN THE WHOLE PENNSYLVANIA SET. 'NO OTHER PATH PROVIDED SUCH EASY GRADES ACROSS PENNSYLVANIA'S MOUNTAINS. For that reason it has been suggested that THE FIRST INDIANS WHO MOVED INTO PENNSYLVANIA FROM THE WEST, THOUSANDS OF YEARS AGO, MAY HAVE COME THROUGH THIS GATEWAY.' Every other route in this domain is dated by a journal, a treaty or a fort. This one is dated by a gradient. THE ARGUMENT IS PURELY PHYSICAL AND THAT IS ITS STRENGTH. Wallace's own framing of the state is that the Alleghenies interposed a barrier no river pierced and that could be surmounted only by long portages; if that is true, then the ONE place where the grades are easy is where people would have come first, and the road there should be older than the record. It is the same reasoning as _meta.glacial_roadbed_rule and AW-419's 'excellent terrain adds confirmation' — the ground testifying about traffic nobody wrote down. IT RUNS UP THE WEST BRANCH AND SINNEMAHONING CREEK TO EMPORIUM, then over the Allegheny Portage at AW-413, crossing at KEATING SUMMIT the height of land between the Susquehanna and Ohio drainages, to Canoe Place at Port Allegany. Chesapeake water on one side, Gulf of Mexico water on the other, and the easiest walking in the state between them. Tier B: Wallace's line is firm; the antiquity is a suggestion and is recorded as one.

routes.name: The Pine Creek Path (Jersey Shore–Genesee)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 91, AND IT IS FIFTY MILES INSIDE A GORGE. From the Indian settlements at Jersey Shore the path runs up the Pine Creek canyon to Ansonia — and Wallace's detail is a lesson in how a path behaves when the walls close in. BELOW THE FIRST FORK IT CROSSES THE STREAM A NUMBER OF TIMES IN ORDER TO AVOID MOUNTAIN SHOULDERS; above it, having found a workable bank, IT STAYS ON THE EAST SIDE. Then through the narrowest part of the gorge to the Third Fork at Ansonia, where it turns west and follows the water past Gaines and Galeton to West Pike. A ROAD IN A CANYON HAS NO ROUTING DECISIONS EXCEPT WHICH BANK, and it spends its fords buying the right one. That is the opposite of AW-463's Virginia Road, which navigates by springs across open country. The same network contains both because Pennsylvania contains both. WALLACE STOPS WHERE HIS EVIDENCE DOES: there is SOME UNCERTAINTY ABOUT THE COURSE IT TOOK NORTH OF WEST PIKE, and this layer stops being confident there too — the last hop into Genesee is drawn because the path is named for its destination, not because he traced it. Tier B for the gorge, and the note carries the caveat rather than the tier hiding it.

routes.name: The Great Island Path (Shamokin–Great Island)
routes.era: pre-contact; Shikellamy at his town on the West Branch from the 1720s
routes.note: WALLACE No. 34, AND IT COMPLETES A HUB. The Great Island at Lock Haven is where the Sinnemahoning, Pine Creek and Sheshequin paths converge — Wallace says so in his Bald Eagle entry — and with this road and AW-398 and AW-426 the layer now holds SIX ROUTES MEETING THERE. It is the West Branch equivalent of Kuskuskies with five and Wyoming with five, and it exists for the same reason: an island in a river below a mountain gap is where crossing is easy and where people therefore stop. THE ROUTE IS TRACED BY A LOCAL HISTORIAN AT HOUSE-BY-HOUSE RESOLUTION. J. P. Meginness has it cross the Susquehanna at Shamokin about a quarter-mile south of the present bridge, ascend the ravine on the west side, follow for three miles the ridge that forms the boundary between Snyder and Union counties, turn toward the river, PASS OVER THE HILL UPON THE MERRILL PLACE, follow the bank through Winfield and Lewisburg to Buffalo Creek WHERE THE IRON BRIDGE NOW SPANS IT, and curve back to the river through Shikellamy's Town. A COUNTY LINE, A NAMED FARM AND AN IRON BRIDGE, used to fix a footpath. It is the same evidentiary texture as the Stone Church at Marklesburg on AW-428 — this domain is reconstructed largely from things that were obvious to somebody local in 1889. Tier B.

routes.name: Old Peter's Road (Downingtown–Conoy Town)
routes.era: Bezaillon's pack trail; his grant at Conoy Town 1719, the rival road cut 1737
routes.note: WALLACE No. 79, AND IT IS THE TYPE SPECIMEN FOR HIS WHOLE THEORY OF ROUTING. He introduces DRY, LEVEL AND DIRECT — his three words for Indian path-making — by contrasting this road with the one that replaced it. Peter Bezaillon's bridle path RAN WITHOUT A SERIOUS OBSTACLE from Downingtown to Bainbridge on the Susquehanna. Then in 1737 the Paxtang Road, now the Horseshoe Pike, was cut to give a shorter way to Harrisburg — and it made a difficult ascent of the South Mountain OVER GROUND MADE WET BY MOUNTAIN SPRINGS. Wallace's verdict is that motorists on the Horseshoe Pike still know what those springs do to the subsoil when they freeze in January and thaw in March. A SHORTER ROAD THAT IS WORSE, AND IT WON. IT IS SAID THAT PETER BEZAILLON WAS GRIEVED. That sentence is in the book, and it is the only place in either domain where this layer knows how a man FELT about a road being superseded — a trader watching a survey line make his life's route obsolete by being straighter and worse. THE FORKS ARE DRAWN BECAUSE BRACKBILL GIVES THEM: at Mount Joy the left branch runs to Conoy Town and the Susquehanna ford below Conewago Falls, the right through Elizabethtown and Middletown to Harrisburg. Conoy Town is where Bezaillon took seven hundred acres in 1719 and where AW-448, the Conoy Path, begins. Tier B.

routes.name: The Lenni Lenape Path — the Old York Road (Philadelphia–New Hope)
routes.era: pre-contact; a laid-out road from 1711
routes.note: WALLACE No. 54, AND IT IS THE CLEAREST CASE OF A FOOTPATH SURVIVING AS A HIGHWAY. It ran from Philadelphia to New Hope on the Delaware, and thence across New Jersey from Lambertville to salt water at Elizabeth — Delaware Bay drainage to the Atlantic, on foot, in two days. Wallace: it was SO WELL ROUTED that when a road was laid out in 1711 it followed the path very closely, and U.S. 611 follows it still. THE IMAGE IS EMOGENE VAN SICKLE'S AND IT IS THE BEST DESCRIPTION OF A HUB IN EITHER DOMAIN. The Indian paths leading out of the Philadelphia area were so numerous that one historian likened them TO THE STICKS OF A LADY'S FAN. This layer has drawn six of those sticks — the Allegheny Path, the Great Minquas Path, the Tulpehocken Path, the Delaware River Path, the Blue Rock Path and now this — and Wallace's own remark elsewhere is that the country around Philadelphia was THE FIRST TO LOSE ITS INDIAN PATHS, already going out of use in William Penn's day. A FAN WHOSE STICKS WERE BROKEN FIRST AT THE HANDLE. Tier B.

routes.name: The Minsi Path (Philadelphia–Kingston)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Munsee on the upper Delaware until the Walking Purchase and after
routes.note: WALLACE No. 66, SUBSTANTIALLY CORRECTED AND UPGRADED v131-B131. The prior geometry (drawn before wallace.txt was on disk) ran Philadelphia–Doylestown on the Old York Road, then Easton, then Minisink Island — A LINE WALLACE NEVER DESCRIBES. His actual text has the Minsi Path leaving Philadelphia at Rising Sun onto Germantown Avenue (past Stenton, James Logan's estate, where Indians frequently congregated), through Chestnut Hill, and following the OLD BETHLEHEM PIKE (US 309) — a corridor well west of the Old York Road / Doylestown line — through Whitemarsh, Ambler and Montgomeryville to Line Lexington, then via Hellertown to a Lehigh ford near the modern Minsi Trail Bridge. AFTER THE LEHIGH THE PATH FORKS TWICE: first at Bethlehem (Elizabeth Ave/Linden St), where the RIGHT branch (US 22) goes to EASTON and the LEFT/MAIN branch (Pa. 191) goes to Nazareth; second at Nazareth, where one branch runs east via Tatamy and Totts Gap to Shawnee on Delaware, and the OTHER — the one Wallace's own motorist directions follow — runs north through Wind Gap and Saylorsburg to Snydersville (where Sullivan's Road forks left and the Minsi Path keeps right), Stroudsburg, and Pechoquealing (Shawnee on Delaware, junction AW-421). From there the path followed the Delaware past Bushkill, Egypt Mills and Dingmans Ferry to Minisink Island, the principal Munsee town, opposite Indian Point at the mouth of Raymond Kill — giving the Munsee communication with their Hudson River kin. From Minisink Island up through Milford, a ford near Carpenter's Point to Port Jervis, then east up the Neversink and down Rondout Creek to Esopus (Kingston). Between Esopus and Port Jervis the Dutch Old Mine Road followed this same path; early settlers Nicholas Depui and Daniel Brodhead (already here by 1727) used it from Esopus to reach their Minisink lands. EASTON IS A REAL, ATTESTED BRANCH — not a wrong guess to erase — but it is not the line Wallace's own recommended route draws, so it is noted here rather than drawn (single_line_is_an_artefact_rule). CONSEQUENCE: AW-425, AW-475 and AW-494 all cited AW-470 at Easton; that claim is now false and has been corrected in the same batch (junction_dependency_rule). The Munsee-communication framing and the Minisinks knot (AW-080, AW-176, AW-446 all touching Minisink Island) are preserved from the prior note.

routes.name: The Lake Shore Path (Sandusky–Buffalo)
routes.era: pre-contact; the south-shore road of Lake Erie
routes.note: WALLACE No. 52, AND IT IS THE LAYER'S SECOND ROAD RUNNING ON A DEAD LAKE. The path follows the south shore of Erie from Sandusky through Conneaut and Erie to Westfield and Buffalo — but Wallace notes that ITS CHARACTER CHANGES AT ERIE. West of the city it stays close to the water; east of it, it keeps about a mile and a half back, RUNNING ALONG A CURIOUS RIDGE SAID TO HAVE BEEN, IN AN EARLIER AGE, THE SHORE OF LAKE WARREN. Lake Warren was a proglacial lake, an ancestor of Erie held up by the ice, and its abandoned beach is the roadbed. AW-455 RUNS ON THE STRANDLINE OF GLACIAL LAKE IROQUOIS AND THIS ONE ON THE STRANDLINE OF GLACIAL LAKE WARREN. Two of the longest, straightest routes in the Northeast are old beaches — see _meta.glacial_roadbed_rule, now on its third case with the Logstown moraine. AND WALLACE ADDS THE NUANCE THAT SAVES THE RULE FROM BEING TOO NEAT: before good bridges this was AN AWKWARD ROAD TO TRAVEL, because the ridge is PERFORATED BY A NUMBER OF DEEP, NARROW CREEK GORGES which must have caused something of a scramble. A glacial roadbed gives you dry and level; it does not give you continuous. The ice built the causeway and then the meltwater cut it to pieces. Tier B. THE GATE REFUSED THIS ROUTE ON FIRST WRITE, v112-B112: pre_check flagged a 187 km hop from Sandusky to Conneaut, over the 120 km tier-B limit. Two nodes were added and they are of DIFFERENT KINDS, which matters. CLEVELAND IS A REAL JUNCTION — the Cuyahoga mouth, where AW-156's portage to the Tuscarawas begins, and Wallace's Cayahaga region takes its name. ASHTABULA IS A SHAPING NODE, added only because the gate demanded one, and it is declared as such here per _meta.densify_warrant_rule: a shaping node is geometry, not evidence, and must never be allowed to read as an attested stop.

routes.name: The Conneaut Path (Conneaut–Cussewago)
routes.era: pre-contact; crossed by the state boundary survey of 1786
routes.note: WALLACE No. 16, AND THE EVIDENCE IS A SURVEYOR'S ACCIDENT. A map of the northern portion of the PORTER-McCLELLAN SURVEY OF PENNSYLVANIA'S WESTERN BOUNDARY IN 1786 shows an Indian path crossing the line A MILE AND FIVE-EIGHTHS SOUTH OF LAKE ERIE. Two men running a state border noted where a footpath cut it, and two centuries later that incidental tick is the fix for a whole route. THIS IS THE SAME EVIDENTIARY CLASS AS THE MASON-DIXON NOTE ON AW-432 and the warrantee survey on AW-429 — BOUNDARY WORK AS THE UNINTENDED ARCHIVE OF INDIGENOUS ROADS. Surveyors were not recording paths; they were recording what they crossed, and a path is a thing you cross. Wallace's introduction says the Bureau of Land Records is the pathfinder's paradise for exactly this reason. THERE WERE SEVERAL WAYS from Conneaut to French Creek and he names the most direct: by Albion and thence south ALONG AN EASY RIDGE to the vicinity of Harmonsburg north of Conneaut Lake, where it joined the Cussewago Path from Sandusky. Tier B.

routes.name: The Cayahaga Path (Venango–the Salt Spring)
routes.era: pre-contact; the eastern approach to the Great Trail
routes.note: WALLACE No. 11, DRAWN SHORT UNDER _meta.shared_tail_rule — from the Salt Spring onward it is AW-405, the Mahoning Path, and thence to Cayahaga, Lower Sandusky and Detroit. This is the reach that is its own. IT IS THE FIFTH NAME FOR ONE ROAD. Wallace already told us the Mahoning Path west of Kuskuskies was also the Salt Lick Path, the Tuscarawas Path, the Sandusky Path and the Detroit Path; the Cayahaga Path is the same corridor approached from Venango instead of New Castle. SIX LABELS, ONE PIECE OF GROUND, and the only reason this layer can hold that without duplicating the road six times is frozen IDs plus the shared-tail convention. WALLACE HEDGES HIS OWN LINE AND THE TIER FOLLOWS: there MAY HAVE BEEN SEVERAL WAYS of getting from the Salt Spring to Venango, and Thomas Hutchins described one running about nineteen miles from the Salt Spring to Shenango Indian Town. Another instance of _meta.single_line_is_an_artefact_rule — the moment a second source appears, the road splits. Pymatuning Indian Town is drawn because Wallace names it on the way. STALE JUNCTION CAUGHT AGAIN, v112-B112, AND THIS IS THE THIRD TIME. This node claimed AW-418 at Venango. AW-418 has ended at Bullocks Ford since B101, when this same researcher shortened it. B108 made the identical mistake with AW-429 in three places. _meta.junction_dependency_rule already says READ THE ROUTE BACK BEFORE CLAIMING A JUNCTION WITH IT, and it was not followed. THE PATTERN IS NOW DIAGNOSABLE: the failures cluster on routes that were SHORTENED under shared_tail_rule, because the researcher remembers the road's full logical extent and the layer holds only its drawn extent. Shortened routes are the highest-risk citations in this layer and should be checked every single time.

routes.name: The Nanticoke Path (Calvert–Nanticoke)
routes.era: the Nanticoke at Nanticoke, Pa., for five years in the 1740s
routes.note: WALLACE No. 70, AND IT IS A ROAD DEFINED BY THE FIVE YEARS SOMEBODY LIVED AT THE END OF IT. The Nanticoke came up from the Eastern Shore of Maryland — Calvert, Oxford, North East, Elkton — and settled east of Wilkes-Barre on the North Branch, and Wallace says the path is KNOWN TO HAVE BEEN USED THROUGHOUT ITS LENGTH by them DURING THE FIVE YEARS WHEN THEY WERE SETTLED THERE. Four hundred kilometres of road, dated by a tenancy. THE ROUTE IS A WATERSHED. Dr. J. Alden Mason: there seems to be general consensus that it FOLLOWED THE RIDGE BETWEEN THE SUSQUEHANNA AND THE DELAWARE — a divide walked as a road, which is the purest form of Wallace's dry-level-direct principle. A height of land has no fords, no floods and no ascents; it is the one line in broken country that never has to cross anything. IT IS THE THIRD REFUGE ROAD IN THIS DOMAIN, after the Tuscarora Path and the Wechquetank. Three nations moving north within a generation, each along its own line, and the layer can now show them together. Tier C: Wallace says plainly the exact route HAS NOT BEEN CLOSELY TRACED except in certain sections, the southern part being best known. UPGRADED v133-B133, SPLIT BY CONFIDENCE (segment_confidence). Wallace's own hedge — 'the exact route has not been closely traced except in certain sections, the southern part being best known' — is now expressed directly in the schema rather than only in prose: the southern leg (Calvert to Reading) carries PA Route 10's attested chain of junctions — Oxford, Russellville, Cochranville (where a fork to Atglen/Gap is noted but not drawn), Parkesburg, Compass, Honey Brook, Morgantown, Reading — confirmed independently by the modern route's own junction list, and is drawn at B. The northern leg (Reading to Nanticoke, via Virginville's Dreibilbis-farm Indian settlement, an unspecified Blue Mountain crossing, Tamaqua, Hazleton, and four unnamed mountains before Warrior Gap where the Lehigh Path from Bethlehem joins) stays at C: Wallace says the Blue Mountain crossing is 'not precisely known' and that north of Hazleton the path 'must have crossed' four named mountains without specifying how. Also recorded: this northern stretch was little used by white men — settlers fleeing after the 1778 Battle of Wyoming avoided it, going instead by Nescopeck, Wyoming, Wapwallopen or Pittston, and none are recorded to have taken the Nanticoke Path itself.

routes.name: The Nescopeck Path (the Forks of the Delaware–Nescopeck)
routes.era: pre-contact; Gnadenhütten 1746–55; a refugee road again after 1778
routes.note: WALLACE No. 72, AND IT CARRIED FOUR DIFFERENT KINDS OF TRAFFIC IN THIRTY YEARS. Wallace lists them: traders and missionaries, DELAWARE WAR PARTIES during the French and Indian War, and SETTLERS DRIVEN FROM THE WYOMING VALLEY AFTER THE BATTLE OF WYOMING. One road, and its users in sequence were merchants, evangelists, raiders and refugees — the same ground doing opposite work as the politics turned over. GNADENHÜTTEN IS THE HINGE. The Moravians built a MODEL TOWN for their Indian converts on the Lehigh at the mouth of Mahoning Creek, and it was destroyed in 1755. AW-425 already passes it, AW-422's Wechquetank was founded in 1760 partly to replace it, and AW-403's Friedenshütten took the survivors' successors north in 1765. FOUR ROUTES IN THIS LAYER NOW TOUCH ONE CONGREGATION'S SERIAL DISPLACEMENT, which is not something any single route could show. Wallace notes the best known section is Bethlehem to Lehighton, and the drawn line reflects that. Tier B.

routes.name: The Tunkhannock Path (Tunkhannock–Great Bend)
routes.era: pre-contact; Ingaren at the Great Bend
routes.note: WALLACE No. 114, AND ITS DESTINATION IS THREE TREES. It runs from the Indian town of Tunkhannock at the creek mouth on the North Branch to a junction with the Lackawanna Path at New Milford, then down Salt Lick Creek to Hallstead and across the Susquehanna to 'an old Tuscorora Town' at the Great Bend. That town was INGAREN, sometimes called APPLE TREE TOWN — and the early settlers knew it as THE THREE INDIAN APPLE TREES. A settlement named by incomers for the orchard its people left behind. WALLACE ALREADY TOLD US THE LACKAWANNA PATH HAD A BRANCH TO APPLE TREE TOWN, in the entry this layer used to correct AW-424 at B100; this is the road that meets that branch. The two together close the loop between the Wyoming Valley, the Great Bend and the Lackawanna country. IT SHARES ITS TAIL AND IS DRAWN TO THE MERGE. From New Milford onward it is AW-424's ground, so the route stops there under _meta.shared_tail_rule. Tier C: Wallace opens with IS SAID TO HAVE RUN, and the tier follows the hedge rather than the detail. STALE JUNCTION REMOVED v114-B114, AND IT IS A NEW VARIANT OF THE FAULT. This node claimed AW-424 at New Milford. AW-424 is drawn on Wallace's MAIN line — Wyoming, Pittston, Old Forge, Scranton, Leggetts Gap, Lanesboro, Oquaga — and New Milford is on its BRANCH TO APPLE TREE TOWN, which he mentions in one clause and which this layer has not drawn. FIFTH STALE-JUNCTION FAILURE, and the first where the target route was neither shortened nor lengthened: the claim was made against a limb that exists in the SOURCE but not in the LAYER. _meta.junction_dependency_rule is widened again — a junction may be true of the road as Wallace describes it and false of the road as drawn, and only the drawn version can be cited. EXTENDED v135-B135 TO ITS REAL END. The prior stop at New Milford was correct given what was in the layer, but Wallace's OWN path-114 entry gives the rest of the line too: from New Milford it 'followed the Lackawanna Path down Salt Lick Creek to Hallstead and across the Susquehanna to an old Tuscarora Town' at Great Bend — Ingaren, called Apple Tree Town by settlers for the three surviving trees of an Indian orchard, remembered as the rallying point for councils, marriages, feasts, war-dances and the fate of prisoners. Since AW-424 (the Lackawanna Path) has never drawn this Apple Tree Town branch, there is nothing to defer to under shared_tail_rule — the ground is attested here, in path 114's own entry, and undrawn everywhere else, so it is drawn here rather than left as a citation to geometry that does not exist. NO JUNCTION IS CLAIMED WITH AW-424 at New Milford: the branch remains undrawn on AW-424's own line, and per junction_dependency_rule only drawn geometry can be cited. A branch to the Salt Springs near Franklin Forks is also mentioned, sourced to a 1951 interview with a local resident describing an Indian trail up Martin's Creek with a documented camp site — not drawn, too locally sourced to place with confidence, but worth recording as an open lead.

routes.name: The Redstone Path (the Half King's Rock–Redstone Old Fort)
routes.era: pre-contact; Gist's plantation from 1753, the Half King there in 1754
routes.note: WALLACE No. 99, AND IT IS TWENTY-FIVE KILOMETRES CARRYING THREE OF THE MOST LOADED PLACE NAMES IN THE COLONIES. It runs from THE HALF KING'S ROCK, about a mile northeast of Summit in Fayette County, by way of CHRISTOPHER GIST'S PLANTATION at Mount Braddock, to the Monongahela at REDSTONE OLD FORT. The Half King was Tanaghrisson, the Seneca who was with Washington at Jumonville Glen in May 1754 and who — by most accounts — struck the blow that turned a skirmish into a world war. Gist's plantation was the frontier's westernmost English settlement and Washington's shelter that same year. The road between them is the ground both men were standing on. REDSTONE OLD FORT WAS AN INDIAN ERECTION and Wallace is precise about it: the ruins lay between the mouths of Redstone and Dunlap creeks, NEARER DUNLAP THAN REDSTONE. An earthwork already ancient when the English named a fort after it, at the head of navigation on the Monongahela — which is why Nemacolin's Path comes here too, and why the Ohio country was reached from this bank. Tier B.

routes.name: The Sewickley Old Town Path (West Newton–New Kensington)
routes.era: the Sewickley Shawnee gone from both towns early in the 18th century
routes.note: WALLACE No. 102, AND IT RUNS BETWEEN TWO PLACES THAT ARE BOTH CALLED 'OLD TOWN' FOR THE SAME REASON. Both took their names from the The-we-gi-la or Sewickley division of the Shawnee — one on the Youghiogheny near West Newton, one on the Allegheny at New Kensington — and Wallace notes that EACH IS BETTER KNOWN FROM THE RECORDS AS SEWICKLEY OLD TOWN, SINCE THE INDIAN OCCUPANTS LEFT EARLY IN THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY. A road whose both ends are memorials, drawn from records written after everyone had gone. It is _meta.old_town_rule at its most complete: not one abandoned node but an entire route consisting of them. THREE NAMES FOR ONE ROAD, and one of them is a farmer's. It is also the Puckety Creek Path and BYERLY'S PATH — Andrew Byerly kept a farm and trading post on Bushy Run where it crossed the Raystown Path, and in August 1763 he was with the advance guard that the Indians almost wiped out there. He and six others escaped and reached the main army, and that was the beginning of the Battle of Bushy Run. A ROAD NAMED FOR A MAN BECAUSE HIS HOUSE WAS ON IT, and the house is why the battle has that name. Tier B.

routes.name: The Kiskiminetas Path (Cherry Tree–Chartier's Landing)
routes.era: pre-contact; Kiskiminetas Old Town abandoned before the surveys that name it
routes.note: WALLACE No. 44, AND ITS EVIDENCE IS A SURVEYOR'S PHRASE. It branches off the Kittanning Path about six miles west of Indiana, passes THE ROUND HOLES near Spring Church and the Indian town of Kiskiminetas, and runs to Chartier's Town. Wallace quotes the record verbatim: 'THE OLD PATH LEADING FROM KISKIMANETES OLD TOWN TO SHARTEE'S OLD TOWN' — a line of land-office spelling that fixes a whole route, and another entry for _meta.boundary_work_as_archive. HE LOCATES THE TOWN TO THE HUNDRED METRES: on the south side of the Kiskiminetas, opposite the mouth of Carnahan Run, about a mile north of Vandergrift Heights. Then almost due west to Chartier's Landing at Edgecliff, at the mouth of the present Chartier Run. THIS ROAD PUTS A FOURTH LINE INTO TARENTUM. AW-409 comes from New Castle, AW-478's twin Sewickley town is just upriver, and the Kittanning Path passes above — Chartier's Town was a Shawnee settlement abandoned around 1745 when Peter Chartier took several hundred of his mother's people west rather than accept English trade terms, and the roads to it outlasted the reason for going. Tier B. SIXTH JUNCTION FAILURE, v115-B115 — AND THE LAST ONE TO BE CAUGHT BY DISCIPLINE. This node cited AW-429 at Cherry Tree using AW-179's coordinate, and the two are 1.5 km apart: CHERRY TREE EXISTS TWICE IN THIS LAYER. That gap is below the 600 m near-miss threshold, so the sweep cannot see it, and the guard only reports it after a merge. The node now carries the coordinate AW-414 and AW-429 share. AW-179 STILL HOLDS THE OUTLIER at -78.81, 40.74 and is flagged here rather than silently edited, because it is not otherwise part of this batch. RESPONSE: claimcheck.py was written this batch — see _meta.claimcheck_tool. Six repeats of one mistake is not a discipline problem, it is a missing tool.

routes.name: The Pigeon Paths (Cornplanter's Town–the pigeon plateau)
routes.era: seasonal, annually, until the passenger pigeon was exterminated
routes.note: WALLACE No. 90, AND IT IS THE ONLY ROUTE IN THIS LAYER WHOSE DESTINATION MOVED EVERY YEAR AND WHOSE DESTINATION IS NOW EXTINCT. Pigeon hunting was a Seneca seasonal activity, and the favourite nesting grounds of Ectopistes migratorius were on the high plateau at the headwaters of the Clarion and Tionesta, where Warren, McKean, Forest and Elk counties meet near Sheffield, Kane and a place called Pigeon. THE ROAD WAS TIMED BY RECONNAISSANCE. After a flight had DARKENED THE SKY over Cornplanter's Town the Indians waited a few weeks, then sent scouts up into the hills to bring back SQUABS — by which the chiefs could judge precisely when it would be best for the people to go. A road opened by a committee reading the age of nestlings. TWO ROUTES CONVERGED AND THEN DISSOLVED. Some went on foot down the Allegheny and up Kinzua Creek to Dunkle's Corner and across the hills to Sheffield; others came down the river BY CANOE to the mouth of Dutchman's Run above Warren and walked through Clarendon to Sheffield, where the two joined. A few miles south the joint path BROKE UP INTO A NUMBER OF MINOR PATHS by which hunters approached the particular places — WHICH VARIED FROM YEAR TO YEAR — where the pigeons were nesting. THE MANAGEMENT NOTE IS WALLACE'S AND IT MATTERS. Hunters took squabs, knocking them from nests with long poles or felling the laden trees, and some netted adults or shot them; BUT AS A RULE INDIANS WERE CAREFUL NOT TO DESTROY THE BREEDING STOCK. The extermination came through commercial slaughter. Tier C: the trunk is Wallace's, the terminal fan is explicitly undrawable.

nodes.n: Up Kinzua Creek to Dunkle's Corner
The pigeon plateau (the paths break up)

routes.name: The Great Path (Pittsburgh–Tuscarawas)
routes.era: pre-contact; the trunk road west, to Detroit
routes.note: WALLACE No. 33, AND ITS NAME IS ITS ARGUMENT. Not named for a place at either end but for what it was: THE GREAT PATH, Pittsburgh to Detroit. It crosses the Allegheny at the Forks and runs along the WEST side of the Ohio through Avalon, Sewickley, Logstown and Crow's Town to Logan's Town and Beaver's Town at the Beaver mouth, then turns away from the river at Beaver and goes by Blackhawk and Clarkson to the Ohio line, and on through Dungannon, Kensington, Minerva and Malvern to the Indian town of Tuscarawas at Bolivar — crossing the river about a mile above the town. FOUR TOWNS IN TWENTY-FIVE KILOMETRES, EACH NAMED FOR A MAN. Logstown, Crow's Town, Logan's Town, Beaver's Town: the lower Ohio was a corridor of leaders' settlements, and the road is the string they were beaded on. IT IS THE SAME GROUND AS THE MAHONING PATH AT ITS FAR END and this layer now approaches Tuscarawas from three directions — AW-405 from Kuskuskies, AW-156's portage from the Cuyahoga, and this from the Forks. Drawn to Tuscarawas; the continuation to Detroit is Ohio country and wants an Ohio roster. Tier B.

nodes.n: Forks of the Ohio (Pittsburgh) — junction AW-137, AW-138, AW-399, AW-406, AW-433

routes.name: The Juniata Path — McKee's Path (Dalmatia–Jack's Narrows)
routes.era: McKee's upper trading post from the 1740s
routes.note: WALLACE No. 41, AND IT IS A TRADER'S FRONT DOOR. From McKee's Upper Trading Post at Dalmatia the path fords the Susquehanna to what is STILL KNOWN AS McKEE'S HALF FALLS, runs west to Thompsontown on the Juniata, follows the river to Kishacoquillas, and past Mount Union joins the Frankstown Path at Jack's Narrows. A ford, a falls and a path all carrying one trader's name three centuries on. THE SENTENCE THAT MAKES IT MATTER IS AN OVERHEARD REMARK. Bishop Cammerhoff, travelling north by the Paxtang Path in 1748, stopped at a house a short distance beyond the mouth of Wiconisco Creek — probably McKee's — and was informed that across the river 'BEGAN THE GREAT PATH TO THE ALLEGHENY COUNTRY'. Not a survey, not a deed: a man at a door telling a passing bishop where the west started. THIS LAYER NOW HAS TWO THINGS CALLED THE GREAT PATH and they are different roads — AW-481, Wallace No. 33, running Pittsburgh to Detroit, and this one, which McKee's neighbours called by the same name because from their doorstep it was the way west. Precisely the hazard _meta.wallace_roster_rule and _meta.id_rule exist for. Tier B.

routes.name: The Kishacoquillas Path (Bald Eagle's Nest–Lewistown)
routes.era: Kishacoquillas living at Lewistown by 1731; walked by Fithian in 1775
routes.note: WALLACE No. 43, AND IT IS THE ONLY ROUTE IN THE LAYER WHOSE TIER RESTS ON ONE MAN'S ADJECTIVES. Philip Fithian walked it in August 1775 from Bald Eagle's Nest to Kishacoquillas, and Wallace reconstructs the line from what he wrote. THE FIRST DAY HE FOLLOWED WHAT HE CALLED A 'BLIND, UNFREQUENTED' PATH — past Bellefonte, Pleasant Gap, Old Fort, Centre Hall, to Potters Mills where Logan's Path came in from the north. ON THE LAST DAY HE TRAVELLED A BETTER ROAD over the Seven Mountains. A TRAVELLER GRADING THE SURFACE AS HE GOES is the nearest thing this domain has to a road survey, and it is _meta.trail_definition_varies_rule stated by someone actually on the path: blind where nobody goes, better where they do. 'BLIND PATH' IS WALLACE'S OWN TECHNICAL TERM. He defines it in the introduction — a path gone out of common use and so overgrown as to be difficult to follow — and Fithian is using it correctly in 1775, which dates this stretch's decline. The path is named for a Shawnee chief known to be living at what is now Lewistown in 1731. Tier B.

routes.name: The Loyalsock Path (Wyalusing–Montoursville)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 59, AND HE SPLITS HIS OWN CONFIDENCE DOWN THE MIDDLE OF ONE ROUTE. J. Andrew Wilt suggested a path beginning opposite Wyalusing that led up Sugar Run, over the divide to the headwaters of the Little Loyalsock at Dushore, and down that creek and the Big Loyalsock to its mouth at Montoursville. Wallace's response is the interesting part: IT IS UNQUESTIONED that an important path ran from the mouth of Sugar Run over the divide to the West Branch — but the specific line down the Loyalsock is Wilt's suggestion, offered as such. THE CORRIDOR IS CERTAIN AND THE ROUTE IS NOT, and those are different claims about the same ground. This is _meta.trail_definition_varies_rule again from the historiographic side: a source can be confident that traffic crossed a divide and uncertain which creek it followed down. IT SHARES BOTH ENDS WITH ROADS ALREADY DRAWN. Sugar Run is where AW-403, the Wyalusing Path, crosses the Susquehanna; Montoursville is Otstonwakin, where AW-401's Sheshequin Path begins and where Weiser could count on finding a canoe. So this is a third answer to the same question those two answer — how to get from the North Branch to the West Branch — and the layer now holds all three. Tier C on Wallace's own division. STRENGTHENED v136-B136: Wallace's doubt is sharper than the prior note captured, and it deserves recording as a negative finding in its own right, not just a hedge. He states plainly that the attested path's WESTERN DESCENT WAS NOT BY THE VALLEY OF THE LOYALSOCK BUT BY THAT OF MUNCY CREEK (AW-403's ground) — not an open question but a specific correction of Wilt's suggestion. His evidence: by water, Forksville (the Big/Little Loyalsock junction) to Montoursville is over 36 miles against a 24-mile crow's flight, and John S. Koch of Allenwood, writing in 1962, doubted any prominent trail ever used the valley at all — 'nine out of ten riffles cannot be waded with hip boots, owing to their swiftness and depth,' even where Indians are known to have forded chest-deep water elsewhere in cold weather. Wallace does allow there were probably 'bits of paths' connecting small camps between Montoursville and Hillsgrove, and his own motorist note calls the drive along the Loyalsock 'delightful' while asking the driver to 'believe' hunters used it at least locally — a much weaker claim than the drawn line implies. Tier stays C; the note now says why with the source's own strongest evidence rather than its softest.

nodes.n: The mouth of Sugar Run (opposite Wyalusing) — junction AW-403
Over the divide to the Little Loyalsock

routes.name: The Chillisquaque Path (Northumberland–Comly)
routes.era: pre-contact; a road on Howell's map by 1792, a county line by 1822
routes.note: WALLACE No. 12, THE SHORTEST ROUTE IN THE PENNSYLVANIA SET AND THE CLEAREST DEMONSTRATION OF HOW A FOOTPATH FOSSILISES. Only a few miles long, from Northumberland over Montour Ridge to the County Line Branch of Chillisquaque Creek near Comly. Wallace's evidence is a sequence of three documents and the sequence IS the argument. IN 1792 it appears on Reading Howell's map of Pennsylvania as a very early road. BY 1822, on Melish's map, THAT SAME HIGHWAY IS SHOWN AS MARKING THE BOUNDARY BETWEEN NORTHUMBERLAND AND COLUMBIA COUNTIES. AND IT STILL MARKS IT. A path became a road, the road became a border, and the border is now the most durable thing about it — a line originally chosen because it was walkable, still dividing two counties two centuries after anyone needed to walk it. THIS IS THE INVERSE OF _meta.boundary_work_as_archive. There, surveyors recorded paths incidentally while running boundaries. Here a path BECAME the boundary — so the modern county line is not evidence about the road, it IS the road. Tier B, on documents rather than on tradition.

routes.name: The Tioga Path (Trout Run–Painted Post)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 110, AND IT IS A BRANCH THAT LEAVES A ROAD THIS LAYER ALREADY HOLDS. It quits the Lycoming valley and the Sheshequin Path at Trout Run north of Williamsport, runs north over the mountains and down the Tioga River to Painted Post — which Wallace calls AN IMPORTANT JUNCTION POINT OF INDIAN PATHS AND CANOE ROUTES. PATHS AND CANOE ROUTES IN ONE PHRASE is the layer's recurring blind spot stated plainly by the source: at Painted Post the land network and the water network are the same network, and a hub that mixes them is invisible to anyone drawing only footpaths. See _meta.absence_of_path_rule. IT RUNS UP A STREAM AND CROSSES IT REPEATEDLY. For two miles and more the path follows the valley of Trout Run, WHICH IT CROSSES SEVERAL TIMES — the same behaviour as the Pine Creek Path in its gorge, buying the workable bank with fords, and the same as Ettwein's thirty-six crossings of Muncy Creek. In steep valleys a path is a sequence of decisions about which side to be on. Painted Post already carries AW-181, the Forbidden Path, and Wallace elsewhere records Mrs Jane Whittaker taken through it in 1779 on a foot path well beaten and quite wide enough in many places for two abreast. Tier B.

routes.name: The New Path (Letort's Spring–Aughwick)
routes.era: much used by traders after about 1749
routes.note: WALLACE No. 73, AND HIS FIRST CLAUSE IS THE WHOLE JOKE: 'THE NEW PATH — ACTUALLY A VERY OLD ONE'. It is a short cut on the Frankstown Path between Paxtang and Aughwick, much used by traders after about 1749, and it was called new because that is when white traders started using it, not when it was made. A NAME THAT DATES THE OBSERVER, NOT THE ROAD — the same failure as 'Warriors Path' at _meta.warriors_path_is_a_colonial_label, where a label records a stranger's relationship to a thing rather than the thing. WHAT IT SAVES IS THE ROXBURY DETOUR. Instead of going round by Roxbury Gap — from which there were alternate routes through Amberson, Doylesburg and Concord, or through Spring Run and Shade Gap — the New Path runs north from Letort's Spring near Middlesex and Carlisle to Croghan's, which is Sterretts Gap. FOUR NAMED VARIANTS OF THE ROAD IT BYPASSES, listed in one sentence, and the layer draws the bypass because that is the entry. AW-397 already carries both Sterretts Gap and Aughwick, so this route is a chord across a road already in the layer — the first one drawn as such. Tier B. CLAIMCHECK CAUGHT A STALE CITATION BEFORE THE MERGE, v118-B118. This node cited AW-428 at Aughwick; AW-428 lost Aughwick at B108 when Wallace's own text moved it onto the Fort Littleton line. SEVENTH INSTANCE OF THIS MISTAKE AND THE FIRST THAT COST NOTHING — the previous six were found by the guard AFTER merging, so each needed a repair edit on a layer already in a violating state. Here the batch file was fixed and the layer never touched. That is the whole argument for building a tool instead of rewriting a rule.

routes.name: The Monocacy Path (Conejohela–Frederick)
routes.era: the Susquehannock castle at Conejohela; the Conoy there in the 18th century
routes.note: WALLACE No. 67, AND ITS NORTHERN END IS A TOWN THAT CHANGED NATIONS WITHOUT MOVING. The palisaded SUSQUEHANNOCK CASTLE north of the mouth of Canadochly Creek, opposite Washington Boro, WAS KNOWN DURING THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY — AFTER THE REFUGEE CONOYS HAD BEEN LIVING THERE — AS CONEJOHELA. One fortification, two peoples, and the later name is the one that stuck. This layer has drowned nodes, abandoned nodes and nodes named for objects carried away; this is a node that outlived its builders and was inherited. THE ROAD SOUTH IS WHY THE CONOY WERE THERE AT ALL. They had already been pushed north out of Maryland — AW-448's Conoy Town on the Susquehanna is the same people again, a generation on — and this path runs back down the way they came, through York to the Monocacy and Frederick. A REFUGEE ROAD READ IN REVERSE IS AN ESCAPE ROUTE, and the layer now holds four of them: Tuscarora, Nanticoke, Wechquetank and this. Wallace gives two branches from Wrightsville into York, one by Hallam and Spring Forge and one from the castle by East Prospect and Canadochly Church; the castle branch is drawn because it is the one with the town on it. Tier B.

routes.name: The Warriors Branch (the Ohio–Brant Summit)
routes.era: pre-contact; a tributary of the Catawba Path
routes.note: WALLACE No. 126, AND ITS DESCRIPTION IS THE ONLY ONE IN THE BOOK GIVEN BY A MAN WHO WALKED IT. A scholar at Waynesburg College who had studied the path AND WALKED OVER MUCH OF IT gave Wallace the account, and it reads as directions rather than history: it crossed the Ohio at the mouth of Graves Creek, another branch came in at the mouth of Fish Creek, the Indians crossed at fords AND THEY IMMEDIATELY GOT TO THE HIGH GROUND. Then Morford Post Office in the extreme southwest corner of Greene County, Centennial Church KEEPING RIGHT ON THE RIDGE, Nettle Hill, the top of Grimes Hill, and from Grimes Hill to Bluff — known to most people as Gabbletown — WHERE IT APPEARS AS A CREASE IN THE HILLTOP. Then Knisely School House, still on the ridge, to Brant Summit. THIS IS A REAL RIDGE TRAIL. THERE ARE NO BIG DIPS. A CREASE IN THE HILLTOP is the only physical trace of a path recorded anywhere in this domain. Wallace's introduction says most traces have been obliterated by farming, lumbering, road making and strip mining, and that it is seldom possible to walk an old Indian path in Pennsylvania. Here is one, on a ridge nobody had a use for, still legible as a dent. James Veech in The Monongahela of Old makes it a tributary of the Catawba Path and notes it was used as a short cut to Wills Creek. Tier B.

Morford (the southwest corner of Greene County)

routes.name: St. Joseph's Path (Powell–Sheshequin)
routes.era: walked by Spangenberg and Weiser on the way to Onondaga, 1745
routes.note: WALLACE No. 100, AND IT IS A SHORT CUT ON A SHORT CUT. It is one of several CROSSING PATHS from Towanda Creek to Sugar Creek in Bradford County, used by travellers on the Sheshequin Path IN ORDER TO AVOID THE WIDE LOOP THROUGH TOWANDA. AW-401 already carries the Sheshequin and AW-402 carries Towanda; this is the chord between them, and it means the network was dense enough that people optimised WITHIN it, not merely between towns. THE NAME IS A NICKNAME FOR A BISHOP. Leo Wilt of Towanda thought it was named in honour of August Gottlieb Spangenberg, KNOWN AMONG THE MORAVIANS AS 'BROTHER JOSEPH', who travelled it on his way to Onondaga with Conrad Weiser in 1745. So the road is named for a man by the name his own congregation used for him — not his office, not his surname. It is the same journey that produced the description of the Sheshequin country as a wilderness where one does not see the sun all day long. SEVERAL SUCH CROSSING PATHS EXISTED and Wallace names this one; the others are another instance of _meta.single_line_is_an_artefact_rule. Tier B.

nodes.n: The Sugar Creek crossing — junction AW-401

routes.name: The Perkiomen Path (Philadelphia–Reading)
routes.era: pre-contact; surviving as Ridge Avenue and the Ridge Pike
routes.note: WALLACE No. 88, AND IT IS THE MOST COMPLETELY SURVIVING ROAD IN THE DOMAIN. He does not reconstruct it, he identifies it: the path WAS IDENTICAL WITH RIDGE AVENUE from Franklin Square on Race Street in Philadelphia to the Falls of the Schuylkill, the Wissahickon, Roxboro and Manatawna; beyond the city limits it followed THE RIDGE PIKE through Barren Hill and across Plymouth Creek to Norristown, then Jeffersonville to ford Perkiomen Creek at Collegeville, and on through Trappe, Limerick and Sanatoga. AN INDIAN FOOTPATH THAT IS NOW A NAMED CITY AVENUE FOR ITS WHOLE LENGTH. Both surviving names describe the same fact — Ridge Avenue and the Ridge Pike — so the road announces its own routing principle twice over, and Wallace's DRY, LEVEL AND DIRECT is legible in a street sign. IT IS ANOTHER STICK OF THE FAN. This is the ninth route in this layer leaving Philadelphia, and the one that most directly tests _meta.road_determinism_caution: Beauchamp would say the ridge determined both the path and the avenue and neither inherited from the other. Here the inheritance is arguable precisely because the alignment is exact rather than approximate — a coincidence of line over eighty kilometres is not a coincidence. Tier B. EIGHTH SWEEP CATCH, v119-B119: Reading was drawn 85 m from AW-180's node, the Tulpehocken Path. Both roads reach the Schuylkill there and the junction is real — the Perkiomen Path comes up the river from Philadelphia and the Tulpehocken goes on north-west to Shamokin, so Reading is a hinge between the Delaware and Susquehanna systems, not a coincidence of drawing.

nodes.n: Philadelphia (Franklin Square) — junction AW-139, AW-180, AW-396, AW-446, AW-469, AW-470

routes.name: The Ichsua Path (Port Allegany–Olean)
routes.era: pre-contact; on the Adlum-Wallis map of 1793 or '94
routes.note: WALLACE No. 40, AND IT COMPLETES A THROUGH-LINE ACROSS THE STATE. Wallace calls it A CONTINUATION of the Sinnemahoning Path from Lock Haven to Emporium and the Portage Path from Emporium to the Canoe Place at Port Allegany — so AW-465, AW-413 and this are one journey in three entries, running from the West Branch of the Susquehanna to the upper Allegheny and the Seneca towns. THE LAYER NOW HOLDS THE EASIEST CROSSING OF PENNSYLVANIA END TO END, which is the road Wallace suggests the first people may have used, thousands of years ago. THE ADLUM-WALLIS MAP OF 1793 OR '94 IS DOING THE WORK AGAIN. It shows the path following the EAST side of the Allegheny to the vicinity of Eldred, fording the river, crossing Indian Creek at what IS STILL KNOWN AS INDIAN CROSSING, and going over the hills to ford the Allegheny again. Two fords and a named crossing, recorded by a surveyor and surviving as a place name — the same map that gave the Great Bend carry its 'Portage 19ms' at AW-415. ICHSUA IS OLEAN, where AW-432, the Catawba Path, begins its run to the Carolinas. Tier B. DUPLICATE RESOLVED v123: this road was drawn TWICE — as AW-492 at B120 and again as AW-497 at B122, because the researcher did not check whether the id range was already occupied by content he had not written. AW-497 is removed and its note kept here. The earlier id is canonical per _meta.id_rule; nothing cited the duplicate, so no junction claims were orphaned. THE NEAR-MISS SWEEP CAUGHT IT — three nodes of one road sitting metres from three nodes of its twin.

routes.name: The Horseheads Path (Grover–Horseheads)
routes.era: pre-contact; Kanawohalla destroyed by Sullivan's army, 1779
routes.note: WALLACE No. 39, AND ITS NORTHERN TERMINUS IS NAMED FOR AN ATROCITY AGAINST ANIMALS. It branches off the Sheshequin Path at Grover, at the head of Lycoming Creek WHERE THE SHESHEQUIN PATH TURNED EAST, and runs north by Canton and Troy, across Sugar Creek and up Wolf Creek through Columbia Cross Roads, to ford the Chemung at Kanawohalla and go on to Horseheads, five miles beyond. HORSEHEADS TAKES ITS NAME FROM SULLIVAN'S 1779 CAMPAIGN. The army, returning from burning the Seneca towns, killed its own worn-out packhorses there and left them; the Iroquois afterwards gathered and arranged the skulls, and the settlers named the place for what they found. A TOWN NAMED BY WHITE SETTLERS FOR A THING INDIANS DID TO THE REMAINS OF AN ARMY'S ANIMALS — and it is on the road that army came back down, AW-494. THE BRANCH POINT IS THE FINDING. Wallace locates it exactly where the Sheshequin Path turns east: a fork exists because another road changes its mind, and this one carries straight on. Tier B. DUPLICATE RESOLVED v123: this road was drawn TWICE — as AW-493 at B120 and again as AW-498 at B122, because the researcher did not check whether the id range was already occupied by content he had not written. AW-498 is removed and its note kept here. The earlier id is canonical per _meta.id_rule; nothing cited the duplicate, so no junction claims were orphaned. THE NEAR-MISS SWEEP CAUGHT IT — three nodes of one road sitting metres from three nodes of its twin.

routes.name: Sullivan's Road (Easton–Kanawohalla)
routes.era: cut in 1779 for the invasion of the Iroquois country
routes.note: WALLACE No. 107, AND IT IS THE ONLY ROUTE IN THIS DOMAIN THAT IS AN ACT OF DESTRUCTION. General John Sullivan in 1779 TURNED AN INDIAN PATH INTO A MILITARY ROAD FOR THE INVASION OF THE IROQUOIS COUNTRY. The layer holds many roads that armies used; this is the one an army made out of a road in order to end the people who made it. IT IS ASSEMBLED ENTIRELY FROM PATHS THIS LAYER ALREADY HOLDS. Wallace traces it precisely: from Easton by Chestnut Hill, Stockertown and Belfast through the Wind Gap to Saylorsburg, then north by Sciota and Snydersville to Bartonsville — where IT PICKED UP THE PECHOQUEALIN PATH and followed it to Wyoming; from Wyoming it FOLLOWED THE GREAT WARRIORS PATH to Tioga; then TOOK THE FORBIDDEN PATH up the Chemung and ENTERED THE SENECA COUNTRY BY THE BACK DOOR at Kanawohalla. Four roads in this layer — AW-421, AW-084, AW-181 — strung into one campaign. THE FORBIDDEN PATH'S NAME BECOMES UNBEARABLE HERE. It was called that because the Iroquois forbade its use to outsiders, and it is the road by which the invasion reached them. Drawn as its own route rather than as edits to the four it uses, per _meta.add_never_overwrite_rule: a military road of 1779 must not overwrite the pre-contact paths it was cut along. Class military, which no other Pennsylvania route carries. Tier B.

routes.name: The Okehocking Path (Pawling Ford–Gradyville)
routes.era: the Okehocking reservation set apart by William Penn in 1701
routes.note: WALLACE No. 78, AND ITS DESTINATION IS THE ONLY INDIAN RESERVATION IN THIS DOMAIN. Okehocking was a tract of five hundred acres on the east branch of upper Ridley Creek, SET APART IN 1701 BY WILLIAM PENN as a reservation for certain Delaware Indians. Five hundred acres, in the county where Penn's own city stood, granted the year before he left the colony for the last time. THE ROAD IS DRAWN FROM RIDGES, NOT FROM DOCUMENTS. Wallace's phrase for the evidence is exact and worth keeping: A TRADITION WELL FORTIFIED BY GEOGRAPHY AND COMMON SENSE. From Pawling Ford — three-quarters of a mile below the Perkiomen mouth and the same distance above Valley Forge — THERE IS A GOOD RIDGE to Paoli, Whitehorse and Okehocking; and south of Okehocking, after crossing Ridley Creek, STILL WITH THE AID OF A GOOD RIDGE, to meet the Great Minquas Path at Gradyville. TWICE IN ONE ENTRY THE ARGUMENT IS 'THERE IS A GOOD RIDGE'. That is _meta.gradient_as_dating_evidence and Wallace's 'an excellent terrain adds confirmation' at AW-419 — the ground offered as testimony where no document survives. Tier C on his own hedge: a tradition, however well fortified.

nodes.n: Pawling Ford (the Schuylkill, above Valley Forge)

routes.name: The Oley Path (Bethlehem–Reading)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Moravian road from Bethlehem into the Oley cove
routes.note: WALLACE No. 81, AND THE NAME IS A LANDFORM DESCRIBED FROM INSIDE IT. Oley is probably a corruption of the Delaware OLINK, meaning hole or cove, and Heckewelder gives OLEY-WALO, A HOLE, as meaning A PLACE SURROUNDED WITH HILLS. It was applied to a fertile cove under the Oley Hills northeast of Reading. A PLACE NAMED FOR WHAT YOU SEE WHEN YOU STAND IN IT — not a river, not a person, not an event, but the shape of the horizon. This layer names roads after towns, people, relics, rapids and trees; this is the first named for an enclosure. THE COVE IS WHY THE ROAD EXISTS. Fertile bottom ringed by hills is exactly what a farming people wants and exactly what a traveller has to climb into, so the path is short, purposeful and worth naming — and the Moravians at Bethlehem used it, which is why it is written down at all. Tier C: Wallace gives the etymology firmly and the course only as an approximate motor route, so the line is his corridor rather than his survey. EXTENDED AND UPGRADED v137-B137. The prior geometry stopped at Oley itself, but Wallace's opening line is explicit that the path continued to Reading, WHERE IT JOINED THE ALLEGHENY PATH (AW-180, at the same hub AW-474 was just joined to) — drawn to that junction here rather than left short. Also added: Macungie, named in Wallace's own opening sentence ('through Emmaus and Macungie') but previously omitted, sitting a few km south of Emmaus on the same corridor. Confidence raised to B: the motorist directions give a specific, continuous line (Pa. 191 fork to L.R. 187, to Emmaus, Shimerville beside Indian Creek, Huff Church, Landis Store, Pleasantville, Oley, Reading), and Count Zinzendorf's own 1742 diary confirms travelers actually rode this line between the Oley Hills and Long Swamp in the dark, badly enough that several of the party fell from their horses on tree limbs — a first-hand account of the road, not just a place-name derivation.
