routes.name: The Oswayo Path (Genesee–Shinglehouse)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 82, AND IT IS THE SHORT WAY ONTO THE FORBIDDEN PATH. On W. W. Thompson's authority it runs from Genesee up Rose Lake Run to Rose Lake, then DOWN Oswayo Creek past Oswayo, Coneville and Millport to Shinglehouse — where it joins the Forbidden Path and follows it through Ceres, Portville, Ichsua and the other Seneca towns on the upper Allegheny. UP ONE RUN AND DOWN ONE CREEK, WITH A LAKE AT THE TOP. It is the simplest routing logic in the whole domain: find the two waters that nearly meet, and walk the seam. Rose Lake sits on the divide and the road is the excuse the water gives it. IT CONNECTS TWO ROADS ALREADY DRAWN. Genesee is where AW-466, the Pine Creek Path, ends after fifty miles of gorge; Shinglehouse puts you on AW-181, the Forbidden Path, whose name records that the Iroquois barred it to outsiders. So a walker could come up the Pine Creek canyon from the West Branch and be on the Seneca road within a day. Tier C: Thompson's account, reported by Wallace without corroboration. CORRECTED v138-B138: added Millport, named by Wallace ('past the towns of Oswayo, Coneville, and Millport') but previously missing from the drawn line. Also corrected the note's own framing — it previously implied Shinglehouse joins AW-181 directly, but AW-181 as drawn runs Athens–Waverly–Elmira–Painted Post–Canisteo–Hornell–Dansville–Geneseo, a corridor roughly 65 km north of Shinglehouse and nowhere near Ceres or Portville. Wallace's 'Forbidden Path' at Shinglehouse is a DIFFERENT stretch of trail than the one this layer has drawn under that name — closer in geography to AW-492 (Ichsua Path, Port Allegany–Olean) and AW-432 (Catawba Path), both of which also touch Ichsua/Olean, but neither reaches Shinglehouse, Ceres or Portville either. No junction is claimed here (none was claimed in the node text before this correction, which was already appropriately cautious); the prose now says so plainly rather than implying a connection that isn't drawn anywhere in this layer. Genuine open gap: the Ceres–Portville stretch of the 'Forbidden Path' as Wallace describes it is undrawn. RESOLVED v142-B142: AW-181 (the Forbidden Path) has been corrected to its real line and now genuinely reaches this point — the junction claimed by Wallace's text is real and drawn. CORRECTION v144-B144: the v142 note said this resolved against AW-181; that was based on a mistaken overwrite of AW-181 (see AW-181's own note). The real junction is with AW-515, Wallace's own path 24, drawn separately.

routes.name: The Conestoga Portage (Conestoga Creek–French Creek)
routes.era: pre-contact; the Susquehannock at Conestoga until 1763
routes.note: WALLACE No. 94E, AND HIS ONE-LINE VERDICT IS THE HEADLINE: THIS WAS THE MAIN CANOE ROUTE BETWEEN THE SUSQUEHANNA AND DELAWARE RIVERS. Not a path — a canoe route, joined by a comparatively short carry between the headwaters of Conestoga Creek, which reaches the Susquehanna at Safe Harbor, and the headwaters of French Creek, which reaches the Schuylkill at Phoenixville. THE LAYER HAS DRAWN THE WHOLE OF PENNSYLVANIA'S EASTERN NETWORK WITHOUT THIS. Eight roads leave Philadelphia in this layer and every one of them walks; the busiest link between the two great rivers was people in boats, and it took a portage entry to find it. That is _meta.absence_of_path_rule stated from the other side — the footpath sources under-represent the wet corridors, and a network drawn only from them will make the water look empty. IT PASSED CLOSE BY THE CONESTOGA SETTLEMENTS, from which the creek took its name — the Susquehannock town at the Susquehanna end of AW-139, whose last twenty people were murdered by the Paxton Boys in December 1763. The same mob that emptied Wechquetank on AW-422. Tier B. RE-ISSUED v123 UNDER A NEW ID. This portage was written into batch120 as AW-492 and reported as merged, but the layer's AW-492 is the Ichsua Path — a route the researcher had not written at that point. The portage never entered the layer and no gate could see the absence, because guard, census and near-miss all check what IS present. It was found only when a later batch redrew Ichsua and the near-miss sweep fired on the twin. See _meta.phantom_merge_note.

nodes.n: The head of Conestoga Creek (to the Susquehanna at Safe Harbor)
The head of French Creek (to the Schuylkill at Phoenixville)

routes.name: The Conococheague Portage (the Conodoguinet–the Conococheague)
routes.era: pre-contact; named on a Maryland map of 1721
routes.note: WALLACE No. 94F, AND A MAP OF 1721 GIVES IT ITS OWN CAPTION. About eight miles, from the Conodoguinet — which reaches the Susquehanna at Harrisburg — to the Conococheague, which reaches the Potomac at Williamsport. A Maryland map of 1721 labels the crossing 'YE LAND CARRIAGE OF 8 MILES TO YE SUSQUEHANNAH'. A cartographer writing the walk into the map because the walk is the connection. WILLIAM B. MARYE FIXES BOTH CANOE PLACES: on the Conodoguinet at the mouth of Rowe Run, formerly Herron's Branch; on the Conococheague at Red Bridge. Between them, in Wallace's quotation, lay A BEAUTIFUL STRETCH OF GENTLY ROLLING COUNTRY — which is the only aesthetic judgement about terrain anywhere in the Pennsylvania set, and it is doing work: gently rolling is why the carry is eight miles instead of a mountain. IT JOINS THE CHESAPEAKE TO ITSELF BY TWO ROUTES. Both these rivers end in the same bay — the Susquehanna at its head, the Potomac two hundred kilometres down — so this carry is not between watersheds but between two long arms of one estuary, saving a voyage round. The only portage in the layer that shortens a journey rather than enabling one. Tier B. RE-ISSUED v123 UNDER A NEW ID. This portage was written into batch120 as AW-492 and reported as merged, but the layer's AW-492 is the Ichsua Path — a route the researcher had not written at that point. The portage never entered the layer and no gate could see the absence, because guard, census and near-miss all check what IS present. It was found only when a later batch redrew Ichsua and the near-miss sweep fired on the twin. See _meta.phantom_merge_note.

nodes.n: The canoe place on the Conodoguinet (Rowe Run, near Orrstown)
The canoe place at Red Bridge (the Conococheague)

routes.name: The Oswegatchie Trail (Oneida Castle–Ogdensburg)
routes.era: on Sauthier's map of 1779, made by order of Governor Tryon
routes.note: REDRAWN v124 AFTER A PHANTOM MERGE. This route was composed and reported at B104 and never entered the layer — see _meta.phantom_merge_note. BEAUCHAMP'S PHRASE IS THE WHOLE ENTRY: among others one went DUE NORTH THROUGH THE WILDERNESS to Ogdensburg, then called Oswegatchie. Eight words for a hundred and eighty kilometres. IT IS THE ONLY ROUTE IN THE NEW YORK SET THAT LEAVES THE SYSTEM. Every other trail here threads between Iroquois towns along valleys that connect them; this one crosses the Tug Hill country, which has no towns, to reach the St Lawrence — the French river, the Canadian frontier, and after 1749 the mission at La Présentation. A road whose entire purpose is to get OUT of the network is evidence about the network's edges, and this layer has been drawing edges for a hundred and thirty batches without often finding one this explicit. 'THROUGH THE WILDERNESS' IS A GENUINE ABSENCE, NOT A RHETORICAL ONE. Tug Hill is the snowiest place east of the Rockies at this latitude and carries no through valley; Beauchamp names no intermediate point because there was none to name. Tier C, three nodes, and the line is the corridor the Black River offers rather than anything he surveyed.

nodes.n: Due north through the wilderness (Tug Hill)

routes.name: The Honeoye Trail (Canandaigua–Chenussio)
routes.era: on Guy Johnson's map of 1771
routes.note: REDRAWN v124 AFTER A PHANTOM MERGE; composed and reported at B105 and never present. ONE OF THREE, AND THE LAYER HAD ONLY THE MIDDLE ONE. Beauchamp, reading Guy Johnson's map of 1771: Canadaragey next appears, and there are THREE TRAILS THENCE TO GENESEE RIVER — the southern goes by Anarara to Chenussio, the middle one direct to the same place, and the third to Canawagus. AW-078, the Seneca Trail, draws the middle. This is the southern and AW-504 is the third. THREE ROADS BETWEEN TWO TOWNS SIXTY KILOMETRES APART is the finding, and it is the shape this layer keeps meeting wherever it looks closely enough: Deardorff's seven ways between Warren and Cornplanter's Town, the Moravians' several trails between Oneida and Onondaga, Wallace's four candidate fords on the Clarion, eleven roads into Caravaca. A SINGLE LINE BETWEEN TWO PLACES IS ALMOST ALWAYS AN ARTEFACT OF THIN SOURCES. Anarara is Honeoye; Chenussio is the great Seneca town on the Genesee that Sullivan burned in 1779, drawn here as Genesee Castle on AW-181 — and AW-494, Sullivan's Road, is how his army got there. Tier C: Johnson's map gives the sequence, not the course.

routes.name: The Canawagus Trail (Canandaigua–Irondequoit Bay)
routes.era: on Guy Johnson's map of 1771
routes.note: REDRAWN v124 AFTER A PHANTOM MERGE; composed and reported at B105 and never present. THE THIRD GENESEE TRAIL, AND IT MAKES A CONNECTION THE LAYER COULD NOT OTHERWISE DRAW. Johnson's map has the third road from Canandaigua running to Canawagus, and ANOTHER RUNNING NORTH-EAST FROM CANAWAGUS TO THE HEAD OF IRONDEQUOIT BAY — which is a node on AW-455, the Lake Ridge Trail. The Genesee country and the Ontario shore road are joined. WHY THIS CORNER MATTERS: Irondequoit Bay is the only good harbour on that stretch of lake shore and Canawagus sits at the Genesee crossing, so a road between them links the deepest inland penetration of Lake Ontario to the richest valley in Seneca country. It is why Denonville landed there in 1687 to burn the Seneca towns — and why Sullivan came overland to do the same thing ninety-two years later. THE NODE COUNT IS THE HONEST PART. Three nodes for eighty kilometres, because Johnson's map is a MAP OF SEQUENCE: it records that these places connect and in what order, not how the ground runs between them. Drawing more would be inventing. Canawagus is Avon, already on AW-078; this route crosses it rather than terminating there.

nodes.n: The head of Irondequoit Bay — junction AW-455

routes.name: Warriors Path: Through Bloody Run (Huntingdon–Oldtown, Md.)
routes.era: attested colonial period; Wallace dates the name's spread to after white settlers displaced the Iroquois' eastern route
routes.note: WALLACE No. 125A, 'Warriors Path: Through Bloody Run.' One of three southbound variants sharing the 'Warriors Path' name in central Pennsylvania (see AW-506, AW-507 for the other two, which run from Frankstown rather than Standing Stone). Wallace: white men called any Indian path not in common trader use a Warriors Path, with milder connotations among Indians themselves, where 'warrior' meant simply an able-bodied man; the Great Warriors Path (Athens–Sunbury) carried mostly peaceful travelers, ambassadors and refugees, not war parties. This variant ran from Standing Stone (Huntingdon), where the Frankstown Path crossed a path from the Great Island through Bald Eagle's Nest, south through Bloody Run (Everett) to Opessah's Town (Oldtown, Md.) on the Potomac — named for the Shawnee leader who held the town before the Iroquois pushed the frontier of settlement west. At Bloody Run it turned southwest along Warrior Ridge/Warrior Mountain, hugging Iron Ore Ridge, into Murley's Gap, and along the summit into Oldtown, where Thomas Cresap kept a trading post frequented by Iroquois war parties. William B. Marye's 'Warriors Paths' (Pennsylvania Archaeologist XIII–XIV, 1943–44) is Wallace's cited authority for the routing. NODE CONFIDENCE: Huntingdon, Marklesburg, Everett/Bloody Run, Oldtown and Warrior Mountain are attested named places with good coordinates; McConnellstown, Shy Beaver, Tatesville and Murley's Gap are named by Wallace but not independently confirmed here and are flagged pending verification (v:true) — Murley's Gap coordinate is derived from Warrior Mountain's own Wikipedia entry, which places it 1.25 mi south of Flintstone, Md., an independent corroboration of Wallace's routing rather than an assumption.

nodes.n: Standing Stone (Huntingdon) — junction AW-179, AW-397, AW-430
Shy Beaver (Woodcock Valley, west wall Tussey Mountain)
Murley's Gap (1.25 mi south of Flintstone, Md.)
Oldtown, Md. (Opessah's Town — Cresap's trading post)

routes.name: Warriors Path: Through Manns Choice (Frankstown–Cresaptown, Md.)
routes.era: attested colonial period
routes.note: WALLACE No. 125B, 'Warriors Path: Through Manns Choice.' Shares its Frankstown–Cessna trunk with AW-507 (Wallace No. 125C, the Raystown variant); per this layer's shared-tail convention that trunk is drawn once, here, and AW-507 begins at the fork rather than re-drawing it. On leaving Frankstown the path stayed the east side of the Frankstown Branch, hugging Short then Dunning Mountain to avoid the wetter west-bank ground, through what was once called Indian Path Valley (now Moses Valley) to the Three Springs landmark — Wallace spends a full paragraph on the competing claims of at least three sets of triple springs in the area, warrantee-surveyed in 1762 and 1767, and this layer follows his preferred siting. At the fork a mile south of Cessna the Manns Choice branch left for speed via the Parting of the Ways near Napier, crossed the Juniata at Manns Choice, and ran down Buffalo Run and Little Wills Creek through Buffalo Mills, Madley and Fossilville to Wills Creek village, then along a ridge west of Wills Creek into Ellerslie and Corriganville, Md. (where the Turkeyfoot Path emerged), then up Braddock Run and south to Cresaptown, where the Manns Choice and Raystown branches reunited for the climb up the North Branch Potomac. NODE CONFIDENCE: Frankstown, Claysburg, St. Clairsville, Manns Choice, Buffalo Mills, Ellerslie, Corriganville and Cresaptown are attested with good coordinates. Osterburg is sited by Wallace as passed 'a little to the east' of the path rather than on it — noted, not drawn as an on-path stop. Cessna, Napier and Fossilville are named by Wallace but not independently confirmed here (v:true).

nodes.n: Frank Stevens' Trading Post (Frankstown) — junction AW-179, AW-397, AW-398, AW-427, AW-428
The Fork (1 mi south of Cessna, Manns Choice branch divides from Raystown branch) — junction AW-507
The Parting of the Ways, near Napier (Glades Path forks off)
Corriganville, Md. (mouth of Jennings Run — the Turkeyfoot Path emerges)
Cresaptown, Md. (on Warrior Run — branches reunite)

routes.name: Warriors Path: Through Raystown (the Fork–Cumberland, Md.)
routes.era: attested colonial period
routes.note: WALLACE No. 125C, 'Warriors Path: Through Raystown.' Identical with AW-506 (the Manns Choice branch) from Frankstown to the fork a mile south of Cessna; per this layer's shared-tail convention that shared trunk is drawn once on AW-506, and this route begins at the fork rather than re-drawing it — drawing it twice would manufacture a junction out of an identity. From the fork the Raystown branch bore left over gentle hills to a point east of Wolfsburg, then hugged the base of the cliffs east of the Juniata to the ford at Raystown (Bedford); Wallace notes an earlier alternate route may have gone via the original Raystown trading post at the mouth of Dunning Creek instead. South of Bedford, Wallace is explicit that the exact course is uncertain and there were probably alternate routes — recorded here rather than resolved, per this layer's practice of citing the source's own hedges. The likelier line ran through Bedford Springs, down the long valley between Wills Mountain and Evitts Mountain, through Centerville, over the Mason–Dixon Line, to the mouth of Wills Creek at Cumberland, Md. NODE CONFIDENCE: Bedford, Bedford Springs and Cumberland are attested with good coordinates. Wolfsburg and Centerville (Bedford County) are named by Wallace but not independently confirmed here (v:true). PATCHED v125-B125 post-ship: the near-miss sweep caught this route drawing its own Bedford node 111 m from the existing four-route Raystown hub (AW-138/427/447/449) instead of joining it — snapped onto the hub coordinate and junction claim added.

nodes.n: The Fork (1 mi south of Cessna) — junction AW-506
Raystown ford (Bedford) — junction AW-138, AW-427, AW-447, AW-449

routes.name: The Allegheny Little Portage Path (Costello–Port Allegany)
routes.era: pre-contact; heavily used by settlers into the early 20th century
routes.note: WALLACE No. 94B, 'Allegheny Portage: Little Portage Path.' Drawn v127-B127 alongside the AW-413 upgrade, using the same source page. An alternative to the Big Portage Path (AW-413): steeper but shorter, from Costello at the mouth of Freeman Run on the First Fork of the Sinnemahoning, up the west side of Freeman Run past Austin, to Keating Summit, where it JOINS THE BIG PORTAGE PATH and the two run together down Little Portage Creek to Port Allegany — drawn here only as far as the join, per this layer's shared-tail convention (see AW-413 for the shared final leg). Wallace quotes Mrs. Marie Kathern Nuschke, formerly of Austin: the trail was precipitous at both ends but reasonably flat on top of the mountain, with its one big bend at the head of Cove Hollow (later Horn Hollow); she is also his source for the Indian priority claim — 'there is no question but what the Indians knew the value of the Little Portage long before the white man saw it' — and for the comparative distances: the First Fork of the Sinnemahoning was navigable farther than the river past Shippen, and the Little Portage was not less than five miles shorter than the Big. Also popular with settlers: Forest House at Keating Summit was long a landmark, and the road-builder who cut the modern route from Costello needed only to widen the old trail beyond the first mountain. NODE CONFIDENCE: Keating Summit and Austin are attested with good coordinates; Costello is named by Wallace but not independently confirmed here (v:true).

nodes.n: Costello (mouth of Freeman Run, First Fork of the Sinnemahoning)
Austin (up the west side of Freeman Run)
Keating Summit (Forest House — joins the Big Portage Path) — junction AW-413

routes.name: Bald Eagle's Path (Milesburg–Clearfield)
routes.era: pre-contact; named for the Munsee Delaware chief Bald Eagle, who lived on Bald Eagle Creek
routes.note: WALLACE No. 3, AND IT IS A BRAID, NOT A LINE. Wallace's own source here is unusual: a 1953 letter to him from Vernoy Davis of Philadelphia, relaying a 1948 map drawn from memory by the late J. A. Bilger, a local hunter who had walked these paths in his youth — keyed to specific letters and elevation marks on old USGS quadrangles. BILGER DESCRIBED AT LEAST THREE DISTINCT BRAIDED VARIANTS crossing the Allegheny Front between Bald Eagle's Nest and Chinklacamoose (Clearfield), each forking again internally: (1) up Wallace Run from Snow Shoe Intersection to Rhodes, down Jonathan Run to the Great Shamokin Path (AW-178); (2) up Dicks Run, forking at the Houston/Rush township line into a northern branch (rejoining the Great Shamokin Path at Snow Shoe) and a southern branch through Philipsburg that forks AGAIN near Pine Hill, one arm ending uncertainly at Clearfield, the other at Klondike School near Osceola; (3) up Laurel Run from Port Matilda to Philipsburg, then following the Warriors Mark Path through Wallaceton to the Great Shamokin Path. THIS LAYER DRAWS ONLY VARIANT (1), the one Wallace's own motorist directions lead with and the clearest to trace — Milesburg, Wingate, Snow Shoe, Moshannon — and records the other two in prose rather than attempting to geocode Bilger's township-line forks and elevation marks, which even Wallace's source (a 1948 hand-drawn recollection) does not claim precision for (single_line_is_an_artefact_rule). THE ROUTE'S TWO ENDS ARE ALREADY IN THIS LAYER: Clearfield is AW-178's own 'Clearfield (Chinklacamoose)' node, reused here rather than duplicated — AW-178 also carries an unnamed shaping node at 41.09/-77.95, about 7 km south of this route's Snow Shoe, which is the kind of coincidence that corroborates the corridor without being formal grounds for a junction claim on a nameless vertex. Tier C throughout: a hunter's 1948 memory, relayed by letter, five years later, is exactly the class of source this layer holds at anchors-only.

nodes.n: Snow Shoe (up Wallace Run, down Jonathan Run — connects with the Great Shamokin Path)

routes.name: The Bottom Path (Winfield–Sunbury)
routes.era: documented by a 1769 New Purchase survey warrant
routes.note: WALLACE No. 5, AND IT IS DATED BY A SURVEY RATHER THAN A DIARY — the same class of evidence as boundary_work_as_archive, applied here to a river-bank tract instead of a township line. The Bottom Path ran at the base of the cliff known locally as Shickellamy's Face, on the west bank of the Susquehanna opposite Sunbury and Northumberland, and was the LOW-WATER SHORTCUT: when the river ran high, travelers from Shamokin (Sunbury) instead climbed the mountain, followed the Penns Creek Path along the summit for about two miles, and came down to the river at Winfield — already drawn on AW-467, the Great Island Path, and reused here rather than duplicated. THE EVIDENCE IS A LAND WARRANT: Application No. 3503 (New Purchase, 1769) and its survey (C 74-119) describe 'a narrow tract extending along the bank of the Susquehanna for over a mile,' reading 'On the West side of Susquehanna opposite to Fort Augusta to include the Bottom Path & Run of water & part of the Mountain from one Narrows to the other' — a legal description written explicitly to include the path, not incidentally crossing it. Tier B: short, precisely bounded by a period survey, though the exact width of 'the Bottom Path & Run of water' at any given point is not given.

nodes.n: Winfield (the summit alternate leaves the river here in high water) — junction AW-467
Opposite Sunbury and Northumberland (west bank, Shamokin)

routes.name: The Cattaraugus Path (Buffalo, N.Y.–Salamanca, N.Y.)
routes.era: pre-contact; possibly used by Étienne Brulé in 1615
routes.note: WALLACE No. 10, AND IT IS MOSTLY NOT IN PENNSYLVANIA — included because Wallace includes it, as the New York hub that fed Pennsylvania's northwestern paths. Ran from Buffalo Creek through Cattaraugus to Salamanca, where it connected west to Cornplanter's Town, Conewango (Warren) and Venango (Franklin), and east to Ichsua (Olean), itself a junction with the Catawba Path (AW-432), the Sinnemahoning Path and the Forbidden Path — none of those connections are drawn as geometry here, since Salamanca is given as a hub for OTHER routes rather than this one's own continuation. TWO ANECDOTES SURVIVE ON THIS ROAD. Jacob Taylor to Thomas Stewardson, February 1807: Nicholas Rosegrantz was found dead toward the head of Little Valley Creek, 'supposed to have perished on his way from Cattaraugus, his Horse was also found Dead some distance back on the Indian path.' And Wallace suggests Étienne Brulé may have used this path in 1615 as a roundabout route to Tioga Point, to avoid Iroquois observation while Champlain prepared to attack them — which would make it, if true, among the oldest European footsteps recorded on any road in this layer. Tier B: the motorist directions (NY 18 through Cattaraugus and Little Valley) give a clear, short, still-followable line.

nodes.n: Little Valley, N.Y. (near where Nicholas Rosegrantz died, 1807)
Salamanca, N.Y. (connections west to Cornplanter's Town, Conewango, Venango; east to Ichsua)

routes.name: The Conestoga–Newport Path (Washington Boro, Pa.–Newport, Del.)
routes.era: pre-contact; the OCR of this entry's place names is degraded and several are uncertain
routes.note: WALLACE No. 14, AND THE SOURCE TEXT ITSELF IS DAMAGED. According to tradition, this path followed the Great Minquas Path (AW-139) from Conestoga (near Washington Boro) to Gap, then took a southeasterly course — later the Gap and Newport Turnpike — through Cochranville, Chatham, and several smaller places whose OCR-scanned names are not confidently legible ('Wondale', 'Kaolin' among them, possibly Landenberg and a genuine Kaolin, Pa.), through Hockessin and Brandywine Springs, to Christina Creek at Newport, Delaware — taking this layer south of the Pennsylvania line for the first time on this particular corridor. NO JUNCTION IS CLAIMED WITH AW-139 at Gap: AW-139's own drawn line runs through Lancaster and Coatesville, a different specific alignment than the Cresswell/Letort/Slackwater/Lampeter/Strasburg motorist route given here, even though both claim the same Conestoga-to-Gap tradition. Tier C throughout, for the reasons above and because Wallace frames the whole route as 'according to tradition' without independent corroboration.

routes.name: The Conewago Path (Manada Gap–Conewago Creek)
routes.era: pre-contact; Derry Presbyterian Church organized 1724 on the path's own spring
routes.note: WALLACE No. 15, AND ITS WHOLE ENTRY IS FOUR SENTENCES. There is a tradition that this path ran from Manada Gap, northeast of Harrisburg, south to the headwaters of Conewago Creek, passing James Galbraith's plantation (Hershey) and the spring beside which Derry Presbyterian Church — organized 1724 — now stands: a church sited on the path's own water source, the same logic as a caravanserai or a Roman mansio, just never named as one because this domain's naming habits differ. Wallace adds only that the same name is sometimes also given to the Conoy Path, a different route entirely (not drawn under this ID; see the Conoy Path if drawn separately). Tier C: 'there is a tradition' is Wallace's own ceiling for this one, and the note follows it.

nodes.n: Hershey (James Galbraith's plantation; the Derry Spring, where Derry Presbyterian Church was organized 1724) — junction AW-396

routes.name: The Fort Hill Path (Fort Hill–Winding Ridge)
routes.era: Fort Hill's Monongahela-culture settlement dated c. 1275-1300 by a 1939-40 WPA excavation
routes.note: WALLACE No. 25, THE SHORTEST ENTRY READ SO FAR — four sentences of text, no diary, no letter, no survey. The Old Fort Hill Road, crossing Negro Mountain near its highest point (Mount Davis, the highest point in Pennsylvania at 3,213 ft), is THOUGHT TO HAVE BEEN a branch of the Turkeyfoot Path (AW-461, already drawn, terminus Confluence) — Fort Hill sits 4.5 miles east of Confluence as the bird flies. Fort Hill itself is the more interesting half of the entry: 'dramatically poised' on the south side of the Casselman River, natural battlements overlooking the B&O Railroad station below, once a palisaded Indian settlement — a 1939-40 WPA excavation directed by Edgar Augustine dated the site to the Monongahela culture, roughly 1275-1300, centuries before any of the colonial-period traffic this layer otherwise records. No junction is claimed with AW-461 at either end: Wallace says only 'thought to have been' a branch, and Confluence to Fort Hill is a 7 km hop in a direction AW-461 does not itself draw. Tier C throughout: the entry offers no first-hand account of the path being walked, only a modern road's name and a site's archaeology.

nodes.n: Negro Mountain (crossing near Mount Davis, the highest point in Pennsylvania)

routes.name: Wallace's Forbidden Path, Southern Branch (Athens–Olean)
routes.era: pre-contact; David Zeisberger first recorded white passage, 1767
routes.note: WALLACE No. 24, DRAWN v144-B144 AS ITS OWN ROUTE, DISTINCT FROM AW-181. Wallace's entry, also titled 'Forbidden Path,' is independently sourced and geographically specific in a way AW-181 (a differently-sourced, pre-Wallace 'Haudenosaunee trails' route to Geneseo) is not — see AW-181's own note for the full account of how these two got conflated and un-conflated. Wallace's own title is explicit: 'From Athens through Canisteo to Olean.' At Painted Post the path forks: the north branch runs up the Cohocton River to Conewago (Avon, N.Y.), not drawn here; 'that to the south bore travelers to the Allegheny' — THIS is that south branch, through Addison, Canisteo (Passigachkunk, head of canoe navigation), Andover, Independence, Eleven Mile Spring (the height of land, named for its distance from canoe navigation on Oswayo Creek), Shinglehouse (where Zeisberger recorded evidence of canoe-making), Ceres, Portville and Ichsua (Olean) to Salamanca. HISTORY: forbidden by the Seneca (Keepers of the Western Door) to protect their heartland; Christian Frederick Post was turned back at Canisteo under threat of death in 1760; David Zeisberger broke through in 1767, challenged by a Seneca chief at the western end — 'how comes it that you travel such an unfrequented road...on which no white man has ever come?'; Sullivan's 1779 army, per Wallace, took THIS path (not necessarily AW-181's line) up the Chemung Valley, guided by an Oneida ally. Zeisberger's account of his first American pine forest near Eleven Mile Spring, 'the wildest and densest woods imaginable,' names the region still called the Pine Barrens. Tier B: Wallace gives a specific, continuous, still-partially-followable line for the whole length.

Spanish Hill (a morainal deposit, not the human-built mound legend claims)
Newtown (Elmira) — site of the Chemung ambuscade laid for Sullivan's army by Brant and Butler
Painted Post (Assinisink) — the path forks here: north branch up the Cohocton River to Conewago/Avon, N.Y., not drawn — junction AW-486
Canisteo (Passigachkunk — head of canoe navigation) — junction AW-460
Andover (bypassed a little to the east)

routes.name: The French Creek Path (Conestoga–Phoenixville)
routes.era: colonial period; one of the earliest court-laid roads in Lancaster County
routes.note: WALLACE No. 29, AND ITS FRENCH CREEK IS NOT THE ONE THIS LAYER ALREADY KNOWS. This is the Chester County French Creek, meeting the Schuylkill at Phoenixville — a different watercourse from the northwestern Pennsylvania French Creek that AW-411 (Presque Isle Portage) and AW-500 (Conestoga Portage) both touch. Checked before drawing, per this layer's standing practice of verifying name matches rather than assuming them. Source: Martin H. Brackbill, 'Peter Bezaillon's Road' (Lancaster County Historical Society Papers XLIII, 1939), charting a line 'after a careful study of a map of the region' — an armchair reconstruction, not a walked survey, which is why this stays tier C. Wallace adds that Indian travel in colonial days actually favored the LOWER Schuylkill, where Dutch and Swedish trading posts stood, reached by two shorter, better-known routes: the Great Minquas Path (compare AW-519, Wallace's own specific line, and AW-139, an independently-sourced older entry with the same name and a different line — see AW-519's note) and Old Peter's Road. This route may therefore represent secondary or supplementary traffic rather than the primary corridor.

nodes.n: Phoenixville (mouth of French Creek) — junction AW-436

routes.name: The Georgetown Road (Nichols Gap–Burnt Cabins, via Cowan Gap)
routes.era: 1722 (Cartledge's Old Road) onward; packers' trade, believed based on Indian trails
routes.note: WALLACE No. 30. Packers' paths up from Georgetown and Baltimore, over Cartledge's Old Road (1722), entered Pennsylvania through Nichols Gap at Monterey (near Waynesboro), where a number of trails converged, then FANNED INTO THREE ROUTES across Franklin County: (1) through Fort Loudon and Cowan Gap to Burnt Cabins — per Hart M. Dymond's research, the earliest and for many years the principal route, and drawn here; (2) through Waynesboro, Greencastle, Mercersburg and Cove Gap to McConnellsburg — cut as a bridle path in 1768 and later 'the main pack trail from Baltimore to the west,' NOT DRAWN; (3) crossing the Conococheague at Social Island and climbing over the North Mountain into Horse Valley, NOT DRAWN. Cowan Gap was a hidden break in the Tuscarora Mountain that saved travelers the steep ascent of the Cove Gap route; one branch of the Raystown Path also used it. Tier C: Wallace credits the routing to Dymond's local research rather than a first-hand account, and 'believed to be based on Indian trails' is itself a hedge about the packers' paths' origin.

routes.name: The Goschgoschink Path (West Hickory–Luthersburg)
routes.era: pre-contact; name recorded by German Moravian missionaries
routes.note: WALLACE No. 32, DRAWN v145-B145. This is a dedicated entry, distinct from and more precise than the brief 'no adequate tracing possible' mention of a Goschgoschink Path inside AW-431 (Wallace No. 58, the Loyalhanna-Goschgoschink Path). AW-431's third leg has been shortened to cite this route directly rather than redraw an approximation of the same ground (shared_tail_rule) — see AW-431's note. From Goschgoschink (West Hickory), forded the Allegheny, ran south to a Tionesta Creek crossing near present Nebraska, continued via Tylersburg and Helen Furnace (where it met the Venango-Chinklacamoose Path), crossed the Clarion River at Clew's Riffle (already drawn on AW-416, about 2 mi east of Clarion — reused here rather than duplicated), turned east through Corsica and Brookville (junction with AW-431 and AW-432, already established) to Luthersburg, where it met the Great Shamokin Path (AW-178) and followed it to Chinklacamoose (Clearfield). A branch ran south from Clew's Riffle to meet the Olean-Kittanning Path near Frogtown, not drawn. NAME NOTE, preserved from Wallace's own footnote: the spelling 'Goschgoschink' is the German Moravian one, chosen because Moravian records are the principal source of information about the place. Tier B: real, continuous motorist directions for the whole length.

nodes.n: Clew's Riffle (the Clarion ford, ~2 mi east of Clarion) — junction AW-416

routes.name: Wallace's Great Minquas Path (Fort Manayunk–Washington Boro)
routes.era: pre-1675 (Susquehannock destruction); named by the Dutch for the Minquas
routes.note: WALLACE No. 35, DRAWN v145-B145 AS ITS OWN ROUTE, DISTINCT FROM AW-139. AW-139 shares this route's name and general theme but is an independently-sourced, pre-Wallace entry (group 'north-america-indigenous', not 'pa-indian-paths'; predates wallace.txt being on disk) with a different, more northerly line through Lancaster, Coatesville and Downingtown — see AW-139's own note and AW-181's note for the fuller account of how a near-identical mistake with the Forbidden Path was caught and corrected in this same session. THIS route follows Wallace's own specific text: from Fort Manayunk (established by Governor Johan Printz on the Schuylkill's west bank, near the later Penrose Ferry Bridge) through Darby, Lima, Gradyville (already drawn, junction AW-495), the Forks of the Brandywine, Mortonville, Parkesburg, Gap, Strasburg, Willow Street, and Rockhill (fording Conestoga Creek) to the Susquehannock settlements near Washington Boro. THE ROUTE IS A KEY TO PENNSYLVANIA'S COMMERCIAL ORIGINS: George P. Donehoo wrote that the Dutch-Swedish-British struggle for the Delaware was fundamentally a struggle to control this trade route with the Susquehannock. NOT DRAWN: Wallace notes many branches at the eastern end running to Chester and other Delaware River points. Tier B: continuous, specific motorist directions for the whole length, though Wallace himself flags the Gradyville-to-Brandywine stretch as not closely followable by modern road.

nodes.n: Fort Manayunk (west bank of the Schuylkill, near the Penrose Ferry Bridge)

routes.name: Wallace's Great Warriors Path (Athens–Sunbury)
routes.era: pre-contact; the designated road for Iroquois ambassadors travelling south
routes.note: WALLACE No. 37, DISTINCT FROM AW-084 (also 'Great Warriors Path', but a continental ~1,300 km corridor from the Susquehanna down the Great Valley to Tennessee, entering this layer's geography only at Great Island and points south/west). Checked before drawing: AW-084 never reaches Athens or the North Branch corridor at all, so there is no overlap to correct — this is the missing northern approach, Athens down the NORTH BRANCH through Wyalusing, Tunkhannock, Wilkes-Barre, Berwick, Danville to Shamokin, where several other paths (Great Shamokin, Penns Creek, Tuscarora, Paxtang, Tulpehocken) also converge. The designated road for Iroquois ambassadors travelling south to 'brighten the chain of friendship' with Philadelphia, Maryland or Virginia. Passed Queen Esther's Town, Old Sheshequin Flats, climbed the Wyalusing Rocks to the town where Moravians later built Friedenshutten, past Tunkhannock and Buttermilk Falls, forded at Pittston, passed the Wyoming battlefield, a Mahican settlement opposite Wilkes-Barre, a Shawnee town at Plymouth (Paxinosa's Town), the Nanticoke town (occupied 1748-1753), a Munsee settlement at the mouth of Shickshinny Creek, several villages each at some point called Nutimus' Town near Briar Creek, a Shawnee town at Bloomsburg, to Shamokin via Shamokin Island. Tier B: continuous, specific, still-followable motorist line for the whole length.

routes.name: The Hays Mill Path (Somerset–Cumberland, Md.)
routes.era: packers' path, said to have been Indian-based; documented in warrantee surveys
routes.note: WALLACE No. 38. A packer's path from the Glades near Somerset to Fort Cumberland, on warrantee surveys called 'the path leading from Simon Hays Mill to Fort Cumberland' or 'the Old Path leading from the Glades to Fort Cumberland.' Left the Glades near Ankeny's Mill (south of Somerset), passed Break Neck, crossed Blue Lick Creek at Hays Mill, joined the Plank Road on the Allegheny Mountain near Pleasant Union. AT A FORK about a mile below the summit: this route (Wellersburg branch) is drawn; the OTHER branch, descending Gladdens Run to meet the Warriors Path at Palo Alto, is what Wallace explicitly says is 'often confused with the Hays Mill Path' under the name 'Cumberland Road' — a different road, not drawn here. At Corriganville the Wellersburg branch met the Warriors Path from Raystown and turned south with it for Cumberland — Corriganville already drawn (AW-506). Tier C: sourced to William H. Welfley's county history rather than a first-hand account.

routes.name: The Kersey Road (near Luthersburg–Elk Creek)
routes.era: road laid out c. 1812, said to have followed an Indian path
routes.note: WALLACE No. 42, PER GEORGE C. KIRK'S ATTRIBUTION. Branched off the Great Shamokin Path (AW-178) about 15 mi west of Clearfield and 4.5 mi east of Luthersburg (AW-518's terminus — close by but not coincident, so no junction claimed), running north over Boon's Mountain, crossing Little Toby's Creek without a bridge where Hellen Mills now stands, up the creek 7 mi to Hogback Hill, over high undulating ground to a mill site on what became Elk Creek, about 2 mi from present Centreville. Tier C: 'according to George C. Kirk...followed an Indian path' is Wallace's own framing of the claim's strength.

routes.name: The Lackawaxen Path (Indian Orchard–Lackawaxen)
routes.era: documented in 1781 and 1784 warrantee surveys
routes.note: WALLACE No. 51 (OCR-mangled to '57' in the body heading; the table of contents correctly gives 51, and the body text is unambiguously the Lackawaxen entry — confirmed by direct comparison before drawing). From Indian Orchard (named for a hundred apple trees the Indians planted there, 2 mi southeast of East Honesdale) southeast to Butcher Pond, between the two Tedyuskung Lakes, past Westcolang Pond, descending to a ford opposite the Indian town of Lackawaxen. A CASE STUDY IN DIRECTNESS: the winding white-man's road took 23 miles to cover this ground, the straightened modern road (Pa. 590/US 6) still takes about 20, and the Indian path took 13 — corroborated by a continuous four-mile run of 1784 warrantee surveys describing 'the path from the Orchard to Delaware.' Local tradition (Allie James, whose father tended the canal lock at Glen Eyre) that 'the path ran up over the hills' rather than following the river's windings. Tier B: two independent lines of evidence (tradition and surveys) agree. GATE NOTE: no shaping node inserted between the two termini — the 20 km hop is well under the tier-B limit, so none was gate-warranted (densify_warrant_rule). The route passing between the Tedyuskung Lakes and past Westcolang Pond is described in prose only.

routes.name: The Loyalhanna Path (Ligonier–Vandergrift)
routes.era: walked by Christian Frederick Post on his second journey to the Allegheny, 1758
routes.note: WALLACE No. 57, DISTINCT FROM AW-431 (Wallace No. 58, Loyalhanna-Goschgoschink Path) despite sharing the Ligonier terminus — checked carefully given this session's earlier confusion between similarly-named paths. From Loyalhanna (Ligonier) followed the Raystown Path (AW-138) to a point ~1.5 mi northwest of Latrobe, then broke away north along the west side of Loyalhanna Creek to its mouth, crossed the Kiskiminetas to Blackleg's Town (Saltsburg), and ran northwest to meet the Kiskiminetas Path (AW-479) near Vandergrift — AW-479's own 'Kiskiminetas Old Town' node sits 1.7 km from Vandergrift's centre, close enough that this is very likely the same crossing; junction claimed. This was Christian Frederick Post's route on his second 1758 journey to the Allegheny. Tier B: precise, continuous motorist directions the whole way.

routes.name: The Mahanoy Path (Lewistown–Selinsgrove)
routes.era: attested as both a 'Warriors Path' and 'Trading Path' in Land Office records
routes.note: WALLACE No. 60. Course 'has not been closely defined,' but attested by Land Office warrant language ('between the Warriors Path and Jacks Mountain'; 'above the Trading Path'). Per Charles Fisher Snyder's research: ran northeast from Kishacoquillas' Town (Lewistown) up Jacks Creek past Maitland and Wagner (both attested in warrants), through Middleburg ('on the old trading path' per an 1766-surveyed tract), to the Susquehanna near Selinsgrove. Named for Mahanoy Creek, the former name of what is now Middle Creek in Snyder County, whose valley it followed for about 10 miles. Tier C: Wallace's own opening sentence is the hedge.

routes.name: The Masthope Path (Indian Orchard–Masthope)
routes.era: documented in an 1775 warrantee survey
routes.note: WALLACE No. 62, SHARING ITS TERMINUS WITH AW-523 (Lackawaxen Path) AT INDIAN ORCHARD — two roads radiating from the same hub in different directions, junction claimed there. Evidence: Warrantee Survey D 109-205 (1775), '...about five mile from the old Indian Orchard in Lehiwaxin...the path Leading from sd Orchard to a place known by the name of Masthope on Dellaware River.' Probably ran east past the old Rock Branch School, crossed Swamp Brook and Wolf Pond Run, followed Rattlesnake Creek to Masthope on the Delaware. Tier C: Wallace's own 'probably ran' for the line between the two attested ends.

routes.name: The Maxatawny Path (Easton–Reading)
routes.era: the white man's road on this line ordered built 1754
routes.note: WALLACE No. 63. From Lechawekink (the Forks of the Delaware — Easton, Bethlehem, Allentown) through the Delaware settlement at Maxatawny (Kutztown vicinity) to Maiden Creek and Reading, where it met the Allegheny Path. WALLACE IS UNUSUALLY HONEST ABOUT THE EVIDENCE'S SHAPE: 'there is a lack of explicit evidence for this traditional Indian path,' but the terrain is so suited to moccasined travel, and the known Delaware presence at Maxatawny so substantial, that highway connections are presumed rather than attested. He also notes a shorter but harder alternative through Oley (see AW-496, already drawn and independently attested by Zinzendorf's own 1742 diary) may have been preferred for direct Forks-to-Reading travel. Tier C on the honesty of that admission.

nodes.n: Reading (joins the Allegheny Path) — junction AW-180, AW-474, AW-496

routes.name: The Minisink Path (Minisink Island–Wilkes-Barre)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 65, A THIRD ROAD FROM THE SAME HUB. Minisink Island already anchors AW-080 (to Kingston on the Hudson, northeast) and AW-176 (to Navesink on the Jersey shore, southeast) — both checked before drawing, both genuinely different directions from this route, which runs WEST through the Poconos to Wilkes-Barre. No conflict: three legitimate roads sharing one junction. From Minisink Island up Indian Point near the mouth of Raymond Kill, along the height of land to Cranberry Ridge, past the Sand Spring near Lords Valley, Blooming Grove, over the hills to Paupack Church (overlooking Wallenpaupack Lake), on by St. Mary's Church and Centerville School to Cooks Pond and Mount Cobb, crossing Moosic Mountain by Indian Spring — H. Hollister's 1885 history records the path there 'so deeply indented as to show its depth and general outline even today' — down through Dunmore and Scranton, forded the Lackawanna to Capoose Meadows where it picked up the Lackawanna Path (AW-424) through Pittston to Wyoming. EAST OF THE DELAWARE, per Lane and Wertenbaker's 'From Indian Trail to Iron Horse,' the path continued across New Jersey through Newton and Lake Hopatcong to tidewater at Springfield — not drawn here, a genuinely separate corridor from AW-176's Navesink line. Tier B: exceptionally detailed, landmark-by-landmark description.

routes.name: The Morrison Cove Path (near King–Martinsburg)
routes.era: local tradition, reported to Wallace on US 220 near the Bedford/Blair line
routes.note: WALLACE No. 68. Local tradition holds several paths climbed Dunning Mountain into Morrison Cove from the Raystown-Frankstown Path. TWO VARIANTS: one left the Raystown-Frankstown Path in Kimmell Township, ~2.5 mi south of King, climbing south-southwest — drawn here. The other left about a mile north of King, climbing northeast to a gap in Dunning Mountain and descending to Martinsburg, NOT DRAWN (single_line_is_an_artefact_rule: two attested forks, one line drawn). Tier C: 'according to a local tradition reported to the writer' is the whole of the evidence.

routes.name: The Muncy-Mahoning Path (Muncy–Danville)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 69. Leaving Muncy (junction AW-178, AW-520) and ascending the hill over Glade Run, ran southeast across the mountains, turned south to the valley of Chillisquaque Creek near Washingtonville, crossed a range of hills to the valley of Mahoning Creek, and followed its east bank to the mouth at Danville (junction AW-520) on the North Branch. Tier C: Wallace gives no first-hand account, only the corridor and a caution that the first few miles south of Muncy are difficult to trace by modern road.

routes.name: The New Castle Path (New Castle, Del.–Peach Bottom)
routes.era: James Logan travelled it 1705; also called the Susquehanna Path
routes.note: WALLACE No. 74, sharing its Pennsylvania terminus with AW-537 (Peach Bottom Path, Wallace No. 84). A short but wet route from New Castle on the lower Delaware to Susquehanna settlements at Peach Bottom, Pequea, Shenks Ferry and Conestoga. James Logan, the Provincial Secretary, took this route on his first visit to Conestoga in 1705; Governor John Evans travelled it the same way to visit Pequea and Conestoga. Tier C: no routing detail is given beyond the two ends, and no motorist section is provided at all — the sparsest kind of entry in this layer, anchors only by necessity rather than editorial choice.

routes.name: The Nippenose Paths (West Branch–Nippenose Valley)
routes.era: named for an Indian recorded at Shamokin in 1760-61
routes.note: WALLACE No. 75, A THREE-WAY FAN INTO ONE VALLEY. Said to have been three approaches into Nippenose Valley from the West Branch: (1) from the east via the Great Island Path (AW-467), crossing North White Deer Ridge near Collomsville — drawn here as the best-attested; (2) from the north via Nippenose Old Town below Long Island opposite Jersey Shore, through a gap cut by Antes Creek (formerly Nippenose Creek), NOT DRAWN; (3) from the west via Love's Gap, NOT DRAWN (single_line_is_an_artefact_rule). The valley, Old Town, Bottom and Creek were all named for an Indian recorded as a familiar figure at Shamokin in 1760-61 per the Indian Commissioners' Day Book. Tier C: 'are said to have been' is Wallace's own hedge for all three.

nodes.n: Great Island (Susquehanna) — junction AW-084, AW-178, AW-398, AW-465
North White Deer Ridge (crossing near Collomsville)

routes.name: The Oil Creek Path (Waterford–Oil City)
routes.era: contested — possibly a white man's road of 1797, not an Indian path at all
routes.note: WALLACE No. 77, AND WALLACE LETS TWO SOURCES CONTRADICT EACH OTHER ON THE PAGE. Walter Jacks (Erie Motorist, Aug. 1945) describes an Indian path from Lake Le Boeuf southeast to the mouth of Oil Creek; John Reynolds, in an unpublished manuscript, contends it was a WHITE MAN'S ROAD MADE IN 1797, not an Indian path at all. Wallace does not resolve the dispute; he adds his own doubt on top of it: the Indians certainly knew Oil Creek and used the surface 'Seneca Oil' there, but whether the Oil Creek watershed was ever a satisfactory THROUGHWAY is a separate question, since the soil there is unsuited to moccasined travel. B. F. Congdon of Salamanca, in an 1862 school essay, describes walking from Meadville to Rouseville on Oil Creek: French Creek's sandy soil dries quickly after rain, but approaching Oil Creek 'the soil becomes clayey and the weary traveler settles often ankle deep into the old detestable Oil Creek mud.' RECORDED AS A CONTESTED NEGATIVE FINDING, same treatment as AW-484 (the Loyalsock Path): the corridor's existence as a THROUGHWAY is doubted by more than one of Wallace's own sources, not merely under-documented. Tier C accordingly, anchors only.

routes.name: The Old Swedes Path (Philadelphia–New Castle, Del.)
routes.era: the King's Road based on it existed before 1681
routes.note: WALLACE No. 80. Tradition, strongly supported by the terrain along the Delaware, holds that the King's Road from Philadelphia through Darby to New Castle was based on the Old Swedes Path, itself based on an Indian path — evidence: the King's Road forded creeks at the head of tide, as an Indian path would, and by-passed Chester (former Swedish Upland) entirely when first laid out before 1681. AT DARBY THE PATH JOINED WALLACE'S OWN GREAT MINQUAS PATH (AW-519, already drawn with Darby as an attested node) and presumably followed it to Fort Manayunk — junction claimed there, exact coordinate match. Evidence for the junction: a rough 1685 chart of William Wood's land shows the King's Road running into an unnamed path 'unmistakably the Great Minquas Path,' the two heading together toward what the chart calls Swedes Mill Creek (Cobbs Creek). Tier C: a documented tradition, not a first-hand walked account.

routes.name: The Paxtang Path (Washington Boro–Sunbury)
routes.era: attested by Nicholas Scull's 1759 map and Cammerhof's 1748 winter journey
routes.note: WALLACE No. 83, CHECKED AGAINST AW-396 and AW-463 first — neither is titled 'Paxtang Path' itself, so no conflict. Full length south to north: from Conestoga (near Washington Boro, the western terminus of the Great Minquas Path, AW-519) through Washington Boro, Columbia, over Chickies Ridge, Marietta, Bainbridge, Falmouth, Middletown, Highspire, Steelton to Paxtang (where the Allegheny Path, AW-396, crosses the Susquehanna) — already an attested junction. North from Paxtang, through the narrows made by Blue Mountain and Second Mountain to Dauphin, then straight over Peters Mountain (leaving the river's wide westward arc) to Armstrong's (Halifax), through the Berry Mountain Narrows to Millersburg and McKee's (Dalmatia), then between the river and Hoofnagler Mountain through Herndon to the Mahanoy Creek crossing, where it merged with the Tulpehocken Path (AW-180) and continued to Shamokin (Sunbury). For the difficulties of this path in winter, Wallace cites Bishop J.C.F. Cammerhof's 1748 'Narrative of a Journey to Shamokin.' Tier B: Nicholas Scull's 1759 map shows the Harris's Ferry-to-Fort Augusta path clearly, and the motorist directions are precise for the whole length.

routes.name: The Peach Bottom Path (Hayesville–Peach Bottom)
routes.era: an offshoot of the Nanticoke Path
routes.note: WALLACE No. 84, AN OFFSHOOT OF AW-474 (the Nanticoke Path, already drawn) AND SHARING ITS PENNSYLVANIA TERMINUS WITH AW-531 (New Castle Path, Wallace No. 74). From Hayesville (2.5 mi north of Oxford, near AW-474's own drawn line but not an exact node on it, so no formal junction claimed) west through Tweedale, across Octoraro Creek at Pine Grove, through Tayloria, Oak Hill, Little Britain, Oakryn and Wakefield to Peach Bottom at the mouth of Peters Creek. Source: the late Harry Wilson's account. Tier C: a single named source's description, no independent corroboration cited.

nodes.n: Peach Bottom (mouth of Peters Creek) — junction AW-531

routes.name: The Perkiomen–Lehigh Path (Oaks–Vera Cruz)
routes.era: tradition; Vera Cruz jasper quarries used since prehistory
routes.note: WALLACE No. 89, DISTINCT FROM AW-491 (The Perkiomen Path, Philadelphia-Reading, a different corridor entirely — checked before drawing). According to tradition, ran north from an Indian town at the Schuylkill/Perkiomen Creek mouth (near Oaks) up the west side of Perkiomen Creek past Schwenksville and Perkiomenville, crossed near Green Lane, through Kleinville, Geryville and Hosensack to the Macungie jasper quarries at Vera Cruz — 'there paths converged from all directions,' Wallace notes, marking it as a genuine hub. Continued north across the Lehigh at Allentown, through Hokendaqua toward Nescopeck and Wyoming. Tier C: 'according to tradition' throughout, no first-hand account.

routes.name: The Pohopoco Path (Weissport–Shawnee on Delaware)
routes.era: still called an 'Indian Path' in surveys as late as 1785
routes.note: WALLACE No. 92. Began at the Gnadenhutten ford on the Lehigh (Weissport/Lehighton), ran up the north side of Pohopoco Creek past the old Levett School, through Kresgeville, Gilbert (site of the Moravian town of Wechquetank), Brodheadsville (where Sullivan's Road crossed it), Sandhill, Snydersville, to Stroudsburg and Pechoquealin (Shawnee on Delaware) — already AW-470's Minsi Path terminus and AW-421's Pechoquealin node, junction claimed there. A MILITARY HIGHWAY IN THE FRENCH AND INDIAN WAR: called 'the high Road towards the Menisinks' in 1756; Fort Allen guarded the western end at Weissport, Fort Hamilton the eastern at Stroudsburg, Fort Norris the middle, commanding a path from Wyoming to Smith Gap and Bethlehem. DESPITE MILITARY IMPORTANCE, still described in 1785 surveys as an 'Indian Path.' Tier B: warrantee surveys give its exact course and continuous motorist directions confirm it.

nodes.n: Pechoquealin (Shawnee on Delaware) — junction AW-421, AW-470

routes.name: The Point Pleasant Path (Schwenksville–Point Pleasant)
routes.era: Parson's Ferry patented 1740
routes.note: WALLACE No. 93, AND HE SHOWS HIS WORK ON HOW LOCAL TRADITION BECOMES A LAYER ENTRY. Reported by Samuel W. Pennypacker, 3rd: an Indian path came up the North East Branch of Perkiomen Creek from Schwenksville, crossed Indian Creek, up the North East Branch valley to Sellersville, over the height of land to a ford at Point Pleasant on the Delaware (Parson's Ferry, patented 1740), connecting with a believed-Indian New Jersey road to Ringoes and the Lenni Lenape Path (Old York Road). WALLACE QUOTES A FULL LETTER from W. J. Taylor of Plainfield, N.J., describing his own fieldwork interviewing Point Pleasant residents — an auctioneer with secondhand knowledge, a Miss Marshall (descendant of the Walking Purchase's Marshall) who named two roads from the ford, 'The Fern Road' west and the 'Tory Road' northwest (named for Tory settlers along it — NOT the same as AW-545, Wallace's separate 'Tory Path' entry through Schuylkill County, checked and confirmed distinct). WALLACE'S OWN VERDICT: 'the route traced on the accompanying map is conjectural.' Tier C accordingly.

routes.name: The Red Hole Path (upper Swatara Creek–West Branch Schuylkill)
routes.era: much used as a rendezvous and hideout during the French and Indian War
routes.note: WALLACE No. 98. The Red Hole, a valley named for its red shale/sandstone, lies north of Pine Grove between Second Mountain and Sharp Mountain — an Indian rendezvous, rest camp and hideout during the French and Indian War. The path left the Tulpehocken Path (AW-180) coming down off Broad Mountain, ran up Swatara Creek to the mouth of Black Creek, crossed, followed Black Creek valley ~7 mi, crossed the divide to Indian Run and down it to the West Branch of the Schuylkill. CONNECTED THE TULPEHOCKEN PATH (west) TO A PATH DOWN THE SCHUYLKILL TOWARD READING (east) — short and functional, a genuine cross-link rather than a through-road. Traces reportedly still visible on the Black Creek/Indian Run divide as of Wallace's writing. Tier C: no first-hand account, corridor description only.

routes.name: The Salt Lick Path (Ligonier–Hunkers)
routes.era: documented in the Papers of Henry Bouquet, August 1758
routes.note: WALLACE No. 101. From Loyalhanna (Ligonier) probably followed the Catawba Path (AW-432) southwest to Laurelville (already an AW-432 node, reused here), branched onto the Glades Path through Mount Pleasant, then onto Braddock's Road for ~5 mi to the Salt Lick — Braddock's Camp No. 16, near present Hunkers, Hempfield Township. DOCUMENTED IN REAL TIME: Major George Armstrong to Colonel Henry Bouquet, 7 August 1758, from the Camp at Drownding Creek: 'Mr Reynolds with an equal party to reconitre the Road from Loyalhanon to the Salt Lick upon Genl Bradocks Road.' Tier B: a period military document naming the exact road and mission.

routes.name: The Standing Stone Path (Huntingdon–Milesburg)
routes.era: attested by William Scull's 1770 map and a 1770 warrantee survey
routes.note: WALLACE No. 105, DISTINCT FROM AW-179 (the Kittanning Path, also starting at Standing Stone/Huntingdon but running WEST via Frankstown and Kittanning Gap to Kittanning) — checked carefully, no conflict: this route runs NORTH via State College to Milesburg instead. Ran from Standing Stone (Huntingdon) up the Standing Stone Creek valley, over Tussey Mountain near Pine Grove Mills, through Bloomsdorf, Struble and State College, to join the Bald Eagle Creek Path (AW-398) at Milesburg. TWO PIECES OF EVIDENCE DISAGREE ON DETAIL: Scull's 1770 map shows the Buffalo Run crossing near its Spring Creek junction; Warrantee Survey A19-26 (also 1770) describes a Buffalo Run (then called Trout Run) crossing about eight miles from Bald Eagle's Nest — six or seven miles higher up than Scull's map shows, suggesting either two branches or a genuine discrepancy Wallace does not resolve. Tier C on that unresolved conflict, plus Wallace's own 'little record has been made of its use.'

Milesburg (joins the Bald Eagle Creek Path) — junction AW-398, AW-509

routes.name: The Susquehanna Path (Harrisburg–Sunbury, west shore)
routes.era: documented on Capt. Joseph Shippen's 1756 map, used by Col. Clapham's regiment
routes.note: WALLACE No. 108, THE WEST-SHORE COUNTERPART TO AW-535 (the Paxtang Path, drawn along the east shore). Evidence: an attributed 1756 map by Capt. Joseph Shippen (PHMC Map 105) showing routes Col. William Clapham's regiment used that July, going north by bateaux and Indian paths to build Fort Augusta. South of the Juniata, Wallace infers (but the Shippen map does not show) a path from the Conodoguinet mouth near Lemoyne to the Juniata mouth at Duncannon, given easy terrain and attested settlements at both ends. NORTH OF THE JUNIATA THE MAP IS EXPLICIT: starting opposite Haldeman Island, north through a gap in Half Falls Mountain, along the bank through Mount Patrick and Liverpool, fording Mahantango Creek, through Chapman, Port Trevorton, Selinsgrove (junction AW-525) and Penns Creek to ford the Susquehanna at Shamokin. Charles Fisher Snyder records a local tradition that Fort Augusta's cannon were dragged on wooden sledges up the hill at the Herrold School on a variant of this path. Tier B: a period map with an explicit, checkable route for most of its length.

nodes.n: Shamokin (Sunbury) — junction AW-084, AW-178, AW-180, AW-434, AW-462, AW-464, AW-467, AW-520, AW-535

routes.name: The Three Springs Path (Shirleysburg–Bedford)
routes.era: pre-contact
routes.note: WALLACE No. 109, A SHORT CROSS-LINK BETWEEN TWO MAJOR TRUNKS. Ran south from Aughwick (Shirleysburg) through Orbisonia and up Three Springs Creek to the town of Three Springs, then southwest to Sideling Hill Creek, meeting the Raystown Path (AW-138) at Waterfall near Sideling Hill Gap — already an AW-138 waypoint corridor, though no exact node exists there to cite formally. From Waterfall it followed AW-138 to Bedford. Tier C: no first-hand account, a connector's description only.

nodes.n: Bedford (following the Raystown Path) — junction AW-138, AW-427, AW-447, AW-449, AW-507

routes.name: The Tory Path (Allemaengel–Catawissa)
routes.era: a Revolutionary War-era Tory haven at its western end
routes.note: WALLACE No. 111, ALSO CALLED THE OLD CATAWISSEY PATH, AND DISTINCT FROM THE 'TORY ROAD' MENTIONED INCIDENTALLY IN AW-539'S ENTRY (a Point Pleasant local road named for Tory settlers, a different road in a different county — checked and confirmed unrelated). A bridle path from Allemaengel (Albany Township, Berks County) over the Blue Mountain to Drehersville, north to McKeansburg, over Second Mountain to the head of Tumbling Run, over Sharp Mountain to Middleport, over Locust Mountain to Mahanoy City, over North Mahanoy Mountain to the Catawissa Creek valley — 'a haven for Tories during the Revolution,' which gives the path its name. From Catawissa, Wallace notes further trails ran north to Muncy, west to Shamokin, east to Nescopeck and Wyoming, though those legs are not detailed here. Tier C: a corridor description sourced to a single warrantee survey (Ir 340), no first-hand account of travel.

nodes.n: Catawissa (Catawissa Creek — a Tory haven in the Revolution) — junction AW-434

routes.name: The Walnut Bottom Path (Carlisle–Shippensburg)
routes.era: documented in an early Blunston license, 1734
routes.note: WALLACE No. 122, A BRANCH OF THE VIRGINIA PATH (AW-463) THAT MAY ONCE HAVE BEEN ITS MAIN STEM. A Blunston license of July 31, 1734 places a tract 'At the Walnut Bottom on the road from Pextan to Potowmac about two miles from Robert Dunning [Mount Rock]' — the other, more westerly branch went via Mount Rock. Family tradition among Joseph Chambers' descendants holds he took this path when he first went to the Falling Spring (Chambersburg). Left Carlisle near the present Law School, ran southwest through Mooredale, Cumminsville, Dickinson and Houckersville to cross Yellow Breeches Creek near Walnut Bottom, continuing through New Lancaster and Lees Crossroads to rejoin the other branch at Shippensburg. Tier B: a specific 1734 land document plus continuous modern-road directions.

routes.name: The Warm Spring Path (Mercersburg–Berkeley Springs, W.Va.)
routes.era: a traditional site of intertribal conferences, north and south
routes.note: WALLACE No. 124, A BRANCH OF THE TUSCARORA PATH (AW-462). Going south from Mercersburg, bore west of the Tuscarora Path, passed Fort Marshall, ran between Two Top and Claylick Mountains into Blair Valley and Maryland, turned west at Union Bethel Church through Stone Cabin Gap (also called Stony Gap, Hanging Rock Gap, Polecat Hollow), followed Lanes Run, crossed to Indian Springs, along the Potomac's north bank to a ford near Hancock, and six miles south to the Warm Spring (Berkeley Springs). A SACRED NEUTRAL GROUND: tradition holds the spring, a constant 74 degrees summer and winter, was visited by Indians from north and south both for its reputed medicinal properties and as a site for intertribal conferences — per Dr. B. Franklin Royer of Greencastle, its waters were 'held so sacred by the Indians that no blood was ever shed in their vicinity,' the same class of claim this layer already records for Sacred Sites elsewhere (extraction is not a sacred story, but a shared peace-ground is). Tier B: precise, continuous motorist directions the whole way.

nodes.n: Mercersburg (bears west of the Tuscarora Path)
Warm Spring (Berkeley Springs, W.Va.) — a neutral ground, no blood shed in its vicinity

routes.name: The Warriors Mark Path (Warriors Mark–Clearfield)
routes.era: referenced in Samuel Wallis's 1798 survey notes
routes.note: WALLACE No. 127, AND HE OFFERS THREE COMPETING GUESSES FOR THE SAME STRETCH WITHOUT CHOOSING. Good evidence for the path's existence (Wallis Papers, 18 Jan 1798, describing tracts 'on the path leading from the Warriors Mark to Clearfield') but little certainty about its precise course. Probably a continuation from Frankstown north through Yellow Spring to Water Street, crossing the Little Juniata to Warriors Mark, then over Bald Eagle Mountain, fording Bald Eagle Creek at the village where Chief Bald Eagle is said to have camped, up the Allegheny Mountain by the old Philipsburg-Tyrone Road line. FROM SANDY RIDGE, THREE POSSIBLE LINES: (1) the convenient ridge to Philipsburg, joining Bald Eagle's Path (AW-509) — drawn here; (2) per Vernoy Davis (the same informant behind AW-509's own braided complex), east down Cabbage Hollow and Cold Stream to the same Philipsburg junction; (3) west down to Osceola Mills, a better Moshannon Creek crossing in bad weather, joining Bald Eagle's Path west of Graham and the Great Shamokin Path near Roaring Run — both alternates NOT DRAWN (single_line_is_an_artefact_rule). Tier C: three named guesses, no chosen winner, is Wallace's own verdict.

nodes.n: Sandy Ridge (Allegheny Mountain, Bright Run valley)

routes.name: The Wysaukin Path (Wysox–Owego, N.Y.)
routes.era: Moravian missionaries camped and named the site 1750
routes.note: WALLACE No. 131, THE LAST NUMBERED ENTRY IN THE BOOK (followed immediately by the appendices). A SHORT CUT off the Great Warriors Path (AW-520), letting travelers up the North Branch avoid the wide loop through Towanda, Sheshequin and Tioga. Left the river at Wysox, ran up Wysaukin (Wysox) Creek through Rome to the headwaters, over an almost imperceptible divide to a branch of Wappasening Creek, down it to Nichols, N.Y., about 8 mi below Owego. ON JUNE 7, 1750, Moravian missionaries Frederick Cammerhoff and David Zeisberger camped at Wysox and named the place Garden of Roses for the wild roses on the plains there — recorded on the same road as Zeisberger's later Forbidden Path crossing (AW-515), seventeen years before he broke Seneca protocol on that western journey. Tier B: precise motorist directions, though the path's own value was as a shortcut rather than a destination in itself.

routes.name: The Owego–Onondaga Trail (Owego–Onondaga at Pompey)
routes.era: 18th c.; three named embassies attested 1737-1753
routes.note: BEAUCHAMP, 'Perch Lake Mounds...and some accounts of Indian trails' (1905), trails section. THREE NAMED EMBASSIES DESCRIBE THIS GROUND, AND THEY DISAGREE WITH EACH OTHER, which is itself the finding (single_line_is_an_artefact_rule again, this time from a New York source rather than Wallace). Conrad Weiser went as ambassador to Onondaga by way of Owego in 1737, and again in 1743 with a larger party including John Bartram and Lewis Evans — Evans mapped the route, Bartram wrote the itinerary. Bartram's line: east side of Owego and West creeks, a steep hill to a Fall Creek tributary, ponds in Cortland, west branch of the Tioughnioga from Homer, a branch of the Susquehanna rising in Pompey, over Pompey Hill, the Indian village at LaFayette, entering the Onondaga valley from the southeast. IN 1745 BISHOP SPANGENBERG TOOK A DIFFERENT LINE (per John W. Jordan's notes on the journal): up Owego and Catatonk creeks, leaving the latter above Candor, crossing West Creek in Richford, over Prospect Hill in Harford, a Fall Creek affluent in Virgil, to Crandall's Pond in Cortland, Big Lake in Preble, and Oserigooch (the largest lake in Tully), then by Cardiff to Onondaga — THIS is the line drawn here, as the most specifically located of the three. IN 1750 CAMMERHOFF AND ZEISBERGER TRIED A DIFFERENT COURSE AGAIN, by canoe to Waverly then horseback via Cayuta Lake and Ithaca down the east side of Cayuga Lake — not drawn, a materially different corridor (the Cayuga Lake route, not the Owego-Onondaga overland one). ZEISBERGER TRIED THE OWEGO ROUTE AGAIN ALONE WITH FREY IN 1753 AND FAILED, losing the trail so often they turned back — their own field note is the best single sentence on what an Indian trail actually was in this country: 'where they cannot distinguish [it] each one runs through the woods according to his own judgment... it frequently occurs that from two to three miles, and farther, there is no visible road.' They succeeded on a second attempt via the east branch of the Tioughnioga by canoe, reaching a clearly defined trail between Homer and Preble that split at Tully, one branch to Onondaga and the other to the village of Tueyahdassoo (not identified, not drawn). TERMINUS: Onondaga at Pompey (the 1677–1700 site, already established on AW-459) rather than the later Syracuse-area node — all three embassies predate the move. NOT DRAWN: hundreds of other trails Beauchamp says left 'neither trace nor tradition' across the same country. Tier B: three independent, named, dated accounts of the same general corridor, even where they disagree on the particulars. PRIMARY SOURCE FOUND v158-B158 for the Spangenberg leg specifically. Beauchamp's edited Moravian Journals give the actual 1745 diary, not just Jordan's later summary: from Tioga up the Susquehanna 'by the narrow path on the mountain by the river,' nooning at a spot named Gashnecariorum ('the dear spring') after a packhorse drowned there, past three islands the party named for the Penn brothers, to Owego (an Indian settlement deserted the previous spring, with red-painted posts where captives were tied and danced around), then up a creek called Tiatachschiunge, crossing another called Ganowtachgerage, over Prospect Hill, to a 'Dry Wilderness' camp with little water, past a chain of small lakes (Ganiataragachrachat and five others draining to the Susquehanna) to Lake Ganneratareske, and on to the large lake Oserigooch — where the water first tasted of Onondaga's salt — arriving at Onondaga on 17 June, eleven days after leaving Shamokin's outskirts. The diary's own place names (Tiatachschiunge, Ganowtachgerage, Ganiataragachrachat, Ganneratareske, Oserigooch) are the same features Jordan's later notes identified as Catatonk Creek, West Creek, Crandall's Pond, Big Lake and Tully's lake respectively — this route already uses Jordan's modern identifications; the diary is corroboration, not new geometry. FURTHER CONFIRMATION v162-B162: Zeisberger and Frey, approaching this same trail from the Tioughnioga side in 1753 after abandoning a failed direct attempt near Owego (see AW-079's note), reached Lake Ganneratareske and recognized it as a place Zeisberger had seen 'nine years ago' — on Spangenberg's 1745 trip, this route's own basis. He found 'the names they had cut into the trees,' left by Spangenberg's party eight years before: the same physical trail, reused, marked, and recognized by a returning traveler, which is about as direct a confirmation of an established route as this kind of source ever provides.

nodes.n: Tully (Oserigooch, the largest lake — the trail forks here toward Tueyahdassoo, not drawn)
Onondaga at Pompey (the 1677–1700 site) — junction AW-459

routes.name: The Cold Spring Creek Trail (Allegany Reservation–New Albion)
routes.era: carried War of 1812 dispatches
routes.note: BEAUCHAMP, trails section, Cattaraugus County: 'a trail ran through Carrollton, following Cold Spring creek and passing into Napoli...thence it went to Niagara Falls and Canada.' Confirmed and extended independently by the Town of Napoli's own local history: the trail ran from the Allegany Reservation through Carrollton, entering Napoli on lot 41 and following Cold Spring Creek into New Albion, continuing to Buffalo, Niagara Falls and Canada. GOVERNOR BLACKSNAKE, the Seneca war chief, CARRIED IMPORTANT MESSAGES OVER THIS TRAIL DURING THE WAR OF 1812 — a specific, dated, named use of an otherwise undated corridor, and the same class of evidence as a boundary survey: incidental, unbiased about which roads anyone thought mattered, and therefore trustworthy. NOT DRAWN: the Buffalo-to-Niagara-Falls-to-Canada continuation, which neither source gives any routing detail for beyond naming the destinations. Tier B: two independent sources agree on the same specific creek-and-township line, one of them citing a named historical courier.

nodes.n: Napoli (entering on lot 41, following Cold Spring Creek)
New Albion (Governor Blacksnake's War of 1812 courier route)

routes.name: The Oneida–Chittenango–Onondaga Trail
routes.era: a 'recent' trail per Beauchamp's own dating, i.e. post-dating the earliest network
routes.note: BEAUCHAMP, trails section, Madison County survey: 'One of these was from Oneida to Chittenango, and thence to Onondaga, passing some distance south of Canaseraga.' Beauchamp explicitly flags Madison County's better-known trails as the RECENT ones, distinct from the many early trails whose traces survive only as portages elsewhere in the state — a rare case of him dating a road's era relative to others without a specific year. NOT PINNED: the Canaseraga referred to here is not confidently identified — there is a village of that name far west in Allegany County, clearly not this one, and no Madison County locality of the same name was confidently located during drawing; the trail is recorded as passing 'some distance south' of it without placing that point. Endpoints reuse this layer's existing Oneida (AW-458) and Chittenango/Onondaga (AW-459) nodes. Tier C: a single sentence, no first-hand account, and one waypoint deliberately not placed.

routes.name: The Oneida–Hamilton–Chenango Canoe Trail
routes.era: a well-defined trail, per Beauchamp
routes.note: BEAUCHAMP, trails section, Madison County: 'A well defined trail went from Oneida through the west part of Hamilton, and down the Chenango river. The Oneidas and Tuscaroras came up that river in canoes as far as they could, and diverged to their several towns.' A MIXED-MODE ROAD: overland from Oneida to Hamilton, then a canoe route down the Chenango, with foot travel resuming wherever the river ran out for a given party's destination — the same category of note-worthy detail as this layer's other river-adjacent routes, recorded here rather than assumed. Tier B: Beauchamp's own 'well defined' is stronger language than most of his single-sentence county entries.
