routes.name: The Canandaigua Branch (Canandaigua Lake–Irondequoit Bay)
routes.era: recorded by George H. Harris
routes.note: BEAUCHAMP quotes George H. Harris's account of Genesee Valley trails: 'a branch trail from Canandaigua lake to the head of Irondequoit bay, then to Genesee falls and along the lake ridge to the Niagara river.' FROM IRONDEQUOIT BAY ONWARD THIS IS AW-455'S OWN GROUND (the Lake Ridge Trail, already drawn Oswego–Rochester–the Tuscarora village), so this route is drawn only as far as that shared point (shared_tail_rule) — the new ground is the Canandaigua-to-Irondequoit leg. Harris is also this layer's source for the general rules Iroquois trail-makers followed: seclusion, then directness, then a dry path, in that order of priority; a beaten trail rarely wider than 15 inches; no bridges (small streams forded, large ones rafted or canoed); fallen trees left in place, the trail routed around or over them. Two convergence points near Rochester: one on the Pittsford road east of Allen's Creek reaching Brewer's Landing (with several branch trails off it), the other reaching the river near Franklin and North St Paul streets. Tier B: a named surveyor's firsthand account, cited with unusual specificity for this section of Beauchamp's text.

nodes.n: The head of Irondequoit Bay — junction AW-455

routes.name: The Esopus–Neversink Trail (Saugerties–Port Jervis)
routes.era: per Jeptha R. Simms's Schoharie County research; Beauchamp flags most such trails as modern
routes.note: BEAUCHAMP, citing Jeptha R. Simms: 'In Ulster county a great trail started from Saugerties, followed the Esopus, crossing to the Rondout at Marbletown, leaving that stream at Napanoch, passing through Mamakating hollow, and reaching the mouth of the Neversink river at Port Jervis' — already an attested layer node (AW-080's Port Jervis). Beauchamp immediately hedges: 'In these and other cases most of the trails are modern,' a caution he does not attach to the Owego-Onondaga embassy routes or the Cold Spring Creek trail elsewhere in this section, and worth preserving as his own judgment on this entry's reliability specifically. Distinct from AW-197 (the Schoharie Path, Mohawk-Esopus), which runs entirely within the Catskills interior and never reaches Saugerties, Marbletown or Port Jervis — checked before drawing. Tier C on Beauchamp's own modern-trail caveat.

nodes.n: Port Jervis (mouth of the Neversink) — junction AW-080

routes.name: Cammerhoff's Cayuga Road (Tioga–Cayuga, via Cayuta Lake and Ithaca)
routes.era: 1750, Bishop Cammerhoff's second embassy to Onondaga
routes.note: BEAUCHAMP, editing Cammerhoff and Zeisberger's own 1750 diary. WHERE SPANGENBERG (AW-401/AW-550, 1745) WENT FROM TIOGA VIA OWEGO OVERLAND, CAMMERHOFF TOOK THE CHEMUNG BRANCH BY CANOE INSTEAD, AND THE DIARY SAYS SO EXPLICITLY: passing the Tiaogu fork, they 'came across the road on which Br. Spangenberg and his company had traveled five years ago, from Tiaogu, via Owego... to Onondago' — and did not take it. Two named, dated, primary-sourced routes to the same council fire, diverging at the same fork, both preserved. Up the Chemung to Ganatocheracht (a Cayuga town near modern Waverly, which they named the Haven of Peace, 200 miles by their own reckoning from Wyoming), where they left the canoe, borrowed a horse from their host, and continued on foot and horseback. THE ROUTE CROSSED GENUINELY DIFFERENT COUNTRY FROM ANY OTHER PATH THIS LAYER DRAWS IN THIS REGION: through a war camp called Kassickahe (named for its unusually tall trees, with painted posts where Gatabe prisoners had been tied), to a lake the Indians called Ganiatarenge (Cayuta Lake, draining south to Owego Creek), over a mountain named Untagechiat into an open plain the missionaries called Edom and Seir, past several creeks to a lake called Ganiataragechiat — CAYUGA LAKE ITSELF, reached near its south end at modern Ithaca — then up the east shore for roughly 50 more miles (the diary's own distance) to the Cayuga towns at the north end. THE GAJUKA GUIDE'S OWN GEOGRAPHY LESSON, recorded en route: Niagara Falls four to five days' journey W.N.W., described by height comparison to the tallest pines (100+ feet) stacked four or five high; Quebec nine days on foot, ten from Schenectady; the Ohio 'as wide as the Susquehanna at Harris's Ferry.' Tier B: a first-hand, dated diary with consistent compass bearings and named camps for nearly every day of travel. ON WHETHER THIS IS A REAL ROUTE OR A ONE-OFF TREK, ADDRESSED EXPLICITLY: the diary frames this as a known ALTERNATIVE to Spangenberg's Owego road, not exploration into the unknown — a choice between two named options, not the invention of a third. The Cayuga guide 'has traveled much through this region' and later drew the surrounding geography from memory on bark, which is knowledge, not improvisation. Nearly every landmark on the route (Kassickahe, Ganiatarenge, Ganiataragechiat, and the smaller creeks) already carried an Indigenous name before the missionaries arrived — unlike their own camp nicknames (Land's End, Pentecostal Spring, the Tabernacle in the War Camp), which they invented and which this route does not use as node names. Cammerhoff himself calls the road 'very strange... such as I had never yet seen anywhere in this country' and the party got lost or half-lost more than once — but that is the same faint-in-the-middle, clearer-near-towns pattern this layer already documents for known trails elsewhere (trail_definition_varies_rule), not evidence the road was invented on the spot. Confidence B reflects that judgment: real, known, guided travel through named territory, with a rough tread rather than no tread at all.

routes.name: The Garlock's Dorf–Schenectady Path (Duanesburgh corridor)
routes.era: used by the first Dutch settlers of Vrooman's Land
routes.note: SIMMS, History of Schoharie County (1845), Judge Brown's third named foot-path: 'commenced at Garlock's dorf, and led to Schenectada through Duanesburgh. By this path, the Dutch who first settled in Vrooman's Land, proceeded from Schenectada. This path was much used for several years by the Schoharie Germans, who went to that ancient city with grists upon their backs to get milling done!' A GENUINE INDIGENOUS FOOT-PATH REPURPOSED FOR A MUNDANE COLONIAL ERRAND: the same line that first brought settlers in became, for a generation after, the road they walked with sacks of grain on their backs because there was no mill at home. Tier B: named at both ends, dated use on both sides of contact, and Brown's own note that the road of his own day still followed close to it.

routes.name: The Kneiskern's Dorf–Fort Hunter Path (Mohawk–Susquehanna corridor)
routes.era: much traveled by natives moving between the Mohawk and Susquehanna valleys
routes.note: SIMMS, History of Schoharie County (1845), Judge Brown's fourth named foot-path: 'led from Kneiskern's dorf down the Schoharie to Sloansville, from thence through the towns of Charleston and Glen to Cadaughrity and ended at Fort Hunter. This path was much traveled by the natives, who went from the Mohawk to the Susquehanna valley.' Fort Hunter (Icanderago/Tionondoroge, the lower Mohawk castle at the Schoharie-Mohawk confluence) is already this layer's node for that site via other routes' territory. Tier B: a through-road explicitly identified by Brown as serving inter-valley travel, not merely local settlement traffic.

nodes.n: Fort Hunter (Icanderago, the lower Mohawk castle) — junction AW-077, AW-197

routes.name: The Kneiskern's Dorf–Canajoharie Path
routes.era: in full use until after 1762, per Judge Brown
routes.note: SIMMS, History of Schoharie County (1845), Judge Brown's fifth named foot-path: 'led from Kneiskern's dorf north-west to Canajoharic. This path...was much traveled by the early Germans, who often went to visit relatives at the German Flats. It continued in full use...until after the year 1762, at which time Sir William Johnson reviewed a brigade of militia...near the upper Indian castle of the Mohawks.' A dated terminal point for the path's documented working life, from a named eyewitness. Tier B: two independent anchors (Kneiskern's dorf, Canajoharie) and an explicit end-date for its use.

routes.name: The Wickquasgeck Trail (Manhattan, Battery–Inwood)
routes.era: first written record 1642 (de Vries); pre-dates Dutch settlement
routes.note: MANHATTAN'S OWN SPINE, AND THE OLDEST CONTINUOUSLY-USED ROAD LINE IN THE LAYER. Named for the Wecquaesgeek, a Lenape band living in northern Manhattan and across the Harlem River, this ran the length of the island along the driest, highest ground available — a ridge choice, not a ceremonial one, exactly the same logic this layer records elsewhere for trail-building on any continent. First written record: Dutch trader David Pietersz. de Vries, 1642, 'the Wickquasgeck Road over which the Indians passed daily.' The Dutch widened it into the Heeren Wegh ('Gentlemen's Way'); the English renamed it Broadway for its unusual width. THE LINE HAS BARELY MOVED IN FOUR CENTURIES: modern Broadway still runs this route from the Battery to where it meets the top of Central Park, continuing north through Manhattan and into the Bronx, where US Route 9 picks up the same line. Not drawn past Kingsbridge — the Bronx and Westchester continuation is a separate research question. Junction with the Bloomingdale Trail (AW-561) at Kintecoying, a documented crossroads and council ground. Tier B: a dated primary-source citation for the line's existence, plus four centuries of unbroken physical continuity as the same street.

nodes.n: Bowling Green (Fort Amsterdam, the island’s southern tip) — junction AW-157, AW-216
Kintecoying (Astor Place — 'Crossroads of Three Nations', a documented council ground) — junction AW-561
Inwood (the island's northern tip, continuing into the Bronx as present US 9)

routes.name: The Bloomingdale Trail (Manhattan, 14th Street–116th Street)
routes.era: legislatively documented as pre-existing by 1703
routes.note: A SECOND, GENUINELY DIFFERENT MANHATTAN TRAIL FROM THE WICKQUASGECK — checked before drawing, since both eventually became parts of what is now Broadway and could easily be conflated. This one struck off northwest across the island rather than following the spine. THE EVIDENCE FOR ITS AGE IS UNUSUALLY PRECISE FOR AN URBAN TRAIL: New York's colonial legislature formally named it a public road on June 19, 1703, and it was laid out only four rods wide, where NEW roads of that era were required to be six — later legal proceedings cited that narrower width as proof the road already existed and was merely being formalized, not newly cut. Ran from 14th Street and the Bowery (near Kintecoying, already this layer's own node on AW-560), crossing the island on a diagonal to the northwest, ending at Adrian Hoogelandt's house near 116th Street and the modern Riverside Drive. The Dutch/English called it Bloomingdale Road; in 1868 it was absorbed into the widened, straightened Broadway and its own separate identity was lost. Tier B: a specific, dated legislative act with an evidentiary argument for pre-existence, not just tradition.

routes.name: The Wiccoppe–Wappinger Trail (Kingsbridge–Fishkill Creek)
routes.era: formalized as the Albany Post Road, 1669–1703; the Native basis predates that
routes.note: THE MISSING LINK BETWEEN THE MANHATTAN TRAILS AND AW-082. When New York's colonial government designated a postal route from New York City to Albany in 1669 (formalized 1703 as 'a public and common general highway,' the Queen's Road), the route was explicitly built on 'old trails used by the Wiccoppe and Wappinger tribes' along the Hudson's east bank — not a road cut fresh through the wilderness. It continued directly from the Wickquasgeck Trail (AW-560) at the Manhattan end. THE GAP THIS ROUTE FILLS: AW-082 (the Mahican-Wappinger River Trail) already covers Wappingers Falls north to Schodack/Albany, itself reconstructed from creek mouths and Mahican/Wappinger council sites rather than surveyed — but nothing in this layer previously covered the stretch south of that, from Manhattan through Westchester to the Fishkill Creek junction. Route, per the documented Post Road alignment: from Kingsbridge (where the King's Bridge crossed Spuyten Duyvil Creek, built 1693, the first fixed link from Manhattan to the mainland) north through the Bronx and Yonkers, along the Hudson's east bank through Dobbs Ferry, Tarrytown, Ossining, and Peekskill, to the Fishkill Creek junction with AW-082. NOT A COLONIAL INVENTION: the road's own 1669 designation explicitly names the Native peoples whose trails it followed, which is the whole basis for drawing this line rather than some other. Tier C, matching AW-082's own honest rating: the corridor is certain (the river dictates it, and two independent period sources name the trail's Native origin), but the specific pre-colonial alignment is inferred from the road that replaced it, not independently surveyed. UPGRADED TO TIER B v168-B168 with C.G. Hine's 'The New York and Albany Post Road' (1906), a far more granular period source than the general encyclopedia account this route was first drawn from — Hine walked the whole road on foot between May and November 1905 and recorded the Native name and meaning at nearly every stop: Weckquaskeck at Dobbs Ferry, Alipconck ('place of elms') at Tarrytown, O-sin-sing itself at Ossining (an Indian village name the Dutch simply kept), Matteawan ('Council of Good Fur') at Fishkill. HINE ALSO SUPPLIES THE DIRECT STATEMENT THIS ROUTE NEEDED: writing of the stretch through Wiccopee Pass south of Fishkill, 'The road over which we have been traveling was once an Indian trail. Shortly before the French and Indian wars Lord Loudoun passed through this country, and in order to get his baggage train through, the trail became a road under his direction' — an explicit, dated trail-to-wagon-road conversion, not an assumption. Two real sites recovered from Hine and added as nodes: the Council Tree of the Weckquaskecks at Hastings, a walnut tree remembered as a meeting place; and Teller's/Croton Point, defended by an Indian castle against up-river tribes, where Chief Croton fell defending his people — 'the last warrior to go down before the invaders,' in Hine's own words.

nodes.n: Kingsbridge (Spuyten Duyvil Creek crossing, continuing north from the Wickquasgeck Trail's Inwood terminus across the water)
Hastings (the Council Tree of the Weckquaskecks, a great walnut)
Dobbs Ferry (the Indian town of Weckquaskeck, ‘the place of the bark kettle’)
Tarrytown (the Indian village of Alipconck, ‘the place of elms’)
Ossining (O-sin-sing — the Indian village bore this name before the Dutch arrived)
Teller's Point (Croton Point — an Indian castle defended it; Chief Croton died here, the last of his people to fall)
